▼ About ScriptLangCore

Overview An embedded scripting language for .NET 11 with NativeAOT support, written by Gérôme Guillemin

ScriptLangCore is an embedded scripting language for .NET 11, shipped as a NativeAOT executable: one self-contained native binary, with no runtime to install and no dynamic code generation. Source text is parsed into an AST, then the top level and every function are compiled to bytecode and executed by an internal VM, with a fallback to direct AST tree-walking for the constructs the VM does not cover. A program is a .slc file, a line typed at the REPL, or a compiled .slcbc bundle. It is written and maintained by Gérôme Guillemin.

Key Features

  • Types: int, long, double, float, decimal, string, bool, char, byte, short, object, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan, nullable (Type?), arrays (Type[]), list literals ([1, 2, 3]), and the framework's own types by name (List<T>, Dictionary<K, V>, Regex, Uri, and the CLR interfaces)
  • Control flow: if/else, while, for, foreach (and await foreach), do-while, break, continue, return, switch, the match expression, and pattern tests with is
  • Functions: named functions, local functions, lambdas (fun / (args) => expr), closures, pure memoization, yield coroutines, default parameter values, params, ref/out, named arguments, and async/await
  • Classes & Structs: Single inheritance, interfaces (with default bodies, implements, is, casts), records, generics, extension members, constructors, destructors, fields, methods, auto-properties ({ get; set; }, { get; private set; }, { get; init; }), object initializers (new Foo { Prop = val }), access modifiers, super/base, struct operator overloads, script-defined enums
  • Delegates: Action<>, Func<>, Predicate<>, event, multi-cast, as casting
  • Additional features: String interpolation ($"...", raw and interpolated forms), null-coalescing (??), null-conditional (?.), range literals (1..5), list comprehensions ([x for x in ...]), destructuring (var (a,b) = ...), using and await using
  • Error handling: try/catch/finally, throw, and refusals that name the position they happened at
  • Built-in APIs: LINQ (30+ methods), JSON, regex, sqlite (typed queries, bulk insert, CSV import), HTTP client and http.Use server pipelines, TCP and WebSocket, COM and Excel automation, Win32 and a Windows UI toolkit (forms, controls, themes), MCI multimedia, clipboard, scheduler, bitwise operations
  • Module system: import cross-file code loading, namespace, RunScript dynamic evaluation, and bytecode bundles (--compile writes a .slcbc, which runs with or without the source text)
  • AOT compatible: the shipped artifact is one native executable built by NativeAOT, with every function running on the internal bytecode VM and a tree-walker fallback for what it does not cover

Modes

CLI modeScriptLangCore.exe script.slc runs a file and exits
REPL modeScriptLangCore.exe interactive shell with dot commands
REPL + auto-runScriptLangCore.exe --repl script.slc starts REPL, runs .run script.slc, then accepts further commands
MCP modeScriptLangCore.exe --mcp MCP server (stdio or --port). Registers tools via RegisterMcpTool() and resources via RegisterMcpResource(). Supports --repl for combined MCP + REPL. See docs/mcp/howto.html.
Compiled bundleScriptLangCore.exe script.slcbc runs a bundle --compile wrote, which needs no source text beside it
ScriptLangCore is written and maintained by Gérôme Guillemin. This reference documents the language as the shipped engine implements it: every entry's rules, refusals and examples are the engine's own behaviour, so what you read here is what a script gets.
Use the search bar above or browse the categories below to find documentation for any keyword, function, or command. Press Ctrl+C at any time in the REPL to interrupt a running script and return to the >>> prompt.

▼ Command line

Command line What the executable runs, and every flag it takes

One argument is a file to run, and its extension decides how: a .slc is parsed and interpreted, a .slcbc is a compiled bundle loaded and run. With no argument the executable starts the REPL. Flags select a different job, and they are listed below in the order you are likely to want them.

--compile <file.slc> [out.slcbc]Builds a bundle from a script and runs nothing, which is how a file that opens a window or never ends can still be compiled. The output goes beside the source unless you name it, and the name is the first argument after the source that is not a flag, so --compile app.slc --source=strip app.slcbc names it too. It also SEALS the bundle: a SHA-256 of the whole file lives in the bundle's own header, so an artifact that changes after it was built is refused by name instead of running, with no companion file to keep in step. It exits 0 when a bundle was written, 2 when the file, the output path or a flag could not be used, and 3 when the file did not parse or the source mode you asked for could not be honoured (the same four numbers a script writes by name as ExitCode.Ok, Usage and Refused). See the Bytecode entry for what a bundle carries, and Keeping a bundle honest for the digest.
<name>.slcbc.sha256 (optional)A SIDECAR, for the stronger two-file check: a SHA-256 in sha256sum's own <hex> <name> shape, which that tool checks too. --compile no longer writes one (the digest travels inside the bundle); a sidecar you place beside a bundle is still honoured by every path load, and a mismatch is refused by name. It is worth having when the expected digest is kept somewhere the artifact itself cannot reach, and Bytecode.WriteBundleManifest(path) writes one for you.
--source=carry|strip|strictWith --compile: which of the engine's three source modes the bundle is written in. carry (the default, and what no flag means) keeps the program text in the bundle; strip leaves it out when that is honest and carries it, saying so in the report, when it is not; strict leaves it out or refuses the compile, naming what could not be carried. A conflicting pair with --no-source, a bare --source, and an unknown spelling are all refused, so the mode is never guessed.
--no-sourceShorthand for --source=strict: leaves the program text out of the bundle, and a body the bytecode cannot reproduce is refused by name instead of being carried, or the bundle would silently differ from its script.
--dump-bytecode <file.slc>Prints the constant table, the locals, the global slots and every compiled function, without running anything. The same compile step as --compile.
--programWith --dump-bytecode: also reports whether the script's TOP LEVEL itself compiled, and if not, which statement declined.
--repl [file.slc]Starts the REPL, and with a file also runs it first (the same as typing .run file.slc at the prompt).
--mcpStarts an MCP server (stdio, or HTTP with --port / --url), and EXECUTES every tool script in the tools directory so they can register themselves with RegisterMcpTool(). --repl combines the server with a prompt. See docs/mcp/howto.html.
--mcp-bcThe same server, but the tools directory holds COMPILED bundles (*.slcbc) instead of sources (*.slc). Each bundle is loaded and run, so its top-level RegisterMcpTool() calls still register: a compiled bundle is not merely a library.
--tools-dir <dir>Where the MCP server looks for tool scripts. Repeatable, and it defaults to tools/ beside the executable. A relative path resolves against the current directory.
--allowed-dir <dir>The directories the MCP server may read and write through its file tools. Repeatable.
--port <n> / --url <url>The HTTP transport's address, instead of stdio.
ScriptLangCore.exe app.slc // run a script ScriptLangCore.exe app.slcbc // run a compiled bundle ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc // write app.slcbc, run nothing ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc app.slcbc // ...where you say ScriptLangCore.exe --dump-bytecode app.slc // what compiled, without running it ScriptLangCore.exe --repl // interactive prompt ScriptLangCore.exe --mcp --port 8765 // MCP server over HTTP ScriptLangCore.exe --mcp-bc --tools-dir ./bundles // ...with compiled tools
A flag is not a script: only the argument naming a file is run, and a file whose extension this build does not know is refused rather than run.
SLC_* environment flags The engine's run-configuration gates: every variable, what it defaults to, and the one rule for reading them

These variables configure a RUN, and the engine keeps them in one registry, so this list is the whole of them: a gate cannot exist without appearing here, and the SLC_ spelling is derived from the name, so the two cannot drift. They are set in the environment before the process starts, and each is only the starting value: a script can flip the same state later with Diagnostics.Trace(name, ...) or with one of the VmSet* members, and Diagnostics.Traces() reports what the process is currently using.

One rule reads every flag: 1 turns it on, 0 and false turn it off, and any other value leaves the gate at its own default. So a stray value cannot switch a trace on, and the two gates whose default is on are turned off by naming the off spelling (SLC_TOPLEVEL_VM=0, SLC_CARRIED_STATEMENTS=0).

SLC_TOPLEVEL_VMFlag, on by default. Whether a script's TOP LEVEL runs on the bytecode VM, statement by statement, or on the tree walker. Off is how you compare the two engines in one process, and the member form is VmSetTopLevelEnabled(false).
SLC_CARRIED_STATEMENTSFlag, on by default. Whether a top-level statement the compiler cannot model is carried into a compiled bundle as its own source text, so a bundle answers like the file it was built from. Off compares the two states, and the member form is VmSetStatementCarrier(false).
SLC_VM_MAXFRAMESValue, not a flag: a positive whole number that sets BOTH call-depth caps, the flat frame cap and the tail-call cap. With nothing set the cap is the platform's own (a fixed figure on the JIT build, memory-derived on the shipped AOT build), and Diagnostics.Trace("VM_MAXFRAMES", 0) restores that default. Naming a number here is also how a script that recurses deeply runs under a runner that would otherwise cut it off.
SLC_VM_TRACEFlag, off. Prints one line per instruction the VM executes: the position, the body, the opcode, the operand-stack height and a short note. This is what names the instruction a bail happened at.
SLC_BAIL_TRACEFlag, off. Prints the source site that raised a VM bail (a shape the VM hands to the tree walker), the first question when a compiled body stops part-way.
SLC_NAMED_TRACEFlag, off. Prints every site that consumes a named-argument marker, with the callee it went to and the parameter names it carried.
SLC_COERCE_TRACEFlag, off. Reports each constructor candidate and whether the argument values fit it, which is how a choice between same-arity overloads is explained. It has no engine field, so it is read from the variable and cannot be flipped per name.
SLC_CORO_TRACEFlag, off. Traces a coroutine's lifecycle: creation, resumption, yield, completion and the status a script reads.
SLC_STACK_TRACEFlag, off. Adds the engine's stack to a reported failure, which is what turns a refusal into a trace a developer can read.
SLC_STACK_MAPFlag, off. Prints the VM's frame map when a body is entered, for reading a trace against the frames it names.
SLC_DISABLE_GUARDSFlag, off. Turns the engine's defensive checks off for a run. It exists for measuring what a guard costs, and a process that sets it can be killed by input the guard would have refused.
SLC_SINGLE_INSTANCEFlag, off. Appends the lock's name to the single-instance refusal. The name is a sanitized full path, which is why it is opt-in and the default message is one short line.

The state a flag backs is one value with two doors, so a script that calls VmSetTopLevelEnabled(false) and a process started with SLC_TOPLEVEL_VM=0 are the same state, not two. Diagnostics.LogTraces(true) turns the TRACE gates on together and deliberately leaves the two path switches and the frame cap alone, because those are not traces.

// turn every trace on, from a script or a suite Diagnostics.LogTraces(true); // or one gate, with a boolean that answers what it set Diagnostics.Trace("BAIL_TRACE", true); // read what the process is configured with print(Diagnostics.Traces()); // the cap is a value, so it is set and reported as a number Diagnostics.Trace("VM_MAXFRAMES", 50000);
Three more variables belong to the LAUNCHER rather than to the engine, and they are documented on the embedding page: SLC_ENGINE_DLL and SLC_ENGINE_HOME say where ScriptLangCore.dll is, and SLC_LAUNCHER_INFO makes the launcher report which engine it loaded.

▼ Types

int keyword 32-bit signed integer. Default: 0

Use for whole numbers in the range -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. The L suffix forces long type; use as int if you need the runtime value to be int. Numeric widening: int values match as long / as float / as double checks, and vice versa.

int x = 42; int y = 42 as int;
// Declaration and assignment int count = 100; count = count + 1;
Integer overflow: Arithmetic overflow wraps silently (like C# unchecked). No compile-time or runtime error is raised. Example: var x = int.MaxValue + 1; print(x); prints -2147483648. Use long with the L suffix (2147483648L) if the value exceeds int range.
long keyword 64-bit signed integer. Default: 0

Use for large whole numbers or when mixing with int in arithmetic (result promoted to long). Append L suffix to force long type: 42L.

long x = 1000000; long y = 42L;
long big = 1_000_000_000; big = big * 2;
double keyword 64-bit floating-point number. Default: 0.0

Standard floating-point type for most decimal calculations. Append d suffix for explicit double type (3.14d).

double x = 3.14;
double pi = 3.14159; pi = pi * 2;
Equality and truthiness are tolerant for floating values: ==, !=, match and an if test compare with a tolerance of 1e-6, the same constant in both engines, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true and a value of 1e-7 is falsy. Library methods are NOT: an array's Contains comes from LINQ and keeps the CLR's exact equality, so [0.3].Contains(0.1 + 0.2) is false. The split is deliberate see AGENTS.
string keyword UTF-16 text. Default: null (reference type)

Supports concatenation (+) and indexing via LINQ methods. Immutable.

string s = "hello";
string greeting = "Hello" + " " + "world"; print(greeting);
Escapes: \\ \' \" \0 \a \b \f \n \r \t \v, the fixed-width \uXXXX and \UXXXXXXXX, and \xH..H with one to four hex digits. A code point above 0xFFFF becomes a surrogate pair, and one past 0x10FFFF is refused. A single-quoted string and an interpolated one take the same set, and a raw string takes none of them (see raw string literals).
A single-quoted literal holding ONE character is a char, escapes included: 'a', '\n', '\0', '\'', '\u00e9', '\x41' and '\U00000041' are chars, while '', 'ab' and '\n\n' are strings. \xH..H is GREEDY, so '\x4142' is the single char U+4142 and not two characters. An escape whose code point needs two UTF-16 units ('\U0001F600') is a string, since one unit cannot hold it. typeof reports which one you got, and a char-target declaration (char tab = '\t';) takes the character.
String interpolation is supported via $"..." syntax see the string interpolation entry.
string interpolation keyword Embed expressions inside strings with $"{expr}" syntax

String interpolation allows embedding expressions directly inside string literals using $"..." syntax, where {expr} is replaced with the expression's evaluated value. Supports any expression including method calls and arithmetic.

The forms, and what a brace means in each

FormHolesUse it for
$"..."{expr}, a literal brace as {{ / }}a line of text; escapes are processed
$@"..." or @$"..."as $"..."text spanning lines with no escape processing; a " is doubled ("")
$"""...""", or more $N braces open a hole, N being the number of $; fewer than N are literal texta raw template: the text is verbatim, quotes and backslashes included
The dollar count is C#'s, and it is what a field of braces wants: with $$""" a hole is {{expr}} and every single { is itself, so a CSS rule stays a CSS rule. A RAW form has no doubled-brace literal (C# refuses a run of 2N braces and so does this engine): a literal brace wants MORE dollars. A raw form also skips the first line break right after the opening delimiter, exactly like """ on its own (see raw string literals).
An ALIGNMENT pads a hole, as in C#: $"{n,5}" right-aligns in five columns, $"{n,-5}" left-aligns, and it applies AFTER a format specifier ($"{n,6:D5}" pads the formatted text).
Inside a hole, a TERNARY needs parentheses: $"{(ok ? "yes" : "no")}". The bare form is refused with the fix named, because the : after the expression starts a format specifier, which is exactly how C# reads it (a bare $"{ok ? "yes" : "no"}" does not compile there either). A format specifier still comes after the expression ($"{n:N2}"), and ?? and ?. are not ternaries.
A template is always a string, even one that holds nothing but holes: $"{42}" is "42", not the number so $"{n}".Length works and $"{n}" + 1 concatenates instead of adding. Each hole goes through the same display rule as print and +.
var name = "world"; var msg = $"Hello {name}"; // "Hello world"
// Variables and expressions var x = 42; print($"x = {x}"); // "x = 42" print($"2+2 = {2+2}"); // "2+2 = 4" // Method calls var s = "Hello"; print($"upper = {s.ToUpper()}"); // "upper = HELLO" // Escaped braces with {{ }} print($"{{literal brace}}"); // "{literal brace}" // Format specifiers (C#-style) var n = 123; print($"{n:D4}"); // "0123" (zero-padded 4 digits) print($"{n:X}"); // "7B" (hex uppercase) print($"{n:N2}"); // "123.00" (2 decimal places)

Format specifiers reference

Format specifiers follow the {expr:format} syntax. They are mapped directly to (expr).ToString("format") at runtime, so all .NET numeric, date/time, and custom format strings are supported.

SpecifierNameExample (n=123, d=now)
DDecimal (zero-padded integer)$"{n:D4}" → "0123"
XHexadecimal (uppercase)$"{(int)255:X}" → "FF"
xHexadecimal (lowercase)$"{(int)255:x}" → "ff"
NNumber (group separators)$"{(int)1234567:N0}" → "1,234,567"
FFixed-point$"{3.1415:F2}" → "3.14"
CCurrency"${(int)42:C}" → "$42.00" (locale-dependent)
PPercent (×100 + %)$"{(double)0.5:P0}" → "50%"
EScientific notation$"{(double)12345:E2}" → "1.23E+004"
GGeneral (compact)$"{123:G}" → "123"
0Zero placeholder (custom)$"{(int)42:0000}" → "0042"
#Digit placeholder (custom)$"{(int)42:####}" → "42"
dShort date$"{now:d}" → "6/11/2026"
D (Date)Long date$"{now:D}" → "Thursday, June 11, 2026"
tShort time$"{now:t}" → "6:30 PM"
TLong time$"{now:T}" → "6:30:00 PM"
yyyy-MM-ddCustom date format$"{now:yyyy-MM-dd}" → "2026-06-11"
HH:mm:ssCustom time format$"{now:HH:mm:ss}" → "18:30:00"
Internally, $"..." is transformed into string.Concat() calls at parse time. The \{ escape sequence produces a literal {. Format specifiers ({expr:format}) are transformed into (expr).ToString("format") calls.
Verbatim interpolation: Use $@"..." or @$"..." for multi-line interpolated strings where \ is treated literally and "" is the escape for a quote character. Example: $@"Hello {name} on two lines with ""quotes""."
bool keyword Boolean (true/false). Default: false

Used in conditions, logical operators, and if/while/for statements.

A number is not a bool, and casting one is an error: (bool)0 does not compile (C# refuses it too), so write the test instead (0 != 0) or the constant (false / true). Converting a bool to a number is allowed ((int)true is 1), and a text that spells a boolean converts from its text ((bool)"true").

bool b = true;
bool isReady = true; if (isReady) { print("ready"); }
char keyword Single UTF-16 character. Default: '\0'

Enclosed in single quotes.

char c = 'A';
char letter = 'Z'; print(letter); // Result: Z
byte keyword 8-bit unsigned integer (0–255). Default: 0

Use for small positive integers or raw byte data.

byte b = 255;
byte b = 200; print(b + 55); // Result: 255
short keyword 16-bit signed integer. Default: 0

Smaller range than int, useful for memory-constrained scenarios.

short s = 100;
short s = 100; print(s * 3); // Result: 300
float keyword 32-bit floating-point. Default: 0.0f

32-bit floating-point. Less precision than double, use for memory-sensitive applications. Append f suffix to force float type: 42f.

float f = 1.5; float g = 42f;
float f = 2.5; print(f * 2); // Result: 5
Equality and truthiness are tolerant for floating values: ==, !=, match and an if test compare with a tolerance of 1e-6, the same constant in both engines, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true and a value of 1e-7 is falsy. Library methods are NOT: an array's Contains comes from LINQ and keeps the CLR's exact equality, so [0.3].Contains(0.1 + 0.2) is false. The split is deliberate see AGENTS.
decimal keyword 128-bit high-precision decimal. Default: 0.0m

Use for financial/monetary calculations where exact decimal representation matters. Append m suffix to force decimal type: 3.14m.

decimal m = 99.95; decimal n = 3.14m;
decimal price = 19.99; print(price * 3); // Result: 59.97
Arithmetic stays decimal. A decimal PAIR computes in decimal in both engines, so 0.1m + 0.2m is exactly 0.3 and typeof(1.5m + 0m) is "decimal", the exactness the text above promises. A MIXED pair (a decimal with a double or an int) still widens through double, which is the lenient reading of what C# refuses to compile outright. crash_numeric_types.slc pins both.
object keyword Base type for all values. Default: null

Use for untyped variables or heterogeneous collections.

object o = "anything";
object val = 42; print(typeof(val)); // Result: "long" val = "hello"; print(typeof(val)); // Result: "string"
DateTime keyword Date and time value type

Available as a built-in .NET type with .Now, .Ticks, etc.

var now = DateTime.Now;
var start = DateTime.Now; sleep(100); var elapsed = (DateTime.Now.Ticks - start.Ticks) / 10000; print("Elapsed ms: " + elapsed);

A DateTime is not a number: arithmetic and a cast on one are refused, and the sentence names the three ways to get a number out of it. .ToOADate() is the serial a spreadsheet counts in (days since 1899-12-30, so 46024.25 is an afternoon) with DateTime.FromOADate to come back, .Ticks is the tick count since year 1, and .ToString(...) is for display.

var at = new DateTime(2026, 1, 2, 6, 7, 0); print(at.ToOADate()); // 46024.25486111111 print(DateTime.FromOADate(46024)); // 01/02/2026 00:00:00 var serial = 1.0 * at.ToOADate(); // 1.0 * at would be refused, and say why

A cell read through COM arrives as a real DateTime, not as a serial: Excel stores VT_DATE and the bridge converts it, so a date column needs .ToOADate() before it can be multiplied while .ToString("s") or a format string is what to print.

void keyword The return type of a body that answers no value

void declares that a body answers nothing: a free function, a class or struct method, and an event handler all take it. Calling one as a STATEMENT is the ordinary use, and a void body leaves with a bare return;; a return that carries a value from it is refused. It is also what a void handler means to the engine, which calls it and ignores what it answered: an http.MapGet handler that writes ctx itself, a button's Click, a middleware that only logs.

void Log(string s) { print(s); } Log("hello"); class Counter { public int N; public void Bump() { N = N + 1; } } var c = new Counter(); c.Bump(); c.Bump(); print(c.N); // 2
nullable (?) keyword Nullable value types using ? suffix

Value types can be made nullable by appending ? allows null assignment.

int? x = null;
int? count = null; count = 42; double? pi = 3.14;
array ([]) keyword Fixed-size collection of elements of the same type

Created with new type[size], new type[] { values }, the array literal shorthand [1, 2, 3], or accessed via index. All three forms produce a native T[].

var arr = new int[3]; var init = new int[] { 1, 2, 3 }; var li = [1, 2, 3]; // also int[] (shorthand)
var a = new int[3]; a[0] = 10; print(a[0]); // Result: 10

Members

Count / LengthHow many elements the array holds.
IndexOf(value)The position of a value, or -1 when it is not there.
Clone()A SHALLOW copy: a new array holding the same elements, so writing to the copy leaves the original alone while a contained instance stays shared.
Sort() / Sort(fn)Sorts IN PLACE, by the element type's own order or through a script comparer (fun(int a, int b) { return a - b; }, which answers a negative, zero or positive number). A comparison that fails keeps its own message.
IsReadOnlyAlways false: an array's elements can be written.
var a = [3, 1, 2]; print(a.Count); // Result: 3 print(a.IndexOf(1)); // Result: 1 a.Sort(); // in place print(a); // Result: [1, 2, 3] a.Sort(fun(int x, int y) { return y - x; }); // a comparer, descending print(a); // Result: [3, 2, 1] var b = a.Clone(); // a new array with the same elements
sbyte type 8-bit signed integer (-128 to 127)

Signed byte type. .NET System.SByte. Useful for compact integer storage. Use (sbyte)value to cast.

var b: sbyte = -100;
sbyte min = sbyte.MinValue; // -128 sbyte max = sbyte.MaxValue; // 127
ushort type 16-bit unsigned integer (0 to 65535)

Unsigned 16-bit integer. .NET System.UInt16. Useful for Win32 API parameters. Use (ushort)value to cast.

var u: ushort = 65535;
ushort val = (ushort)500;
uint type 32-bit unsigned integer (0 to 4294967295)

Unsigned 32-bit integer. .NET System.UInt32. Common in Win32 for handles, flags, and DWORD values. Use (uint)value to cast.

var u: uint = 0xFFFFFFFF; var v = (uint)4000000000;
uint flag = 0x80000000; // Win32 style bitmask print(flag); // 2147483648
ulong type 64-bit unsigned integer (0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615)

Unsigned 64-bit integer. .NET System.UInt64. Large bitmasks and unsigned arithmetic. Use (ulong)value to cast.

var u: ulong = 12345678901234567890; var v = (ulong)100000000000;
ulong ptr = 0x7FFE00010000; // memory address style
DateTimeOffset type Date/time with explicit timezone offset

Represents a point in time relative to UTC with a timezone offset. Unlike DateTime, it unambiguously identifies a single point in time.

var dto = new DateTimeOffset(DateTime.Now, TimeSpan.FromHours(2));
DateTimeOffset now = DateTimeOffset.Now; print(now.Offset); // +02:00:00 print(now.UtcDateTime); // UTC DateTime
TimeSpan type Represents a time interval (duration)

Represents an elapsed duration of time. Can be created from hours, minutes, seconds, or milliseconds.

var ts = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);
TimeSpan ts = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1500); print(ts.TotalSeconds); // 1.5 var sum = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3) + TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
Result type Return value of RunScript() carries execution outcome

Returned by RunScript(). Contains error info, return value, and exit code. Serializable via Json.Serialize().

PropertyTypeDescription
.HasErrorboolTrue if the script encountered an error
.ErrorMessagestring?Error message string
.ErrorInfoErrorInfo?Structured error (code + message)
.ReturnValueobject?The script's return value
.As<T>()T?Typed access coerces the return value through the engine (CoerceTo, so int→long/double/string work); on a mismatch returns default(T) (0/false for value types, null for reference types use a nullable T like int? to observe null); never throws
.Return<T>()TStrict typed access coerces like As, or throws ScriptException (TypeMismatch pattern used by native methods)
.ExitCodeintProcess exit code
.AbortedboolTrue when the script ended itself with exit() (.ExitCode carries the code it asked for)
.CancelledboolTrue when the run was stopped by the token it was given (HasError is true too, and the message reads Stopped: the run was cancelled). Its own flag rather than a code to compare, so a runner says r.Cancelled instead of knowing ErrorInfo.Code
.StackTracestring?.NET stack trace on error

What the three outcome fields say for each way a run can end (a run stopped by its token is an OUTCOME, not a failure: it reads Cancelled, it keeps no error position, and a harness reports it as CANCEL rather than as an error):

The run....Cancelled.HasError.Aborted.ExitCode
finished normallyfalsefalsefalse0
failed (1 / 0, a refusal, a script throw)falsetruefalse0
ended itself with exit(3)falsefalsetrue3
was stopped by the token it was giventruetruefalse0
var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(); var task = Task.Run(fun () { return RunScript(src, false, false, cts.Token); }); sleep(100); cts.Cancel(); // the run stops at its next statement, loop back-edge or sleep chunk var outcome = task.Result; if (outcome.Cancelled) print("stopped on request");
var r = RunScript("return 42;"); if (r.HasError) print(r.ErrorMessage); else print(r.ReturnValue); // 42 print(Json.Serialize(r)); // {"HasError":false,"ExitCode":0,"ReturnValue":42}
var n = r.As<int>(); // 42 var m = r.As<long>(); // 42 (widened via CoerceTo) var t = r.As<string>(); // "42" (coerced to text) try { var bad = r.Return<bool>(); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Code); } // TypeMismatch (native error pattern)
Array keyword Base class for all array types int[], string[], etc.

Type annotation for any native array. Accepts all array types (int[], string[], decimal[], etc.) regardless of element type. Useful for function parameters that take array literals [1, 2, 3].

Array arr
// Function accepting any array void printLen(Array items) { print(items.Length); } printLen([1, 2, 3]); // 3 int[] accepted printLen(["a", "b"]); // 2 string[] accepted // printLen(42); // runtime error not an array
Array provides runtime validation: passing a non-array value to an Array-typed parameter throws a runtime error. For fixed-type arrays, use object[], int[], string[] etc.
Function type The callable contract type lambdas, named functions, bound methods, combined delegates, natives

Function is the first-class callable contract type. It has no runtime representation of its own typeof of a callable reports "Function" but it is usable with is and as, and as a signature annotation type on parameters and return types. v is Function is True for lambdas (fun and => arrow), named functions, bound methods, combined delegates, and native functions; False for non-callables (int, bool, string, ...). as Function returns the value unchanged when callable, and null otherwise.

As a signature type, Function works in named functions, fun/arrow lambdas, methods, and local functions: a parameter declared Function fn accepts any callable (invoked directly as fn(args) inside the body), and a function declared to return Function may return any callable. Passing a non-callable argument or returning a non-callable value is a typed runtime error (Expected a Function, got X.).

A contract names the VALUE, not an ARRAY of them. Function[] fns = [One, Two]; holds two callables and fns[0]() calls one; the same holds for Iterable[] and RandomAccess[]. Element coercion does not apply here: a contract is a shape test, so every element either satisfies it or does not, and only a value that is not a function is refused.

Two declarations of one function name with DIFFERENT parameter lists are an OVERLOAD SET, and each call resolves by argument count then by type: the exact type beats a widening one (Pick(int) wins for an int argument over Pick(long)), and a tie goes to the first declaration. A ref/out position is part of the signature, so F(ref n) reaches F(ref int) even when the argument's value would also fit F(int) beside it, and a params tail is weighed by its ELEMENT type. Named arguments choose the member their NAMES fit: with Nm(int a, string b) and Nm(string a, int b), Nm(b: 1, a: "s") is the second one. A declaration whose signature MATCHES an existing one does not overload, it REPLACES the earlier body, which is what retyping a line at the prompt does. A call no member accepts is refused naming what the name holds, for example No overload of 'Ar' takes 1 argument(s) that fit: the name holds (int), (int, int)., and a by-reference position is spelled with its keyword, as in (ref int), (string).
// One name, two arities, one set: each call picks its member string Ar(int a) { return "one:" + a; } string Ar(int a, int b) { return "two:" + a + "," + b; } print(Ar(7)); // one:7 print(Ar(3, 4)); // two:3,4 // the name is a value too, and the set travels with it var f = Ar; print(f(9) + " / " + f(9, 9)); // one:9 / two:9,9
// A Function-typed parameter is called directly inside the body int Apply(Function fn, int v) { return fn(v); } print(Apply(fun (int x) { return x + 1; }, 1)); // 2 lambda passed as Function // is Function guard fun lambdas, arrows and named functions are callable var f = fun (int x) => x * 2; print(f is Function); // True var g = (int x) => x * 3; print(g is Function); // True arrow lambda print(42 is Function); // False a scalar is not callable print(f); // func <lambda>(int) -> object its own signature print(typeof(f)); // "Function" typeof names the contract, not the storage class // Function return type a factory returns a lambda Function Make(int n) { return fun (int x) { return x + n; }; } print(Make(5)(10)); // 15 // A non-callable argument is a typed runtime error try { Apply(42, 1); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // Expected a Function, got Int32
Printing a callable answers its SIGNATURE; typeof answers the contract. print(fn) reads func Add(int, int) -> int for a named function, func <lambda>(int) -> object for a fun or arrow lambda (a lambda declares no return type, so it reports object), and func print(object...) -> object for a native. A body that returns nothing omits the arrow entirely (func NoRet()), and a script function's params tail prints as its element type (func Variadic(int, int) -> int) while a native's variadic tail keeps the dots. So a value that holds a callable reads as what it does, and typeof stays the one-word answer: "Function".
A callable is a Function; the engine's internal storage name for that type is NOT exposed to scripts. Writing the internal name in a script is a runtime error (unknown or undefined type), so Function is the callable contract.
Built-in type keywords match case-sensitively. Function, Iterable, RandomAccess, Tuple, DateTime, ... are real types a lowercase function is NOT one: function foo() { ... } or x is function reports Type 'function' is unknown or undefined (the legacy pseudo-type was treated as object with a warning; it is now rejected). There is no function declaration keyword: name a function by its return type (string Foo(), void Bar(), int Coro()), and reserve the Function type for parameters and returns that hold a callable a lambda or a function pointer such as Function Make(int n) { return fun (int x) { return x + n; }; }.
CLR interfaces type The .NET interfaces a script can name and use, and what each one is for

A framework interface is a type name like any other: it can be written in a declaration, as a parameter type, in an is/as test and in a cast, and the engine resolves it against the assemblies the process has loaded. A generic spelling carries its arguments, including a nested one (IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<string, int>>), and one written WITHOUT arguments is refused with the fix in the message, which is C#'s own rule. The behaviour behind each interface works too; the table is what a sweep of them measured, on the development build and on the shipped one.

InterfaceWhat works
IDisposableusing, d.Dispose(), and as a parameter type
IAsyncDisposableawait using and await d.DisposeAsync()
IEnumerable<T> / IEnumerator<T>foreach over a script list and over a CLR collection, a parameter type, is
IAsyncEnumerable<T> / IAsyncEnumerator<T>await foreach, and a hand-driven GetAsyncEnumerator() / MoveNextAsync() / Current
ICollection<T> / IList<T> / IReadOnlyList<T>a parameter type that takes a script list or an array, and Count, IndexOf and indexing on the value
IDictionary<K, V>a parameter type that takes a { } literal, plus Count and key indexing, on a raw CLR dictionary too
IComparable<T> / IComparer<T>CompareTo, both as parameter types, and StringComparer.Ordinal as a comparer
IEquatable<T>is IEquatable<string>, and Equals
ICloneableClone(), on an array as well
IFormattable / IFormatProviderToString(format, provider), and both as parameter types
A name nothing defines is refused, in the type and in a type ARGUMENT. x is IAsyncEnumerable<NoSuchType> is refused with the name in the message rather than answered false, the wording an unknown outer name already gets. A TYPE PARAMETER is resolved in a type position, which is what makes a generic body's own test work: o is IEnumerable<T> answers for the instantiation's binding (true for Gen<string>(new List<string>())), in a return, an if, a &&, a var initializer, a bare is T, a loop body and a lambda alike.
Not covered, and worth knowing before planning around it: IQueryable<T> and Expression<T> cannot be named, because nothing the engine does loads the assemblies they live in. Sorting a VALUE is covered (list.Sort() and list.Sort(comparer), see the List<T> and array entries), and an ORDERED SEQUENCE (OrderBy's result) is covered too: OrderBy(key, comparer) takes a comparer for the KEYS, OrderByDescending answers the same members, and .ToList() / .ToArray() materialize it. What is still refused is Comparer<int>.Default, so a comparer is written as a function (fun(a, b) { return b.CompareTo(a); }) where the default order will not do.
Internal Types type Registry of script-exposed internal types script-facing names, is/typeof/print alignment, Dispose

ScriptLangCore exposes several internal types to scripts through a central registry. The script-facing name carries no Script prefix and no namespace it is a functional name shared by is / as, typeof, print() and nameof() (via ToString()). Every value also answers a callable Dispose(): real cleanup for resource-owning types, a safe no-op otherwise.

A type name is one the engine registers. The primitive names are lowercase (string, int, long, bool, char, double, float, decimal, byte, sbyte, short, ushort, uint, ulong, object); the CLR-cased spelling is the script name only where the CLR type is the script type (DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan). A declaration written String, Int, Long or Object is refused with the spelling to use instead: 'String' is not a name this engine registers for a type: write 'string'. A CLR type the engine has no script name for is unaffected (StringBuilder, Control, List<T>), and a name nothing defines stays the usual unknown-type warning rather than an error.

Script-facing nameprint / typeof / nameofDispose()
TupleTupleno-op
KeyValuePairKeyValuePairno-op
LazyDeserializedListthe declaration the read was asked for (List<int>, string[], IList)no-op
ErrorInfoErrorInfo (print/nameof show Message)no-op
ResultResultno-op
WeakRefWeakRefno-op
MetaMetano-op
MemBufferMemBufferreal frees pointer, drops Mem.LiveBuffers()
DynamicLibraryDynamicLibraryreal frees the loaded library
OrderedEnumerableOrderedEnumerableno-op
FileStreamReaderFileStreamReaderreal closes the reader
FileStreamWriterFileStreamWriterreal closes the writer
MessageInfoMessageInfono-op
CipherInfoCipherInfono-op
CronExpressionCronExpressionno-op
CronType (enum)enum member namen/a (enum)
SqliteIteratorSqliteIteratorreal releases the statement
SqliteMappingIteratorSqliteMappingIteratorreal forwards to the inner iterator
SqliteRowSqliteRowno-op the row owns nothing, the cursor does

Iterable a predicate type

Iterable is a guard, not a value type. It has no runtime representation and never appears in print()/typeof. It is usable with is and as: v is Iterable is True for arrays, lists, tuples, dicts, HashSets, LINQ results, coroutine generators, and strings, and False for scalars (int, bool, double, ...). as Iterable returns the value unchanged when iterable, and null otherwise. typeof still reports the concrete type name (int[], List<int>, Tuple, ...) Iterable is a contract, not a replacement name.

It exists so one guard covers every collection kind foreach and LINQ can enumerate, instead of chaining v is List, v is Array, v is Tuple, v is Dictionary, ... together.

// One guard for heterogeneous collection handling void Process(object v) { if (v is Iterable) { var n = 0; foreach (var e in v) { n = n + 1; } print("iterable, " + n + " elements"); } else { print("not iterable"); } } Process([1, 2, 3]); // iterable, 3 elements Process((10, 20)); // iterable, 2 elements Process(42); // not iterable

Iterable a signature type (params and returns)

Iterable is also a usable signature type: a parameter declared as Iterable accepts any iterable, and a function declared to return Iterable may return any iterable. It works in named functions, fun/arrow lambdas, methods, and local functions. Passing a non-iterable argument or returning a non-iterable value is a typed runtime error (Expected an Iterable, got X.).

// A generic count helper accepts any iterable int ItCount(Iterable it) { var n = 0; foreach (var e in it) { n = n + 1; } return n; } print(ItCount([1, 2, 3])); // 3 array print(ItCount((1, 2, 3))); // 3 tuple print(ItCount("ab")); // 2 string var d = new Dictionary<string, int>(); d["a"] = 1; print(ItCount(d)); // 1 dict (enumerated as KeyValuePairs) print(ItCount([1, 2, 3].Where(fun (x) { return x > 0; }))); // 3 LINQ result print(ItCount(FpCoro2.pairs(3))); // 3 generator // A non-iterable argument is a typed runtime error try { ItCount(42); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // Expected an Iterable, got Int32 // Iterable return type any iterable may be returned Iterable Range(int n) { var a = new int[n]; for (var i = 0; i < n; i = i + 1) { a[i] = i; } return a; } var s = 0; foreach (var x in Range(3)) { s = s + x; } print(s); // 3 array holding 0,1,2 // fun and arrow lambdas accept the same annotation var f = fun (Iterable it) { var n = 0; foreach (var e in it) { n = n + 1; } return n; }; print(f((1, 2))); // 2 var g = (Iterable it) => { var n = 0; foreach (var e in it) { n = n + 1; } return n; }; print(g([1, 2, 3])); // 3

RandomAccess indexable + re-enumerable contract

is/as RandomAccess is True for arrays, lists, tuples, and strings values that are both indexable (v[i]) and re-enumerable. It is False for dicts, HashSets, LINQ results, generators, and scalars. RandomAccess is a strict subset of Iterable: every RandomAccess value is iterable, but not every iterable is random access (dicts and LINQ results are single-pass). It is usable as a signature type too. typeof keeps the concrete type name (int[], Tuple, string, ...) never RandomAccess.

// is RandomAccess indexable + re-enumerable print([1, 2] is RandomAccess); // True array print((1, 2) is RandomAccess); // True tuple print("ab" is RandomAccess); // True string print(d is RandomAccess); // False dict is iterable but not random access var ra = [10, 20] as RandomAccess; if (ra != null) { print(ra[1]); } // 20 still indexable after the cast // RandomAccess-typed parameter index directly int First(RandomAccess ra) { return ra[0]; } print(First([5, 6])); // 5

Iterable combinators Replayable/Memoize, Tuple.Map/Fold, Iterable.* natives

Replayable(it) / Memoize(it) cache-once re-enumerable wrappers. A one-shot Iterable a coroutine generator, a LINQ result, a dict can only be enumerated once. Wrapping it in Replayable (alias Memoize) makes it re-enumerable: the first enumeration consumes the source and records each element as it is produced, and once it completes, every later enumeration replays the recorded elements. The cache grows with the number of elements enumerated.

// A coroutine generator is one-shot wrap it to enumerate twice namespace NumCoro { int nums(int n) { var i = 0; while (i < n) { yield i; i = i + 1; } return -1; } } var rp = Replayable(NumCoro.nums(3)); var s1 = 0; foreach (var p in rp) { s1 = s1 + p; } var s2 = 0; foreach (var p in rp) { s2 = s2 + p; } print(s1, s2); // 3 3 the wrapped generator replays // LINQ results are single-pass too Memoize caches them var rm = Memoize([1, 2, 3, 4].Where(fun (x) { return x % 2 == 0; })); var m1 = 0; foreach (var v in rm) { m1 = m1 + v; } var m2 = 0; foreach (var v in rm) { m2 = m2 + v; } print(m1, m2); // 6 6 print(rp is Iterable); // True the wrapper is itself an Iterable

Replayable/Memoize values are Disposable. A wrapper's cache is released deterministically: using (var r = Replayable(...)) { ... } (or the using var r = ... declaration form) calls r.Dispose() at block exit, and an explicit r.Dispose() works anywhere. Dispose() clears the cached elements and drops the wrapped source, so the memory is freed immediately; re-enumerating a disposed wrapper yields nothing (an empty sequence). Without a using or Dispose(), the cache lives until the wrapper is garbage-collected.

// Replayable/Memoize are Disposable dispose releases the cache and the source using (var r = Replayable(NumCoro.nums(3))) { var n = 0; foreach (var p in r) { n = n + 1; } print(n); // 3 first pass consumes the generator and caches it } // Dispose() runs here the cache and the source are released var rd = Replayable(NumCoro.nums(2)); var m = 0; foreach (var p in rd) { m = m + p; } // 0 + 1 = 1 rd.Dispose(); // deterministic release var m2 = 0; foreach (var p in rd) { m2 = m2 + p; } print(m, m2); // 1 0 re-enumeration after dispose is empty

Tuple.Map(tuple, fn) applies fn to every element and returns a tuple of the same arity with the element names preserved; Tuple.Fold(tuple, seed, fn) is an eager left fold the seed, then fn(acc, element) over each element in order. See the tuple entry for a names-preserved example.

// Tuple.Map same arity, element names preserved (int n, int m) src = (10, 20); var up = Tuple.Map(src, fun (x) { return x + 1; }); print(up.n, up.m); // 11 21 names survived the map print(typeof(up)); // Tuple still a concrete Tuple value var tot = Tuple.Fold((1, 2, 3), 0, fun (a, e) { return a + e; }); print(tot); // 6 left fold

The Iterable namespace adds FP combinators over any Iterable: Map, Filter, Fold, Zip, Append, Concat (an alias of Append) and Range plus ToList. Map/Filter/Zip/Append/Concat/Range are lazy (deferred) they return a re-enumerable result and run the function only as elements are pulled; Fold and ToList are eager. The first argument of every combinator is any Iterable; a non-iterable argument is a runtime error (Expected an Iterable, got X.). Iterable.Range(start, count) lazily yields start, start+1, ..., start+count-1 as ints. Iterable.ToList(it) eagerly copies any iterable into a new List<T> (copy semantics, like ToArray()); the element type is inferred when it is certain arrays use their element type and lists/sets use their ElementType, so Iterable.ToList([1, 2, 3]) is a List<int> and List<object> otherwise (tuples, strings, generators, dicts, LINQ results, mixed elements).

// Map lazy, re-enumerable; Filter keeps matching elements var sq = Iterable.Map((1, 2, 3), fun (x) { return x * 2; }); print(sq.Count()); // 3 var ev = 0; foreach (var v in Iterable.Filter((1, 2, 3, 4), fun (x) { return x % 2 == 0; })) { ev = ev + v; } print(ev); // 6 // Zip pairs up to the shorter source; Append/Concat join two Iterables var zp = 0; foreach (var p in Iterable.Zip((1, 2), (10, 20, 30), fun (a, b) { return a + b; })) { zp = zp + p; } print(zp); // 33 11 + 22, the longer source is clipped var ap = 0; foreach (var x in Iterable.Append((1, 2), (3, 4))) { ap = ap + x; } print(ap); // 10 // Fold is eager; Range is a lazy arithmetic sequence print(Iterable.Fold((1, 2, 3), 0, fun (a, e) { return a + e; })); // 6 var rg = 0; foreach (var x in Iterable.Range(5, 3)) { rg = rg + x; } print(rg); // 18 5 + 6 + 7 // ToList is eager and typed a fresh copy, not the source var tl = Iterable.ToList([1, 2, 3]); print(typeof(tl)); // List<int> typed when the element type is known print(typeof([1, 2, 3].ToList())); // List<int> the array method form print(typeof(Iterable.ToList("ab"))); // List<char> strings iterate as chars, like foreach

Namespace / type-name coexistence. The Tuple and Iterable namespaces live alongside the same-named type predicates: member access (Tuple.Map(...), Iterable.Zip(...)) resolves through the namespace objects, while is Tuple / is Iterable, as casts and typeof keep resolving through the type-name path unchanged.

// The same names stay valid as predicates and keep concrete typeof names print((1, 2) is Tuple); // True the predicate is unchanged var u = Tuple.Map((1, 2), fun (x) { return x; }); print(u is Tuple, typeof(u)); // True Tuple print([1, 2] is Iterable); // True try { Iterable.Map(42, fun (x) { return x; }); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // Expected an Iterable, got Int32
// Every internal type: same name on all four surfaces + callable Dispose() var it = Sqlite.Query(db, "SELECT id, name FROM t"); print(it); // SqliteIterator print(typeof(it)); // SqliteIterator print(it is SqliteIterator); // True it.Dispose(); // real release never throws // Non-disposable natives are safe no-ops var dict = new Dictionary<string, int>(); dict.Dispose(); // no-op dict stays usable
Adding a new script-exposed internal type requires one entry in the central type registry (which drives is/typeof/print names) and, for a resource-owning type, a real Dispose(). The Script prefix is stripped automatically never expose it in script-facing names.

▼ Variables

var keyword Implicitly-typed local variable

Type is inferred from the initializer expression. Must have an initializer.

var x = 42; // int var y = "hello"; // string
var a = 10; var b = 20; print(a + b); // Result: 30
A name holds ASCII letters, digits and underscore, plus the ACCENTED LATIN-1 letters. The accented range is the Latin-1 Supplement's letters (à to ö and ø to ÿ), so hé, café, Straße, niño and ação are ordinary names in a variable, a class, a property, a function and a dictionary key, and they travel into a compiled bundle. A character outside that range (CJK, Greek, Cyrillic) is not part of a name: it belongs inside a string or a comment, and the lexer refuses it with the rule in the message.
// accented names, the whole Latin-1 range var hé = 10; string Straße = "strasse"; class Été { public int Degré { get; set; } } print(hé + " " + Straße); // Result: 10 strasse
A KEYWORD cannot be a variable name, and @ is how a name that collides is kept. Writing var out = 1; is refused naming the keyword and the escape: @out is that name spelled so the parser sees an identifier, and the same holds for @when, @ref, @case and the rest. A handful of keywords are tolerant instead, and a variable may take one with a warning (var class = 5; works and says it may confuse a reader), so the refusal names the escape rather than a rule about all keywords.
// a keyword needs the @ escape var @out = 41; print(@out + 1); // Result: 42
// a keyword needs the @ escape var @out = 41; print(@out + 1); // Result: 42
typed declaration keyword Explicit type declaration for variables

Types can be specified explicitly instead of using var.

int x = 42; string name = "Alice";
int x = 10; int y = 20; print(x + y); // Result: 30
const keyword Immutable variable cannot be reassigned

Attempting to reassign a const variable throws ConstAssignment error.

const pi = 3.14159;
const rate = 0.05; var result = 1000 * rate; print(result); // Result: 50
destructuring keyword Unpack array elements into multiple variables with var (a, b) = expr or [a, b] = expr

Destructuring unpacks an array or list into multiple variables in one statement. Two syntaxes are supported: parenthesized var (a, b) = expr for declarations, and bracket [a, b] = expr for assignments to existing variables.

var (a, b) = [10, 20]; // declares a and b [x, y] = source; // assigns to existing x, y
// Declaration destructuring var (first, second, third) = [1, 2, 3]; print(first); // 1 // Assignment destructuring [a, b] = [100, 200]; print(b); // 200 // With range literal [x, y] = 1..10; print(x); // 1
The source expression must evaluate to an array or list. The number of variables must not exceed the number of elements in the source.
tuple (a, b) keyword Lightweight multi-value container (10, "hello"), named elements, destructuring

A tuple literal groups several values into one Tuple value. Tuples support positional access (t[0]), Item1..ItemN, Length, destructuring (var (a, b) = t), and Json.Serialize (as a JSON array). Element names come from the declared return type ((int i, string s)) or, for lambdas returning a matching-arity tuple, are inferred from the parameter names.

var t = (10, "hello", 3.5); (int i, string s) Fn() => (10, "hello");

1 · Basic literal, positional access, named elements, destructuring

// Tuple literal typeof, positional access, ItemN, Length, JSON array var t = (10, "hello", 3.5); print(t[0]); // 10 print(t.Item2); // hello print(t.Length); // 3 print(typeof(t)); // Tuple print(Json.Serialize(t)); // [10,"hello",3.5]
// Declared tuple return type → named elements (int i, string s) Test() => (10, "hello"); var r = Test(); print(r.i); // 10 print(r.s); // hello
// Lambda returning a tuple names inferred from the parameter names var mk = fun (int a, int b) { return (a, b); }; var p = mk(1, 2); print(p.a); // 1 print(p.b); // 2
// Destructuring with a discard var (x, _, z) = (1, 2, 3); print(x + z); // 4

Declared return type (int a, int b) Fn()t.a, t.b ✅t[0], t.Item1 ✅
Lambda param-inferred fun (int a, int b) { return (a, b); }t.a, t.b ✅t[0], t.Item1 ✅
Unnamed fun (int v) { return (a, b); } (arity ≠ param count)t.a ❌ "Property not found"t[0] / t.Item1 / t.Length ✅

2 · Advanced tuple parameters, tuple returns, namespaces, classes, coroutines

Functions, lambdas (fun and => arrow forms), methods, local functions and coroutines can declare a tuple parameter. In the unnamed form the element names become usable directly in the body; in the named form the parameter name binds the whole tuple and elements resolve via name.field.

// Tuple parameters unnamed: elements usable directly in the body var sum = fun ((int n, int m)) { return n + m; }; print(sum((3, 4))); // 7 // Arrow form var mul = ((int n, int m)) => n * m; print(mul((5, 6))); // 30 // Named form the name binds the tuple; elements via name.field var diff = fun ((int a, int b) p) { return p.a - p.b; }; print(diff((9, 4))); // 5 // Named function + namespace + method + coroutine forms are all supported
// Tuple-typed variable declaration declared element names bind directly (int c, int d) name = (10, 20); print(name.c); // 10 print(name.d); // 20
// Functions and lambdas RETURNING tuples (int, int) Tp() { return (21, 2); } print(Tp()[0]); // 21 unnamed return, positional access (int a, int b) LocalPair(int v) { return (v, v * 2); } print(LocalPair(21).a); // 21 named return accessed inline // Recursive fibPair-style a tuple-param lambda returning a 2-tuple var fibPair = fun ((int n)) { if (n <= 1) return (n, 1); var prev = fibPair((n - 1)); return (prev[1], prev[0] + prev[1]); }; var fp = fibPair((10)); print(fp[0]); // 55 print(fp[1]); // 89
// Tuples in namespaces and classes namespace functions take AND return tuples namespace Geo { (int x, int y) Shift((int a, int b) p, int dx) { return (p.a + dx, p.b + dx); } } var g = Geo.Shift((1, 2), 10); print(g.x); // 11 print(g.y); // 12 // Class methods take tuple params; a method returns a tuple via `object` + (Tuple) cast class Pt { public int Sum((int a, int b) p) { return p.a + p.b; } public object Get() { return (3, 4); } } var pt = new Pt(); print(pt.Sum((10, 32))); // 42 var tgt = (Tuple)pt.Get(); print(tgt[0]); // 3
// Coroutines yielding tuples direct generator path namespace PairCoro { int pairs(int n) { var i = 0; while (i < n) { yield (i, i * 2); i = i + 1; } return -1; } } var gen = PairCoro.pairs(2); print(gen.MoveNext(), gen.Current[0], gen.Current[1]); // True 0 0 print(gen.MoveNext(), gen.Current[0], gen.Current[1]); // True 1 2 print(gen.MoveNext()); // False // ... or destructure the yielded tuple var gen2 = PairCoro.pairs(1); gen2.MoveNext(); var (a, b) = gen2.Current; print(a, b); // 0 0
// A tuple-param lambda passed as a Func<object,int> argument namespace ApplyNs { int Apply(Func<object, int> fn) { return fn((3, 4)); } } print(ApplyNs.Apply(fun ((int n, int m)) { return n + m; })); // 7

Type check is Tuple

In a script the tuple type is addressed as Tuple, which is also what typeof reports. Use is Tuple to test whether a value is a tuple, and inspect .Length / .Names:

string describe(object v) { if (v is Tuple) { var t = (Tuple)v; return "tuple(" + t.Length + ")" + (t.Names == null ? "" : " " + string.Join(",", t.Names)); } return "not a tuple"; } print(describe((1, 2))); // tuple(2) (int a, int b) Pair() => (1, 2); print(describe(Pair())); // tuple(2) a,b print(describe(42)); // not a tuple

Tuple.Map / Tuple.Fold element-wise combinators

Tuple.Map(tuple, fn) applies fn to every element and returns a tuple of the same arity with the element names preserved; Tuple.Fold(tuple, seed, fn) is an eager left fold the seed, then fn(acc, element) over each element in order. See the Internal Types → Iterable combinators block for the full reference.

// Tuple.Map same arity, names preserved (int a, int b) src = (10, 20); var mapped = Tuple.Map(src, fun (x) { return x + 1; }); print(mapped.a, mapped.b); // 11 21 names preserved through the map print(mapped is Tuple); // True still a Tuple value // Tuple.Fold left fold: 1 + 2 + 3 print(Tuple.Fold((1, 2, 3), 0, fun (a, e) { return a + e; })); // 6

3 · Edge cases

// Arity mismatch on a tuple-param bind runtime error var f1 = fun ((int n, int m)) { return n + m; }; f1((1, 2, 3)); // ✗ Parameter '__tup0' expects a 2-element tuple, got 3 elements // Non-tuple argument to a tuple param runtime error f1([1, 2]); // ✗ Parameter '__tup0' expects a tuple argument, got 'Int32[]' // Destructuring is LENIENT on arity extra elements are dropped; a missing element stays unbound var (x, y) = (1, 2, 3); // x = 1, y = 2 no error var (u, v, w) = (7, 8); // w is NOT bound using it is an "Undefined variable 'w'" error var (a, b) = 42; // ✗ Cannot destructure type 'Int32'. Expected array or list
Destructuring also works in two new positions: foreach (var (a, b) in items) destructures each iteration item (tuple / array items, coroutine yields, dictionary KeyValuePair items a → Key, b → Value), and match tuple patterns case (int a, int b) => ... bind the element names in an arm-scoped scope. See the foreach and match entries.
// Unnamed tuples expose ItemN / [0] only named access is a runtime error var plain = (7, 8); print(plain.Item1); // 7 plain.a; // ✗ Property 'a' not found on tuple
// Nested tuples each element is itself a tuple var nst = (1, (2, 3)); print(nst[0]); // 1 print(nst[1][0]); // 2 print(nst[1].Length); // 2
// Tuples inside lists and dictionaries var lst = [(1, 2), (3, 4)]; print(lst[1][0]); // 3 var d = new Dictionary<string, object>(); d["k"] = (9, 10); print(((Tuple)d["k"])[1]); // 10
// A tuple param inside a coroutine namespace CoroEdge { int gen((int a, int b) p) { yield (p.a + p.b, p.a - p.b); return -1; } } var eg = CoroEdge.gen((9, 4)); print(eg.MoveNext(), eg.Current[0], eg.Current[1]); // True 13 5
// Engine edge a tuple-param element name colliding with a global is misdetected // as an external capture (the prologue-destructured element isn't registered as a // lambda parameter). Results stay correct the element still wins but the lambda // takes a full closure snapshot instead of the shared capture-free one. var n = 100; // a global `n` ... var f = fun ((int n, int m)) { return n + m; }; print(f((3, 4))); // 7 the tuple element wins over the global
Tuple parameters are supported in functions, lambdas, methods and local functions. Delegates, constructors and operator overloads reject tuple parameters with a parse error (Tuple parameters are not supported in this context.) such declarations have no body to destructure into.
Tuple element names exist only when declared ((int i, string s) Fn()) or inferred from matching lambda parameters. An undeclared tuple like fun () => (10, "hello") exposes Item1..N / [0] only. Tuples run in both the tree interpreter and the bytecode VM (MAKE_TUPLE).

▼ Control Flow

if/else keyword Conditional branching

Executes thenBranch if the condition is truthy, elseBranch otherwise.

if (condition) { /* then */ } else { /* else */ }
if (x > 10) { print("large"); } else { print("small"); }
using keyword Resource acquisition and automatic disposal

The using statement acquires a disposable resource, executes a block of code, and then disposes the resource even if an exception occurs. The variable declared in the using expression is scoped to the block and disposed when the block exits.

using (var f = Application.CreateForm("MyForm")) { // use f inside the block f.Width = 300; } // f.Dispose() called automatically, even on exception
using var b = Mem.Buffer(64); // declaration form no block; disposed at enclosing scope exit
// Declaration form (C# semantics): the resource lives until the enclosing scope exits void work() { using var b = Mem.Buffer(200 * 1024 * 1024); Mem.Fill(b.Ptr, 200 * 1024 * 1024, 0xFF); print(Mem.ReadByte(b.Ptr, 0)); // 255 } // b disposed here no explicit Mem.Free / b.Dispose() needed

A top-level using var is disposed when the run ends, because there is no enclosing block to leave. In a file that is the end of the program; at the REPL each line is a run, so the resource is released before the next line is read. The block form disposes at its own } wherever it appears, which is the one to reach for when the release has to be observed.

The forms are using (var x = init) { }, using var x = init;, and using (expression) { } for a resource you already hold: the expression is evaluated once and bound to a name the body cannot see. await using spells the same three shapes for a resource that implements IAsyncDisposable, and awaits the disposal: await using (var x = init) { }, await using var x = init;, await using (expression) { }.

await using (var lines = File.ReadLinesAsync("data.csv")) { await foreach (var line in lines) { print(line); } } // DisposeAsync awaited when the block exits, even on exception

Which one a value needs is the interface it implements, and a mismatch is refused by name rather than silently doing nothing: a value implementing only IDisposable under await using is told to write using, one implementing only IAsyncDisposable under using is told to write await using, and a value implementing neither is refused too. A disposal that cannot be observed is worth knowing about: a CLR async sequence opens its file when it is created, so a sequence that is created and never enumerated holds it, and the same is true after disposing that sequence by hand.

// With a form (implements IDisposable) using (var form = Application.CreateForm("Demo")) { form.Width = 400; form.Height = 300; } // form.Dispose() called automatically // Nested using blocks using (var f1 = Application.CreateForm("Outer")) { using (var f2 = Application.CreateForm("Inner")) { print(f2.Width); } // inner disposed } // outer disposed // With a script class destructor class Resource { int id; public Resource(int v) { id = v; } ~Resource() { print("cleanup " + id); } } using (var r = new Resource(1)) { print("using resource"); } // ~Resource() runs here
Which types support using?
  • IDisposable .NET types: Form, StreamWriter, MemoryStream, TcpClient, ProcessHandle (via is IDisposable)
  • Script class instances with ~Destructor() the destructor chain runs on block exit
  • Any object with a Dispose() method resolved via duck-typing reflection fallback
while keyword Loop while condition is truthy

Coroutine-aware supports suspension and resumption at any point inside the loop body.

while (condition) { /* body */ }
var i = 0; while (i < 5) { i = i + 1; } print(i); // Result: 5
for keyword C-style for loop with initializer, condition, and increment

Coroutine-aware supports suspension inside the loop body. The increment expression runs after each iteration.

for (init; condition; increment) { /* body */ }
var sum = 0; for (var i = 0; i < 10; i = i + 1) { sum = sum + i; } print(sum); // Result: 45
foreach keyword Iterate over collections, arrays, coroutines

Supports any Iterable arrays, lists, tuples, dicts, HashSets, LINQ results, generators, and strings. Coroutine-aware.

Dictionary iteration: foreach(var kv in dict) yields KeyValuePair objects, and KeyValuePair(key, value) builds one (the same bare-call shape Rect(l, t, r, b) has, since a bare new KeyValuePair(a, b) reaches the CLR generic and cannot infer its type arguments). Access the key via kv.Key and the value via kv.Value. This works on native Dictionary<K,V>, script Dictionary<K,V>, and the boxed rows a sqlite cursor yields.

foreach (var item in collection) { /* body */ }
var nums = new List<int>(); foreach (var n in nums) { print(n); }

Destructuring form: foreach (var (a, b) in items) destructures each iteration item into the given names over tuple items, array items, coroutine yields, and dictionary KeyValuePair items (a → Key, b → Value). A non-destructure-able item (e.g. a plain int) is a runtime error.

// foreach destructuring tuples and arrays var total = 0; foreach (var (a, b) in [(1, 2), (3, 4)]) { total += a + b; } // total = 10 foreach (var (x, y) in [[1, 2], [3, 4]]) { total += x * y; } // total = 24 array items // ... and over coroutine yields foreach (var (n, m) in PairCoro.pairs(3)) { csum += n; } // csum = 3 // A non-destructure-able item is a runtime error foreach (var (u, v) in [1, 2]) { } // ✗ Cannot destructure type 'Int32' ...

Tuples & enumeration

LINQ results: a filtered (or otherwise LINQ-produced) tuple sequence enumerates like any other collection use the plain form, or the destructuring form over the filtered items.

// (1) Filter a tuple list with Where, then enumerate foreach (var t in [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)].Where(fun (t) => t[0] > 1)) { print(t[0], t[1]); // 3 4 / 5 6 (1, 2) filtered out } // The destructuring form works over the filtered result too var total = 0; foreach (var (a, b) in [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)].Where(fun (t) => t[0] > 1)) { total += a + b; } print(total); // 18 (3+4 + 5+6)

break / continue behave normally inside the destructuring form.

// (2) break / continue in a destructuring foreach var sum = 0; foreach (var (a, b) in [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), (7, 8)]) { if (a == 3) continue; // skips (3, 4) if (a == 7) break; // exits before (7, 8) sum += a + b; } print(sum); // 14 (1+2 + 5+6)

Bare tuple iteration

// A bare tuple iterates element-wise yields 1, 2, 3 var ts = 0; foreach (var x in (1, 2, 3)) { ts = ts + x; } print(ts); // 6 // Named tuples iterate the same way yields 10, 20 (int p, int q) pair = (10, 20); var psum = 0; foreach (var v in pair) { psum = psum + v; } print(psum); // 30 // A tuple-of-tuples iterates its inner tuples yields (1, 2), (3, 4) foreach (var t in ((1, 2), (3, 4))) { print(t[0], t[1]); } // 1 2 / 3 4 // The destructuring form works over the inner tuples too var s = 0; foreach (var (u, w) in ((1, 2), (3, 4))) { s = s + u + w; } print(s); // 10
foreach (var (k, v) in dict) destructures each KeyValuePair the iteration item is a KeyValuePair, destructured as k → Key and v → Value. This works on native Dictionary<K,V>, script Dictionary<K,V>, and the boxed rows a sqlite cursor yields. The same destructuring also works in statement form: var (k, v) = kv;. Use kv.Key / kv.Value when you need the pair object itself, as shown under Dictionary iteration above.

Coroutine yields (single-var form): a coroutine's yielded values enumerate generator-style in foreach or drive the coroutine directly with MoveNext() / Current.

// (5) generator-style enumeration of coroutine yields namespace Gen { int nums(int n) { var i = 0; while (i < n) { yield i * 2; i = i + 1; } return -1; } } foreach (var x in Gen.nums(3)) { print(x); } // 0 2 4 // Direct driver loop MoveNext() / Current var co = Gen.nums(2); while (co.MoveNext()) { print(co.Current); } // 0 2 see the Coroutine entry

Async streams (await foreach)

An asynchronous sequence (IAsyncEnumerable<T>) produces its elements one await at a time, so it is read with await foreach. A plain foreach over one is refused, and the refusal says what to write: Cannot iterate over an asynchronous sequence of string with a plain foreach: its elements arrive one await at a time, so write `await foreach (var item in …)`. await foreach over something that is NOT asynchronous is refused too, naming the type that has no GetAsyncEnumerator.

await foreach (var line in asynchronousSequence) { /* body */ }

It is allowed in the same two places an await is: at the top level of a file (where the engine waits for each element, the way an async entry point does) and inside an async function. break and continue behave normally, and the sequence is disposed on every exit, including a break out of the loop, so a file handle is released.

// Read a file line by line, stopping after the header var n = 0; await foreach (var line in File.ReadLinesAsync("data.csv")) { if (n++ == 10) { break; } print(line); } async Task<int> CountLines(string path) { var total = 0; await foreach (var line in File.ReadLinesAsync(path)) { total = total + 1; } return total; }
A source-less bundle carries such a file's source: an await foreach runs on the tree walker, because the bytecode VM has no state for an async enumerator, so --compile --no-source refuses that file by name and the default (source carried) behaves as the script does. The same is true of a match pattern only in the opposite direction: patterns DO travel now (as their own source text), see the Bytecode entry.
break keyword Exit the current loop immediately

Works inside while, for, and foreach loops. Coroutine-safe.

break;
var i = 0; while (true) { if (i >= 3) break; i = i + 1; } print(i); // Result: 3
continue keyword Skip to the next iteration of the current loop

Works inside while, for, and foreach loops.

continue;
var sum = 0; var i = 0; while (i < 5) { i = i + 1; if (i == 3) continue; sum = sum + i; } print(sum); // Result: 12 (skips 3: 1+2+4+5)
match keyword Pattern matching expression compare a value against multiple patterns

The match expression compares a subject value against a series of patterns, returning the value associated with the first matching pattern. Patterns are separated by commas, and a wildcard _ pattern matches everything (must be the last arm).

Two equivalent forms are supported: the postfix form subject match { ... } and the prefix form match (subject) { ... }. The case keyword before a pattern is optional in both forms.

Patterns: a match arm uses exactly the same pattern grammar as switch constants, wildcard _, type patterns with an optional binding, relational patterns, tuple patterns, logical (and/or/not, with (…) grouping), property patterns and list patterns. An arm may add a guard with when expr, evaluated after the pattern's bindings are in scope.

// type patterns, bindings, guards and logical/property/list patterns all work in match var r = o match { int n when n > 0 => "positive", int and > -100 => "other int", { Name: "bob" } => "bob", [1, ..] => "starts with 1", _ => "other" };
expr match { 1 => "one", 2 => "two", _ => "other" }
// Matching integers var status = 404; var label = status match { 200 => "OK", 404 => "Not Found", _ => "Unknown" }; print(label); // "Not Found" // Matching strings var level = "warn" match { "error" => 500, "warn" => 400, _ => 200 }; print(level); // 400 // With enum enum Http { OK=200, NotFound=404 } var name = Http.NotFound match { 200 => "OK", 404 => "Not Found", _ => "?" };

Tuple patterns

A tuple pattern case (int a, int b) => ... matches the subject on tuple-ness + arity: the subject must be a tuple with exactly that many elements. The element types are informational (not checked); only the shape matters. The element names bind in an arm-scoped scope visible in that arm's value expression only, never after the match. _ is a discard (binds nothing), and unnamed elements case (int, int) are a shape check with no bindings. On a mismatch (non-tuple subject or wrong arity) the arm is skipped and matching falls through to the next arm.

// Tuple patterns prefix and postfix forms, optional `case` var r1 = match (1, 2) { case (int a, int b) => a + b, _ => 0 }; // 3 prefix form, with `case` var r2 = (1, 2) match { (int a, int b) => a + b, _ => 0 }; // 3 postfix form, `case` omitted var shape = (1, 2) match { (int, int) => "2-tuple", _ => "other" }; // "2-tuple" shape check, no bindings var d = (1, 2) match { case (int _, int b) => b, _ => 0 }; // 2 `_` is a discard var f = match "x" { case (int a, int b) => 1, _ => 7 }; // 7 non-tuple subject falls through var g = match (1, 2, 3) { case (int a, int b) => 99, _ => -1 }; // -1 arity mismatch falls through // Arm-scoped names: `a` and `b` are undefined after the match no leakage

Samples tuples in real flows

Tuple patterns shine where real code produces tuples: function return values, foreach destructuring pipelines, namespace functions, and mixed pattern arms. match arms do not support when guards (unlike switch), so a conditional arm uses a value pattern on the relevant element instead.

// (1) Match on a tuple returned by a function (int, int) Pt() { return (3, 4); } var m = match Pt() { case (int a, int b) => a + b, _ => 0 }; print(m); // 7 // (2) foreach + match pipeline the arm is a value pattern (match arms have no `when` guard) var labels = new List<string>(); foreach (var (a, b) in [(1, 2), (7, 8)]) { labels.Add(match b { 8 => "eight", _ => "other" }); } print(labels[0], labels[1]); // other eight // (3) Tuples from a namespace function, matched with tuple patterns namespace Geo { (int, int) Origin() { return (0, 0); } (int, int) Offset() { return (5, 6); } } var sum = match Geo.Origin() { case (int x, int y) => x + y, _ => -1 }; var prod = match Geo.Offset() { case (int x, int y) => x * y, _ => -1 }; print(sum, prod); // 0 30 // (4) A tuple-pattern arm combined with value patterns on the same subject var combo1 = match 0 { 0 => "zero", case (int a, int b) => a + b, _ => "other" }; // "zero" the value pattern wins on an int subject var combo2 = match (5, 6) { 0 => "zero", case (int a, int b) => a * b, _ => "other" }; // 30 the tuple arm handles a tuple subject print(combo1, combo2); // zero 30 // (5) Nested tuple patterns are NOT supported `case (int, (int, int))` is a parse error. // Patterns are flat: shape is tuple-ness + arity only, so a nested-tuple VALUE matches a flat pattern. var nested = match ((1, 2), 3) { case (int, int) => "pair", _ => "other" }; print(nested); // pair
match is a soft keyword: a function literally named match that is called and followed by a block match(x) { ... } parses as a match expression (subject x), not a call. Without the block, match(x) still resolves to the identifier/function.
The last arm must be a wildcard _ to ensure exhaustive matching. Patterns are compared using == (equality).
case / when keyword A switch label, and the guard that narrows it

case introduces a label in a switch statement or expression, and when adds a GUARD to it: the label only matches when the guard is truthy, which is how one case covers several values without repeating its body. default is the label that matches when nothing else did, and a match arm takes the same guard (pattern when cond => value). The switch and match entries have the rest (patterns, several labels on one arm, the wildcard a match expression requires).

var n = 3; var label = ""; switch (n) { case 1: label = "one"; break; case 3 when n > 2: label = "three"; break; default: label = "other"; break; } print(label); // three print(5 match { > 3 when true => "big", _ => "small" }); // big
switch keyword C#-style switch statement with pattern matching constant, type, var, when guards

Pattern kinds (shared by switch, match and is): constant (1, "x", null), wildcard _, var name, type (int, string) with optional binding (int n), relational (> 5, <= 0), logical (p and q, p or q, not p, grouped (p)), tuple ((int a, int b)), property ({ Name: "bob", Age: > 18 } instances, dictionaries by key, named tuples by element name; an unknown member is a non-match), list ([1, 2], [1, ..], [.., 3], [1, .., 9], [1, .. var rest], [1, .. _] subjects are arrays, Lists, tuples and strings, whose elements are chars ("abc" is ['a','b','c'] is true; ["a", ..] is not, since a char is not a 1-character string); one slice max; the .. var rest capture follows the subject kind a List yields a List (element type preserved), a string yields char[], arrays/tuples yield an array; .. _ is an explicit discard). Binding rules: a name may be bound once per pattern; both sides of or must bind the same names; is bindings live only in an if/while true branch. Diagnostics (warnings, never errors): a switch with no _/default arm warns as non-exhaustive, an arm placed after a wildcard warns as unreachable, and two structurally equal constant arms warn as duplicates (1 vs 1 collides; 1 vs 1L does not).

The switch statement evaluates a subject expression and executes the first matching case. Supports constant patterns, type patterns with binding (case int i:), var patterns (case var v:), discard (case _: / default:), when guards, and multiple labels (case 1: case 2:). No fallthrough each case must exit via break or return.

Also available as a switch expression (expr switch { pattern => value, ... }), returning a value from the first matching arm.

Switch statement

switch (expr) { case 1: return "one"; case 2: return "two"; default: return "other"; }
// Constant patterns int test1(int x) { switch (x) { case 1: return 10; case 2: return 20; default: return 0; } } // Type patterns with binding string test3(object x) { switch (x) { case int i: return "int: " + i; case string s: return "str: " + s; default: return "other"; } } // When guard string test4(int x) { switch (x) { case int i when i < 0: return "negative"; case int i when i == 0: return "zero"; case int i: return "positive: " + i; } return ""; } // Multiple labels share one body int test7(int x) { switch (x) { case 1: case 2: case 3: return 123; default: return 0; } } // Break exits the switch (not surrounding loop) int test9() { var sum = 0; var i = 0; while (i < 10) { i = i + 1; switch (i) { case 3: break; // exits switch, loop continues case 5: break; // exits switch, loop continues default: sum = sum + i; } } return sum; // 1+2+4+6+7+8+9+10 (skipped 3,5) }

Switch expression

return x switch { 1 => "one", 2 => "two", _ => "other" };
// Switch expression with constant + discard int test8(int x) { return x switch { 1 => 11, 2 => 22, _ => 0 }; } // With when guard in expression var label = code switch { 200 => "OK", 404 => "Not Found", int c when c > 500 => "server error", _ => "unknown" }; // Lambda shorthand (o) => o switch { ... } var classify = (o) => o switch { int i when i < 0 => "negative", int i => "int: " + i, string s => "str: " + s, _ => "other" }; print(classify(42)); // "int: 42" print(classify("hi")); // "str: hi"

Pattern reference

PatternSyntaxExample
Constantcase value:case 42:, case "hello":
Type (no bind)case Type:case int:, case string:
Type (with bind)case Type name:case int i: i usable in body
Varcase var name:case var v: always matches, binds to v
Discardcase _: / default:Catch-all matches anything
When guardcase pattern when cond:case int i when i > 0:
Multiple labelscase A: case B:case 1: case 2: case 3: body
Named .NET type patterns
Callablescase Function:Matches script function values
case Coroutine:Matches running coroutines
Delegate typescase Delegate:Matches any .NET delegate
case Func:Matches Func<> instances
case Action:Matches Action<> instances
case Predicate:Matches Predicate<T> instances
System typescase Regex:Matches Regex objects
