Break semantics: break; inside a switch exits the switch, not the surrounding loop. If no switch is active, break exits the innermost loop as usual.
return keyword Return a value from a function

In void functions, return; without a value is allowed. Returning a value from a void function is an error.

A returned value is coerced to the function's declared return type, as in C#: an int function returning 2.5 gives 2, and a value the declared type cannot hold is refused (Cannot convert string 'hi' to int) rather than travelling on unchanged. A coroutine is the exception: return in a generator supplies the generator's final value, which the coroutine API hands back as it is, so a yield-based body is not constrained by the declared type.

return value;
int square(int x) { return x * x; } print(square(7)); // Result: 49

⚡ return.Value inspect the pending return inside finally

Inside a finally block, return.Value reads the value that is about to be returned from the enclosing try. This is a super power compared to C#: C# finally cannot observe the return value without an extra local variable, and return inside a C# finally is a compile-time error.

return.Value
// ⚡ finally can inspect the pending return value int testFinallyReturn() { try { return 42; } finally { var retVal = return.Value; print("Finally runs before return, value is: " + retVal); } } print(testFinallyReturn()); // Output: // Finally runs before return, value is: 42 // 42

⚡ return inside finally overrides the pending value

Unlike C# (which forbids return inside finally), ScriptLangCore allows it. A return executed inside a finally block replaces the original pending return value. Any nested finally still runs and sees the new value.

// ⚡ return in finally overrides the original return int testOverrideReturn() { try { return 42; } finally { print("First finally sees: " + return.Value); return 77; // overrides 42 → function returns 77 } } print(testOverrideReturn()); // Output: // First finally sees: 42 // 77
// Nested try/catch/finally inside finally return.Value is read-only at runtime int testNestedFinally() { try { return 42; } finally { try { return.Value = 15; print("(0)Finally runs before return: " + return.Value); } catch { print("(1a)Finally runs before return: " + return.Value); return 77; print("(1b)Finally runs before return: " + return.Value); } finally { print("(2)Finally runs before return: " + return.Value); } } } print(testNestedFinally()); // Output: // (1a)Finally runs before return: 42 // (2)Finally runs before return: 77 // 77

Notes:

  • return.Value is only meaningful inside a finally block whose corresponding try contains a return. Outside that context, it is null.
  • return.Value is read-only at runtime assigning to it throws a ScriptException with the message "Cannot assign to 'return.Value' it is read-only.". This exception is catchable by a wrapping try/catch.
  • A return statement inside a finally block overrides the pending return value. The function returns the last value returned, regardless of the original return in the try.
  • Nested finally blocks always run before the function actually returns, and they see the latest pending return value at the moment of execution.
  • At the top level a return ends the script and its value becomes the RUN'S ANSWER, which is ScriptResult.ReturnValue: what RunScript hands a script, what slc_file puts in the JSON it answers, and what the ABI reports. A bare return; answers nothing, a statement written after it never runs, and a return inside an if ends the run there. The value is NOT the process exit code: that comes from exit(n), abort(n) or an exitcode = n assignment (return 42; leaves the process at 0, while exitcode = 7; return 0; leaves 7). A script that ends without an explicit return exits with code 0, and one that encounters an unhandled error exits with 1.

⚡ return at the top level is the run's answer

The top level is a body like any other for return, so a script answers with an explicit value instead of trailing an expression statement. That matters where the answer is a result rather than a printed line: RunScript(file) reads .ReturnValue, slc_file(path) serializes it into the JSON it returns, and a host reading the ABI's verdict gets the same value.

// the same file, five shapes, and what the run answers return "blub"; // ReturnValue: "blub" (a statement after it does not run) return 42; // ReturnValue: 42 return { ok: true, n: 7 }; // ReturnValue: {"ok":true,"n":7} if (done) { return "early"; } // ends the run there, the rest of the file never runs 1 + 2; // no return at all: the last expression statement is the answer, 3 return; // answers nothing: the JSON has no ReturnValue member

Any value travels: a scalar, a string, a list, a dictionary literal, a struct or a class instance (its fields become the document), and a list of instances inside one. What does NOT travel is a computed member: a method is not serialized and the language has no computed property, so a summary you want in the answer is a FIELD you fill before returning.

That makes a script a small report factory: run each step, record what happened, and answer with the whole log in one value.

class StepLog { public string Name; public string State = "pending"; public string Detail = ""; } class RunLog { public string Suite; public string Verdict = "pending"; public List<StepLog> Steps = [].ToList(); public void Add(string name, string state, string detail) { var s = new StepLog(); s.Name = name; s.State = state; s.Detail = detail; this.Steps.Add(s); } public long Count(string state) { var n = 0; foreach (var s in this.Steps) { if (s.State == state) { n = n + 1; } } return n; } } // one step: run it, record it, and never let a failure end the run RunLog Step(RunLog log, string name, Func<int> work) { try { var code = work(); if (code == 0) { log.Add(name, "passed", ""); } else { log.Add(name, "failed", "exit " + code); } } catch (var ex) { log.Add(name, "failed", ex.Message); } return log; } var log = new RunLog(); log.Suite = "nightly"; Step(log, "compile", fun() { return 0; }); Step(log, "unit", fun() { return 2; }); Step(log, "smoke", fun() { throw "no database beside the exe"; }); log.Add("publish", "skipped", "no credentials"); if (log.Count("failed") > 0) { log.Verdict = "failed"; } else { log.Verdict = "passed"; } print("nightly: " + log.Count("passed") + " passed, " + log.Count("failed") + " failed"); return log; // the whole report is the run's answer

The run answers one document, so the reader queries it instead of parsing lines: json_extract(slc_file(path), '$.ReturnValue.Verdict') is the verdict, and json_each turns the log into rows (select value from json_each(slc_file(path), '$.ReturnValue.Steps') where json_extract(value, '$.State') = 'failed' gives the failures). The same file answers .ReturnValue through RunScript, and the example strips, so a bundle answers it too.

Two boundaries are worth knowing before relying on it. A typed line in the REPL is not a run: return 5; at the prompt echoes = 5 and the session continues, where the same line in a file ends the script. And the answer is not the exit code, so a script whose answer says "failed" still exits 0 unless it says otherwise with exitcode.

debugger keyword A breakpoint you can leave in the source

debugger; is a statement that hands control to the script debugger when it is on (.debug), and does nothing at all when it is off. That is what makes it safe to leave in a script: a normal run, a compiled bundle and every suite step straight past it, and the same line becomes a breakpoint for the session in which the debugger is on. It takes no arguments and needs its semicolon.

var total = 0; while (total < 3) { total = total + 1; debugger; // stops here only while .debug is on } print(total); // 3
do/while keyword Execute loop body at least once, then repeat while condition is truthy

The do keyword introduces a loop that executes its body once unconditionally, then repeats while the condition remains truthy. The while keyword and condition appear after the body.

do { /* body */ } while (condition);
var i = 0; do { i = i + 1; } while (i < 5); print(i); // Result: 5 // Always runs at least once, even if condition is false var x = 10; do { x = x + 1; } while (x < 5); print(x); // Result: 11

▼ Functions

fun / arrow lambda keyword Anonymous function expression (lambda) fun syntax or C#-style (args) => expr / x => expr

Lambdas capture their enclosing scope (closure). Two syntaxes are available: the fun keyword, and the C#-style (args) => expr form (no fun keyword). Both produce the same AST and behave identically. Supports expression body (=>) or block body ({ }).

// fun keyword (explicit types) fun (int x) => x * 2; fun (int x) { return x * 2; } // C#-style arrow (types optional, default object?) (x) => x * 2; (x) => { return x * 2; } () => 42; (int x, int y) => x + y; // C#-style bare single parameter (parens optional for exactly one untyped param) x => x * 2; x => { var n = x * 2; return n + 1; };
// fun keyword with expression body var dbl = fun (int x) => x * 2; print(dbl(21)); // 42 // Same lambda with C#-style arrow (type inferred as object?) var dbl2 = (x) => x * 2; print(dbl2(21)); // 42 // Zero parameters var answer = () => 42; print(answer()); // 42 // With closure var mult = 10; var adder = (int x) => x + mult; print(adder(50)); // 60 // Block body var abs = (x) => { if (x >= 0) return x; return -x; }; print(abs(-5)); // 5 // Higher-order function with arrow callback var nums = [1, 2, 3]; var doubled = [x*2 for x in nums]; print(doubled[0]); // 2 // Bare single-parameter form same lambda without parens (C#-style, untyped param) var sq = x => x * x; print(sq(5)); // 25 // Block body, bare form var twice = x => { var n = x * 2; return n + 1; }; print(twice(5)); // 11 // LINQ with bare lambda hs10.Select(x => x * 2).Count() == 4 var hs = new HashSet<int>(); hs.Add(1); hs.Add(2); hs.Add(3); hs.Add(4); print(hs.Select(x => x * 2).Count()); // 4
// Verified coverage bare single-parameter arrow lambdas (from iterable_test.slc, group 11) Check("11a. LINQ bare lambda: hs10.Select(x => x * 2).Count() == 4", hs10.Select(x => x * 2).Count() == 4); var f11 = x => x * 2; Check("11b. bare expr lambda: f = x => x * 2; f(5) == 10", f11(5) == 10); var g11 = x => { var n = x * 2; return n + 1; }; Check("11c. bare block lambda: g = x => { ... }; g(5) == 11", g11(5) == 11); Check("11d. chained bare lambdas: [1,2,3].Select(x => x + 1).Where(y => y > 2).Count() == 2", [1,2,3].Select(x => x + 1).Where(y => y > 2).Count() == 2); Check("11e. bare lambda on tuple: (1,2,3).Select(x => x * 3).Count() == 3", (1, 2, 3).Select(x => x * 3).Count() == 3); VmSetEnabled(false); var treeCount11 = [1,2,3].Select(x => x * 5).Count(); VmSetEnabled(true); Check("11f. bare lambda tree-mode parity: Select(x => x * 5).Count() == 3", treeCount11 == 3); Check("11g. discard lambda: [1,2].Select(_ => 7).Count() == 2", [1,2].Select(_ => 7).Count() == 2); var five11 = 5; Check("11h. match bare-identifier PATTERN still a pattern (suppression): 5 match { five11 => \"yes\", _ => \"no\" } == \"yes\"", (5 match { five11 => "yes", _ => "no" }) == "yes");

Arrow lambda rules:

  • (args) => expr expression body (no fun required)
  • (args) => { ... } block body with =>
  • Bare single parameter: x => expr and x => { ... } (C#-style) the parens are optional when there is exactly one untyped parameter; multiple untyped params still need parens ((x, y) => ...), and typed params keep the paren form ((int x) => ...)
  • Parameters without explicit type default to object?
  • Typed parameters work the same as fun: (int x, int y) => x + y
  • Closures, delegates, and higher-order functions work identically
  • Generic functions still require fun/named function syntax

Generic functions use <T> syntax: T Identity<T>(T x) { return x; }. Type arguments can be inferred from call arguments or specified explicitly: Identity<long>(42). See assets/language/repl/generics_showcase.slc for a complete reference.

Generic return types. Generic functions may use T[], List<T> or Dictionary<K, V> and arrays of these, e.g. List<T>[] as their return type (or as a generic collection type anywhere in the signature). Inside a generic function, typeof of such a generic collection reports the concrete instantiation "List<int>", not a bare "List". List<T>.ToArray() and HashSet<T>.ToArray() return a typed T[] (e.g. int[], string[]) never object[], so the elements are not boxed and a generic function returning T[] delivers the concrete array type, which typeof reflects: typeof(evens) is "int[]" for Filter<int>(...).
T[] Filter<T>(Array items, Predicate<T> pred) { var result = new List<T>(); foreach (var i in items) { if (pred(i)) result.Add(i); } return result.ToArray(); } var evens = Filter<int>([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], (x) => x % 2 == 0); print(evens.Length); // 2 Filter<int> returns int[] var collect = Collect<int>([1, 2, 3]); // List<T> Collect<T>(T[] items) { ... } print(typeof(collect)); // "List<int>" the concrete instantiation
Type-argument mismatch warning. A generic type argument that does not match the runtime value produces an early call-site warning (never an exception): Type mismatch: Type argument 'int' for 'T' does not match the runtime type 'string' of argument 1. The call keeps running the coercion still errors (catchably) later if the mismatched value is actually used.
// [WARNING] Type mismatch: Type argument 'int' for 'T' does not match the runtime type 'string' of argument 1. var warned = Filter<int>(["a", "b"], (x) => x == "a"); // warns only no exception // the string→int coercion still throws (catchably) when the value is used inside the function
Bare Identifier => ... in match/switch-expression arms is a PATTERN, not a lambda. Inside subject match { ... } (and switch arms), a bare identifier followed by => is parsed as an arm pattern (Function => "Function" matches a value that is Function, or five => "yes" compares the subject to the constant five) exactly the pre-existing behavior. The bare-lambda form applies only in ordinary expression positions.

Function, Iterable and RandomAccess are usable signature annotation types on parameters and return types, in named functions, fun/arrow lambdas, methods, and local functions. Function is the callable type (lambdas, named functions, bound methods, combined delegates, natives) and can be invoked directly inside the body. See the Internal Types entry for the full contract.

See also assets/language/repl/crash_arrow_lambda_test.slc for a comprehensive test of all patterns.

Closure capture: Closures capture variables (bindings), not value snapshots later assignments are visible inside the closure. Captured locals are RefCell-backed, so the closure and the enclosing scope share the same cell and writes go through on both sides; captured const values stay snapshots. Closures can mutate global variables. Method calls on reference types (like List.Add()) work because the object reference itself is shared. Local functions capture the same way and when they run on the VM their captures are VM-bound (materialized into the VM frame from the same RefCells), so mutation is visible on both sides there too.

// ✅ Closures CAN mutate global variables int result = 0; var fn = () => { result = 42; }; fn(); print(result); // 42 // Also works via method call on shared reference var items = new List<int>(); var fn2 = () => items.Add(7); fn2(); print(items[0]); // 7
Prefer proc.ExitCode after WaitForExit() over the onExited callback the callback runs on a ThreadPool thread and cannot reliably modify script variables. Stdout/stderr callbacks work correctly but still need sleep(300) after WaitForExit() for async draining.
Recursion depth limit: the interpreter runs script calls on a flat heap call stack deep non-tail recursion grows the heap, not the native thread stack, so legitimate recursion can go very deep (sumTo(5000), sumTo(100000) all run fine the cap is 1000000 nested VM calls under NativeAOT (30000 in Debug/JIT), bounded by memory, and it works even in JIT builds where the old re-entrant path overflowed at ~2000). A true runaway (e.g. int boom(int n) { return boom(n + 1) * 2; }) throws a catchable ScriptException (Maximum call depth exceeded (1000000) possible runaway recursion. under NativeAOT) it never crashes the process, and the guard is silent (no console warning). Tail-recursive calls are optimized into a loop and run in constant stack (tailRec(100000, 0) runs in constant stack; the 1000000-iteration tail-loop guard bounds an infinite tail loop, and SLC_VM_MAXFRAMES lowers it). Functions that fall back to the tree-walker (coroutines, unsupported constructs, or after VmSetEnabled(false)) are still bounded by the interpreter guard (3000 under NativeAOT, 24 in Debug/JIT see the VmSetEnabled entry for the full table), and the AOT build keeps a 32 MB process stack as a safety net.

Recursive lambdas two-step binding

A lambda that calls itself needs its own name, but the var binding does not exist until its initializer has finished evaluating. Declare the binding first, then assign the lambda:

// Two-step pattern binding first, lambda second (verified: prints 4181; VM and tree paths identical) var fibPair; // binding first fibPair = ((int n)) => { if (n <= 1) return (n, 1); var prev = fibPair(n - 1); // closure sees the late assignment return (prev[1], prev[0] + prev[1]); }; print(fibPair(19)[0]); // 4181

The one-liner does not work:

var fib = ((int n)) => { /* ... fib(n - 1) ... */ }; // invoking it raises Undefined variable 'fib'

The lambda is evaluated before fib exists the closure snapshot is taken at creation time, so there is no capture for fib to resolve against. The initializer itself completes, but the first call raises Undefined variable 'fib' (cleanly, on both the VM and tree paths never a VmFallback leak and never a crash). The two-step form works because the binding exists in scope when the closure is created: closures capture the variable (binding), so the later assignment is visible.

Design note: JS-style hoisting (auto-defining the declaration name before evaluating its initializer, so the one-liner would work) was considered and deliberately rejected it would change the semantics of every var x = init (var x = x; self-assignments, order surprises). The engine keeps its C#-flavored var semantics.

Alternative: a local named function can also recurse local functions run on the VM exactly like top-level functions. A local function is lazily compiled to bytecode on its first invocation, and its recursion is VM-flat: it grows the VM's flat heap frame list, not the C# call stack. Deep local recursion is therefore no longer capped by the Debug tree-walker (MaxCallDepth 24 in JIT builds) the bound is now the VM's frame cap (VmMaxFrames: 30000 in Debug/JIT, 1000000 under NativeAOT). Verified against the Debug exe: var Deep(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n + Deep(n - 1); } recursing to Deep(1000) returns 500500.

A local function is in scope for the whole body it is declared in, as in C#, so a closure written above it can still call it. The name is bound when the body starts and the declaration fills it, so the closure sees the function when it runs. This is the shape a callback written before its helper has, and it works at the top level, inside a function, inside an if and inside a loop:

// The handler is written ABOVE the function it calls, and both work var hits = [].ToList(); var handler = fun (string s) { Note(s); }; // created before Note exists var label = "late"; // declared between them, and Note still sees it void Note(string s) { hits.Add(label + ":" + s); } handler("one"); print(hits[0]); // late:one

One limit comes with it: calling a local function before its declaration runs is refused, naming it (The function 'Note' is used before the declaration that defines it in this block ...), because the function itself is created when the declaration executes. Order therefore matters for the CALL, never for a name a closure captured. The shape runs on the bytecode VM like any other body: the slot exists from the start of the block, a closure created above the declaration captures it as a cell, and the declaration fills that cell (measured on a 2,000-call loop through such a handler: VM: 4001 (100.0%) | Tree: 0).

The two-step pattern also works nested inside a function closures capture variables (bindings), so the closure created inside the function sees the later assignment to fibPair and recurses through the same RefCell. Verified against the Debug exe (prints 4181; VM and tree paths identical):

// Nested two-step pattern binding first, lambda second (verified: prints 4181; VM and tree paths identical) var NestedFib() { // local function (untyped) Function is a return-type keyword var fibPair; // binding first fibPair = ((int n)) => { if (n <= 1) return (n, 1); var prev = fibPair(n - 1); // the captured binding is live recursion works return (prev[1], prev[0] + prev[1]); }; return fibPair(19); } print(NestedFib()[0]); // 4181
// Deep local recursion the named-function alternative runs VM-flat (verified against the Debug exe: prints 500500) var Host() { var Deep(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n + Deep(n - 1); } return Deep(1000); } print(Host()); // 500500 (previously: Maximum call depth exceeded (24) on the Debug tree path)
// Delegate-typed lambda parameters Action / Func<,> / Predicate<T> work in both lambda forms var run = fun (Action a, Func<int, int> g) { a(); return g(21); }; print(run(fun () { }, fun (int x) { return x * 2; })); // 42 // Arrow form same delegate-typed params var arrowRun = (Action a, Func<int, int> g) => g(21); print(arrowRun(fun () { }, fun (int x) { return x * 2; })); // 42 // Predicate<T> param too var isBig = fun (Predicate<int> p) { return p(5); }; print(isBig(fun (int x) { return x > 3; })); // True
named arguments keyword Pass arguments by name f(x: 1, y: 2) order-independent

Arguments can be passed by name using name: value syntax. Named arguments are reordered to match the callee's parameter list at the call site, so they can appear in any order and be mixed with positional arguments (positional must come first, like C#).

f(x: 1, y: 2); obj.Method(name: "a", count: 3); new Person(name: "Alice", age: 30);
void draw(int x, int y, string label) { /* ... */ } draw(x: 10, y: 20, label: "origin"); draw(label: "pt", y: 5, x: 1); // any order draw(0, label: "zero", y: 0); // mixed: positional first
Named arguments work on script functions, methods, and constructors. Calls using named arguments are compiled to the bytecode VM: the compiler emits the arguments in source order plus a name-mapping const, and the VM reorders them against the callee's parameter list before binding. Named arguments on a local/parameter callee (e.g. a lambda stored in a local variable) still fall back to the tree interpreter.
On an overloaded name, the NAMES choose the member: with Nm(int a, string b) and Nm(string a, int b), Nm(b: 1, a: "s") is the second one, because each candidate is asked whether its parameter list has those names (C#'s rule), and the call is then bound through that same mapping. A name no parameter has, and the same name twice, are refused as such Named argument 'c' does not match any parameter., Named argument 'a' specified more than once. rather than as an arity problem.
local functions keyword Nested named functions declared inside a method/function body

A function declared inside another function's body is a local function. It is scoped to the enclosing block, can capture and mutate the enclosing locals, and supports all normal function forms (typed, void, var, expression body, tuple return).

Two declarations of one name with DIFFERENT parameter lists are an overload set, exactly as for a top-level function (see Function): each call resolves by argument count and type, the exact type beating a widening one, and a tie going to the first declaration.

int outer(int n) { int double_(int x) { return x * 2; } return double_(n) + 1; }
// Capture + mutate an enclosing local int counter() { var acc = 0; int add(int x) { acc = acc + x; return acc; } add(3); add(4); return acc; // 7 } // void and var forms int useVoid() { var total = 0; void bump(int v) { total = total + v; } bump(5); return total; // 5 } // Tuple-returning local function inside a lambda var outer = fun (int v) { (int a, int b) mid(int w) { return (w + 1, w + 2); } return mid(v); };
Local functions are not visible outside the enclosing body. They reuse the lambda closure machinery mutable captures are promoted to RefCell so writes propagate back to the enclosing scope. Local functions run on the bytecode VM like top-level functions (lazily compiled on first invocation), with their captures VM-bound: the same RefCells are materialized into the VM frame, so mutation is visible on both sides and recursion stays VM-flat.
pure keyword Pure function results are memoized

Pure functions must be deterministic same inputs always produce the same output. Results are cached in _pureMemoCache.

pure int square(int x) { return x * x; }
pure int fib(int n) { if (n <= 1) return n; return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); } print(fib(10)); // Result: 55 (memoized)
Memoization is keyed by the function name + argument values. Cache can be cleared with ClearPureCache().
yield keyword Suspend a coroutine and produce a value direct call returns a Generator (MoveNext / Current / foreach)

Functions containing yield are auto-detected as coroutines. Call the function directly to get a Generator a lazy iterable driven with MoveNext()/Current or consumed with foreach or pass it to Coroutine.Start() to run it as a background coroutine. Generator arguments are preserved: the first MoveNext() runs to the first yield with the original arguments in place.

What a coroutine is

  • Cooperative multitasking on one thread many logical executions interleaved at explicit yield points, no OS-thread overhead.
  • Stateful, resumable, controllable the status lifecycle (NotStarted/Suspended/Waiting/Completed/Dead), Continue()/Abort()/Reset() actions, LastYieldedValue (the last yielded value after completion it keeps that last yield and is what an iterator's Current reads; the body's return value is Coroutine.ReturnValue, null until it completes naturally), per-coroutine memory.
  • Await-style requests yield Coroutine.Sleep(ms) / Wait(evt) are deferred: the coroutine expresses "don't resume me until X," and the driver (the Pump() loop) enforces it. This is the one green-thread-like trait: the coroutine can suspend for a reason rather than a fixed number of steps. Coroutine.Pump() drives the interpreter of the RUN that calls it, so a pumping loop behaves the same in an embedded session (ScriptLangCore.Launcher.exe) as from the command line.
yield value;
// As a coroutine (background execution) int countTo(int max) { var i = 0; while (i < max) { yield i; i = i + 1; } return i; } var co = Coroutine.Start(countTo, 3); // auto-starts the first yield (0) is consumed inside Start print(co.Resume()); // Result: 1 print(co.Resume()); // Result: 2 print(co.Resume()); // Result: 3 // As a Generator direct call, explicit MoveNext()/Current (no thread, no pump) print(typeof(countTo(3))); // Result: "Generator" the name a script can also write: `gen is Generator` var gen = countTo(2); // nothing runs until the first MoveNext() print(gen.MoveNext()); // Result: True runs to the first yield print(gen.Current); // Result: 0 argument 2 reached the body (preserved on first resume) print(gen.MoveNext()); // Result: True print(gen.Current); // Result: 1 print(gen.MoveNext()); // Result: False the function returned, enumeration is over // The same Generator, consumed by foreach foreach (var n in countTo(3)) { print(n); // 0, 1, 2 } // Nested generators a coroutine may call another coroutine by bare name int pairs(int n) { var i = 0; while (i < n) { yield (i, i * 2); i = i + 1; } return -1; } int nested(int n) { foreach (var v in pairs(n)) { yield v; } return -1; } foreach (var t in nested(2)) { print(t[0], t[1]); } // 0 0, 1 2 generator loop frames stay isolated

The yielded sequence vs. the return value

A generator produces two distinct things: the yielded sequence exactly the yield values, which foreach/MoveNext iterate and the return value, which terminates the sequence and is never an element. The return is not mandatory at runtime on the VM path: falling off the end of the body simply ends the generator (after death Current shows null instead of a stored value). It is required on the tree-walker path (VmSetEnabled(false)), which raises Coroutine 'X' must return a value. for a body that ends without one and it is the honest type-contract for a function declared int. return -1; is the conventional sentinel used in these examples: it satisfies both paths and closes the sequence without contributing a value to the consumers.

// foreach sees ONLY the yields the return value is never an element int gen() { yield 1; yield 2; return -1; // terminates the sequence NOT an element } var s = ""; foreach (var x in gen()) { s = s + x + ","; } print(s); // "1,2," // MoveNext step by step the return value only appears once the generator is done. // g.Status tracks the lifecycle: NotStarted → Suspended (while iterating) → Completed (natural end). var g = gen(); print(g.Status); // NotStarted print(g.MoveNext(), g.Current, g.Status); // True 1 Suspended print(g.MoveNext(), g.Current, g.Status); // True 2 Suspended print(g.MoveNext(), g.Current, g.Status); // False -1 Completed ran to its return naturally print(g.Status == CoroutineStatus.Completed); // True (naturally exhausted) // Action vocabulary Continue()/Abort()/Reset() complete MoveNext()/Dispose(). // A break-abandoned generator is Suspended, NOT stuck: Continue() resumes it. int gen2() { yield 1; yield 2; return 0; } var g2 = gen2(); foreach (var x in g2) { break; } // abandoned → Suspended (yield 1 consumed) print(g2.Continue(), g2.Current); // True 2 resumed from the yield point print(g2.Continue(), g2.Status); // False Completed ran to its return var g3 = gen2(); foreach (var x in g3) { break; } g3.Abort(); // ≡ Dispose → Dead, state freed print(g3.Status); // Dead var g4 = gen2(); g4.MoveNext(); g4.Reset(); // safe destroy → Dead, no exception print(g4.Status, g4.MoveNext()); // Dead False
Read Current only while MoveNext() returned True. After the generator returns, MoveNext() stays False forever; the return value is the coroutine's completion result (stored as LastYieldedValue / returned by the final Resume()), but the foreach/MoveNext contract is defined over the yielded values only. To check where a generator is in its lifecycle, read g.Status: NotStarted before the first MoveNext, Suspended/Waiting while iterating, and once exhausted Completed if it ran to its end naturally or Dead if it was disposed/abandoned (e.g. g.Status == CoroutineStatus.Completed); the raw Coroutine is also reachable via g.InnerCoroutine. Action vocabulary: g.Continue() ≡ MoveNext() (resumes an abandoned break generator from its yield point), g.Abort() ≡ Dispose() (→ Dead, state freed), g.Reset() = safe destroy (→ Dead, no exception generators are one-shot, so re-create for a fresh run).
VM-safety gate gap the loud fallback: a generator body is compiled to VM bytecode when the compiler's analysis considers it VM-safe. That analysis is conservative but not exhaustive, so a body may still contain a construct the VM cannot execute e.g. delegate subtraction f - g, which is not a defined operation on any path (the tree raises Cannot convert 'func …' to number; only f + g combines delegates). When the VM meets such a construct at runtime it falls back loudly instead of silently re-running the body: before the first yield it throws a catchable VM generator 'X' cannot execute its body on the bytecode VM … (possible VM gate gap; the generator stayed VM-backed because its body appeared VM-safe), and after a yield it throws VM generator 'X' cannot be resumed after the bytecode VM fell back (…). Side effects executed before the failure run exactly once the fallback never double-executes the body. The same construct on the tree path (VmSetEnabled(false)) produces the standard runtime error.
async / await keyword Suspend an async function on a Task without blocking a thread: a call returns a Task

async marks a function whose body may await. Calling one returns the Task this engine already had: the body starts, runs to its first suspension, and the caller holds a task that completes with the body's return value, or faults with whatever the body threw. Nothing blocks a thread while the body waits, and that suspension belongs to the runtime rather than to a compiler-generated state machine: the engine builds against .NET 11 with <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>, and Task.Delay is an async engine method.

A .NET task is awaited the same way: a member taken from the CLR surface of a namespaced facade (see File) hands the script this engine's own Task, so var text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync("./report.txt"); reads a file without blocking a thread, and a failure travels as the engine's mapped refusal rather than an AggregateException.

async Task<Type> Name(params) { await expr; ... } // or, with an expression body async Task<Type> Name(params) => await expr;

Declaring an async function

FormSpellingNotes
typed functionasync Task<int> Fetch(int ms) { ... }the return value becomes the task's result
no resultasync Task Log(string s) { ... }no result, and the call still hands back a Task
expression bodyasync Task<int> Answer() => 42;await may sit in the expression
local functionasync Task<int> Local(int v) { ... }the same forms, declared inside another body
modifier orderpure async Task<int> F() { ... }async comes after the other modifiers, as in C#
async Task<int> Fetch(int ms) { await Task.Delay(ms); // suspend here, no thread is held return ms; // becomes the Task's result } async Task Log(string text) { await Task.Delay(1); print(text); } async Task<int> Answer() => 42; // expression body, no await needed async Task<int> Sum(int ms) => await Task.Delay(ms) + 1; // await inside an expression body void Outer() { async Task<int> Local(int v) { // a local async function await Task.Delay(0); return v * 3; } print(Local(7).Result); // 21 }

What can be awaited

  • the Task another async call returned, which is what lets async bodies compose;
  • Task.Delay(ms), the delay that holds no thread, and Task.Delay(ms, token), which faults the task instead of completing it when the token fires;
  • a Task that is already complete, including Task.CompletedTask, which costs no suspension at all;
  • the awaitable requests the coroutine machinery already had, the same set yield accepts: Coroutine.Sleep(ms), Coroutine.Wait(evt), Coroutine.Fetch(url), ReadLineAsync().

Statements that take await

Two STATEMENTS are awaited, and both spellings are C#'s: await foreach reads an IAsyncEnumerable<T> one MoveNextAsync at a time and disposes the enumerator on every exit (the foreach entry has the detail), and await using awaits an IAsyncDisposable's disposal (the using entry does). Neither compiles to bytecode, so a source-less bundle carries such a file's source instead of stripping it.

await foreach (var line in File.ReadLinesAsync('data.csv')) { print(line); } await using (var seq = File.ReadLinesAsync('data.csv')) { // DisposeAsync awaited when the block exits, even on an exception }

An await keeps a window alive

An awaiting script's window stays live: the pump a suspension is driven from also dispatches the queued messages, so a pending repaint is delivered and a queued click runs its handler during the wait. That is C#'s own behaviour on a UI thread, where a continuation is resumed through the message loop, and it is what makes await usable in a tool that owns a form. The boundary is deliberate: sleep dispatches nothing, so a handler never re-enters a statement that is merely blocking, while every other pump caller (an await, Task.Wait(), .Result, a coroutine sleep, Application.DoEvents()) is a wait that already gives the window a slice. Pinned by await_window_liveness_test.

async Task Work() { await Task.Delay(700); // the form keeps painting and taking clicks through this } Work().Wait();

An async Task body may fall off its end, exactly as a bare return; does, so a body whose last statement is a call, an await or an await foreach needs no closing return. An async Task<T> body owes a value on every path, which is C#'s own rule, and the refusal says so.

async Task<int> Twice(int ms) { var a = await Fetch(ms); // await another async call var b = await Fetch(ms); // then a second one, sequentially return a + b; } async Task<string> Sleepy() { await Coroutine.Sleep(10); // the awaitables yield already accepted are awaitable return "woke"; } async Task<int> Quick() { var done = Task.Delay(0); print(done.IsCompleted); // True return await done + 3; // already complete: the await does not suspend } async Task<int> Total() { var a = await Task.Delay(1); // one await per top-level statement var b = await Task.Delay(2); var c = await Task.Delay(3); return a + b + c; // 6 }

Async members and lambdas

A method carries the modifier the way a function does, and the receiver travels with the body, so this reads the instance. An async fun lambda is a value like any other lambda, and calling it returns the Task. Task.CompletedTask is a Task that is already complete, which an await takes without suspending.

class Loader { public int Base = 40; public async Task<int> Grow(int by) { await Task.Delay(1); return this.Base + by; // the receiver is bound } } print(new Loader().Grow(2).Result); // 42 var f = async fun(int n) { await Task.Delay(1); return n * 2; }; print(f(4).Result); // 8 async Task<int> Work() { await Task.CompletedTask; return 42; } // no suspension at all print(Task.Run(Work).Result); // 42 an awaited method handed to Task.Run is unwrapped

Where an await may sit

An await belongs in the body, and any of the ordinary statements can hold it: the top level, an if, a try, a plain block, or a while, a for and a foreach body, as a statement, as the value of an expression (t = t + await f()), or bound to a local. A local bound from the awaited value survives, a loop body keeps the element or the index its iteration is on, and a fault raised there is caught by the enclosing try. A file's TOP LEVEL is where a script's own await belongs, as C#'s async Main is for a program: it may await, and it may just as well run ordinary code. A top-level await WAITS rather than suspending, because the outermost frame has nothing to resume it, which makes it equivalent to .Result there.

await f(); // statement var r = await f(); // bound to a variable return await f(); // the awaited value as the return value

Pointers, refs and unsafe code

A suspension here holds nothing in a register: the engine records the body's position and its locals and resumes the body in the same process, and one cooperative pump drives every body on the same thread. So a raw pointer or a native handle you hold across an await is still usable afterwards, and a local of any type survives the suspension. That is a deliberate difference from C#, where the state of a suspended method lives in a heap object, the scheduler may run the continuation on another thread, and a pointer across an await therefore needs pinning.

C# refuses two shapes across an await, and both are about a suspension moving the state to the heap or resuming it on another thread: a fixed pointer (the compiler reports "cannot await in context of a 'fixed' statement") and a by-ref local ("a ref local cannot be kept across an await or yield boundary"). Everything else around unsafe code is ordinary there too: a stackalloc buffer, an address taken from a local, and an unsafe block are all accepted in an async body, and an await may sit in a try, a catch and a finally alike. Here none of the two applies, because nothing is pinned and no local moves, so the body you write is the body that runs: a pointer from Mem or a native library is safe to carry across an await, and a by-ref parameter stays live across one.

The Task you get back

An async call hands back the ordinary Task, so its whole surface applies unchanged. The wait members drive the coroutine pump for you, which is what lets a task reach completion without the script having to pump anything itself.

MemberOn a Task an async call returned
.Status"Running" while the body is suspended, then "Completed" or "Faulted"
.Wait()drives the pump until the body finishes; rethrows a fault
.Resultthe body's return value; drives the pump, and throws if the body faulted
Task.WhenAll(list)accepts these Tasks, and the composite is driven by waiting on it
.ContinueWith(fn)runs fn on the main thread once the body completes, chained arbitrarily
Task.Run(fn)accepts an async function, and the task is UNWRAPPED as in C#, so it carries the async body's value instead of a nested Task. A WORK function runs on the interpreter the script is running on, so its body reads and writes the same globals the calling code does, including inside a nested RunScript. Given a token (Task.Run(fn, cts.Token)), that token is the body's KILL SIGNAL while it runs, and a pre-cancelled one means the body never starts
awaitthe awaited value of the body, which is how one async body waits for another

Inside an async body, await the task: that is the spelling to prefer, and it is how one async body waits for another. At a file's top level the two are equivalent, because a top-level await waits on the spot, so await reads the same there and is the spelling to reach for: .Result and .Wait() stay available, and are the tools to pick when you want the wait to be visible in the code or when you are in a body that cannot await.

var t = Fetch(30); print(t.Status); // Running t.Wait(); // drives the body to completion print(t.Status); // Completed print(t.Result); // 30 // Task.Run accepts an awaited method: C# unwraps it, so the task carries the VALUE async Task<int> Load() { await Task.Delay(5); return 7; } var loaded = Task.Run(Load); print(loaded.Result); // 7, not a Task async Task<int> Plus1() => await Task.Run(Load) + 1; // 8 the unwrapped value, awaited var a = Fetch(10); var b = Fetch(15); Task.WhenAll([a, b]).Wait(); // the composite drives its constituents print(a.Result + " " + b.Result); // 10 15 var seen = 0; var c = Fetch(5); c.ContinueWith(fun(t) { seen = t.Result * 4; return null; }); c.Wait(); // completes the body and queues the continuation print(seen); // 20

Faults

A throw with no enclosing try in the body faults the Task instead of unwinding the caller, which is C#'s rule. The fault then surfaces wherever the caller touches the task.

async Task<int> Fails() { await Task.Delay(1); throw "boom"; } var bad = Fails(); // the call itself does not throw try { print(bad.Result); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // boom print(bad.Status); // Faulted async Task<string> Handled() { // a fault awaited at the body's top level travels on var t = Fails(); var r = await t; return "unreachable"; } try { print(Handled().Result); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // boom

Contextual keywords

Both words are contextual, exactly as in C#: inside an async body and at a file's top level await is the operator (at the top level a following operand decides, so print(await) keeps its name), and inside any other body it is an ordinary identifier, so a script may still call a variable await. A function that is not declared async cannot use the operator, and that refusal names the fix.

var await = "a legal name"; // outside an async body this is just an identifier print(await); // a legal name async Task<int> Ok() { return await Task.Delay(1); } int NotAsync() { return await Task.Delay(1); // Error: 'await' is only the await operator, and only inside an `async` function }

Coming from C#

The habits that carry over, and the places where this engine answers differently.

C# habitHere
await the taskthe same, and the spelling to prefer inside a body
.Result / .Wait()work, and they block while they drive the body, which is why C# discourages them. They are for a script's top level, where no body can await; inside a body use await
Task.Run(...), named by WHAT it wrapsan ASYNC method wrapped this way adds nothing, since an async body already waits without holding a thread, so await Load() directly. A BLOCKING call is what it is for, and this engine's File members are all synchronous (and its own refusal lists what it holds: no File.WriteAllTextAsync among them), so await Task.Run(fun() { File.WriteAllText(path, text); }); is the right spelling for one
async void, only for an event handlerREFUSED here: this engine has one untyped Task, and an async call always hands back an awaitable Task, so C#'s unawaitable form cannot be expressed. Write async Task
fire-and-forget, _ = F();the Task holds the fault, so a failure is visible only if something reads that task. Await it, or read .Result inside a try
start the independent work, then Task.WhenAllthe same, and it is how several waits run together. A foreach of awaits serialises them, and does not deliver its values anyway, see below
Task.CompletedTask, Task.FromResultCompletedTask is a Task that is already complete, and FromResult makes one that carries a value, so a caller can await it or read it without waiting for anything
ConfigureAwait(false)accepted as a NO-OP that answers the same task, so ported code reads unchanged. The engine owns one cooperative pump and has no synchronisation context to marshal away from
Task<T>, ValueTask, await foreachabsent. The engine's Task is untyped, and .Result or await carries the value

Supported, and not yet

The boundary is written down rather than left to be discovered, and assets/language/probes/probe-async-await.slc runs every shape below and reports a verdict per check, so a row and its instrument can be read together.

CapabilityNowNotes
async on a top-level, local, class or struct function or method✅ Yesa call returns a Task. On a member the receiver is bound, so the body reads this
async on an extension member✅ Yesthe same wrap. A NAMED receiver block (extension(string s)) does not expose its alias inside the body, which the coroutine form of the same member shares
async fun lambdas✅ Yesasync fun(...) { ... } and async fun(...) => expr. The bare async x => x form is not accepted, so write async fun (x) => x
await a Task from another async call, or Task.Delay✅ Yesone body may await another, to any depth
await an already-completed Task, or an existing awaitable request✅ Yesa completed Task does not suspend at all
await at the body's top level (statement, variable, or returned value)✅ Yesthe placement the resume understands
the Task surface on the returned Task: .Status, .Result, .Wait(), WhenAll, ContinueWith✅ Yeswaiting on a task also drives its body
a fault faulting the returned Task✅ Yessurfaces at .Result, .Wait(), or an await at the body's top level
Task.WhenAll over failing constituents✅ Yesthe composite carries the fault, and it names every failure in one line (Multiple failures) through .Wait(), .Result and await alike. One failure stays the plain exception a single task throws, and a composite of successes completes as before
await/async as contextual keywords✅ Yesno existing script is affected by the two names
await inside an if, a try, or a plain block✅ Yesthe value is delivered, a block-local bound from it survives, return await in a branch returns it, and a fault raised there is caught by the enclosing try
await inside a while or a for body✅ Yesas a statement, as the value of an expression (t = t + await f()), or bound to a local in the body, to any nesting
await inside a foreach body✅ Yesthe element stays the one the iteration is on, so t = t + await f(n) accumulates every element
catching a fault that a suspension raises inside a try in the body✅ Yesthe catch sees the awaited task's fault, which is C#'s rule
async on an interface member❌ Not yetrefused by name: an abstract member has no body to suspend in. A class or a struct method is the place for it
Task.CompletedTask✅ Yesa Task that is already complete, and a fresh one per read
pure on an async function❌ Refusedby name: the memo cache holds a return value, and an async call returns a Task. Drop one of the two modifiers
Task.Run(anAsyncFunction), including from a body evaluated by RunScript✅ Yesthe body starts on the interpreter that is RUNNING the script, so the pump that drives it and the pump its caller waits in are the same one
cancellation: an optional CancellationToken on every Task that EXECUTES work, Task.Run, Task.Delay and RunScriptAsync; a missing one means CancellationToken.None✅ Yesa token that fires faults the task, and one that is already cancelled never starts the body. The fault reads the awaited operation was cancelled before it completed, an engine message rather than a localized runtime one
a source-less bundle (--compile --source=strict)✅ Yesthe strip carries what a body IS, so a program whose top level waits on an async call runs from its bundle and prints what the file prints: the async-ness of a declaration travels with it, and a call from a compiled body hands its caller a Task either way. A body the compiler declined is still skipped and named in the export report
ConfigureAwait✅ Yes, as a no-opawait t.ConfigureAwait(false) awaits the same work: this engine has one pump and no synchronisation context to marshal a continuation away from, so the flag has nothing to change and the call answers the task itself
Task<T> results, ValueTask, await foreach✅ For the SPELLING, ❌ for an enforced payload typeasync Task<T> is the spelling and T is the body's result type, while the engine's Task stays UNTYPED at run time, so .Result is what carries the value. An enforced payload type, ValueTask and await foreach are still not there
a Task as a JSON value✅ Yes, as null by designa Task is a handle to running work rather than data, so there is nothing to write and nothing a reader could rebuild: Json.Serialize answers null for one, pending or complete, and for a task held in a list or a dictionary. C# writes the bookkeeping instead (Id, Status, IsCompleted) and that is just as unusable, so the rule is the same on both sides: serialize the INPUTS and the OUTCOME, never the task, which is what a job queue does (a payload plus a handler name). t.Status is a string and t.Result is the value
the outermost wait in a FILE✅ Yes, with await or with .Result / .Wait()a file's top level can await, so var r = await Work(); works there, and a top-level await WAITS rather than suspending (the outermost frame has nothing to resume it). Inside an async body use await and never .Result. Waiting drives the pump, so it cannot deadlock the way a CLR .Result can against a synchronisation context
two awaits in ONE expression, as in (await a) + (await b)✅ Yes in an async bodyan async body compiles, so a second await resumes at the next instruction instead of re-entering the statement. A body the compiler DECLINES (one holding an is pattern, a using body or a nested function) runs on the tree, where re-entry would re-issue the first await, so that shape is refused by name with the fix: var x = await a; var y = await b;
How it runs. The engine's suspension is cooperative and single-threaded: an await yields an awaitable to the coroutine pump, the pump wakes the body when the awaited Task completes, and a wait on the Task (.Wait(), .Result, or waiting on a combinator) is what drives that pump. An async body COMPILES and runs on the bytecode VM, where its await is the AWAIT opcode and the resume continues at the NEXT instruction (which is what lets one statement hold two awaits). A body the compiler declines, one holding a try, an is pattern, a using body or a nested function, is tree-walked instead, and there the once-per-statement await rule applies. The C#-flavoured surface above was added as a proof of concept, so treat the tables as the contract for now.
Coroutine built-in Coroutine API Start, Pump, Sleep, Wait; or call a coroutine directly for a Generator

The Coroutine namespace provides static methods for managing coroutines. Functions containing yield are auto-detected as coroutines. Calling a coroutine function directly returns a Generator lazy, with no thread and no pump needed driven with MoveNext()/Current or foreach; Coroutine.Start() remains the pump-style API for background scheduling.

Coroutine.Start(fn, args..., autoStart?); // autoStart defaults to true Coroutine.Pump(); yield Coroutine.Sleep(ms); yield Coroutine.Wait(evt); var gen = myCoro(2); // direct call → Generator (no Start needed)
// Direct call → Generator: MoveNext()/Current arguments are PRESERVED on first resume int countTo(int max) { var i = 0; while (i < max) { yield i; i = i + 1; } return i; } var gen = countTo(2); // nothing runs until the first MoveNext() print(gen.MoveNext(), gen.Current); // True 0 argument 2 reached the body print(gen.MoveNext(), gen.Current); // True 1 print(gen.MoveNext()); // False the function finished // foreach iterates the same generator foreach (var v in countTo(3)) { print(v); } // 0, 1, 2 // Nested coroutines a coroutine calls another coroutine by bare name int pairs(int n) { var i = 0; while (i < n) { yield (i, i * 2); i = i + 1; } return -1; } int outer(int n) { foreach (var v in pairs(n)) { yield v; } return -1; } foreach (var t in outer(3)) { print(t[0], t[1]); } // 0 0, 1 2, 2 4
// Start and pump (background scheduling) var co = Coroutine.Start(myFunc); while (co.IsResumable) { Coroutine.Pump(); } // stops on Completed or Dead // Manual pump-style alternative: Coroutine.Start(fn, args..., false) + co.Resume() var co2 = Coroutine.Start(countTo, 2, false); print(co2.Resume()); // 0 first Resume reaches the first yield print(co2.Resume()); // 1 print(co2.Resume()); // 2 the return value; Status is now Completed (natural end) // Action vocabulary Continue ≡ Resume (safe on any status), Abort ≡ Dispose, // Reset = safe destroy (Dead; later Continue/Resume → null instead of throwing) var co3 = Coroutine.Start(countTo, 2, false); print(co3.Continue()); // 0 same as Resume() co3.Abort(); // → Dead, state freed (like Dispose) print(co3.Continue() == null); // True already Dead (Continue returns null) var co4 = Coroutine.Start(countTo, 2, false); co4.Reset(); // safe destroy → Dead (no exception) // Sleep inside a coroutine yield Coroutine.Sleep(1000);
The direct-call Generator path is AOT-safe: Generator<T> is preserved for NativeAOT builds, so scripts can call MoveNext()/Continue()/Current/Dispose()/Abort()/Reset() on a direct-call generator under AOT same vocabulary as the Coroutine instance (Resume()/Continue()/Dispose()/Abort()/Reset()). Coroutines run through the tree-walker (they are not VM-compiled), so they are skipped at bytecode export.
CoroutineStatus enum Coroutine lifecycle states

Values returned by co.Status. Lifecycle: NotStarted → Suspended/Waiting while running or awaiting a request → Completed (the body ran to its end/return naturally) or Dead (disposed, abandoned, or errored).

CoroutineStatus.NotStarted // not yet started CoroutineStatus.Suspended // yielded a value resumable CoroutineStatus.Waiting // yielded a request (sleep/http/…) resumable CoroutineStatus.Completed // body ran to its return/end finished naturally CoroutineStatus.Dead // disposed / abandoned / errored not Completed
// Hand-driven loops: use IsResumable so a naturally-completed (Completed) // coroutine stops the loop too (Status != Dead alone would spin forever on it). while (co.IsResumable) { Coroutine.Pump(); } if (co.Status == CoroutineStatus.Completed) { print("finished, return=" + co.LastYieldedValue); }
params keyword Variable-length parameter collects excess call arguments into an array

The params keyword marks the last parameter of a function as a variable-length argument collector. When the function is called, any excess arguments beyond the required ones are collected into an Array (native object?[]). The parameter type must be Array or an array type like int[].

void printAll(params Array items) { foreach (var x in items) print(x); } printAll(1, 2, 3, "hello"); // items = [1, 2, 3, "hello"]
// Parameters can be passed individually or as an array literal int sum(params int[] nums) { var total = 0; foreach (var n in nums) total = total + n; return total; } print(sum(1, 2, 3)); // 6 params collect excess args print(sum([10, 20, 30])); // 60 single array literal also works

params can only appear on the last parameter. A function can have at most one params parameter. If a single argument is already an Array, it is passed through directly rather than double-wrapped.

Tail elements are by value. The array the callee receives is created for the call and filled with by-value elements, so a ref or out argument cannot occupy a tail position: there is no caller variable for the callee to write back to. Declare the parameter ref T[] xs and pass the array when the callee must write the array itself back.

.NET native methods with params are now supported e.g. Console.WriteLine(format, arg0, arg1, ...), string.Format(format, args...), StringBuilder.AppendFormat(format, args...). The interpreter detects [ParamArrayAttribute] on the last parameter and collects excess arguments into a typed array automatically.

Array literals vs. .NET params: A single array literal [a, b, c] passed to a .NET params method is not expanded it is passed as a single object argument. Always pass format values as individual arguments for .NET native methods like Console.WriteLine, string.Format, or StringBuilder.AppendFormat.

// .NET params methods work with multiple individual arguments Console.WriteLine("{0} {1} {2}", "Hello", "from", "params"); // Console table header with 13 positional args var row = "| {0,-4} | {1,-15} |"; Console.WriteLine("{0} {1} {2} {3} {4} {5} {6}", row, "Id", "Name", "CronExpr", "TzId", "MaxIter", "Status"); // string.Format var msg = string.Format("{0} + {1} = {2}", 1, 2, 3); // StringBuilder.AppendFormat var sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.AppendFormat("{0:D4} {1:F2}", 42, 3.14);
default parameter values keyword Optional parameters with default values caller may omit trailing arguments

Function parameters can have a default value specified with = expr. When the caller omits trailing arguments, the default is used. Default parameters must appear after all non-default parameters.

void Greet(string name = "world") { print("Hello " + name); }
// Function with default int Power(int x, int exp = 2) { var r=1; while(exp>=0){exp=exp-1;r=r*x;} return r; } print(Power(3)); // 9 (3²) print(Power(2, 10)); // 1024 // Multiple defaults string Concat(string a = "a", string b = "b") { return a + b; } print(Concat()); // "ab" print(Concat("x")); // "xb" print(Concat("x", "y")); // "xy"
Default values work on named functions, lambdas, and class methods. They also work with params for variadic functions.
ref keyword Pass argument by reference allows the callee to modify the caller's variable

The ref keyword marks a parameter as passed by reference. The callee can read and modify the caller's original variable. Works on function parameters and method parameters. Supports all value types: int, long, double, string, bool, char, structs, and class instances.

void Increment(ref int x) { x = x + 1; } var a = 5; Increment(ref a); print(a); // 6
// Swap two values void Swap(ref int x, ref int y) { var tmp = x; x = y; y = tmp; } var c = 10; var d = 20; Swap(ref c, ref d); print(c + "," + d); // 20,10 // With class instance mutating a field through ref class Box { public int val; } void DoubleBox(ref Box b) { b.val = b.val * 2; } var bx = new Box(); bx.val = 21; DoubleBox(ref bx); print(bx.val); // 42 // A FIELD, a PROPERTY or an ELEMENT can be passed by ref, and a ref local can point at one class RLBox { public int F; } void Bump(ref int v) { v = v + 1; } var h = new RLBox(); h.F = 3; Bump(ref h.F); // h.F is 4 ref int rf = ref h.F; // rf IS h.F rf = 30; // h.F is 30 int[] a = [1, 2, 3]; var re = ref a[1]; // the index runs ONCE re = re + 20; // a[1] is 22 Bump(ref a[2]); // a[2] is 4 print(h.F + "/" + a[1] + "/" + a[2]); // 30/22/4 // An `in` parameter is read-only and by value, and the keyword is optional at the call int Scale(in int v) { return v * 3; } var n = 4; print(Scale(in n) + "/" + Scale(n) + "/" + Scale(7)); // 12/12/21 // A REF RETURN: the call answers a REFERENCE, so reading it dereferences and assigning writes through int total = 0; ref int Slot() { return ref total; } Slot() = 9; // total is 9 ref int r9 = ref Slot(); // r9 IS total r9 = r9 + 1; // total is 10 print(Slot() + "/" + total); // 10/10 // A ref-returning METHOD is an lvalue the same way class Pool { public int n; public ref int Cell() { return ref this.n; } } var pool = new Pool(); pool.Cell() = 4; // pool.n is 4 ref int pc = ref pool.Cell(); // pc IS pool.n pc = pc * 2; // pool.n is 8 print(pool.Cell()); // 8 // All primitive types supported var rl = 50L; // long var rd = 10.0; // double var rs = "hello"; // string var rb = true; // bool var rc = 'A'; // char

Rules:

  • Both the declaration and the call site must use ref: Fn(ref x). Naming the keyword for a parameter that is not declared that way is an error, and the two keywords are not interchangeable: ref for an out parameter, or out for a ref one, is refused. The argument is never quietly passed by copy instead.
  • ref parameters cannot be used with const variables (throws ConstAssignment)
  • An argument passed by ref or out must be a VARIABLE, a FIELD or an ELEMENT (Fn(ref h.F), Fn(ref a[i])): a literal, a call and an operator result have no storage to write back to. An element's index is evaluated ONCE, and a bad index is refused at the call rather than on a later read
  • The variable a ref argument names must already hold the declared parameter type, because a reference is never converted: converting would retype the caller's variable. void P(ref int v) called as ref s where s holds "abc" is refused, and ref object is the spelling for "any variable". A numeric family still passes, so ref double accepts an int variable
  • A ref local binds a reference: ref int r = ref x; or var r = ref x;, and the target may be a variable, a field or an element (ref int r = ref h.F;). The local IS that storage, so a read dereferences it and an assignment writes through, an element's index is evaluated once, and the local travels into a lambda like any other capture. The written type is documentation: typeof(r) answers what the reference points at. Rebinding (r = ref y) is not supported
  • A ref overload and an out overload of the same parameters cannot coexist: a call cannot tell them apart, so the second declaration is refused
  • An in parameter is read-only and passed by value: int Scale(in int v). The keyword is optional at the call, a temporary is allowed (Scale(7)), and a body that writes the name, passes it by ref/out, or takes a ref local over it is refused WHERE IT IS DECLARED, with the fix named. The declared type still checks the argument
  • ref works in lambdas (fun(ref int x) => ...), constructors, and delegates, in classes and in structs alike
  • A ref return declares what the reference points at and answers the reference itself: ref int Slot() { return ref v; }. Reading a call dereferences (Slot() + 1), while Slot() = 9; and ref int r = ref Slot(); use the reference and write through it, on a free function and on a method (ref int Field() { return ref this.F; }). Such a body compiles, and so do both LVALUE uses: a plain read is a flat VM call, and for Slot() = 9; and ref int r = ref Slot(); the compiler marks the call so the VM hands the reference back instead of the value. A ref on a call that answered a VALUE is refused with the fix named, and a ref return of a LOCAL is allowed here where C# refuses it, because the reference is a heap cell rather than a native address
  • A ref argument cannot occupy a params tail position (see params)
  • ref works with events via delegate types that accept ref parameters (discouraged for multicast events), but an EVENT itself cannot be passed by ref: it holds a handler list, not a value
  • Coroutine Coroutine.Start() supports ref arguments
  • What it costs, and on which engine. A compiled body encodes a reference in bytecode (a slot reference for an argument, a cell the engine builds for a global, a field or an element) and the VM dereferences it; the tree walker closes a RefCell over a getter/setter pair per position. That is where the difference comes from: on the AOT build a loop passing a ref argument took 3% to 15% of the tree walker's time (a ref to a global or an out position about 5%), with allocations of the same order of magnitude apart. A ref LOCAL over a LOCAL variable is an ALIAS, the cheapest shape of the family (about 580 ns per iteration on the VM against 10,100 on the tree, and a few kilobytes allocated where the tree allocates megabytes); over a global, a field or an element it is a cell, so every read and write goes through it. A ref RETURN compiles too, and so do its two LVALUE uses: a read dereferences, `F(..) = 7;` writes through the reference, and `ref int r = ref F(..);` binds `r` to it. The compiler marks such a call so the VM hands the CELL back instead of the value (a plain read stays a flat VM call, so a compiled caller pays no interpreter re-entry), and the write goes through one helper the tree uses as well. A ref-returning METHOD is an lvalue too (box.F() = 7;, ref int r = ref box.F();). Two narrower shapes are the exceptions, and they differ in kind: a BARE call to the class's own method as an lvalue (Cell() = 12; inside a method) works, with that method's body walked rather than compiled, because its marker would have to sit under a receiver the arm builds first; and a call that NAMES its arguments cannot be assigned through at all (box.F(n: 0) = 9; is refused by the language, identically from a file and from a bundle, because a call that names its arguments is not a reference target, while READING it is fine). ref int r = ref F(..); also needs F to be provably a ref return, and the tree refuses it by name otherwise. assets/language/repl/bench_ref_vm_tree.slc measures all of it in one process, switching engines with VmSetEnabled
  • Internally, ref is implemented via a RefCell wrapper that captures a getter/setter pair for the target; a field or an element reuses the very resolver a compound assignment writes through, so a reference and h.F = v are one storage
in keyword A read-only parameter, and the foreach separator

in has two jobs, and neither is a boolean operator. Before a parameter's type it declares a READ-ONLY, by-value parameter (int Scale(in int v)): the body reads v and a write to it is refused, and the CALLER may write the keyword or leave it out, since the modifier is about the callee's side. In a foreach header it separates the iteration variable from the collection. Both spellings are keywords, so in cannot be a variable name, while In is an ordinary identifier (keywords are case-sensitive). The ref entry has the modifier's neighbours.

int Scale(in int v) { return v * 3; } var n = 4; print(Scale(in n) + "/" + Scale(n)); // 12/12, the keyword is optional at the call var sum = 0; foreach (var x in [1, 2, 3]) { sum = sum + x; } print(sum); // 6
out keyword Pass argument by reference callee must assign a value before returning

The out keyword marks a parameter as an output parameter. Unlike ref, the caller's variable does not need to be initialized before the call. The callee must assign a value to every out parameter before the function returns, otherwise a runtime error is thrown. Available in functions, methods, lambdas, constructors, and delegates. The call site must name the keyword the parameter declares, out for an out parameter and ref for a ref one, because the two are not interchangeable. Class and struct constructors both take out parameters, and an out argument cannot occupy a params tail position.

Three call-site syntaxes

// 1. Existing variable variable must exist or is auto-created void InitValue(out int x) { x = 42; } var a; InitValue(out a); print(a); // 42 // 2. Inline declaration (C# 7.0 style) declares and captures in one step InitValue(out var b); print(b); // 42 // 3. Discard value is thrown away, no variable created InitValue(out var _); // true discard, no scope pollution InitValue(out _); // also discards, but _ is a real variable
// Multiple out params inline declaration void Split(out int first, out int second) { first = 10; second = 20; } Split(out var x, out var y); print(x + "," + y); // 10,20 // ref + out in same call void ReadThenInit(ref int source, out int dest) { dest = source + 5; } var src = 10; ReadThenInit(ref src, out var dst); print(dst); // 15 // With class constructor class OutCtor { constructor(out int created) { created = 2024; } } var obj = new OutCtor(out var val); print(val); // 2024 // With lambda var factory = fun(out int v) { v = 77; }; factory(out var res); print(res); // 77 // Discard with out var _ factory(out var _); // value discarded, no _ variable created

Rules:

  • Both the declaration and the call site must use out: Fn(out x)
  • The caller's variable does not need to be initialized beforehand out var name declares it inline; out name auto-creates it if undefined
  • The callee must assign a value to every out parameter before the function returns failure to do so throws: "The 'out' parameter 'X' must be assigned before the function returns."
  • A parameter cannot be both ref and out
  • out works in plain functions, class methods (instance and static), lambdas (fun and arrow), constructors, and delegates
  • out works with events (declared as delegate void Handler(out int x)) following C# conventions: technically supported, but discouraged for multicast events since only the last subscriber's assignment is observable
  • Type compatibility: When an out parameter has a named class type (e.g. List<int>, StringBuilder), assigning a value of an incompatible type throws TypeMismatch: "cannot assign value of type 'X' to out/ref parameter 'Y' of type 'Z'." Primitive types (int, string, double, etc.) are auto-coerced and not checked
  • Internally, out is implemented via the same RefCell mechanism as ref, but with an assignment tracker and the ability to capture undefined variables

▼ Classes & Structs

extends keyword Single inheritance for classes

The extends keyword creates a class that inherits fields, methods, constructors, and events from a parent class. The child can override methods and must call super() in its constructor.

class Child extends Parent { constructor(params) { super(baseArgs); /* ... */ } }
class Animal { public string Name; constructor(string n) { this.Name = n; } public string Speak() { return "..."; } } class Dog extends Animal { public string Breed; constructor(string n, string b) { super(n); this.Breed = b; } public string Speak() { return "Woof!"; } } var d = new Dog("Rex", "Lab"); print(d.Name + " says " + d.Speak());

Access modifier defaults:

  • class / struct declarations → private (not visible from importing scripts unless marked public)
  • Class members (fields, methods) → private
  • Struct members (fields, methods) → private
  • Top-level functions → private (not exported from modules unless marked public)
  • Top-level const / var → public (module constants are visible to importing scripts)

Access matrix (class/struct declarations):

ModifierSame-fileImported moduleAs type arg (import)
none (defaults private)✅❌ blocked❌ blocked
private✅❌ blocked❌ blocked
protected✅❌ blocked❌ blocked
internal✅✅ accessible✅ accessible
public✅✅ accessible✅ accessible

Constructor access matrix:

ModifierSame-file globalImported class
none (defaults public)✅ callable✅ callable
public✅ callable✅ callable
private❌ blocked❌ blocked
protected❌ blocked❌ blocked (only via super())
internal✅ callable✅ callable

Member defaults: Class fields/methods default to private. Struct fields/methods also default to private. private/protected members are blocked from global code even in the same file.

Constructor access: Constructors support access modifiers too (public, private, protected, internal). A private constructor can only be called from within the class itself (singleton pattern). A protected constructor is only accessible from derived classes via super(). internal constructors are accessible from importing scripts. Default is private (same as fields).

Only single inheritance is supported. Generic classes use <T> syntax: class Box<T> { ... }. Access modifiers: public, private, protected, internal. Destructors via ~ClassName() { } adds automatic Dispose() method with inheritance chaining. Static members via static keyword on fields and methods. See assets/language/repl/class_access_test.slc, destructor_comprehensive_test.slc, static_test.slc.

new keyword Create an instance: script class, struct, CLR type or bag

new creates an instance and answers it. The name after it is a script class or struct, a CLR type (new StringBuilder("ab"), which is what the CLR fallback resolves) or one of the bag types (new List<int>()). A CLR CONSTRUCTOR is chosen by the argument TYPES and not only by their count, so new StringBuilder("x") fills the builder and new StringBuilder(10) only reserves. An OBJECT INITIALIZER fills properties and fields in the same statement (new Box() { V = 5 }), which is also the only moment an init or get-only property can be given a value. The constructor and object-initializers entries have the rest.

class Box { public int V; public string Tag { get; set; } } var b = new Box() { V = 5, Tag = "t" }; print(b.V + "/" + b.Tag); // 5/t var sb = new StringBuilder("ab"); sb.Append("c"); print(sb.ToString()); // abc var list = new List<int>(); list.Add(3); print(list.Count); // 1
constructor keyword Special method called when creating a new class or struct instance; static variant runs once per type

Constructors initialize a new instance. They can take parameters, assign fields, and call the base constructor via super(). Multiple constructors with different parameter lists are supported (overloading).

A .NET type's constructor is chosen by the arguments themselves. When several constructors accept the same NUMBER of arguments, the first whose parameters accept the values is used, so new StringBuilder("x") takes StringBuilder(string) and new StringBuilder(10) takes StringBuilder(int).

Alternative syntax: Instead of constructor(params), you can use the class name itself as the constructor name identical to C# syntax. Both forms are equivalent and share the same overload set:

public ClassName(params) { /* initialization */ } // same as constructor(params)

Restriction: Methods cannot share the same name as the class attempting to declare void ClassName() produces a parse error suggesting the ClassName(...) constructor syntax instead.

Static constructors (static constructor()) run automatically once before the first instance is created or the first static member is accessed. They are parameterless, cannot have an access modifier (public, private, etc.), and cannot reference instance fields via this. They run in base-to-derived order across the inheritance hierarchy like C# static constructors.

constructor(params) { /* initialization */ } // instance constructor static constructor() { /* one-time type init */ } // static constructor
// Instance constructors use class name or constructor() class Point { int X; int Y; public Point(int x, int y) { this.X = x; this.Y = y; } public constructor() { this.X = 0; this.Y = 0; } } var p1 = new Point(3, 4); // calls Point(int, int) var p2 = new Point(); // calls constructor() // ClassName() syntax identical to constructor() class NativeLib { private var _lib; public NativeLib(string dllName) { _lib = LoadLibrary(dllName); } ~NativeLib() { if (_lib != null) FreeLibrary(_lib); } } var nl = new NativeLib("user32"); // calls NativeLib(string) constructor // Static constructor runs once, auto-executed before first use class Shape { public string Name; private constructor(string n) { this.Name = n; } static Shape RedCircle; static Shape BlueSquare; static constructor() { Shape.RedCircle = new Shape("circle"); Shape.BlueSquare = new Shape("square"); } } print(Shape.RedCircle.Name); // circle (static ctor ran automatically)

Rules:

  • Instance constructors support access modifiers: public, private (singleton pattern), protected (only via super()), internal
  • Static constructors are always private and cannot have an access modifier or parameters
  • Static constructors cannot use this there is no instance at the time they run
  • The execution order is base class → derived class, matching C# semantics
destructor (~) keyword Finalization method called when a class instance is garbage-collected or disposed

A destructor (also called a finalizer) is declared using the tilde ~ prefix followed by the class name, with no parameters and no return type. It is called automatically by the garbage collector when the object is collected, or explicitly via the built-in Dispose() method.

~ClassName() { // cleanup code }
class Resource { private IntPtr _handle; public bool Disposed; // plain field public Resource(IntPtr h) { _handle = h; } ~Resource() { if (this.Disposed) return; this.Disposed = true; print("cleaned up"); } } var r = new Resource(0); r.Dispose(); // calls destructor → "cleaned up" print(r.Disposed); // true

Important: Destructors are non-deterministic when called by the GC you cannot predict when (or if) the GC will run. For deterministic cleanup, call the built-in .Dispose() method on the instance to invoke the destructor immediately. Calling Dispose() multiple times is safe (the destructor should guard with a flag like Disposed).

Dispose() method Uniform cleanup call real dispose for IDisposable/native resources, safe no-op otherwise

Dispose() is callable on every value (uniform "virtual dispose"). Behavior by receiver kind:

  • Script class instance invokes the class destructor chain (~ClassName) immediately for deterministic cleanup; you never need to define Dispose() yourself.
  • IDisposable .NET types (Mem.Buffer → MemBuffer, LoadLibrary → DynamicLibrary, File.OpenRead → FileStreamReader, Sqlite.Query → SqliteIterator, Process.Start → ProcessHandle, ...) releases the underlying resource.
  • Anything else (int, string, Dictionary, arrays, ...) safe no-op, never throws.
obj.Dispose();
class FileHandle { private IntPtr _handle; public bool Disposed; // plain field constructor(string path) { _handle = CallNative(...); } ~FileHandle() { if (this.Disposed) return; CallNative("CloseHandle", _handle); this.Disposed = true; } } var fh = new FileHandle("data.txt"); // use fh... fh.Dispose(); // deterministic cleanup: destructor runs now // Uniform no-op on non-disposable values var dict = new Dictionary<string, int>(); dict.Dispose(); // safe no-op dict stays usable 42.Dispose(); // safe no-op

For script classes, Dispose() is always available write cleanup code in the destructor and call .Dispose() for deterministic release (file handles, native pointers). The destructor should be idempotent (guard re-entry with a flag like Disposed). For non-disposable values the call is a harmless no-op, so .Dispose() can be used uniformly in cleanup paths.

extension members keyword Declare members on a type you do not own C# 14 `extension` blocks

An extension block declares members on a type the script does not own.
