A member declared public static is called on the extended type itself (List<int>.Create()); a member written without static is called on a value of the extended type ("abcd".Len()), with the receiver bound as this. A block may be written at top level, or inside a static class container: a container class that is not static is refused, as it is in C#, and a top-level block needs no container at all. A block registers for the file that DECLARES it and no other: an extension block declared in an imported module does not reach the importer (the import entry has the measurement), so declare it where it is used. A nested static class is a container too (class Outer { public static class Exts { extension(…) { … } } }): static is accepted wherever a nested class or struct is declared. The extended type is matched by name and arity, never by reflection, so a List<int> value reaches List<T>.

// ── 4. A block over an INTERFACE: it speaks for every value that MATCHES the contract ── interface ISized { int size(); } extension(ISized) { public string label() { return "size " + this.size(); } } class Measured implements ISized { public int size() { return 3; } } // declared the contract class Loose { public int size() { return 5; } } // merely shaped like it struct Pt implements ISized { public int size() { return 7; } } // and a struct var p = new Pt(); print(new Measured().label()); // "size 3" print(new Loose().label()); // "size 5": structural matching reaches the block too print(p.label()); // "size 7" // A STATIC member cannot work this way, and is refused with the reason: // 'ISized' is an INTERFACE, and a static member is reached through a TYPE name: a value never reports an // interface, so that member could never answer. Write it as an INSTANCE member, which a block over 'ISized' // provides to every value that matches the contract.
The target is a TYPE, and a receiver reaches its base classes too. Dispatch matches the receiver's type name, then each base class up the chain NEAREST FIRST, so a Dog value reaches a block on Animal and the most derived block wins. object is the last step of that walk, which makes extension(object) the one spelling that speaks for every value. What is still refused: extension<T>(T), a block cannot extend its own type parameter, and a CONTRACT name (Iterable, RandomAccess, Function, Class, Struct), which is a guard for is/as rather than a type. A STATIC member is reached through the type it was written for, so it is not inherited by a derived type name: the walk applies to values.
extension[<T>] (Target [name]) { public static ReturnType Member(args) => …; public ReturnType Property => …; }
The receiver may be NAMED. extension(string s) gives the block's members a second spelling of the value beside this, as C# 14 does: inside every member of that block s and this are the same object, and a member's own parameter of that name still shadows it. The name is an alias, not a parameter it cannot be reassigned as an argument, and a static member of the block has no receiver, so a body reading it is refused exactly as one reading this is.
// ── 0. A NAMED receiver: `s` beside `this` ────────────────────────────────── extension(string s) { public int Len() => s.Length; // the name is the receiver public int Both() => s.Length + this.Length; // and `this` is the same value } // Anonymous form writes no name at all, and the members below behave identically. extension(string) { public int Len2() => this.Length; } // ── 0b. A PROPERTY: computed, because a block adds no storage ───────────────── extension(string s) { public int Len => s.Length; // read as a property, no parentheses public int Capped { get => s.Length > 3 ? 3 : s.Length; } // get only } extension(string) { public static string Kind => "text"; } // reached through the TYPE print("abcd".Len); // 4 print("abcde".Capped); // 3 print(string.Kind); // text // A setter sees the assigned value as `value`, and writes it wherever the block says: // `public int X { get => …; set { holder = value; } }` is the shape on a receiver you own.
// ── 1. The basic shape: a block at top level, one INSTANCE member ─────────── // Without `static` the member is reached on a VALUE of the extended type, and the // receiver is bound as `this`. The type is matched by name and arity, never reflection. extension(string) { public int Len() => this.Length; public string Twice(string sep) => this + sep + this; } print("abcd".Len()); // 4 called on any string print("ab".Twice("-")); // ab-ab this, then the parameters // ── 2. Both halves, and a class YOU declared ─────────────────────────────── // `public static` is the TYPE half: it is called on the extended type itself. extension(string) { public static string Greet() => "hello"; public static int Measure(string s) => s.Length; } print(string.Greet()); // hello through the TYPE print(string.Measure("abcd")); // 4 class Animal { public string Name = "rex"; } extension(Animal) { public string Shout() => this.Name + "!"; } print((new Animal()).Shout()); // rex! a script class instance is a receiver // ── 3. A GENERIC target: T comes from the receiver ───────────────────────── extension<T>(List<T>) { public int HowMany() => this.Count; } // A list literal is an ARRAY, not a List ToList() is what makes a real List<int>. var xs = [1, 2, 3].ToList(); print(xs.HowMany()); // 3 a List<int> value binds T = int (an int[] would not match) // ── 4. Where a member already exists, the value's OWN member wins ────────── // C# spec 7.6.5.2: an extension never shadows what the type already answers with. extension(string) { public int Trim() => 999; } print(" a ".Trim()); // a String.Trim wins: the extension is declared but never used class Beast { public string Shout() => "own"; } extension(Beast) { public string Shout() => "ext"; } print((new Beast()).Shout()); // own the class's own member wins // ── 5. Advanced: T bound from the CALL SITE, a returned literal typed by the ─ // declared type, and the two halves that must not leak into each other extension<T>(List<T>) { public static List<T> Create() => []; public static T[] None() => []; } print(typeof(List<int>.Create())); // List<int> [] became a List<int> print(typeof(List<string>.None())); // string[] and it follows the call site extension(string) { public static string Bark() => "bark"; } print(string.Bark()); // bark try { print("x".Bark()); } // Method 'Bark' not found on type String -- the value half's refusal catch (var e) { print(e.Message); } // the refusal names the member it looked for

extension is a contextual keyword, exactly like enum: it is a declaration keyword only where a declaration may start, so a variable named extension keeps working.

How "the value wins" is checked. By NAME and ARITY over every overload, plus properties and fields, following the interpreter's comparer, since the check can only block an extension. The first implementation asked GetMethod(name, flags), which throws AmbiguousMatchException as soon as a type has two overloads of that name, as String.Trim does, inside a try with an empty catch, and a swallowed exception reads as "owns no such member". That let an extension shadow String.Trim until crash_extension_members.slc declared the collision and caught it; the check that pretended to guard the rule had declared no block at all.
Instance members. A member written without static is reached through a value of the extended type, "abcd".Len(), a.Shout(), xs.HowMany(), and only when nothing the value owns answers: instance members take priority over extensions (C# spec 7.6.5.2), so " a ".Trim() still calls String.Trim, and a class's own Shout() still wins. Script classes, structs and the built-in types all work as receivers, and a List<int> value reaches extension<T>(List<T>) by name, and its type parameter is bound from the RECEIVER a List<int> value binds T = int and a dictionary binds BOTH of its parameters, a generic class instance the arguments it was instantiated with so the signature and body are concrete on either half.
A member is a METHOD or a PROPERTY, and nothing else. A block declares methods and COMPUTED properties: a field, an operator, an event, a constructor, an indexer or a nested type is refused at declaration, because these are what a block adds from outside a type. A property has no storage here (the block adds none), so its only forms are Name => expr; and Name { get => …; set { … } }, and an auto-accessor (get;) is refused with that reason. What a METHOD MAY be is broad: ordinary parameters, params, its own type parameters (public string Tag<U>(U v), with U inferred at the call), a coroutine body (yield), and it may be written public or private (the modifier is accepted and restricts nothing). A ref or out parameter is ordinary too: the call site names the variable to write back to, exactly as a function's does ("abc".Fill(ref n)). One shape is refused with the reason: this, or the receiver's name when the block gave it one, inside a static member, because a static member has no receiver. A name may be declared once per target and per half: two members with the same name are a duplicate even when their parameters differ (O() next to O(int)), so extension members do not overload, while one static and one instance member of the same name are two members, each reached through its own door (string.Dual() and "x".Dual()). An OPERATOR is `static` and takes BOTH operands (a class operator takes only the other one, because its receiver is the left), and one of them must be the extended type, which is what makes it findable. A PROPERTY and a method may share a name: they are different members, as they are in C#.
What is refused. A duplicate member for the same target is refused at declaration, and a block whose type parameters do not match the target's arity (say extension<T, U>(List<T>)) is refused with the count it expected. The target must be a NAMED type: extension<T>(T), a CONTRACT name (Iterable, RandomAccess, Function, Class, Struct, guards for is/as, not types), and an ARRAY (extension<T>(T[]), extension(string[])) are each refused with the reason and the spelling that works, because a block over any of them would register and then never fire. A static member no block declares reports No static extension member 'X' for 'List<int>', and the two halves do not leak into each other: a public static member is not reachable through a value, and an instance member is not reachable through the type.
A member's NAME follows the interpreter's case flag. Member names are compared with the interpreter's own comparer, like every other member lookup, so in the default (strict) mode Len and len are different members - "abcd".len() is an error there and resolves under .lax. The extended TYPE name follows the interpreter's comparer, like every other name.
Blocks register in the order they run, so a member is declared before its first use, as with any other top-level statement.
Type arguments are BOUND, and a returned literal is typed by them. The block's type parameters are bound from the call site's arguments, matched positionally against the extended type's, so List<int>.Create() instantiates the member with T = int (its parameters and return type become concrete). A member whose body is nothing but a returned list literal then takes its container from that declared type C# collection expressions: List<T> Create() => [] hands back a List<int>, and T[] None() => [] an int[]. Anywhere else the declared type stays descriptive, as it is everywhere in this language: a body computing a string for a declared int still returns the string, and a literal that reaches a var first loses the expectation.
Which engine runs what (VmStats() counts function invocations, not statements). A compiled function that calls an extension member stays on the bytecode VM: the type reference travels as the same TypeInfo the engine already carries for is, and the VM delegates the member lookup to the same registry the tree uses. A public static member's body is compiled as well, as long as its block has no type parameters. An instance member's body runs there as well it is compiled with a method's context and invoked with the receiver as the trailing this local. A generic block's member is instantiated per call site, and that instantiation is compiled too: the concrete clone has no type parameters left, so it runs flat as well. What stays interpreted is what the compiler cannot take: a coroutine member (wrapped the way a coroutine method is, so the interpreter walks it while it yields), and a body using a construct it declines such as a try/catch or a pattern match. The values are identical either way, which is what crash_extension_members.slc asserts.

Against C# 14's own extension blocks. The table is this language beside that spec, so what to expect is a lookup rather than a guess. A cell that differs is spelled out; the last table is what this language has and C# does not.

FeatureC# 14ScriptLangCore
Where a block may sit
At top level, no container✘ a static class is required✔: a top-level block needs no container
Inside a static class✔✔
Inside a class that is not static✘✘
Nested inside another type✘ the class must be non-nested✔: a nested static class is a container
A generic container (static class E<T>)✘ non-generic only✔
The receiver
Unnamed, extension(string)✔ this is the STATIC block✔ and the same block holds instance members too: static is per MEMBER, and the receiver is always this
Named, extension(string s)✔ the receiver becomes a parameter of that name✔ the name is a second spelling of this inside the block
ref / in / ref readonly / scoped receiver✔✘ a parse error
where T : … constraints✔✘ a parse error
Matching a base type or an interface✔ an implicit conversion from the receiver✔: the base CLASS chain, nearest first, with object last. An INTERFACE IS a target: the block speaks for every value that MATCHES the contract, nominal or structural, and a contract name such as Iterable stays refused
What a member may be
Instance method✔✔ this is the receiver
Static method✔✔ reached through the TYPE
Instance property (get/set, no backing field)✔: computed, no backing field✔: computed, Name => expr; or Name { get => …; set { … } }
Static property✔✔: reached through the type
User-defined operator (static), incl. += in an instance block✔✔: both operands, and one of them is the extended type. Compound += comes free, since the language desugars it
params parameters✔✔
The member's own type parameters✔✔ inferred, or written as Tag<long>(9)
Events, fields, constructors, indexers, nested types, finalizers✘ not supported yet✘ refused
Resolution and scope
A real member wins over an extension✔✔
Invoked as if it were on the receiver✔✔
Overloading between candidates✔ normal overload resolution, then the ambiguity is reported✘ one member per name and per half: O() next to O(int) is a duplicate
What carries a blockthe using scope of the enclosing namespacethe FILE that declares it, an imported block does not reach the importer
The old this-parameter syntax✔ kept working✘ a parse error; the block form is the only spelling

And the other direction here, and not in C# 14's spec (each is usable today, and pinned by the extension suites):

/tr>
What this language hasC# 14
A block at top level, with no container at alla non-static class, or none, is refused, the class is required
A NESTED static class as the containerthe class must be non-nested
A GENERIC container classnon-generic only
ONE block holding both halves, chosen per member (static on the member), so Dual() and static Dual() live side by sidethe RECEIVER's shape decides, so that is two blocks, extension(string s) and extension(string)
A member reaching a SIBLING through this (public int Doubled() => this.Len() * 2;)no this in an extension body, the receiver is a parameter
A COROUTINE member (public int Steps() { yield 1; yield 2; })no coroutines in the language
Task.FromResult(value)✅ Yesa Task that is ALREADY complete and carries the value, the pair of Task.CompletedTask, so Task<int> A() => Task.FromResult(42); is a legal forwarder, awaited or read through .Result
RunScriptAsync(source [, concurrent])✅ Yesa nested script run handed back as a Task, so it composes (await, Task.WhenAll) instead of blocking. By default the run is PUMP work, performed on the next pump pass, so nothing runs on another thread; RunScriptAsync(src, true) starts it on a background thread the way Task.Run does. Both accept an optional CancellationToken, told apart from the flag by its TYPE, and a token that has already fired means the run never starts
interface keyword A named contract of method signatures a class declares it implements

An interface declares a contract: a name and the method signatures a class must provide. A class says what it implements with implements, after its optional base class, and the engine checks it when the CLASS DECLARATION EXECUTES, before any instance exists, so a missing member is reported at the declaration rather than at the first call. An interface is checked TWICE, and both readings hold. A class that writes implements is validated when its declaration executes (so a missing member is refused at the declaration), and any value that provides every member a contract demands ALSO matches it structurally, whether or not it wrote implements: implements is a promise you state on purpose, and is asks the shape. An interface is declared at the top level, and a declaration is a statement, so an interface must run before the class that implements it and before the interface that extends it.

interface Name [extends Other[, More]] { ReturnType Member(args); // or ... { default body } }
// ── 1. The basics: a contract, a class, and what `is` says ──────────────────── interface IShape { int area(); // abstract: the class must implement it string describe() { return "a shape of " + this.area(); } // DEFAULT: inherited when the class writes none } class Square implements IShape { public int area() { return 16; } } var s = new Square(); print(s.area()); // 16 print(s.describe()); // "a shape of 16": the default body reached the class's own member print(s is IShape); // True var view = s as IShape; // the SAME value: an interface reference is a checked view, and nothing is wrapped
// ── 2. A property is a NAME plus the shape a member must have ───────────────── interface ISized { int Size { get; set; } // a FIELD or a property of that name answers this int Doubled => this.Size * 2; // a default PROPERTY: served when the value writes none } class Box implements ISized { public int Size; } // the field answers both accessors struct Point implements ISized { public int Size; } // and a struct's field does too var box = new Box(); box.Size = 3; print(box.Doubled); // 6 var p = new Point(); p.Size = 5; print(p.Doubled); // 10 // ── 3. What a refused declaration says ─────────────────────────────────────── interface INamed { string name(); } class Bad implements INamed { } // REFUSED when the class declaration runs, before any value exists: // Class 'Bad' implements 'INamed' but does not implement 'name/0'. // Add 'public <type> name() { }' to 'Bad', or give 'INamed.name/0' a default body. // The ARITY is part of the contract, so `public string name(int x)` is refused with the same words.
// ── 4. Two contracts, one name, two bodies: the contract is named at the CALL SITE ── interface IShapeA { int area(); } interface IContainerA { int area(); } class Both implements IShapeA, IContainerA { int IShapeA.area() { return 10; } // not in the class name table: reached by naming its contract int IContainerA.area() { return 20; } } var b = new Both(); print(IShapeA.area(b)); // 10 print(IContainerA.area(b)); // 20 print(b is IShapeA); // True, and True for IContainerA: one name satisfies both demands // b.area() IS refused, with the spellings to write instead: // 'area/0' is an EXPLICIT implementation on class 'Both', so it is not in the class name table. // Name the contract you mean: IShapeA.area(value) or IContainerA.area(value) // ── 5. Inheritance, an override, and the nearest one winning ────────────────── interface IRoot { int area(); string who() { return "shape"; } } interface IScaled extends IRoot { string IRoot.who() { return "scaled"; } } // an OVERRIDE, named by contract interface IScalable extends IRoot { void scale(int k); } class Grower implements IScaled, IScalable { public int area() { return 1; } public void scale(int k) { } } var g = new Grower(); print(g.who()); // "scaled": the NEAREST override wins print(IRoot.who(g)); // "shape": naming a contract reaches THAT contract's body print(g is IRoot); // True, through the parent // ── 6. A shape is enough, a trait matches everything, a library value is not a shape ── interface IShaped { int area(); } interface IMarker { } // a contract that demands nothing class Loose { public int area() { return 7; } } // never wrote `implements` print(new Loose() is IShaped); // True: it PROVIDES every member the contract demands print(new Loose() is IMarker); // True: a trait matches every class and struct print("abc" is IShaped); // False: a library value's surface belongs to the library // ── 7. A generic contract, and an extension block over a contract ───────────── interface IBox<T> { T get(); } class IntBox implements IBox<int> { public int get() { return 7; } } print(new IntBox() is IBox<int>); // True print(new IntBox() is IBox<string>); // False: the ARGUMENTS are part of the match // `class Bad implements IBox { }` is refused: // 'IBox' is a GENERIC interface, so write its arguments: `IBox<T>`. // A generic contract is matched by DECLARATION only, since a shape cannot witness the arguments. interface IShaped2 { int area(); } extension(IShaped2) { public string tag() { return "area:" + this.area(); } } class Declarer implements IShaped2 { public int area() { return 3; } } class Shaped { public int area() { return 5; } } struct Point2 implements IShaped2 { public int area() { return 7; } } var pt = new Point2(); print(new Declarer().tag()); // "area:3", a class that declared the contract print(new Shaped().tag()); // "area:5", a class that merely matches it print(pt.tag()); // "area:7", and a struct
An interface declares methods and properties. A property is that name plus the SHAPE a member must have, and a body on an accessor is a default; a field or a nested type cannot be a member of one, because an interface owns no storage. A member written as ReturnType Name(args); is abstract and every implementing class must provide it; a member with a body is a DEFAULT, and a class that writes none inherits it. One class method of the right name and arity satisfies two interfaces that demand it, and an implementation in a BASE class satisfies the contract too.
Checked at the declaration, with the member and its arity named. A class that implements a contract without implementing a member is refused where it is declared, and the message names what is missing and what to add: Class 'Bad' implements 'IShape' but does not implement 'area/0'. Add 'public <type> area() { }' to 'Bad', or give 'IShape.area/0' a default body. The arity is part of the contract, so area(int x) does not satisfy area().
An extension target, and one thing it cannot carry. A block over an interface speaks for every value that MATCHES the contract, nominal or structural, so extension(IShape) serves a class that declared it and a struct that merely has the members; a STATIC member in such a block is refused, since a static member is reached through a type name and a value never reports an interface. The built-in names (Iterable, RandomAccess, Function, Class, Struct) are guards for is/as rather than contracts, so declaring an interface with one of those names is refused.
The structural reading: a contract is a shape. x is I is True when the value PROVIDES every member I demands, name and arity, so a class or a struct that never wrote implements still matches, and a match brings the interface's DEFAULT bodies with it: such a value can call a member the interface supplies even though it declared nothing. A member with a default body is not asked for (the interface supplies it), a member of the wrong ARITY does not count, and a contract that demands nothing matches every class and struct, which is how a defaults-only trait is written. Only a script class or struct matches, so "abc" is ISomething is False rather than an error: a library value's surface belongs to the library.
Explicit implementations: the contract is named at the call site. A member can be qualified by the interface it serves, int IShape.area() { ... }. Dispatch is by name, so the receiver's type cannot differ per contract: such a member is deliberately NOT in the class's name table, and it is reached by naming the contract, with the value as the first argument, IShape.area(value). That is what lets two contracts demand one name with two different bodies, and a bare call is refused with the spellings to write: 'area/0' is an EXPLICIT implementation on class 'Both', so it is not in the class name table. Name the contract you mean: IShape.area(value) or IContainer.area(value). An explicit member satisfies exactly the contract it names and never another one, a member the value itself owns is still called on the value, and a DEFAULT body running inside a contract composes through that same contract, so this.area() inside IShape.describe reaches the IShape implementation. A struct may carry explicit members the same way.
Generic contracts are TEMPLATES, and one is matched by DECLARATION. interface IBox<T> declares one; a class instantiates it as implements IBox<int>, and the closed form is what the engine records and answers is IBox<int> for, so the ARGUMENTS are part of the match: IBox<int> and IBox<string> are two different contracts, and a bare IBox is refused with the recipe write its arguments: `IBox<T>`. A generic contract is matched by DECLARATION only, because a shape cannot witness which arguments were written, so a value that merely has the members does not match one. An interface may extend an instantiated contract (interface ID extends IBase<int>). A member is still pinned by NAME and ARITY, as everywhere else in a contract, so the argument types are not checked. Not here: variance, and constraints, since this engine parses no where clause anywhere yet.
What `is` and `as` mean here. x is I is True when the class of x, or one it inherits from, declares I (or an interface that extends it), and False for null. x as I is the same value when that holds and null otherwise: an interface reference is a checked view, so nothing is copied and nothing is wrapped.

Against the interface rules of C#. The table is this language beside that spec, so what to expect is a lookup rather than a guess. A cell that differs is spelled out, and a third mark means ALLOWED BY A DIFFERENT RULE, which the cell states. Every row below was measured on the shipped engine, and each refusal quotes the message it produces.

FeatureC#ScriptLangCore
What an interface member may be
An abstract method✔✔ int area();
A method with a body (a default)✔ C# 8✔ int describe() { ... }, served where nothing else answers
A property (abstract or with a body)✔✔ a property is a NAME plus the SHAPE a member must have: int Area { get; } demands a readable member, { get; set; } a readable and writable one, satisfied by a field or by a property on the implementing type, and a body (Area => expr; or { get => ...; }) makes it a DEFAULT
An indexer✔✘ Expected '(' after the name of a method, or '=>' or '{' for a property: an interface declares methods and properties, and a member may carry a DEFAULT body
An event✔✘ Expected a method or a property in the interface body. An interface declares METHODS and PROPERTIES, so a field or a nested type cannot be a member of one, and a property is written with accessors (`{ get; }`) rather than as a field
A static member (field, method, property)✔ C# 8✘ refused by the same rule as an event: Expected a method or a property in the interface body, so static is not a modifier an interface member takes
static abstract / static virtual, operators✔ C# 11✘ refused at the same place (Expected a method or a property in the interface body): it needs static abstract members and constraints, and constraints are missing engine-wide
A generic interface (interface I<T>)✔✔ a contract is a TEMPLATE: interface I<T> declares it, implements I<int> instantiates it, and is I<int> asks for it. A SCRIPT contract is matched by DECLARATION only, since a shape cannot witness the arguments, while a CLR one is matched by the arguments the value carries; a generic written WITHOUT them is refused with the fix in the message, and an unknown argument is refused naming the name (see the CLR interfaces entry)
Variance on a type parameter (in / out)✔✘ variance is not implemented, and the parse says so: Expect '>' after the interface's type parameters. (the in is then read as an identifier, which also draws the reserved-keyword warning)
A where T : ... constraint✔✘ constraints are missing engine-wide: no where clause is parsed anywhere, and the clause is refused where it would sit (Expect '{' before the interface body.)
An access modifier (public, private, protected, internal)✔ C# 8, private helpers are the point✘ a member is written bare, and a modifier is refused as a member that is neither a method nor a property (Expected a method or a property in the interface body); the ACCESS of the implementing member uses this language's own rules
virtual, abstract, sealed, override on a member✔✘ refused at the member (Expected '(' after the name of a method, or '=>' or '{' for a property): a default is always virtual (a class member always wins) and there is no sealed to stop it
A nested type (class, struct, enum, delegate)✔ C# 8✘ Expected a method or a property in the interface body, the refusal that names what an interface may declare
An instance field, constructor, finalizer or instance operator✘ C# rejects these too✘ An interface declares METHODS and PROPERTIES, so a field or a nested type cannot be a member of one, and a property is written with accessors (`{ get; }`) rather than as a field; a constructor is refused earlier, at Expect the interface member's name.
An abstract auto-property (int Area { get; set; })✔✔ it PARSES, and it is not storage here: a property is a NAME plus the SHAPE a member must have, so { get; set; } demands a readable and writable member (row 3 above)
Inheritance and dispatch
Multiple interface inheritance (interface A : B, C)✔✔ interface IC extends IA, IB: every parent's members are required, and is answers for each
A parent default is inherited by an implementer✔✔ a class implementing only the child answers the parent's default
One name demanded by two contracts, one implementation✔✔ one member of the right name and arity satisfies both
An EXPLICIT implementation (void IFoo.Bar())✔✔ grounded, and spelled at the CALL SITE: int IShape.area() { ... } is reached as IShape.area(value)
...and the bare name of one✔ it is hidden⚠ it is not in the class name table, and asking for it says which contract to write: 'M/0' is an EXPLICIT implementation on class 'OnlyExpl', so it is not in the class name table. Name the contract you mean: IX.M(value) (two contracts are both listed). A class that ALSO has an ordinary member of that name answers the ordinary one by the bare name, which is C#'s own rule
A derived interface OVERRIDES a parent default with a body (void IBase.M() { })✔ C# 8, the explicit form✔ a derived interface writes the override NAMED BY ITS CONTRACT (string IBase.M() { ... }), the nearest override wins, a re-declaration of the member makes it abstract again, and naming a contract reaches that contract's own body
Two unrelated interfaces with a default for ONE member (a diamond)✘ an error unless the class overrides it✔ refused LOUDLY, the same rule as C#, and the message names both the member and every contract to write: 'Who/0' has a DEFAULT in both 'ID1' and 'ID2', and 'NoAnswer' does not implement it. Add the member to its own type, or name the contract you mean: ID1.Who(value) or ID2.Who(value)
A default is visible on the VALUE by its bare name✘ C# 8 requires ((IFoo)obj).M()⚠ served by the same miss path a member goes through, so obj.describe() works: that is what a duck-typed language means
Who implements, and how it is reached
A class declares what it implements✔ nominal✔ implements, validated when the CLASS DECLARATION runs, naming the member, its arity and the recipe
A STRUCT as an implementer✔ C# 13✔ a struct DECLARES implements, validated when its declaration executes, and it matches a contract structurally as well
is, a cast, and a call through the interface✔✔ is and a cast are one membership test, and a cast yields the SAME value (no wrapper). A call through the contract, IFoo.M(obj), reaches an EXPLICITLY implemented member ONLY; for a member the value itself owns the bare name is the way, and naming the contract says so: 'IA' has no member 'M/0' that 'Two' implements EXPLICITLY. Write `IA.M(value, ...)` to reach an explicit implementation, and `value.M(...)` for a member the value itself owns
An extension member on an interface✔ C# 14✔ a block over an interface speaks for every value that MATCHES it, nominal or structural, and a STATIC member in one is refused

What this language has and C# does not. Two rules, both measured, and both are the same property seen twice: a declared contract is also asked of a value as a SHAPE.

FeatureC#ScriptLangCore
A value matches a contract WITHOUT declaring it✘ C# is nominal✔ a class or struct that provides every member matches, and a match brings the interface defaults with it
A contract that demands nothing (a trait)✘ a marker interface still has to be declared✔ it matches every class and struct, which is how a defaults-only trait is written
implements keyword The interfaces a class or struct fulfils

implements lists the interfaces a class or struct fulfils, with several separated by commas: class Dog implements IAnimal, INamed. It is a CONTEXTUAL word, read as a clause only right after the class's optional extends parent, so a field or a method named implements is unaffected. A member the interface declares and the type does not is refused where the type is declared, and an instance satisfies the interface afterwards: d is INamed answers true, which is how a collection of one interface type can hold several implementations. The interface entry has the default-body and property rules.

interface INamed { string Name(); } class Dog implements INamed { public string Name() { return "Rex"; } } var d = new Dog(); print(d.Name() + " is INamed: " + (d is INamed)); // Rex is INamed: True
class keyword Reference type with fields, methods, constructors, inheritance

Supports single inheritance, access modifiers, nested classes, operator overloading, and events. Classes can also be generic: class Box<T> { ... }.

class Name extends Base { // fields, methods, constructors }
class Point { public int X; public int Y; constructor(int x, int y) { this.X = x; this.Y = y; } public int Sum() { return this.X + this.Y; } } var p = new Point(3, 4); print(p.Sum()); // 7 // Nested class private inner class accessed by outer class method class WithPrivateInner { private class PrivateInner { public static string Hidden = "secret"; } public static string GetSecret() { return PrivateInner.Hidden; } } print(WithPrivateInner.GetSecret()); // "secret" // Nested struct inside a class class Outer { public struct InnerPoint { public int X; public int Y; } public InnerPoint Pos; } var o = new Outer(); print(o.Pos.X); // 0 (default)

See the static entry for details on static members, and the generics entry for type parameter syntax.

operator keyword Declare an operator overload on a type

operator declares an overload as an ordinary method whose name is the token itself, and because the LEFT operand is this it declares EXACTLY ONE parameter: public Pt operator +(Pt other) adds this and other. The tokens are + - * / % < > <= >= == !=. A class or struct that declares one is used like a built-in on both engines, and a token the type does NOT declare is the engine's own refusal (Operator '+' is not defined for 'Bare') rather than a silent numeric answer. The class and struct entries show where the body sits among the other members.

class Pt { public int X; public Pt operator +(Pt other) { var r = new Pt(); r.X = this.X + other.X; return r; } } var p = new Pt(); p.X = 2; var q = new Pt(); q.X = 3; print((p + q).X); // 5
record keyword Reference type with structural (value) equality == compares fields, not references

A record is declared like a class but with structural value equality: two record instances are == when all their fields are equal (compared recursively), regardless of whether they are the same object. Plain classes keep reference equality (== is identity).

record Point { public int x; public int y; }
record Point { public int x; public int y; } var p1 = new Point(); p1.x = 1; p1.y = 2; var p2 = new Point(); p2.x = 1; p2.y = 2; print(p1 == p2); // True (structural equality) // Nested records compare recursively record Inner { public int v; } record Outer { public Inner inner; public string tag; } // Records support constructors like classes record Person { public string name; public Person(string n) { name = n; } }
Structural equality applies to both the tree interpreter and the bytecode VM. Records work with ==/!=; enums and null semantics follow the same value-aware equality used by match patterns.
enum keyword Named integer constants define a set of related values

Enums define a set of named integer constants. Members auto-increment from the previous explicit value (starting at 0). Values can be explicitly assigned with = expr. Enums are exposed as static fields on a synthetic class, so members are accessed via the enum name.

enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } enum Http { OK = 200, NotFound = 404 }
// Access members via the enum name print(Color.Red); // 0 print(Color.Blue); // 2 // Explicit values print(Http.OK); // 200 // Auto-increment after explicit value enum Mixed { A, B = 10, C } print(Mixed.A); // 0 print(Mixed.B); // 10 print(Mixed.C); // 11 // In switch/match var c = Color.Blue match { 0 => "red", 1 => "green", 2 => "blue", _ => "?" };
Enums can be declared at the top level. Use public to export them from modules. Access modifiers: public, internal, private (default). The underlying type is always long. The underlying type is long, and a member carries its enum as well: typeof(Color.Red) is "Color", Color.Red is Color and Color.Red is Enum are both true, and Json.Serialize(Color.Red) is 0 - while Color.Red is long stays true and arithmetic, comparison and match keep working on that underlying value. The enum's own name is matched as any script-declared type name is, exactly: Color.Red is color is an unknown-type error (in .lax too), while a CLR type name is written as C# spells it (DateTime): the lowercase forms were retired, and only .lax accepts another case. That is how the registry is keyed. Json.Serialize(Color) serializes an enum type as a JSON object: {"Red":0,"Green":1,"Blue":2}.
readonly keyword Prevents mutation of a struct after construction readonly struct

The readonly modifier on a struct prevents field mutation after the constructor completes. Fields can only be set inside a constructor or via a with expression (which bypasses the restriction during the non-destructive copy). Accessing a readonly struct's field for mutation throws an AccessViolation error.

readonly struct Point { public int x; public int y; public Point(int vx, int vy) { this.x = vx; this.y = vy; } }
// Constructor can set readonly fields var p = new Point(1, 2); // Mutation outside constructor is rejected // p.x = 10; // AccessViolation // with expression bypasses readonly restriction var p2 = p with { x = 99 };
struct keyword Value type with fields, methods, and operator overloads

Structs are value types assigned and passed by value (copy). Supports fields, methods, constructors, and operator overloads (same syntax as classes: Point operator +(Point other)).

struct Name { /* fields, methods, operators */ }
struct Rect { public int W; public int H; } var r = new Rect(10, 20); print(r.W); // 10 // Operator overload example struct Point { public int X; public int Y; public Point operator +(Point other) { return new Point(this.X + other.X, this.Y + other.Y); } }

Callables take the same argument forms as a class. A struct constructor and a struct method accept defaults, a params tail, and ref/out parameters, under the same keyword rules described for ref and out. A bare field name inside a struct method or constructor writes that instance field, exactly as it does inside a class method.

auto-properties keyword Declare fields with automatic get/set/init accessors via { get; set; } syntax

Auto-properties combine a field declaration with automatic accessor methods. The compiler generates a hidden backing field (<Name>k__BackingField) and redirects reads/writes through the accessors. Supported on both classes and structs.

Type Name { get; set; } // public read/write Type Name { get; private set; } // public read, private write Type Name { get; init; } // public read, init-only write
// Full public read/write class Person { public string Name { get; set; } public int Age { get; set; } constructor(string n, int a) { this.Name = n; this.Age = a; } } var p = new Person("Alice", 30); print(p.Name); // Alice p.Age = 31; // public set // Read public, write private class Counter { public int Value { get; private set; } constructor(int v) { this.Value = v; } public void Increment() { this.Value = this.Value + 1; } } var c = new Counter(10); print(c.Value); // 10 (public get) // c.Value = 5; // runtime error (private set) c.Increment(); print(c.Value); // 11 (class method can write) // Init-only immutable after construction class Config { public string Name { get; init; } public int Version { get; init; } constructor(string n, int v) { this.Name = n; this.Version = v; } } var cfg = new Config("app", 1); // cfg.Name = "other"; // runtime error: init-only

Accessor modifiers: Each accessor can optionally carry its own access modifier (public, private, protected, internal). The getter must be at least as accessible as the property itself. Example: public int Id { get; private set; }.

Init vs set: init is a write-once accessor that can only be called during the initialization phase (inside a constructor or an object initializer). After construction, any attempt to write to an init-only property throws AccessViolation. Structs also support init with the same guard.

Regular fields vs properties: Both can coexist in the same class/struct. Properties expose a backing field through accessor syntax; regular fields (like public int X;) are direct storage with no accessor layer.

get / set / init keyword The three property accessors, and who may write

A property's accessors say who may read and who may write: { get; set; } is read-write from anywhere, { get; private set; } is read from outside and written inside the class (a constructor, a method), { get; init; } is written only while the instance is being built (an object initializer or a constructor) and a later write is refused as init-only, and { get; } has no setter at all, so the object initializer is the only moment it takes a value and every later write is refused as no setter. A property here is an AUTO-property: a body is not expressible, so a computed value is a method (the auto-properties entry has that rule and the access checks).

class Settings { public int Volume { get; set; } public int Max { get; private set; } public string Name { get; init; } public int Id { get; } public constructor() { Max = 100; } } var s = new Settings() { Volume = 3, Name = "main", Id = 7 }; print(s.Volume + "/" + s.Max + "/" + s.Name + "/" + s.Id); // 3/100/main/7 // s.Name = "late"; refuses: init-only, outside initialization // s.Id = 9; refuses: the property has no setter
object initializers keyword Initialize properties/fields at creation time via new Type { Prop = val }

Object initializers allow setting properties and fields immediately after construction using { Prop = val, ... } syntax. They work with both classes and structs, and can be combined with constructor arguments. The initialization phase sets IsInInitPhase = true so that init-only properties can be assigned.

new Type { Prop1 = val1, Prop2 = val2 } new Type(ctorArgs) { Prop = val }
// Basic object initializer no constructor args class Point { public int X { get; set; } public int Y { get; set; } } var p = new Point { X = 3, Y = 4 }; print(p.X); // 3 // Constructor args + object initializer class Person { public string Name { get; set; } public int Age { get; set; } constructor(string name) { this.Name = name; } } var p2 = new Person("Alice") { Age = 30 }; print(p2.Name + " is " + p2.Age); // Alice is 30 // Init-only property via object initializer class Config { public string Key { get; init; } } var cfg = new Config { Key = "abc" }; // init allowed during init phase // cfg.Key = "xyz"; // runtime error (outside init phase) // Struct with object initializer struct Coord { public int X; public int Y; } var c = new Coord { X = 10, Y = 20 }; print(c.X); // 10 // Explicit struct/class keyword (sugar symmetric to new struct / new class) var s = new struct Coord { X = 1, Y = 2 }; var o = new class Point(3, 4) { X = 5 };

Object initializers set IsInInitPhase = true on the instance during initialization, which allows init-only properties to be assigned. After the initializer block completes, the flag is reset to false and any further write to an init property is rejected. Regular fields, public setters, and constructor arguments are all supported in the same initializer block.

this keyword Reference to the current class/struct instance

Used inside instance methods and constructors to access fields and methods of the current object.

this.fieldName
class Person { string Name; constructor(string name) { this.Name = name; } }
super keyword Call base class constructor or access base members

For constructor calls: super(args) must be the first statement in the derived constructor. For member access: super.method().

super(args); super.method(args);
class Base { int X; constructor(int x) { this.X = x; } } class Derived extends Base { int Y; constructor(int x, int y) { super(x); this.Y = y; } }
base keyword Access base class members (similar to super)

Used to access methods and fields of the base class from within a derived class.

base.method(args);
class Parent { string Greet() { return "Hello"; } } class Child extends Parent { string Greet() { return base.Greet() + " world"; } } print(new Child().Greet()); // Result: Hello world
public keyword Accessible from anywhere

Public members are accessible from any code inside the class, from derived classes, from outside code in the same file, and from importing modules.

// Public means accessible everywhere class Visible { public int X; // field: anyone can read/write public int GetX() { return this.X; } // method: anyone can call } var v = new Visible(); v.X = 42; // allowed (public field) print(v.GetX()); // allowed (public method) → 42
Top-level class declarations also support public used to export the class from a module so it's visible to import statements. Default is private for top-level declarations.
private keyword Accessible only within the declaring class

Private members are only accessible from within the declaring class itself. Not visible to derived classes, outside code, or importing modules.

// Private field and method only visible inside the class class Bank { private int _balance; public void Deposit(int n) { _balance = _balance + n; } public int GetBalance() { return _balance; } } var b = new Bank(); // b._balance = 100; // runtime error private b.Deposit(100); print(b.GetBalance()); // 100 via public method
// Private nested class only the outer class can reference it class Outer { private class Inner { public static string Msg = "visible inside"; } public static string Read() { return Inner.Msg; } } // Outer.Inner.Msg runtime error (private nested class) print(Outer.Read()); // "visible inside" outer class can access
Default access level for class/struct members and nested types is private. Private constructors enable the singleton pattern.
protected keyword Accessible within the class and its derived classes

Protected members are accessible from the declaring class and from any derived class. Not visible to unrelated code or global scope.

// Protected member visible in base and derived classes class Animal { protected string Name; protected string GetLabel() { return "Animal: " + this.Name; } } class Dog extends Animal { public void SetName(string n) { this.Name = n; } // allowed (protected) public string GetDogLabel() { return this.GetLabel(); } // allowed (protected) } // Animal.Name runtime error (protected from global code) var d = new Dog(); d.SetName("Rex"); print(d.GetDogLabel()); // "Animal: Rex"
internal keyword Accessible within the same module (cross-file)

Internal members are accessible anywhere within the same module/scope including across files loaded via import. Not visible to code outside the module. Useful for sharing state between files of a multi-file script without making it fully public.

// In module_a.slc: internal int sharedCounter = 0; public void Inc() { sharedCounter = sharedCounter + 1; } // In main.slc (after import "./module_a"): // Inc(); sharedCounter = 5; // both accessible because module imported // But code from another top-level file can't see sharedCounter
internal is the default access for top-level declarations (functions, classes, variables) when no modifier is specified and the file is part of a module (import scenario). Standalone scripts treat internal the same as public since there's only one scope.
static keyword Shared member across all instances of a class; static constructors for one-time type initialization

Static fields and methods belong to the class itself, not to any instance. Accessed via the class name: Config.AppName = "MyApp"; or Config.GetApp(). The static keyword can appear before or after the access modifier: public static int Count() and static public int Count() are both accepted.

Static constructors (static constructor() { }) run automatically once before any instance is created or any static member is accessed. They are parameterless, cannot have an access modifier, and cannot reference this. Execution follows base-to-derived order.

class Config { static string AppName; static string GetApp() { return Config.AppName; } static constructor() { Config.AppName = "MyApp"; } // runs once } print(Config.GetApp()); // MyApp
// Static method with explicit public modifier class Counter { static int Total; constructor() { Counter.Total = Counter.Total + 1; } public static int GetCount() { return Counter.Total; } } var a = new Counter(); var b = new Counter(); print(Counter.GetCount()); // 2 (shared across instances) // C#-style factory pattern with static constructor class Shape { public string Name; private constructor(string n) { this.Name = n; } static Shape RedCircle; static Shape BlueSquare; static constructor() { Shape.RedCircle = new Shape("circle"); Shape.BlueSquare = new Shape("square"); } } print(Shape.RedCircle.Name); // circle (static ctor ran before access) // Singleton pattern with lazy initialization and private constructor class Singleton { public string Name; private static Singleton _instance; private constructor(string n) { this.Name = n; } public static Singleton GetInstance(string n) { if (Singleton._instance == null) Singleton._instance = new Singleton(n); return Singleton._instance; } } var s1 = Singleton.GetInstance("first"); var s2 = Singleton.GetInstance("second"); print(s1 == s2); // true same instance print(s1.Name); // "first" second call ignored

Rules:

  • Static members are accessed via the class name, not an instance variable
  • Static methods can only access static fields and other static methods directly
  • Static constructors run automatically once before first instance creation or first static member access
  • Static constructors are parameterless and cannot have access modifiers
  • Static constructors cannot use this there's no instance at that point
  • Base class static constructors run before derived class ones
  • Generic classes have per-concrete-type statics: Tracker<int>.Count and Tracker<string>.Count are independent
  • The class name resolves to the open generic inside the class body, so Tracker.Count works in class Tracker<T>
  • Singleton pattern: Combine private constructor with a private static field and a public static GetInstance() method. Static fields initially null for reference types are correctly resolved.

Static-only classes & structs:

  • The language does not support a static class modifier. Any class or struct can contain static members alongside instance members. A class with only static members can still be instantiated no compile-time guard exists.
  • Structs support static fields and static methods: static int Add(int a, int b) { ... } inside a struct body is valid. Access them via the struct name: Calc.Add(3, 4).
  • Nested class hierarchies where every level only contains static members work via dotted path access: Outer.Inner.InnerName. No static keyword is needed on nested classes.
  • Static field inheritance: Reading an inherited static field (e.g., Dog.Kingdom where Kingdom is declared on Animal) walks the parent chain. Writing an inherited static field via the derived class name writes to the declaring class's field (the same shared value).
Generic Methods (<T>) language feature Type parameters on class methods

Class methods can declare type parameters with <T> syntax. There is no hard limit the parser accepts any number of comma-separated type parameters. The interpreter supports up to 16 type parameters (matching the AotInvoker limit). Type arguments are specified explicitly at the call site.

class Wrapper { V Query<T, V>(string sql) { return Sqlite.Query<T, V>(_sqlite, _path, sql); } } var list = db.Query<Person, List<Person>>("SELECT * FROM people");

Type arguments propagate through nested method calls via AST substitution. When Query<T> calls Sqlite.Query<T>(...), T is replaced with the concrete type.

A .NET generic method is closed the same way: Array.Empty<int>() instantiates Empty<int> instead of reporting the definition as unusable, and the name resolves exactly as it does for is so Array.Empty<ComNode>() is ComNode[], not object[]. A name the engine does not know is refused. Compiled bodies carry the type arguments in the bytecode, so these calls work inside a function too, not only at the top level.

On the NativeAOT build the runtime can only instantiate a generic method whose instantiation the AOT compiler already generated. A reference type (a class, string) always works; for a value type the engine ROOTS the ones a script plausibly asks for int, long, double, bool, DateTime, TimeSpan, Guid so Array.Empty<DateTime>() does close on the shipping build. A value type outside that list (Array.Empty<decimal>()) is reported by name instead of running, and never substituted. The JIT build has every instantiation.

▼ Error Handling

try/catch/finally keyword Structured exception handling

Catches both script exceptions and .NET runtime exceptions. The finally block always runs.

A refusal names the statement it happened in, whether that statement ran compiled or on the tree walker, so a message reads the same either way: ex.Message ends with (at line L, column C), where the column is the statement's own, not the column of the operator or member that failed. The message text itself names what failed (Division by zero, Method 'Nope' not found on type string with 0 argument(s)).

A thrown value is always an ErrorInfo, whatever was thrown, so a typed clause is matched against that wrapper rather than against the value: catch (int ex) never matches a thrown 42, while catch (ErrorInfo ex) and catch (var ex) match everything. Read the value in ex.Message. Two spellings therefore catch everything (catch (var ex) and catch { }, and so does catch (ErrorInfo ex)), and a clause written after any of them can never run: that is a compile error here rather than a silent dead arm.

try { /* code */ } catch (var ex) { /* handle */ } finally { /* cleanup */ }
try { var z = 0; var crash = 10 / z; } catch (var ex) { print("caught: " + ex.Message); // Result: caught: Division by zero }
// ⚡ Super power: finally runs before return int testFinallyReturn() { try { return 42; } finally { print("Finally runs before return, value is: " + return.Value); } } print(testFinallyReturn()); // "Finally runs before return, value is: 42" then "42"
throw keyword Throw a script exception

Throws a ScriptException with the given message, caught by the nearest try/catch.

throw "error message";
try { throw "something went wrong"; } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); // Result: something went wrong }
ErrorInfo type Error information object caught by catch

When a catch block catches an error, the caught value is an ErrorInfo value. It provides programmatic access to the error code and message. Can be serialized via Json.Serialize().

Properties

.MessageThe error message string. For a throw "msg", this is the thrown string. For a .NET exception, the .Message property of the original exception.
.CodeErrorCode enum value programmatic category of the error (Success, InvalidOperation, IOError, etc.).
.FramesThe script frames the error unwound through, innermost first, at most 16. Each reads Inner [L12:C5]: the function, then the position it was entered at (an engine-invoked body such as a Com.Run callback has no script call site, so its frame carries the declaration's position). Empty for an error raised at the top level.
.ToString()Returns the Message string.

Example

try { throw "my custom error"; } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); // "my custom error" print(ex.Code); // InvalidOperation print(Json.Serialize(ex)); // {"Code":"InvalidOperation","Message":"my custom error"} }
You can match on ex.Code to differentiate error types programmatically: if (ex.Code == ErrorCode.IOError). The ErrorCode enum includes: Success, InvalidOperation, IOError, AccessViolation, DivideByZero, Overflow, SyntaxError, and others.

▼ Operators

and / or / not keyword Pattern combinators, not boolean operators

and, or and not combine PATTERNS: x is int and > 3 is one pattern that needs both sides, x is string or int matches either, and not negates a pattern (x is not string) or makes the null check is not null. They are keywords, so they are also unusable as names. For boolean LOGIC write &&, || and !: the words do not stand in for those, which surprises a reader arriving from Python or VB. The is and match entries have the pattern rules.

object o = 7; print(o is int and > 5); // True print(o is string or int); // True print(o is not string); // True print(o is not null); // True print(true && false); // False, the BOOLEAN operator
is keyword Type check operator

Returns true if the value is of the specified type. Supports all primitive types (int, long, short, ushort, byte, sbyte, uint, ulong, float, double, decimal, bool, char, string), named C# types (Array, List, IScriptList, IScriptDictionary), delegates, and script classes.

value is TypeName
if (x is int) { print("x is an int"); } if (x is string) { print("x is a string"); } if (fn is Func<int,int>) { print("fn is a Func"); } if (new List<int>() is List) { print("a typed list is a List"); } if (new int[3] is Array) { print("array is Array"); }

Patterns after is the same grammar switch uses: constants (x is 2), relational (x is > 5), is not <pattern>, logical (x is int and > 3), property (p is { Name: "bob" }) and list (a is [1, ..]) patterns, plus types (x is int, x is int n) and tuple patterns. List and tuple patterns also accept strings, whose elements are chars ("abc" is ['a', ..]), and a .. var rest capture follows the subject kind (a List for a list, char[] for a string, an array for arrays/tuples). Names bind only in an if/while true branch.

Patterns run on the bytecode VM, not only on the tree walker, so a handler or a parser that tests a shape keeps the fast path: the emitters are the ones a switch arm already uses, which is why the two spellings cannot disagree. Measured on a body using all of them: VM: 9 (100.0%) | Tree: 0. Two rules a reader needs: a pattern that BINDS names (other than the inline x is int n form, which binds anywhere) is allowed only in an if/while/for condition and is refused by name elsewhere (Pattern variable 'n' is only allowed in if/while conditions.), and the same body also runs correctly in a --no-source bundle, because a pattern that needs the engine's matcher travels as its own source text.

Type-qualified property patterns test a type AND its members in one pattern, which is what a factory or a dispatcher wants: o is Shape { Sides: 4 }, and negated, o is not Shape { Sides: 3 }. It is a type test combined with a property test, so it reports false for a different class that happens to hold the same member. Combinators compose with everything above, so v is null or int, s is not null and not string and n is int and > 10 and < 100 all read the way &&/|| would, with one rule from C#: not binds tighter than and/or, so s is not null and not string is (not null) and (not string). The same grammar is the match/switch arm grammar, so o match { Shape { Sides: 4 } => "four", _ => "?" } works and means the same thing.

Positional tuple patterns match a tuple, array or list element by element:

value is ("bird", 10, false)
if (v is ("bird", 10, false)) { print("bird, 10, false"); } if (p is (int x, int y, _)) { print(x + "," + y); } // literals compare with engine equality (10 matches 10.0); typed elements are exact // (use string?/int? to match null); arrays/lists match positionally; arity or // non-positional subjects are simply false. Named variables bind only inside the // if/while true branch.

Every type name is / as accepts, grouped, with what each one matches and what typeof() reports for a matching value. Matching is case-sensitive, C#-strict: a name is accepted exactly as the table spells it, so x is DateTime works and x is datetime is reported as an unknown type. Only the REPL's .lax mode matches any case. A written type's shape and arguments are part of the match: x is int[] is true for an int[] and false for a string; xs is List<int> is false for a list of strings; and as answers exactly as is does. is function, and the engine's internal storage name for a callable, remain runtime errors, so the callable contract is Function.

Name(s) in is / asMatchestypeof() returns
Primitives and their .NET aliases numeric widening applies both ways
string / Stringa string"string"
char / Chara char"char"
bool / Booleana bool"bool"
int / Int32an int, or a long (widening)"int" / "long"
long / Int64a long, or an int (widening)"long" / "int"
byte / Bytea byte, or a long / int"byte"
sbyte / SBytean sbyte, or a long / int"sbyte"
short / Int16a short, or a long / int"short"
ushort / UInt16a ushort, or a long / int"ushort"
uint / UInt32a uint, or a long"uint"
ulong / UInt64a ulong, or a long"ulong"
float / Singlea float, or a double"float"
double / Doublea double, or a float"double"
decimal / Decimala decimal"decimal"
object / Objectanything always trueany name
DateTimea DateTime"DateTime"
DateTimeOffseta DateTimeOffset"DateTimeOffset"
TimeSpana TimeSpan"TimeSpan"
Enumany .NET enum value (ConsoleColor.Red, TaskStatus.Completed)the enum's own name
Collections and their interfaces
Lista script list: new List<int>(), a .ToList(), a comprehension"List" / "List<int>"
Dictionarya script dictionary: a dict literal or a parsed JSON object"Dictionary" / "Dictionary<string, int>"
IDictionarya raw .NET dictionary only a script dict is a Dictionary, so d is IDictionary is False"Dictionary"
HashSeta script set"HashSet" / "HashSet<int>"
Arrayany native array [1,2,3], new int[3], new object[2]"int[]" / "object[]"
Tuplea tuple"Tuple"
KeyValuePairone pair from iterating a dictionary"KeyValuePair"
LazyDeserializedLista list produced by a typed Json.Deserializethe declaration the read was asked for, List<int> or string[] or IList
OrderedEnumerablea LINQ OrderBy / ThenBy result"OrderedEnumerable"
ReplayableEnumerableReplayable() / Memoize()"ReplayableEnumerable"
LazyEnumerableIterable.Map / Filter / Zip / Append / Range"LazyEnumerable"
Contracts a guard, not a name typeof() gives up
Iterablearrays, lists, tuples, dicts, HashSets, LINQ results, generators, stringsthe concrete name (int[], List<int>…)
RandomAccessarrays, lists, tuples, strings indexable and re-enumerablethe concrete name
Functionany callable: lambda, named function, bound method, combined delegate, native"Function"
Class / ClassInstance / class instancea class or record instancethe declared class name, e.g. "Animal"
Struct / StructInstance / struct instancea struct instancethe declared struct name, e.g. "Pt"
ClassInfoa class / record / struct / enum name used as a value, or a generic type reference such as Dictionary<string, object>the declared name ("Animal", "Pt", "Color"), or the whole spelling ("List<int>")
Delegate / Func / Action / Predicatea .NET delegate not a script lambda (that is Function)the delegate's own type name
Resultwhat RunScript() returns"Result"
ErrorInfoa caught error"ErrorInfo"
Coroutinea coroutine / generator"Coroutine"
EventInfo / eventan event"EventInfo"
CombinedDelegate / delegatethe result of f1 + f2"CombinedDelegate"

Namespacea namespace object: Json, Iterable, the Win32 namespace…"Namespace"
Nativea native such as print"Native"

WeakRefa weak reference"WeakRef"

CronExpressiona parsed cron schedule"CronExpression"

Runtime types the interpreter hands out
Metaa loaded bytecode bundle's metadata"Meta"
DynamicLibrarya LoadLibrary handle"DynamicLibrary"
FileStreamReader / FileStreamWriterstream wrappersthe same names
MessageInfo / CipherInfoa parsed message / a cipher handlethe same names
SqliteIterator / SqliteMappingIterator / SqliteRowdatabase iteration and a mapped rowthe same names
Nativea resolved native entry point"Native"
TaskTask.Run / Task.Delay"Task"
ScheduledTaskwhat Scheduler.Add / Enqueue / Schedule returns"ScheduledTask"
SleepRequest / EventWaitRequest / HttpRequest / ReadLineRequestthe yield requests Coroutine.Sleep / Wait / Fetch / ReadLine returnthe same names
Types the interpreter's own surfaces hand out: UI, SQLite, COM and the Win32 API
Button / ButtonBase / CheckBox / ComboBox / DateTimePicker / GenericControl / Label / ListBox / ListView / NativeApp / OpenFileDialog / RadioButton / Rebar / SaveFileDialog / StatusBar / SysLink / TabControl / TextBox / TheTimer / ToolBar / TrackBar / TreeViewa UI object of that kind, from the Application / Form surfacethe name as spelled
KeyEventArgs / MouseEventArgs / MouseButtons / KeyCodes / HotKey / ItemsCollection / ControlCollectionan event argument, a key or mouse code, or a control's child collectionthe name as spelled
ComObject / ComScope / ComNodea COM object, scope or node from Com.CreateObject / GetObjectthe name as spelled
.NET and system types bound in scope
Console / ConsoleColor / Convert / Directory / DockStyle / Encoding / Environment / File / FileAttributes / GC / Guid / Math / Path / Rect / RegexOptions / Size / StringBuilder / TimeZoneInfo / ClientStatus / CoroutineStatus / TaskStatus / CancelEventArgs / EventArgs / CancellationToken / CancellationTokenSource / Control / Form / MdiChild / MdiForman instance of that type Guid.Empty is Guid, Encoding.UTF8 is Encoding, ConsoleColor.Red is ConsoleColor, DockStyle.Bottom is DockStyle. The static-only names (Console, Convert, Directory, Environment, File, GC, Math, Path) never match a value: is Math is a legal False, not an unknown name.the name as spelled ("Guid", "Rect", "ConsoleColor"…)

The callable contract is Function; the engine's internal storage name for that type is NOT exposed to scripts, so writing it is a runtime error (unknown or undefined type).

When adding a new internal type, give its name a Type in ScriptTypeRegistry (TypeAliases.cs). A contract (a predicate over several types, like Iterable, RandomAccess or Function) needs an arm in TryMatchKnownType (VisitExpressions.cs) instead. crash_typeof_matrix.slc asserts both halves.

The registry entry is not the same thing as binding the name in scope, and a type a VALUE can be written back as needs both. The is / as default arm reads ScriptTypeRegistry directly, while typename() and the bare-identifier fallback go through ResolveTypeToClr (that table, then a global-scope Type, then the CLR's own lookup). Measured: with DockStyle bound in the global scope alone, DockStyle.Bottom worked and typeof(bar.Dock) already answered "DockStyle", while bar.Dock is DockStyle was a silent False (the failure shape the is switch's default arm was written to stop producing). One entry in the registry is what makes the name a script can WRITE agree with the name a value REPORTS.

as keyword Type cast operator (returns null on failure)

Safe cast returns null if the value is not of the specified type, rather than throwing. Supports all primitive types (int, long, short, ushort, byte, sbyte, uint, ulong, float, double, decimal, bool, char, string), named C# types (Array, List, IScriptList, IScriptDictionary), delegates, and script classes.

value as TypeName
var fn = fun(int x) { return x * x; }; var casted = fn as Func<int,int>; if (casted is not null) { print(casted(21)); } // Primitive examples all numeric types support cast var v1 = 42 as int; // 42 var v2 = 42 as long; // 42 var v3 = 42L as long; // 42 var v4 = 42f as float; // 42.0 var v5 = 3.14m as decimal; // 3.14 var v6 = (short)100 as short; // 100 var v7 = (byte)255 as byte; // 255 // Collection types var lst = new List<int>() as List; var arr = new int[3] as Array; // Returns null on mismatch var bad = 42 as string; // null
is not null keyword Non-null check pattern

Pattern matching syntax for null checks. Returns true when the value is not null.

value is not null
var maybeFunc = fn as Func<int,int>; if (maybeFunc is not null) { print("result: " + maybeFunc(42)); }
ternary (?:) keyword Conditional expression operator

Returns trueValue if condition is truthy, falseValue otherwise.

condition ? trueValue : falseValue
var label = (x > 0) ? "positive" : "non-positive";
with keyword Non-destructive copy of a struct or class with field overrides expr with { field = value, ... }

The with expression creates a deep copy of a struct or class instance, applying specified field overrides. The original instance is not modified. Works with readonly structs and init-only properties (bypasses mutation restrictions during the copy).

var p2 = p with { x = 99 };
// Struct copy with override struct Point { public int x; public int y; } var p = new Point(); p.x = 10; p.y = 20; var p2 = p with { x = 99 }; print(p2.x); // 99 (overridden) print(p2.y); // 20 (preserved) print(p.x); // 10 (original unchanged) // Class copy with override class Person { public string name; public int age; } var alice = new Person(); alice.name = "Alice"; alice.age = 30; var bob = alice with { name = "Bob" }; print(bob.name); // "Bob" print(bob.age); // 30 (preserved)
+ - * / % operator Arithmetic: add, subtract, multiply, divide, modulo

Standard arithmetic operators. Integer division truncates toward zero. Mixed numeric types promote to the wider type (int + long → long, int + double → double).

Modulo follows the same promotion: with two integers it is an integer remainder and a zero divisor throws, while a double or float operand, or a decimal paired with another type, computes in floating point (7.5 % 2 is 1.5, and a 0.0 divisor gives NaN).

Small integer promotion: sbyte, byte, short, ushort, and char are automatically widened to int before arithmetic so the result stays precise. Example: sbyte.MaxValue + 1 returns int 128 (not double).

a + b // addition a - b // subtraction a * b // multiplication a / b // division a % b // modulo (remainder)
123 + 10 = 133 123 - 10 = 113 123 * 10 = 1230 123 / 10 = 12 // integer truncation 123 % 10 = 3 // remainder 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 // int promoted to double
Division by zero throws a runtime error. Use try/catch when dividing by a variable that could be zero.
== != < > <= >= operator Comparison operators equality, inequality, ordering

Compare two values. == and != work on all types (including null). Ordering (<, >, <=, >=) works on numeric types and strings.

a == b // equality a != b // inequality a < b // less than a > b // greater than a <= b // less than or equal a >= b // greater than or equal
123 == 10 → false 123 != 10 → true 123 < 10 → false 123 > 10 → true
&& || ! operator Logical AND, OR, and NOT short-circuit evaluation

&& and || short-circuit: the right operand is only evaluated if needed. ! negates a boolean value. Any value can be used as a condition falsy values are false, null, and 0.

a && b // logical AND a || b // logical OR !a // logical NOT
if (x > 0 && x < 100) { print("in range"); } if (x == null || x == 0) { print("falsy"); } if (!done) { print("not done yet"); }
& | ^ ~ << >> operator Bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT, left shift, right shift

Bitwise operators work on integer types. ~ is the bitwise complement (one's complement). << shifts bits left (multiply by power of two), >> shifts bits right (divide by power of two).

A shift count is masked by the width of the promoted left operand, as in C#: & 31 for a 32-bit type and & 63 for a 64-bit one, so 1 << 33 is 2 and stays an int, while 1L << 33 is 8589934592 and stays a long. The result keeps the promoted operand's type, which is also why ~ and unary minus of an sbyte, byte, short or ushort answer an int.

a & b // bitwise AND a | b // bitwise OR a ^ b // bitwise XOR ~a // bitwise NOT (complement) a << b // left shift a >> b // right shift
0b1010 & 0b1100 → 8 // (0b1000) 0b1010 | 0b1100 → 14 // (0b1110) 0b1010 ^ 0b1100 → 6 // (0b0110) ~5 → -6 10 << 2 → 40 12 >> 1 → 6
= += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= operator Assignment and compound assignment, and the order in which a target is evaluated

= stores a value and the expression is worth what it stored, so assignments chain and can be captured: a = b = 5 leaves both at 5, and var r = (k += 2) puts the new k in r.

The compound forms are += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>=; each reads the target, applies the operator of the same name to the given value, and stores the result. += on a string concatenates, and the arithmetic ones keep the numeric rules of + - * / %. ??= assigns only when the target is currently null (see ??=), and ++/-- are the one-step spellings (see ++ --).

The target is resolved ONCE, in C#'s order: the receiver first, then any indices from left to right, then the current value is read, then the right operand is evaluated, then the operation, then the store. So Arr()[Next()] += 5 calls the receiver once and the index once, and the read and the write land on the SAME element. Evaluating the index a second time for the write would write an element that was never read, which is the defect this order exists to prevent.

A target may be a variable, a field or a property (their access rules apply, so a private setter from outside is refused), or an array element, which is a variable. The stored value is converted to the target's declared type by the same rule every other door uses, a plain assignment included, so string[] s = ["x"]; s[0] = 42; stores "42" exactly as string a = 42; does, and a value that cannot convert is refused there with the same sentence. A List element holding a struct is not a variable: the indexer hands back a copy, so list[0].X = 1 is refused and the fix is to take the element into a variable, change it, and store it back with list[0] = item. A const cannot be assigned at all.

// the target is evaluated once, so the read and the write agree var items = [1, 2]; items[0] += 10; // items is [11, 2] // chained assignment and the value of the expression var a = 0; var b = 0; a = b = 5; // both 5 var k = 3; var r = (k += 2); // k is 5, r is 5 // += concatenates a string var s = "a"; s += "b"; // "ab"
++ -- operator Prefix and postfix increment/decrement

Both prefix and postfix forms are supported: ++x/--x modify the variable and return the new value; x++/x-- return the old value then modify. They work on local variables, global variables, and property/index targets (c.N++, arr[i]--). An independent member of the assignment operators, and they follow the same rule: the target is resolved ONCE (receiver, then indices), so arr[Next()]++ reads and writes the same element.

++x // increment then return new value --x // decrement then return new value x++ // return old value, then increment x-- // return old value, then decrement
var x = 10; print(++x); // Result: 11 print(--x); // Result: 10 print(x++); // Result: 10 (returns old value) print(x); // Result: 11 // On globals and members ++gCount; // prefix on a global obj.Score++; // postfix on a property arr[0]--; // postfix on an index target
?? operator Null-coalescing returns left side if not null, else right side

The ?? operator returns the left operand if it is not null; otherwise it evaluates and returns the right operand. Short-circuits: the right side is not evaluated if the left side is non-null.

left ?? right
var name = null ?? "default"; print(name); // "default" var x = 42; print(x ?? 99); // 42 (short-circuits, 99 not evaluated) // Chaining var result = null ?? null ?? "fallback"; print(result); // "fallback"
Short-circuit ensures the right operand is only evaluated when the left is null side effects in the right expression may not run.
Precedence is C#'s: ?? binds looser than a comparison, so x ?? "" == y parses as x ?? ("" == y) and answers its LEFT operand whenever that is not null (a truthy value) instead of comparing anything. Parenthesize the value you compare: (x ?? "") == y.
??= operator Null-coalescing assignment assign right side only if the target is null

The ??= operator assigns the right operand to the target only if the target is currently null; otherwise the target keeps its value and the right operand is not evaluated (short-circuit). Works on local variables, global variables, array elements, class/struct fields, and dictionary entries. It is the null-only member of the assignment operators and follows the same rule: the target is resolved ONCE, so Map()[Next()] ??= v looks the entry up one single time and either keeps it or stores into it.

target ??= value
var x = null; x ??= 5; // x was null → x = 5 x ??= 99; // x is 5 (non-null) → keeps 5, 99 NOT evaluated print(x); // 5 // Dictionary entry var cache = new Dictionary<string, object>(); cache["key"] ??= "computed"; // Array element var arr = new object[1]; arr[0] ??= 42;
Short-circuit semantics match ??: the right side is only evaluated when the target is null, so side effects in the right expression may not run. Variable targets run in the bytecode VM; array/field/dict targets use the tree interpreter.
?. operator Null-conditional access member only if target is not null

The ?. operator accesses a property or method only if the target is not null. Returns null if the target is null, avoiding NullReference errors. Supports property access, method calls, and chaining.

obj?.Property obj?.Method()
class Node { public Node Next; public int Id; } var n = new Node(); print(n?.Id); // 0 print(null?.Id); // null (no crash) print(n?.Next?.Id); // null (chained null-safe access)
