Scheduler.Schedule(name, delayMs, callback) ScheduledTask Delayed one-shot: runs the callback after delayMs milliseconds, then auto-removed. Callback receives the task name as first parameter.
Scheduler.Schedule(name, dateTime, callback) ScheduledTask Delayed one-shot: runs the callback at a specific DateTime, then auto-removed. Callback receives the task name as first parameter.
Scheduler.ContinueWith(parentTask, childName, callback) void Registers a continuation: callback fires after parentTask completes successfully. Child callback receives the child task name as first parameter.
Scheduler.Remove(name) bool Stops a task by name (only if status is "Scheduled"). Returns true if found, false otherwise. Case-insensitive.
Scheduler.List() ScheduledTask[] Returns a snapshot of all currently active (Scheduled) tasks. Stopped/completed tasks are auto-removed.
Scheduler.Tick() int Fires any due callbacks now on the calling thread. Returns the number of callbacks fired.
Scheduler.WaitAll() void Blocks until all active tasks are stopped or completed. Drives callbacks on the calling thread.
Scheduler.Clear() void Removes all registered tasks.

ScheduledTask properties

PropertyTypeDescription
.NamestringUnique identifier (defaults to the CRON expression)
.CronExpressionstringThe original CRON expression string
.NextOccurrenceDateTimeOffset?The next scheduled date/time with local timezone offset, or null
.StatusTaskStatusTaskStatus.Scheduled, TaskStatus.Running, TaskStatus.Stopped, TaskStatus.Failed, or TaskStatus.Completed
.IsRunningbooltrue while the task is waiting for its next occurrence (status = Scheduled). false while running, stopped, failed, or completed.

Methods on ScheduledTask

MethodDescription
.Stop()Cancels the task, prints a trace, removes it from the global list
ScheduledTask.Remove(name)Static stops a task by name (same as Scheduler.Remove(name))
// Recurring CRON task callback receives task name Scheduler.Add("DailyReport", CronExpression.Parse("0 8 * * *"), (tName) => { print("Generating report for " + tName); }); // Fire-and-forget Scheduler.Enqueue("Notify", (tName) => { print("Immediate task: " + tName); }); Scheduler.Tick(); // Delayed Scheduler.Schedule("Reminder", 2000, (tName) => { print("2 seconds later: " + tName); }); // Continuation (runs after parent succeeds) var parent = Scheduler.AddOrUpdate("Backup", CronExpression.Parse("0 3 * * *"), (tName) => { print("Running " + tName); }); Scheduler.ContinueWith(parent, "NotifyBackup", (tName) => { print("Backup done " + tName); }); // List active tasks foreach (var t in Scheduler.List()) print(t.Name + ": " + t.Status); // Remove by name Scheduler.Remove("DailyReport");
Callback signature: All script callbacks receive the task name as the first parameter: (tName) => { ... }. The name is passed automatically by the scheduler you do not need to capture it yourself. All callbacks run synchronously on the calling thread via WaitAll() or Tick(). No background threads. Use WaitAll() for fire-and-forget scripts, or a custom Tick() loop when you need to stop tasks from outside callbacks.
SchedulerRunner class High-level task runner with DB persistence, monitoring, and history

The SchedulerRunner class wraps Scheduler with SQLite persistence, automatic task loading, error tracking, execution history, and a monitoring loop. It is the recommended way to run scheduled tasks in production scripts.

Constructor

SignatureDescription
SchedulerRunner(sqlitePath, dbPath)Initializes the runner: loads the sqlite3 library, creates/opens the database, runs schema migrations

Public methods

MethodReturnsDescription
.Run() void Full lifecycle: print header → reset infinite tasks → seed demo tasks → load from DB → print next occurrences → fire due tasks → report infinite tasks → monitor → print history → clear. Enters a blocking monitoring loop until all tasks complete.
.Schedule(name, cronType, callback, cronExpr, tz) void Register a single task. cronType selects the schedule type CronType.Queue, .OneShot, or .Cron. The callback receives the task name. Parameters cronExpr and tz are only used for CronType.Cron.
.GetSqlitePath() string Returns the sqlite3 library path passed to the constructor
.GetDbPath() string Returns the database file path passed to the constructor

Usage examples

// 1. Full auto-run (seed + DB load + monitor) var runner = new SchedulerRunner("tools/sqlite3", "tasks.db"); runner.Run(); // 2. Schedule tasks directly via the public API var r = new SchedulerRunner("tools/sqlite3", "custom.db"); // Enqueue fires on next Tick, then self-removes r.Schedule("Notify", CronType.Queue, (tName) => { print("Sending: " + tName); }, null, null); // OneShot fires at next minute boundary r.Schedule("Report", CronType.OneShot, (tName) => { print("Generating " + tName); }, null, null); // Cron recurring every 5 minutes r.Schedule("Health", CronType.Cron, (tName) => { print("Check: " + tName); }, "*/5 * * * *", null); // Cron with timezone var tz = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("Romance Standard Time"); r.Schedule("ParisTask", CronType.Cron, (tName) => { print("Bonjour " + tName); }, "0 9 * * *", tz);

Callback signature: (tName) => { ... } the task name is passed by the scheduler (via WrapNamedCallback), no closure capture needed.

REPL mode: When Script.IsRepl is true (a prompt is driving, not a file run), .Schedule() automatically calls Scheduler.Tick() after registering the task, so due tasks fire immediately. If pending tasks remain, a hint is printed inviting you to call runner.Run(false) to start the monitoring loop. In CLI mode, Run() handles Tick() in the correct lifecycle order.

Monitoring: Run() enters a blocking loop that calls Scheduler.Tick() every second. To build your own monitoring loop, call Scheduler.Tick() manually in a while loop after scheduling tasks with .Schedule().

Persistence: All task state (status, iteration count, timestamps, errors, elapsed time) is written to the SQLite database. On restart, Run() reloads unfinished tasks and resets infinite tasks that were completed/failed.

Script namespace Runtime information about the script execution environment

The Script namespace describes the run itself: which directory it belongs to, whether a REPL session is driving it, and the interpreter behind it. Useful for adapting behavior in REPL vs CLI mode.

Members

MemberTypeDescription
Script.Directory()stringThe directory of the file being run, which is what a "./name" path is resolved against (see File). In the REPL it is the process directory. Empty when the run has no directory of its own. A callback has no current file: a request handler, a timer, an event handler or a feed.Start body runs later, on somebody else's turn, so Script.Directory() there answers the PROCESS's directory rather than the file's. Read it ONCE while the file is running and keep the value (var appDir = Script.Directory();), which is how the htmx board serves its own icon from wherever the engine was started.
Script.IsReplbooltrue when a REPL PROMPT is driving the interpreter. One thing sets it: the REPL mode itself. A direct CLI run (ScriptLangCore.exe script.slc) sees false, and so does a file run with .run from the prompt, because a file is not the prompt and its top level compiles exactly as a plain run's does. It previously followed .state, which made a .run file report true.
Script.HasErrorboolWhether the interpreter recorded an error. The flag is set when a run FAILS, and a failing top-level run has already ended by then, so a script cannot read it as true.
Script.InstanceInterpreterThe interpreter running the script, for a diagnostic that wants to identify the session, for example Script.Instance.GetHashCode().
// Skip seeding when running in REPL var runner = new SchedulerRunner("tools/sqlite3", "tasks.db"); runner.Run(!Script.IsRepl); // Conditional behavior if (Script.IsRepl) { print("Running interactively"); } else { print("Batch mode"); }
Script.IsRepl is set by the interpreter's REPL mode, which is how a script detects that a REPL session is driving it and skips one-shot seeding. A file run with .run from the prompt is in that mode; a script started from the command line is not.

▼ Collections

array literal [...] syntax Shorthand syntax for creating a native T[] array no new keyword needed

An array literal [1, 2, 3] creates a native T[] where T is inferred from the elements. Supports nesting, emptiness, indexing, foreach, and all array operations (.Length, not .Count).

var a = [1, 2, 3]; // int[] var b = ["a", "b"]; // string[] var c = []; // object[] (empty) var d = [1, "hello", 3.5]; // object[] (mixed) var e = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]; // nested arrays (int[][]) var f = [1.23m, 23.14m]; // decimal[]
var nums = [10, 20, 30]; print(nums.Length); // Result: 3 print(nums[1]); // Result: 20 nums[1] = 99; foreach (var x in [100, 200]) { print(x); } // inline iterable print(typeof(nums)); // Result: int[]
Element type inference: all-int → int[], all-string → string[], int+double → double[] (promoted), mixed types → object[]. To create a List<T> instead, use new List<T>().
Array literals in .NET method calls: When an array literal [a, b, c] is passed as a single argument to a .NET params method (e.g. Console.WriteLine("{0}", items)), it is treated as one object argument, not expanded into individual elements. The format placeholder sees the array itself (prints System.Object[]). To fill multiple format placeholders, pass each element as its own argument: Console.WriteLine("{0} {1} {2}", a, b, c).
dict literal { } keyword Dictionary literal creates Dictionary

{ key: value, ... } creates a Dictionary like Python/JavaScript dicts. Keys can be any type (string, int, bool, etc.). Access and mutate with d[key].

A key is written as a bare name ({name: 1}, which is the STRING "name"), a quoted string, a single-quoted one-character key (which is a char), a number, or a bracketed expression. A literal is an EXPRESSION and never a statement, so {a: 1}; on its own line is refused with the two spellings that work: a declaration (var d = { a: 1 };) or parentheses (({ a: 1 });). A { that starts a statement is a BLOCK, which is what makes the bare form ambiguous.

var d = {}; // empty dict var d2 = {name: "Alice", age: 30}; // unquoted keys are strings d2["name"] // "Alice" d2[42] = "answer"; // non-string keys work too {[]: "array key", 0: "int key"} // expression keys [{}] // Dictionary<object, object>[]
// Create and use var cfg = {host: "localhost", port: 8080}; print(cfg["host"]); // "localhost" // Mutation cfg["port"] = 9090; print(cfg.Count); // 2 // Non-string keys var dk = {}; dk[42] = "int key"; dk[true] = "bool key"; print(dk[42]); // "int key" void check(string n, bool c) { if (c) print("OK " + n); else print("FAIL " + n); } // ContainsKey check if (cfg.ContainsKey("host")) { print("found"); } // Array as key (any expression works) var ek = {[]: "empty key", 0: "number key"}; // Dict in array typed as Dictionary<object, object>[] var da = [{}]; check("type", typeof(da[0]) == "Dictionary"); // Remove entry var dr = {x: 1, y: 2}; dr.Remove("x"); check("remove", dr.Count == 1);
Unquoted identifiers used as keys ({name: val}) are treated as string literals unlike regular expression context where they would be variable references. Use {"name": val} for quoted string keys (behaves identically).
Expression keys: Any expression can be a key, including arrays: {[]: "empty array key", [1,2]: "values as key"}. Numbers also work directly: {0: "zero", 1: "one"}.
Type inference: [{}] creates a Dictionary<object, object>[] the runtime type of the first non-null element determines the array element type. Mixed-type arrays fall back to object[].
comprehension [ for ] keyword List comprehension transform and filter arrays with [expr for var in source if cond]

Comprehensions provide a concise syntax for creating arrays by iterating over a source collection, optionally filtering with if. The result is a native array (object?[]).

[expr for var in source] [expr for var in source if condition]
// Basic comprehension square each element var nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; var squares = [x*x for x in nums]; print(squares[0]); // 1 print(squares[4]); // 25 // With filter only even numbers var evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]; print(evens[0]); // 2 print(evens[1]); // 4 // From a range literal var tripled = [x*3 for x in 1..5]; print(tripled[2]); // 9
Comprehensions work on arrays, lists, strings (iterating characters), and anything implementing IEnumerable. They do not create a lazy iterator the result array is fully materialized immediately.
List<T> type Generic dynamic array ordered, indexable, growable

Creates a resizable list of elements of type T. Supports Add, Remove, indexing via [index], Count, ToArray, ToList, Sort, and all LINQ methods. Use new List<T>() for resizable lists; the array literal [1, 2, 3] creates a native int[] instead. list.ToList() returns a new typed copy a fresh List<T> with the same elements (copy semantics, like ToArray()); a List<int> typeofs as "List<int>".

Sort() sorts IN PLACE by the element type's own order, and Sort(fn) sorts through a comparable script function: fun(int a, int b) { return a - b; } ascending, y - x descending, and any negative/zero/positive number means "before / same / after". The elements are written back through Add, so the element type is enforced exactly as it is for an added element, and a comparison that FAILS reports its own message (a y / 0 in the comparer says Division by zero, not the runtime's "Failed to compare two elements"). An ARRAY has the same member (see the array entry).

var list = new List<int>(); // resizable list var pre = new List<string>(1000); // explicit with capacity var seeded = new List<int>([1, 2]); // filled from a collection; each element is coerced, so a wrong one is refused var set = new HashSet<int>([1, 2]); // the same for a set, and a Dictionary from another dictionary var arr = [1, 2, 3]; // int[] (native array, not a List) var rows = new List<(string s, int i, bool b)>(); // tuple types are valid generic args rows.Add(("x", 1, true)); // Add validates arity + element types var grid = new (string, int)[] { ("k", 1) }; // tuple-typed arrays too
var nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].ToList(); // List<int> with 5 elements (the array literal itself is an int[]) print(nums.Count); // Result: 5 var i = 0; while (i < 100) { nums.Add(i); i = i + 1; } print(Count(nums)); // Result: 105 // ToArray extracts all elements into a typed native array int[] here, not object[] var arr = nums.ToArray(); print(arr[0]); // Result: 1 // ToList copies into a fresh typed list List<int> here var copy = nums.ToList(); print(typeof(copy)); // Result: List<int>
Dictionary<K,V> type Key-value map with fast lookup Keys(), Values(), indexing

Creates a dictionary mapping keys of type K to values of type V. Keys are unique. Supports ContainsKey, Keys(), Values(), indexing via [key], and all LINQ methods.

Tuple keys use value equality: two distinct tuples with equal scalar/string/nested-tuple elements are the same key (so d[(1, 2)] finds a key stored as a separately-created (1, 2); numeric widening applies, e.g. (1L, 2L) aliases (1, 2)). Elements that are arrays/lists/dicts/objects keep reference identity. The ==/!= operators on tuples are unchanged.

Iteration: foreach over a dictionary yields KeyValuePair objects, and KeyValuePair(key, value) builds one (the same bare-call shape Rect(l, t, r, b) has, since a bare new KeyValuePair(a, b) reaches the CLR generic and cannot infer its type arguments) with .Key and .Value properties. This works on both native Dictionary<K,V> and the boxed rows from Sqlite.Query.

var d = new Dictionary<string, int>(); var pre = new Dictionary<string, int>(500);
var d = new Dictionary<string, int>(50); d["key"] = 42; print(d["key"]); // Result: 42 print(Count(d.Keys())); // Result: 1 // Iterate with foreach yields .Key and .Value foreach (var kv in d) { print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value); } // Keys() and Values() return arrays (O(1) bulk copy) var allKeys = d.Keys(); var allVals = d.Values();
KeyValuePair type A key and its value, as one object what a dictionary iteration yields

A single key-value row: .Key and .Value. A foreach over a Dictionary yields these, so the common way to hold one is to receive it; KeyValuePair(key, value) builds one when a script needs to make its own. typeof answers "KeyValuePair" and is KeyValuePair is true.

.Value holds anything: a number, a string, a tuple, a list, or null. A tuple value is read by index (.Value[0]) or by the CLR element name (.Value.Item1), and it still travels inside a List<KeyValuePair<string, object>>.

Build it with the BARE CALL, not new: a bare KeyValuePair name resolves to the CLR generic, whose constructor takes (TKey, TValue) and cannot infer them from the arguments, so new KeyValuePair("a", 1) refuses. KeyValuePair(key, value) is the shape Rect(l, t, r, b) has. A wrong arity is refused by name: KeyValuePair expects 2 arguments: key and value.

A pair answers Dispose() as a safe no-op (so using and is IDisposable behave uniformly), and printing one shows the type name rather than its contents; Json.Serialize is what shows the contents.

var kv = KeyValuePair("alpha", 42); print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value); // alpha = 42 print(typeof(kv)); // KeyValuePair print(kv is KeyValuePair); // True // A tuple as the value, read both ways: var packed = KeyValuePair("row", (1, 2, "three")); print(packed.Value[0]); // 1 print(packed.Value.Item3); // three // And it travels in a typed list: var rows = new List<KeyValuePair<string, object>>(); rows.Add(packed); print(Count(rows)); // 1 // The usual way to hold one is to receive it: var d = new Dictionary<string, int>(); d["a"] = 1; foreach (var item in d) { print(item.Key + " = " + item.Value); } // a = 1
HashSet<T> type Unordered collection of unique elements with O(1) lookup

Creates a hash set of elements of type T. Duplicates are silently ignored. Supports Add, Remove, Contains, Count, Clear, ToArray, ToList, foreach, and all LINQ methods. Use new HashSet<T>() for a mutable set; there is no literal syntax. With tuple elements (HashSet<(int,int)>) duplicates are detected by value: two distinct tuples with equal scalar/string/nested-tuple elements count as the same element (numeric widening applies); composite elements keep reference identity.

set.ToList() returns a new typed copy a fresh List<T> (a HashSet<int> .ToList() is a List<int>); the element order follows the set's iteration order, which is undefined.

var set = new HashSet<int>(); var pre = new HashSet<string>(1000); // explicit capacity
var ids = new HashSet<int>(); ids.Add(42); ids.Add(99); ids.Add(42); // ignored already present print(ids.Count); // Result: 2 print(ids.Contains(42)); // Result: True print(ids.Contains(1)); // Result: False ids.Remove(99); print(ids.Count); // Result: 1 // Iteration via foreach foreach (var x in ids) { print(x); } // ToArray extracts elements into a typed native array int[] (order is undefined) var arr = ids.ToArray();
Order of elements in a HashSet<T> is not guaranteed and may change between runs. Use List<T> if insertion order matters. HashSet<T> is backed by System.Collections.Generic.HashSet<T> and uses the default equality comparer for the element type.

▼ UI Subsystem (Win32)

Application UI Win32 application create forms, dialogs, message loop

Application provides the Windows message loop, form creation, and file dialogs. Use Application.Run() to start the GUI message loop.

Properties

FilePathFull path to the RUNNING executable (e.g. D:\...\ScriptLangCore.exe). In an EMBEDDED run that is the HOST's exe (ScriptLangCore.Launcher.exe or a packaged app), while Path is the engine's own folder, so the two can name different directories: a script that wants to spawn "the same program again" asks FilePath, and one that wants the engine's assets\ asks Path.
PathDirectory path of the running executable (e.g. D:\...\bin\Release\net11.0). An EMBEDDED run reports the folder of the ScriptLangCore.dll it loaded instead, which is where the engine keeps its own files (see Where the engine is when it is embedded).
ExeIconThe running executable's own icon, as a handle, out of its resource (the project's ApplicationIcon). This is what a form takes when the script assigns none; 0 when the build has no icon resource.
ArgsWhat the executable was invoked with, as a list of strings, with the executable's own path left out: the list a C# Main(string[] args) receives. So ScriptLangCore.exe app.slc --flag gives ["app.slc", "--flag"], which is why a script's own flags start at [1] there. The list is rebuilt on every read, so editing the one you were handed does not change what the next read reports. A run started from a session carries its own: .run tool.slc -- a b makes Application.Args ["tool.slc", "a", "b"] for that run only, and the session's own list is back afterwards.
CurDirRead and write. The PROCESS's current working directory, which is the directory a BARE relative path resolves against: after Application.CurDir = "data", File.ReadAllText("x.txt") reads data\x.txt, while a path that starts with ./ still means "beside this script" and is untouched (see the path rule in the File entry). Assigning refuses a value that is not a string, and a directory that does not exist, naming what arrived (Application.CurDir must be a directory path, not 'int', Directory not found: 'X:\nope'). Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() and Directory.SetCurrentDirectory(...) are the same two operations spelled as methods.
SingleInstanceRead and write, default false. One application, the way VB's IsSingleInstance means it, with two effects. IN PROCESS, Application.CreateForm(title) answers the form already carrying that title instead of building a second window, so a snippet pasted twice reuses its panel. ACROSS PROCESSES, turning it on takes a named lock for this run's script, so a SECOND run of the same file ends at the assignment rather than building a second set of windows: it logs ONE line at ERROR level (SingleInstance: already running in another process, so this run ends.) and exits with ExitCode.Refused (3), which a launcher can tell from a genuine failure (1). The lock's name is appended to that line only when the SINGLE_INSTANCE diagnostic is on (SLC_SINGLE_INSTANCE=1), because it is a sanitized full path. Windows releases the lock when the first run's process ends. It takes a boolean and nothing else (SingleInstance takes true or false, not 'int'), and false releases the lock. Set it at the TOP of a script: the assignment is where both effects begin.

Where the engine is when it is embedded

A script normally runs inside ScriptLangCore.exe, so Application.Path is the executable's own folder. An EMBEDDED run is different: a host loads ScriptLangCore.dll and may keep that DLL anywhere, and then Application.Path reports the folder the engine came from, because that is where the engine's own assets\, tools\ and sqlite3.dll were published. The shipped launcher finds the DLL in four steps, and the first hit wins:

StepWhat it looks for
SLC_ENGINE_DLLthe FILE named by that environment variable
beside the exethe host's own folder, which is the shape a packaged app uses, and a copy here WINS over the two steps below
SLC_ENGINE_HOMEthat DIRECTORY, holding ScriptLangCore.dll
PATHeach directory in its own order, first hit wins

A copy beside the exe comes before the environment on purpose: an INSTALLED engine declares SLC_ENGINE_HOME for every process on the machine, so an app that ships its own engine would otherwise run the installed one and silently change version. A declared location is OBEYED rather than consulted: when nothing is beside the exe and SLC_ENGINE_HOME names a folder without ScriptLangCore.dll, or SLC_ENGINE_DLL a missing file, the launcher refuses and names what it was told instead of falling back to another copy, so a typo can never load a different engine than the one you named. A host of your own decides this for itself, since the host is what loads the DLL; what a script can rely on is that Application.Path is the folder of the engine it is running in, while ./ and Script.Directory() keep naming the file being run, and Application.CurDir the process's working directory.

Application methods

InputBox and CreateInputBox have a section of their own, since a prompt carries a good deal more than a method signature: see InputBox.

CreateForm(title [, configure])Create a new Form object with its native window already made, and hidden: form.Created is true at once while form.Visible stays false until Show(), so every control and item can be built before the form appears (form.SetMenu(bar) works there too). A TITLE IDENTIFIES THE WINDOW when Application.SingleInstance is on: a repeat answers the form the script already has (with a warning naming its handle) instead of a second window. With it off a repeat still creates the second window and WARNS about the duplicate title, which is what a pasted-twice snippet used to leak silently.
FindForm(title)The form this run already has under that title, or null: the other half of CreateForm, and the question form.Created cannot answer (that one says whether the instance you hold has a window, not whether the form existed before). It is what makes a startup idempotent without an exception: var p = Application.FindForm("panel"); if (p == null) { p = Application.CreateForm("panel"); ...init... } runs the init once however many times the snippet is pasted.
MonitorCount()How many monitors this machine has, so a script can pick one: form.Screen takes 0 .. MonitorCount() - 1 and refuses anything else by name.
ThemeActive()1 when this machine is running with visual styles, else 0. Ask it BEFORE drawing a themed part: e.ThemePart answers -1 when there is no theme.
CursorPos()The mouse position in SCREEN coordinates, as [x, y]. A posted message cannot move it, which is what makes it the stable reference a drag wants.
MessagePos()The screen position carried by the message being handled (a packed x/y in one value).
ForegroundWindow()The handle of the window the user is currently on, or 0.
WindowFromPoint(x, y)The handle of the window at a SCREEN point, or 0. Useful for a hit test the engine has no member for.
AsyncKeyState(vk)1 while a virtual key is down, else 0. It reads the key AT THE CALL, so it is how a drag asks about the left button without assuming the event carried it.
SystemMetrics(index)A system metric at the SYSTEM dpi (SM_CXSCREEN is 0, SM_CYSCREEN 1).
SystemMetricsForDpi(index, dpi)The same metric measured for a given dpi, which is what a scrollbar or a frame size has to be asked for on a per-monitor box.
AdjustWindowRectExForDpi(rect, style, menu, exStyle, dpi)Grow a client RECT (a Mem buffer) into the window rect its frame needs at that dpi. It writes back into the buffer and answers 1 on success.
SetProcessDPIAware()Tell Windows the process scales itself. The engine asks for per-monitor v2 where it can, so this is for the rare host that must be told early.
GetPixel(x, y), GetPixel(dc, x, y)The pixel at a SCREEN point, for anything outside a window's client: a caption, a scrollbar, another process's window. A control's own client is ctrl.GetPixel(x, y), which takes client coordinates. The reading is a COLORREF, so Colors.FromPixel(...) turns it back into a colour. With two arguments the dc is opened and closed around the one read; with three it reads through a dc the script holds, which is what a sweep over hundreds of pixels wants.
GetDC(), ReleaseDC(dc)The screen dc those reads can share, and the call that hands it back. Hold one across a loop instead of opening one per pixel.
FormToJson(host [, options]), FormFromJson(doc)A HOST as a stored TEMPLATE, where a host is a form, an MDI frame or an MDI document window: the first writes the document (the same one Json.Serialize(host) writes, and it takes the SAME options as the serializers, so {"pretty": true}, a bare option name or a JSON text of them all work), and the second builds a NEW host from it, WHICHEVER its root Kind names: a Form, an MDI frame (with its document windows) or a document window (which gets a frame of its own to be parented to). This is the pair a database of forms is read and written with: one row holds the document, and a form comes back out of the row.
CreateMdiForm(title [, configure])Create a new MDI frame (MdiForm), with an optional trailing configure callback like CreateForm's.
CreateChildMdiForm(title, parentForm [, configure])Create an MDI frame embedded in a parent Form, with an optional trailing configure callback like CreateForm's.
Run([form] [, tabIndex])Start the message loop, which runs until the LAST form closes. It waits on the forms this run has shown: a form created with Application.CreateForm() and never shown does not keep the loop alive (its window exists from creation, so waiting on mere existence would wait for ever), which also means Run() with nothing shown returns at once. A form passed here is shown first, and it takes the window that owns the focus, so a child of it can be focused without a click. The control that gets the focus is the first in TAB ORDER, or the one whose TabIndex is given here: Run(form, 2) opens onto that stop, and Run(2) asks the same of a form that is already running, so a script does not have to keep a form to be understood. A form with no stop that can take the focus keeps the focus it has.
RunFor(timeoutMs [, form])The same loop with a DEADLINE: after that many milliseconds every open form gets a WM_CLOSE, so a demo or a screen ends itself instead of needing a hand-rolled timer. It posts the CLOSE rather than calling Close() on purpose, so a form's Closing handler can still REFUSE and keep the application up. It is a name of its own because Run(number) already means "take the focus to that TabIndex".
Quit([code])Post WM_QUIT to stop the message loop, carrying a CODE to the process when one is given: Application.Quit(7) leaves 7. With no code the process keeps the one it has, which is 0 unless the script set another, so this is not a second spelling of exit(n): that one ends the SCRIPT where it stands, unwinding and running finallys, while this ends the LOOP and lets the script carry on the message loop.

File dialogs

CreateOpenFileDialog()Returns an OpenFileDialog with properties Title, Filter, InitialDirectory, and method ShowDialog() returning 1 (OK) or 2 (Cancel). On success, FileNames[0] contains the selected path.
CreateSaveFileDialog()Returns a SaveFileDialog with same properties plus DefaultExtension. On success, FileName contains the selected path.

Message loop control

IsRunning()Returns true while the message loop is active.
PeekMessage()Non-blocking returns a MessageInfo or null.
WaitMessage()Blocking waits for a message, translates and dispatches it, then returns a MessageInfo. The MessageInfo it answers carries Hwnd, Message, WParam, LParam and Time, and DECODES the packed halves a message is built from: msg.LowWord(msg.WParam) is the id in a WM_COMMAND and msg.HighWord(...) its notification, with msg.LowByte/msg.HighByte for the 8-bit form; msg.MakeLong(lo, hi) and msg.MakeWord(lo, hi) build a value to post back.
DispatchMessage(msg)Dispatch a previously peeked message.
DoEvents()Process pending messages without blocking.
ShowConsole(true); var f = Application.CreateForm("Demo"); f.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; f.Width = 400; f.Height = 300; f.CreateButton("Click me", 10, 10, 100, 30); Application.Run(f);

The same form with the configure callback, which is the other spelling of every line above (they can be mixed freely, and a script that builds many controls reads better this way):

ShowConsole(true); var f = Application.CreateForm("Demo", (frm) => { frm.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; frm.Width = 400; frm.Height = 300; frm.CreateButton("Click me", 10, 10, 100, 30); }); Application.Run(f);
Full example: assets/ui/demos/rich_editor.slc
Form UI Window object container for managed controls

Created via Application.CreateForm(title), which builds the native window at once and keeps it hidden: Created and Handle are true immediately, Visible stays false until Show(), so the whole form is built while nothing is on screen (every control, the items in a list, a menu bar, the event handlers, the theme) and the window appears once, complete. It provides factory methods for all managed controls and event handlers for user interaction. All controls are automatically parented to the form and receive dark mode coloring via WM_CTLCOLOR* messages.

Properties

form["ChildControlName"]The CHILD control carrying that name, or null. The index is a CHILD's name and never the form's own, which is form.Name and is what its caption is built from. It is the handle a document's names are FOR: a document carries the look rather than the behaviour, so re-attaching behaviour means reaching a child by the name it gave it. It works the same on a Form, an MdiForm and an MdiChild, because the index IS the one lookup they share. The name follows the interpreter's own case rule, like every other name, and the first match wins where a script has given two controls one name. Indexing is the ONLY spelling: Find(name) was retired once the index covered it. A miss is loud rather than silent: form["typo"].Text is refused as Cannot access property 'Text' on null, with the position, so a name rebuilt at run time cannot quietly do nothing. ?. is the null-safe way to READ one (form[n]?.Text answers null on a miss), but it is refused as an ASSIGNMENT target (form[n]?.Text = "x" is a parse error), so re-attaching is a guard: var b = form[n]; if (b != null) b.Click = fun(...); (a ?. FURTHER OUT in a target is IGNORED rather than refused, which is not protection: see the ?. entry). A non-string index is refused by name rather than coerced, and a WRITE (form["x"] = c) is refused: a control is reached by name, never replaced by one.
ThemeA ThemeMode, so it is written form.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark: Light or Dark for the two native looks, System to follow Windows' own app-mode setting, and Custom to paint the palette below. Reading DarkMode answers the effective leg, which for Custom follows the palette background's brightness.
ThemeBackground, ThemeText, ThemeBorder, ThemeSelection, ThemeDisabledThe colours a Custom form paints with, written 0xRRGGBB. A colour left unset comes from the effective leg, a control's own BackgroundColor/TextColor still wins, and a part the engine does not draw (a scrollbar, a themed button face) follows the palette background. Changing one re-applies the theme to the form and to every control, so a palette can be adjusted while the window is up.
Width, Height, Left, TopWindow position/size. A width or height written BEFORE the form is shown is a DESIGN measurement in the system DPI's units, so the same number is the same physical size on a 100% and a 150% monitor (900 renders 900 px on the reference monitor and 600 px on the other); after Show() a write is a live size in pixels.
StartPosition0 = manual, 1 = center screen, 2 = center parent. 1 is applied when the window APPEARS (the first Show()) and against the size it then has, so the order of this assignment and of Width/Height does not matter; it also centres a form whose window already exists as soon as it is assigned.
CloseBox, MaximizeBox, MinimizeBox, Resizable, Modalbool the four window-style properties (CloseBox, MaximizeBox, MinimizeBox, Resizable) default to true and toggle the close box (the system menu and the X in it), the maximize and minimize boxes, and the thick (resizable) frame: set them any time before Show(), since each applies a style bit to the window Application.CreateForm already made and a form with no close box is still closable from a script with Close(). Modal is the odd one and defaults to false: it is not a style but an instruction to Show(), which then DISABLES this form's owner while the form is up and restores it when the form dies, so dlg.Modal = true; dlg.Show() is how a dialog owns its caller and dlg.Close() releases it.
Screenint, 0-based in the order Windows enumerates the monitors (the one Windows calls DISPLAY1 is 0). Assigning it BEFORE Show() is what makes a form OPEN on that monitor: the window is not created yet, so the request is honoured where it is created instead of the form appearing somewhere else and jumping. Assigning it later moves the form, centred in that monitor's work area with its size untouched. A value with no monitor behind it is refused, naming how many exist; Application.MonitorCount() is that count.
Paddingint, the space the DOCK layout keeps between the window's edge and the controls it places (DockStyle.Left, .Top, .Right, .Bottom, .Fill), so a docked box's scrollbars do not sit on the window's border. Zero by default; a control positioned absolutely ignores it; the value scales with the DPI like every other design measurement. A control's own Margin then REPLACES it on the sides that control names, which is documented with the controls.
GridSize, GridColorA designer grid drawn by the form itself: GridSize is the dot spacing in client pixels (0 or 1 = no grid) and GridColor the dot colour. The dots are drawn before any Paint handler, and the form clips its children, so a placed control is never overpainted.
HandleThe underlying HWND (IntPtr, accessible as long in scripts).
CreatedWhether this instance already has its native window, which is the question Handle != 0 answers spelled in one word. A FORM's window is created with Application.CreateForm() (hidden), so a form reports true from the moment you hold it and its controls and their items can be built before Show(); form.Visible is the question "is it on screen", which stays false until Show(). A child control reports true once it has been constructed. It says nothing about WHO created the form: a form answered by a repeated Application.CreateForm is a real form, so it reports true as well. Ask Application.FindForm(title) for "does this form exist already".
ControlsThe controls this form holds, in the order they were created. form.Controls.Count is how many and form.Controls.Get(i) is the one at index i, refused with the range when i is past the end. An MDI frame or child holds a plain list, so Controls.Count reads the same there: one spelling for both.

Form methods

SetIcon(icon, [size], [color])Set the window's icon, in one spelling for three cases. A CHARACTER is rendered into an icon: form.SetIcon("✅") draws it at 32 px in the colour the host needs (white on a dark form, near-black on a light one, re-rendered if DarkMode changes), form.SetIcon("✅", 48) picks the size, and form.SetIcon("✅", 32, 0x1F7A1F) the colour, written 0xRRGGBB. A NUMBER is an icon handle the script already has, Application.ExeIcon being the one the engine hands out, with 0 meaning no icon at all; the size and the colour apply to a rendered character, not to a handle. A form nobody sets one on takes the RUNNING EXECUTABLE's own icon, in both sizes. The size is checked before anything changes, so a refused call leaves the window as it was, and a character no font covers leaves it with the icon it had. Set before Show(), it is applied where the window is created, so nothing flickers. Returns the handle the window now holds, which is how a script reads the icon back.
AdoptChild(hwnd, insetL, insetT, insetR, insetB)Parent a foreign child window (e.g. the HWND returned by Com.HostActiveX) into the form, turn it into a real child (WS_CHILD, clears WS_POPUP) and keep it fitted to the client area minus the insets re-applied automatically on every WM_SIZE. hwnd is the long handle from HostActiveX.
Show()Create the window handle (if not already created) and display the form on screen.
Activate()Be the window the user is looking at: the thread's ACTIVE window, the z-order and the desktop foreground, which are one thing and are what a click used to supply. Show() does this too, so a script calls it to raise a window it already has. A window that does not exist yet is left alone.
InitHandle()Make sure the form has a window while leaving it invisible. A form from Application.CreateForm already has one (created, hidden), so this is an idempotent no-op there and a script does not need it; it is the named way to say "a hidden window must exist" for an object that has none yet (the engine's own dialogs use it). The script pattern is build the form and its controls, then Show().
Quit([code])Close the form AND end the run: it does what Close() does, then stops the message loop (WM_QUIT), so Application.Run returns even when other forms are still up. With a CODE the process leaves with it, exactly as Application.Quit(code) does: form.Quit(5) leaves 5, measured on the shipped build. Close() alone is the window, which ends the loop only when it was the last form.
Close()Send WM_CLOSE to the form. Triggers the Closing event set e.Cancel = true to prevent closure.
SendMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Send a window message to the form's own window and return the message's result. The same operation ctrl.SendMessage performs on a control, so no .Handle is needed.
PostMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Queue the message to the form's window and answer whether it was queued, without waiting for it to be handled. The same operation ctrl.PostMessage performs on a control.

Control factory methods

These build a control and hand it back, and they belong to the FORM because the form is what holds it: a control cannot make a sibling. The kinds they return are described in the Controls entry, which is about the controls themselves.

Every one of them takes an optional trailing configure callback, and so does Application.CreateForm (and the two MDI hosts). The callback runs on the thing the factory just made, AFTER it was parented and given its window, and the factory still returns that same instance. The two spellings are equivalent, and they mix freely; the callback one says "create and finish this" in one statement, which is what a form with many controls reads best as:

// the form itself takes the callback too, so the whole window is one statement var form = Application.CreateForm("player", (frm) => { frm.Width = 520; frm.Height = 240; frm.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; }); // the statement-by-statement spelling of two controls var btn = form.CreateButton("OK", 10, 10, 100, 30); btn.Enabled = false; btn.Click = fun(Control sender) { print("ok"); }; var list = form.CreateListBox(8, 50, 220, 120); list.AddItem("one"); list.SelectedIndex = 0; // the same two controls, created and finished in the statement that makes them form.CreateButton("OK", 10, 10, 100, 30, (b) => { b.Enabled = false; b.Click = fun(Control sender) { print("ok"); }; }); form.CreateListBox(8, 50, 220, 120, (l) => { l.AddItem("one"); l.SelectedIndex = 0; }); form.Show();

Four rules it keeps. It runs after the control is adopted, so .Handle is real and form.Controls already holds it. Its parameter is the concrete type (CheckBox, ListBox, Form), so a cast is never needed. A form's callback runs only on a form that call created, never on a reused one (with SingleInstance on, the second CreateForm hands the first window back and its callback does not run again: use Application.FindForm for a get-or-create). And an argument that is not callable is REFUSED by name rather than ignored.

ScrollBar = true gives a control the engine’s own NARROW bar. Windows paints a native scrollbar in the theme’s colours and offers no supported call to change them (measured on five theme variants, all the light 0xF0F0F0 face), so a dark form read its bar as a white stripe. With ScrollBar the native bar is not asked for at all: the engine draws a strip about 45% of the native width, in the host’s background with a blended thumb, keeps the text off it with EM_SETRECT, and drives the control itself: a click in the track pages, the wheel moves three lines, the thumb can be dragged, and the pointer over the strip is not the class’s own cursor (a RichEdit gives its whole client an I-beam, and the strip lives inside it): the THUMB takes the hand, the track the plain arrow, and the text keeps its I-beam. Supported on a multiline EDIT and a RichEdit; any other control is refused by name. The window must be created WITHOUT WS_VSCROLL: a class puts that bit back once it has one, so the setter refuses a window that already carries a bar and names the fix. A multiline EDIT/RichEdit also turns WS_VSCROLL on and off by itself from its content, which is why a native bar disappears while the text fits.
CreateLabel(text, x, y, w, h)Label static text.
CreateButton(text, x, y, w, h)Button clickable with .Click event.
CreateTextBox(text, x, y, w, h), CreateRichTextBox(text, x, y, w, h)TextBox is a single-line or multi-line EDIT with a .Text property; RichTextBox is the class that formats each RUN, which is what a coloured log needs, and it WRAPS by default (a rich text box is read rather than typed into, and a long line has no horizontal bar to reach its end): a RichEdit takes its wrap when its window is CREATED, so set .WordWrap before the control is shown. .WindowClass answers the class it really got (RICHEDIT50W, RichEdit20W, or EDIT when neither library is there), which is what a tool reports or checks before it colours a run. The rich one picks its own Windows class once per process (RICHEDIT50W from msftedit, RichEdit20W as the fallback, EDIT last) and both take .WordWrap.
CreateCheckBox(text, x, y, w, h, [checked])CheckBox toggle with .Checked property.
CreateRadioButton(text, x, y, w, h, [checked])RadioButton mutually exclusive option.
CreateListBox(x, y, w, h)ListBox scrollable list with AddItem(), SelectedItem, SelectedIndex.
CreateComboBox(x, y, w, h)ComboBox dropdown list with AddItem(), SelectedItem.
CreateTrackBar(x, y, w, h)TrackBar slider with Minimum, Maximum, Value and an assignable .Scroll handler (fires on user drag).
CreateTreeView(x, y, w, h)TreeView hierarchical tree with InsertItem(text, parent, insertAfter), Expand(item, expand), SelectedItem, GetItemText(item). Note: InsertItem has a struct marshalling issue on x64 items return valid handles but TVM_GETCOUNT may report 0.
CreateListView(x, y, w, h)ListView tabular grid with InsertColumn(index, text, width), InsertItem(index, text), SetItemText(row, col, text), ItemCount, DeleteItem(index), BeginUpdate() and EndUpdate(). Created double buffered, and a refill costs one repaint when it is wrapped in BeginUpdate() / EndUpdate(). Fill it in place with ItemCount to overwrite the rows that exist and DeleteItem for the tail, rather than clearing first: a cleared list is a state the screen can show, so refresh it when its rows actually change rather than on every interaction.
CreateStatusBar(x, y, w, h)StatusBar bottom status pane (_partWidths={-1} fills width, SB_SETBKCOLOR sets dark background).
CreateTabControl(x, y, w, h)TabControl tabbed panel with AddTab(text). Adding a tab and letting the message pump run both work: a tab control made this way reports TCM_GETITEMCOUNT = 2 after two AddTab calls and survives the dispatch the old note here warned about, so the raw SysTabControl32 workaround is retired.
CreateDateTimePicker(x, y, w, h)DateTimePicker date picker control.
CreateToolBar(x, y, w, h)ToolBar common control toolbar.
CreateSysLink(text, x, y, w, h)SysLink hyperlink control.
CreateHotKey(x, y, w, h)HotKey hotkey input.
CreateRebar(x, y, w, h)Rebar rebar container.
CreateWinControl(className, text, x, y, w, h, [style], [exStyle])GenericControl any Win32 class via CreateWindowExW. Registered in Controls collection.

Quitting, and what each call does to the other windows. The two verbs are not the same act: one stops the RUN and one stops a WINDOW, and only a form you close yourself goes away.

callwhat it closesthe exit code
Application.Quit([code])Nothing. Every form you opened is still standing when Run returns, with its window intact, and closing them stays your script's job.code, when it is not 0. This is the code the process leaves with if the script then ends normally.
form.Quit([code])That form only, exactly as its Close() does. Any OTHER form is still up and the run has ended, so its window outlives the loop.code, when it is not 0.
form.Close()That form only. The run ends when it was the LAST form, which is why a Close on one of several leaves the loop pumping.None: the process keeps the code it already has.

A 0 is deliberately not assigned, so it cannot force the process back to 0 once a non-zero code is set: use a real code, or exit(0), which is the script's own verdict. With several quits in one run the LAST one posted is the one that survives, because the loop drains what is left of its queue on the way out. To close two windows and leave one code, close both and quit once: a.Close(); b.Quit(7);

form.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; form.StartPosition = 1; // Center form.CreateLabel("Name:", 20, 20, 60, 25); form.CreateTextBox("John", 90, 20, 200, 25); form.CreateButton("OK", 200, 100, 60, 25);
Controls UI What every control shares, the kinds a form creates, and the styles, messages, tooltips and events they answer

Every control comes from a factory on its form (form.CreateButton(...)) and each one is a window the engine wraps, so the members below are shared by all of them, the form included. What is NOT here is what a single kind has on its own: a Checked, an AddItem(), a Minimum, the cell members of a ListView. Those are named in the factory row below and in that kind's own entry.

Every control the factories return comes up carrying WS_TABSTOP, and Tab and Shift+Tab move the focus between them IN TABINDEX ORDER: the engine answers those two keys itself, before a key can reach a control and become a character in it, which is what a Tab used to be inside a multi-line input. The order is sorted by TabIndex with ties following the order the controls were added, and it SKIPS anything that cannot take the focus (not a tab stop, disabled, or hidden, the last two asked of the window so a disabled or hidden parent counts). A control that becomes a tab stop is FOCUSED as well, which is what makes the change visible, and the focus cue is turned back on with it, since Windows hides that cue after mouse input. A label is the one exception: a STATIC takes no focus, so Tab has nothing to stop on there. A Form is not one either, and that is not a choice: WS_TABSTOP is the same bit as WS_MAXIMIZEBOX, so a form given one grows a maximise box.

Every control also carries an Id: unique in the process, assigned as its window is created and carried as the window's own child id, so WM_COMMAND reports it and form.GetId(id) finds the control by it. GetId() is the same value as a method, and GetId(id) is the control BEHIND an id, so form.GetId(15).Handle reaches a control a script built dynamically without keeping its handle anywhere. An id no live control carries answers null.

Members every control shares

GetId(), GetId(idOrHandle)The control's own ID, the same value as a method, and the control BACK from EITHER a number or a window: form.GetId(15).Handle and form.GetId(btn.Handle).Handle reach the same control, so a script never has to know which of the two it holds. An id is asked of the window first (the Win32 way) and a handle is answered by the engine's registry, where a handle is unique in the process. The id IS the window's Win32 child id, read live FROM the window, so a script that assigns one itself with SetWindowLongPtr is not a second mechanism. It belongs to CHILD windows: a Form's own id is 0, because GWLP_ID is the low word of the slot a top-level window keeps its menu handle in. Auto ids start at 0x8000, above the ids Win32 reserves (1 is IDOK) and the range a resource editor hands out; 0 is a window that does not exist yet, a number nothing carries, or one that has no child id at all.
ClassHandlesMouseSet true when this control's own Windows class must see its mouse messages first, which the engine steps aside for: it takes no capture on the press and does not forward them to the script handlers. The engine already does this for the classes it knows (a ListBox, a TrackBar, a DateTimePicker and the rest, because taking the capture cancelled what they had pending), so this is the same rule for a class that list does not name. Default false, which is the engine's normal handling.
SetMenu(menu)Wear a MENU as this window's bar, and the id of the item that fired, read inside the Command handler. The Menu type itself is its own entry below, with the items, the submenus and the popups.
MessageBox(text [, caption] [, type])Say something on THIS window, owned by it. With no window to own the box, the BARE global MessageBox(text [, caption] [, type]) is the same call with a null owner, which is what a tool that has no window prompts with; it is not on a namespace because nobody owns it. A message box wants an owner's handle and a control already holds one, so the receiver IS the owner: form.MessageBox("Saved", "Status") is the whole call, with the plumbing done. The typing matches the handle-taking spelling, TYPE flags included (1024 is MB_SYSTEMMODAL), and the return is the button the user chose.
Invalidate([x, y, width, height]), InvalidateUnion(x1, y1, w1, h1, x2, y2, w2, h2)Mark the control for REPAINTING. With no arguments the whole client, which is what a script that changed a drawing asks for; with the four numbers, just that rectangle, in client coordinates. InvalidateUnion takes two rectangles and invalidates the union, which is the drag shape: the only pixels that can have changed are where the control WAS and where it IS. A three-argument form takes the old origin and an OBJECT, and reads X, Y, W and H off it by name: the caller knows where the thing was, and the thing knows its own place and size. The engine owns the arithmetic, so a caller does not compute it, and the two are the reason a drag does not repaint a form's whole grid and flicker.
WindowRectThe window's OWN rectangle, which is what the control BECAME rather than what was asked for: Left/Top/Width/Height are the request, and the two differ whenever the engine adjusted it.
ClientRect, ClientWidth, ClientHeightThe CLIENT rectangle: the room this control can actually paint in, which is WindowRect minus the frame and any scrollbar the window reserved. A layout that wants to know how much space it has wants THIS one. The two singles are that rectangle's size in DESIGN units, the same units as Left, Top, Width and Height, so they can be compared with the geometry of what was placed in the window; a FORM publishes both as document rows.
DpiThe DPI of the monitor this window is ON, read from the window rather than remembered, so a form moved between two monitors answers differently. 0 before the window exists, which is how a caller tells "not created" from a real reading.
ReferenceDpiThe DPI this form's DESIGN measurements were written against (the system's, i.e. the primary monitor's), as opposed to Dpi, which is the monitor the window is on right now. A script that lays controls out itself in pixels needs both: the gaps and offsets it authored are design units while a control's Width comes back in pixels, so round(design * form.Dpi / form.ReferenceDpi) is the whole conversion, and on the reference monitor it answers the design value unchanged.
Focused, SetFocus([idOrHandle])Whether the control holds the keyboard focus, and the way to take it, which turns the focus cue back on with it. With an argument it focuses a control OF THIS WINDOW, named by an id or a window handle, which is what a form needs to focus something it only has a number for. The pair a script uses instead of fetching a handle and calling into the API.
TabIndexWhere the control sits in its container's TAB ORDER, the VB property: 0 is the first stop. It is an ORDERING VALUE and nothing else, independent of the handle, the id and the Z-order position, and two controls may share one, in which case the tie follows the order they were added. Nothing moves when it is set, and a control starts at the place it was created in.
SetBounds(x, y, width, height)Places and sizes in ONE call, in design units. Left/Top/Width/Height are four properties and each one moves the window on its own, so laying out a form with them pays four window calls for what this pays one.
MoveWindow(x, y, width, height [, repaint])Place and size in PIXELS, which is what a layout computed from a window rectangle needs: SetBounds above is the same job in DESIGN units, and the two do not convert into each other. The last argument repaints the window and defaults to true.
ToTop(), ToBottom()Move the control to the top or the bottom of its siblings' Z-ORDER, without moving, resizing or activating it. A control created LATER sits above an earlier one, which is why a size handle has to be raised as it is positioned, and something drawn behind a control (a ring around a selected one) has to be sent down.
SetFont([name] [, size] [, bold])The font in one call, through the same three properties a script can set one by one, so the two cannot disagree: a name left out keeps the engine's font, a size of 0 the engine's size.
Invalidate()Marks the control for repainting, which is what a script that changes a DRAWING asks for. Nothing is painted here and nothing waits: the engine deliberately avoids the synchronous redraws that flicker.
Theme (on a form)A RichTextBox follows it like every other text surface: its client is its own, so it is given the host's background and ink (a Custom palette first, else the leg's pair) unless the script set a colour itself, and switching back to light hands both back. An MDI frame hands the leg to its DOCUMENT WINDOWS as well, whose own dark flag and colour palette are what colour the controls inside them. A CheckBox and a RadioButton take NO theme sub-app under a dark or Custom host, because a themed toggle paints its own face while it is held down: that face is the theme's button colour, and on a dark panel it read as a grey band across the whole control and its caption. With no sub-app the toggle keeps the host's colour in every state and its feedback is the glyph.
PaintsHow many times this window has been asked to paint. It is the instrument a "it flickers" report needs: a child's WM_PAINT is not forwarded to a script handler, so no script could otherwise count them. Read it around a change to tell a repaint storm from a single repaint (measured on the clipboard runner's Wrap toggle, 3 paints of the rebuilt box before the bracket below existed and 1 after it).
BeginUpdate(), EndUpdate()Freeze this control's painting for a bulk change and repaint ONCE at the end, which is what a fill or a rebuild needs: outside the bracket a bulk write pays a paint per item the pump happens to dispatch, inside it pays none, and EndUpdate repaints the control and its children exactly once. It works on ANY control, a FORM included, and freezing the form is the shape a panel uses when it replaces one of its children: the band the destroyed child leaves is the form's own background, so the form is what has to be frozen. The pair is a hint rather than a lock, so an unmatched EndUpdate just repaints.
UpdateWindow()Paint it NOW, synchronously, where Invalidate() only marks it dirty. The exception rather than the rule, because a synchronous redraw is the flicker the engine avoids, so reach for it when something has to be on screen before the next statement: reading pixels back, or any measurement of a drawing.
Text, AppendText(text), Hide()The caption or content. AppendText adds to it in place, which is what keeps a log box from flashing where re-assigning Text repaints the lot; Hide() is Visible = false.
TextLengthThe number of characters in the text, in ONE message and without building the string, for a check that runs on every pass. It counts a line break the way Text reads it, so it is NOT the position SelectionStart and Select use: a RichEdit addresses its content with one character per break.
AppendText(text, rgb)Append one run IN ONE COLOUR, which is what a log needs: the call inserts the text and colours exactly the run it added, with the same colour path SetTextColor uses. A control that is not a RichEdit appends the text and ignores the colour, because a plain EDIT has no per-run format.
SelectionStart, SelectionLength, SelectedTextThe selection, in the control's OWN character positions: assigning the start moves the caret and keeps the length, assigning the length keeps the start. A RichEdit counts a line break as ONE character while its Text reads two, so the two numbers are not text offsets. SelectedText is the range itself, which is what a Find feature reports, and ASSIGNING it replaces that range in one message: an empty string deletes it, which is how a companion column trims itself when the text it numbers gets shorter (and it touches nothing outside the range, so no whole-document write and no repaint of the lot).
Select(start, end), SelectAll()Set the range in the same positions SelectionStart reads, or take the whole text. A NEGATIVE position is refused rather than clamped, because LineIndex answers -1 for a line the control has no layout for yet and clamping that to 0 selects the whole document: guard it, or ask LineIndex(LineCount) for the end position, which is in the same unit.
LineCount, LineIndex(n), FirstVisibleLine, ScrollToCaret(), CharPosition(index)The rows of a text control. LineCount counts what a READER sees, so a text that ends with a line break is not given a phantom last row (a RichEdit's own count does that), an empty document is ZERO rows, and a WRAPPED line contributes one row per row it takes, which is the unit LineIndex and CharPosition speak. LineIndex turns a line into a position for Select, and answers -1 for a line past the end or one the control has not laid out yet: that -1 is a real answer to check, never a 0. FirstVisibleLine reads and sets the row at the top, which is how a second window beside a log follows it. ScrollToCaret() works on a read-only control nobody has clicked, where EM_SCROLLCARET alone scrolls nothing. CharPosition answers [x, y] in the control's client area, for lining up a companion window.
CharHeight, LineSpacingThe text's height and the row spacing, in TWIPS (1/1440 inch), which is the unit a RichEdit really uses. LineSpacing above zero states an EXACT row height, the shape that keeps two controls' rows equal whatever a line holds (a line carrying a glyph the ASCII metrics do not cover draws 2 px taller); zero returns to the control's single spacing.
ReadOnlybool. A text control refuses EDITS while still allowing selection, copying and scrolling, because this is the control's own state rather than a style bit. A control with no such notion remembers the value and ignores it, so one flag can be set on a panel without checking what it holds.
HasKeyboardFocusbool: whether the keyboard focus is on this control OR anywhere inside it, which is the question a panel asks before deciding that a copied value came from itself.
TextHeightPxThe height the control's font is DRAWN at, in pixels for the control's own DPI: the number the font was created with. A companion window lining its rows up with the text needs it, and it cannot be reproduced from FontSize alone because the monitor's DPI and the engine's default size are part of the arithmetic.
Left, Top, Width, HeightPosition and size in design pixels, scaled with the DPI. Assigning one re-applies the window bounds.
Visible, Enabledbool. A disabled control's text takes ThemeDisabled on a Custom form.
DockA DockStyle, so it is written with the enum's own names: DockStyle.None, .Left, .Top, .Right, .Bottom or .Fill. The whole number is accepted too (4 is DockStyle.Bottom), but the name is the spelling to prefer. Docking is re-applied by the engine on every resize and after a DPI change, so a docked control stays docked when the window moves between monitors. A Dock assignment REPLACES the position the control was created with, so the coordinates in a Create... call are what an UNDOCKED control gets.
Margin, MarginLeft, MarginTop, MarginRight, MarginBottomThe inset a DOCKED control keeps inside the band the layout gives it, in design pixels and scaled with the DPI like the container's Padding. Margin sets all four sides and a side set on its own WINS, so box.Margin = 4; box.MarginLeft = 20; is 20 on the left and 4 everywhere else; a side set to -1 hands it back to Margin. This is what stands one docked box off an edge without padding the whole container, and an absolutely positioned control ignores it, having been put where it belongs. A negative value is refused by name.
FontName, FontSize, FontBoldThe control's own font. The engine applies it to the window, and a control the engine paints itself selects it for its drawing.
TextColor, BackgroundColorA colour pair, written 0xRRGGBB, that WINS over the form's theme or palette; left unset it follows the form. A Custom form's palette is what a child takes when it sets neither. A RichTextBox takes the background through its own message, so the value reaches its client like any other control's.
SetTextColor(rgb)The colour of the text this control holds RIGHT NOW, written 0xRRGGBB like every other colour: on a RichEdit it colours the CURRENT SELECTION, which is how a log paints the run it just inserted (with nothing selected the whole text takes it), and on any other control it is TextColor. The byte order a control message wants is derived inside, so a script never has to swap red and blue: handing a raw value to EM_SETCHARFORMAT's crTextColor paints a red as violet.
ScrollBarbool, a NARROW bar drawn by the engine instead of the native one: 45% of the metric wide, in the host’s background with a blended thumb, and it drives the control (a track click pages, the wheel moves three lines, the thumb drags, and the pointer is the hand over the thumb and the arrow over the track). The text is kept off it with EM_SETRECT. A multiline EDIT and a RichEdit only, and the window must be created without WS_VSCROLL, which is what the refusal names.
Handle, Parent, Name, TagThe HWND (IntPtr, usable as long), the control it sits in, a script-side name, and a slot for anything a script wants to hang on it.
ClientToScreen(x, y), GetPixel(x, y)A client point as screen coordinates, and a client pixel. A pixel is a COLORREF (0x00BBGGRR), so compare colours through a colour property rather than through one, and a point outside the client answers CLR_INVALID rather than a colour.
ReadStyle([bEx]), HasStyle(name), SetStyle(name, on)The style word as a number, a style FLAG asked by its NAME (HasStyle("WS_BORDER")), and one set by name. bEx selects the extended word. ModStyle, StyleAdd and StyleRemove take bits rather than a name, which is what the block below covers.
Dispose()Releases the control's window. A using block disposes it at the end of its scope, which is the shorter spelling of the same thing.
SetWindowHandler(fn)Sends THIS window's messages to fun(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam), whose answer is the result Windows gets. It is the one hook a script has for a message the engine does not name, and a handler forwards what it does not take to DefWindowProc.
DefWindowProc(msg, wParam, lParam)Windows' own handling of a message for this window, which is what a handler answers for the messages it does not take (and what keeps the window valid underneath the handler).
CallWindowProc(previous, msg, wParam, lParam)Sends a message to a window procedure a script already holds, which is how a chain of handlers is kept going.

A docked control's inset is its own Margin, and the number written is the distance it gets. Padding belongs to the WINDOW (it insets every docked edge equally, and is what keeps a docked box's scrollbars off the frame); Margin belongs to the CONTROL, per side, and REPLACES the padding on the sides it names, so one docked box can stand 20 px off the left while the rest of the window keeps its padding. Between two controls the same number is the gap between them. A side set on its own wins over Margin, and -1 hands a side back to it:

// this left edge is at 20, whatever the padding says
logBox.Dock = DockStyle.Fill;
logBox.MarginLeft = 20;

// all four sides; a side set on its own wins, and -1 hands a side back to Margin
logBox.Margin = 4;
logBox.MarginLeft = -1;

// 0 is an answer of its own: flush with the client edge, padding included
logBox.MarginLeft = 0;

A text colour is 0xRRGGBB however it is built, and SetTextColor takes it that way too. On a RichEdit it colours the CURRENT SELECTION, which is what a log needs (it paints the run it has just inserted); with nothing selected the whole text takes it, and on any other control it is the same as TextColor. The one value that must NOT be handed to it is a GetPixel reading: that is a COLORREF, so convert it with Colors.FromPixel first.

// the forms the argument takes: a literal, a named colour, or one composed from its parts
logBox.SetTextColor(0xE05252);              // a red, written as every other colour is
logBox.SetTextColor(Colors.Red);            // the same red by name
logBox.SetTextColor(Colors.RGB(224, 82, 82));   // and composed

// a RichEdit's per-run colour: select the range, then colour it. This is what a log does per entry.
logBox.SendMessage(EM_SETSEL, start, end);
logBox.SetTextColor(0x4FC3F7);                 // the run just selected

// the WHOLE control, through the property (a RichEdit takes it on all of its text)
logBox.TextColor = 0xF0F0F0;

// a colour read off the screen has to be converted first: a pixel is a COLORREF
logBox.SetTextColor(Colors.FromPixel(logBox.GetPixel(4, 4)));

A Fill box with form.Padding = 4 and MarginLeft = 20 starts at x = 20 with its right side still on the padding, and a Bottom bar with MarginBottom = 6 leaves 6 px below it. The value is in design pixels and scales with the DPI like Padding, only the DOCK layout reads it (an absolutely positioned control already sits where it was put), and a negative value is refused by name.

A control is MADE by the form that holds it: form.CreateButton("OK", 8, 8, 80, 24) and the rest of the factories are Form methods, listed under Form.

Window styles and window messages (on every control)

ctrl.ModStyle(add, remove [, bEx])Add add and remove remove in one change, then re-apply the frame.
ctrl.StyleAdd(bits [, bEx])Add one or more WS_* style bits.
ctrl.StyleRemove(bits [, bEx])Remove one or more WS_* style bits.
ctrl.SendMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Send a window message to the control's own window and return the message's result.
ctrl.PostMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Queue the message and answer whether it was queued, without waiting for it to be handled.

These are the raw-HWND operations applied to the control's own handle, so a wrapped control needs no .Handle in the call. They exist on every control the factories return (button, text box, check box, status bar, tab, and the form itself), and bEx = true selects the extended style word (GWL_EXSTYLE: WS_EX_*) instead of the plain one (GWL_STYLE: WS_*). Read a word back with ctrl.GetWindowLongPtr(-16) (plain) or -20 (extended), and write one with ctrl.SetWindowLongPtr(-16, word), the pair's two halves:

// a status bar pinned to the bottom of its form, with a raised edge var bar = form.CreateStatusBar(0, 0, 200, 24); bar.StyleAdd(0x00800000); // WS_BORDER bar.StyleAdd(0x00000200, true); // WS_EX_CLIENTEDGE, on the extended word bar.ModStyle(0x00200000, 0x00800000); // add WS_VSCROLL, drop WS_BORDER, in ONE change bar.StyleRemove(0x00000200, true); // take the extended edge back off // the same bar through the configure callback: no variable, and the style work happens where the control is born form.CreateStatusBar(0, 0, 200, 24, (sb) => { sb.StyleAdd(0x00800000); sb.StyleAdd(0x00000200, true); });

The two message members are the same raw-HWND operation applied to the control's own handle, so no .Handle appears in the call. They exist on every control the factories return, and on the form itself. PostMessage answers a boolean, so it reads directly as a condition:

// expand a tree item, then scroll a log box down one line, with no handle in sight tree.SendMessage(0x1102, 2, item); // TVM_EXPAND, TVE_EXPAND var queued = log.PostMessage(0x0115, 0, 0); // WM_VSCROLL, SB_LINEUP, answered true or false

Use the handle-taking spelling for a window nothing wraps: both doors make the same call.

A tooltip on any control

ctrl.SetToolTip(text)Attach the control's tooltip, or change its text if it already has one. Returns the tooltip's window handle.

This is the handle-taking tooltip call applied to the control's own handle, and it is the same tooltip: one per window, created on the first call, re-texted after that rather than given a second tool, and destroyed with the control. A window the engine does not wrap keeps working through the handle-taking spelling, whose tooltip is created once per handle and kept for the process.

// both spellings reach the SAME tooltip for a wrapped control var box = form.CreateTextBox("", 12, 12, 200, 24); var tip = box.SetToolTip("Type the account number here"); box.SetToolTip("Type the account number (8 digits)"); // same window, new text // and the same box created with its tip already on it form.CreateTextBox("", 12, 12, 200, 24, (tb) => { tb.SetToolTip("Type the account number (8 digits)"); });

Events (assign as script functions)

ResizeEventfun(Form sender, ResizeEventArgs e) called on WM_SIZE: e.Width and e.Height are the new client size.
Commandfun(Form sender, CommandEventArgs e) menu commands (WM_COMMAND), where e.Id is the id the item was added with, and WM_NOTIFY notifications, where e.Id is 0x10000 + code. A notification is not a command, and the ones a control sends while it paints arrive here too (a themed control's custom draw is 0x10000 + NM_CUSTOMDRAW, twice per paint), so dispatch on the ids you know. e.Time, and e.UtcDateTime for a date, say WHEN the message arrived: two events with the same time are one delivery seen again, which is what a handler that must act once compares.
Timerfun(Form sender, TimerEventArgs e) WM_TIMER from a Win32 timer armed on the form: e.TimerId is the one that fired.
Closingfun(Form sender, CancelEventArgs e) set e.Cancel = true to prevent close.
Closedfun(Form sender, CancelEventArgs e) after the form has closed.
AcceptDroppedFilesWhether this WINDOW takes a dragged file, and the switch that turns it on: a window that never accepted a drop is sent none, so a DropFiles handler needs this set to be reached at all. It is the window's WS_EX_ACCEPTFILES bit, so a script reads the state back, and turning it off stops the drops. It is on every control and not only on a form, because the drop goes to the window under the cursor: a RichEdit that covers its form takes drops of its own, and so does a button.
DropFilesfun(Control sender, DropFilesEventArgs e) files dropped via WM_DROPFILES, for ANY window whose AcceptDroppedFiles is on: a form, a button, a RichEdit, a GenericControl. Every window needs its own, and that is Win32 rather than this engine: the message goes to the window under the cursor and is never passed up to the parent, so a control that covers its host is the only window that sees the drop. The event answers the FILES (e.FileCount(), e.FileName(i)), and the engine releases the drop list when the handler returns, so a script never allocates a buffer or calls DragFinish. The raw handle is still there as e.HDrop for a caller that needs it. Do not subclass a control to get its drops: SetWindowHandler REPLACES the engine's window proc, and with it the painting, the theme and the colours the control had.
KeyDownfun(Form sender, KeyEventArgs e) WM_KEYDOWN: e.KeyCode is the numeric virtual-key (0x74 is F5, 65 is A), e.KeyValue the same key as a NAME, and e.Alt / e.Control / e.Shift the modifiers held at the key event.
Paintfun(Form sender, PaintEventArgs e) custom GDI painting. The DC is the one the engine already holds (e.Hdc, with the clip rect as e.Left/e.Top/e.Right/e.Bottom), and the drawing members work THROUGH it so nothing fetches a second one: e.Fill(x, y, w, h, color) a solid rectangle, e.Frame(x, y, w, h, color [, lineWidth]) an outline, e.Disc(x, y, w, h, color) a filled ellipse, e.Ellipse(x, y, w, h, color [, lineWidth]) an outline ellipse, e.Line(x1, y1, x2, y2, color [, lineWidth]), e.Text(x, y, text [, color]) at a point and e.Text(text, x, y, w, h, color [, format]) inside a box with DrawText's flags, e.SetTextColor/e.SetBkMode/e.SetBkColor for the colour that follows (GDI keeps it, the way it does for VBA). Each of those makes and deletes what it needs, so a repaint loop leaks nothing; a script that wants a HANDLE of its own calls e.CreateBrush/e.CreatePen, selects it with e.SelectObject (which answers the object it displaced, so it can be put back), draws with e.Stroke/e.StrokeEllipse/e.StrokeLine/e.FillRect (the DC's current pen or brush), and then e.DeleteObject. e.StockObject(5) is the hollow brush and e.StockObject(8) the no-line pen. A THEMED part of this window is drawn the same way: e.ThemePart(windowClass, part, state, x, y, w, h) and e.ThemeText(windowClass, part, state, text, x, y, w, h [, flags]) open and close the theme handle around the one call, so a repaint cannot leak one, and both answer -1 when this machine has no theme for that class.
EraseBackgroundfun(object sender, nint hdc) return true to prevent default background erase (flicker reduction).
Loadfun(Form sender, EventArgs e) once, on the first Show(), after the window is on screen. The window itself exists from Application.CreateForm (hidden), so this is the event that marks "about to be seen", and a handler assigned right after CreateForm still runs: build everything, attach the handlers, then Show(). A form that is never shown never raises it, and showing a form again does not raise it twice.
SetWindowHandlerfun(long hwnd, long msg, long wParam, long lParam) EVERY window message, the ones the engine does not name included, and it is a member rather than an event: its answer is what Windows gets back, so a handler returns DefWindowProc(msg, wParam, lParam) for the messages it does not take. This is how a script receives WM_CLIPBOARDUPDATE from AddClipboardFormatListener (the recipe is in the Clipboard entry), a notification from a native library, or a message another process posts to the window.

Child control events

Click, DoubleClickfun(Control sender, EventArgs e)
MouseDown, MouseUp, MouseMovefun(Control sender, MouseEventArgs e)
GotFocus, LostFocusfun(Control sender, EventArgs e)
Event payloads are fixed by the raise site, not by the handler's declared parameter types. Form-level events (Closing, Closed) deliver sender = Form and a real CancelEventArgs instance Closing is the single veto point: e.Cancel = true prevents the close. Control events (Click, DoubleClick, MouseDown, …) deliver sender = the control (e.g. Button) and a plain EventArgs the click already happened, so there is nothing to cancel: e.Cancel fails with "Property 'Cancel' not found on type EventArgs", and e as CancelEventArgs returns null because EventArgs (a struct) and CancelEventArgs (a class) are unrelated types. Declared handler parameter types are decorative: the engine passes the raw payload regardless (named-object coercion is a pass-through), so a handler typed fun(Form sender, CancelEventArgs e) on a button's Click runs silently with (Button, EventArgs) and the mismatch is only visible when you touch e.Cancel. Prefer untyped fun(sender, e) and inspect the real runtime types with typeof(sender) / typeof(e). To veto a close triggered from a button, set e.Cancel = true in the form's Closing handler instead.
Full demo: assets/ui/demos/rich_editor.slc
Menu UI A menu bar or a popup, built by name: the items, the submenus, and the Command event a click arrives as
