A menu is built BY NAME rather than by handle, the same division ClassHandlesMouse and the Invalidate family make: the ids and the Win32 flags are the engine's, and the words are the script's. Menu.Create() is a bar for a window, Menu.CreatePopup() a context menu, and a submenu is a popup added to another menu, so the object that owns an item is always the one it was added on. Nothing needs a menu handle: form.SetMenu applies one and Menu.Of reads back what a window wears.

Menu members

Menu.Create(), Menu.CreatePopup()Both return a DISPOSABLE object. An empty MENU, for a window's bar, and an empty POPUP, which is a context menu or a submenu. Each starts with no items, and each owns a Win32 handle that Dispose() destroys, or a using block at the end of its scope.
Add(text, id)Append an item. The id is the number the click will report, which is what a handler compares against; the text is what the user reads, and a & in it marks the accelerator ("&File" underlines the F).
AddSeparator()A divider, which is what a menu wants between groups rather than a blank item. It carries no id and cannot be picked.
AddPopup(text)Add a SUBMENU and ANSWER it, so its items are added on the object that owns them. It appends to whatever menu it is called ON, so a popup holds a submenu as well as a bar does: var recent = file.AddPopup("&Recent"); is a submenu inside a popup, and it nests further (recent.AddPopup("More")). A nested item still reports its own id to the form's Command event, however deep it sits: var file = m.AddPopup("&File"); file.Add("&Open...", 1001);. Any depth works, since a submenu is itself a menu.
Popup(owner), Popup(owner, x, y)Show this menu as a CONTEXT menu: with no point, at the CURSOR, which is what a right-click wants; with x and y, at a point the caller names, which is what a keyboard menu wants. It returns when a pick is made or the menu is dismissed, and a pick arrives through the SAME Command event a bar item uses, so there is one handler for both.
Menu.Of(form)The menu a window is WEARING, or null. It asks the WINDOW rather than remembering, so it agrees with what is really applied, and a form with no menu answers null.
Dispose()Destroy the menu and its items. A using block disposes it at the end of its scope, the shorter spelling of the same thing. Take a bar off its window with form.SetMenu(null) before destroying it.

Where a click arrives, and the one order that matters

An item is picked from either place through the same event, so a script writes one handler. The id the item was added with is read from e.Id, which the engine hands the handler, and the same object says WHEN it arrived: e.Time is the key for acting once, e.UtcDateTime the same moment as a UTC date for a log line.

CommandThe form's event, raised when a menu item is picked. It is the same event a control's notification arrives as, and both are the engine dispatching WM_COMMAND: a control carries its window in the message and a menu item carries nothing but the id, which is the whole difference.
e.Id, e.Time, e.UtcDateTime, e.Hwnde.Hwnd says WHICH window sent it: a CONTROL carries its own handle there, while a MENU item carries 0, because a menu is not a window and its id travels in the message instead. So e.Hwnd == 0 is how a handler tells "a menu item" from "a control" with no extra bookkeeping.

form.SetMenu(menu)Wear a menu as the window's bar; null takes the bar away without destroying the menu. A later SetMenu replaces the bar, and the engine does not destroy the one it replaced, so a script that builds bars in a loop owns what it replaces.

The handle has to exist first. A form has no window until it is shown, so a SetMenu called before Show() applies nothing and Menu.Of answers null; the same is true of a popup's owner. Set the bar after the window exists, which is where a Load handler runs. A pick is delivered by the message loop, so a program that builds a menu and ends never sees one: Application.Run() is what pumps it, which is why the sample below is a whole program rather than a fragment.

// a bar with a submenu, and a context menu on a right-click var form = Application.CreateForm("Menu demo"); form.Width = 480; form.Height = 220; form.Show(); // the window, and so the handle, exists from here var m = Menu.Create(); var file = m.AddPopup("&File"); file.Add("&Open...", 1001); file.AddSeparator(); file.Add("E&xit", 1000); m.Add("&Help", 1099); form.SetMenu(m); // a bar applies to a window that EXISTS, so Show comes first var pop = Menu.CreatePopup(); // a context menu: same items, same event pop.Add("Cut", 2001); pop.Add("Paste", 2002); form.Command = (s, e) => { // a bar item and a popup item both arrive HERE if (e.Id == 1000) form.Close(); // Exit if (e.Id == 1001) form.Text = "opened"; // Open if (e.Id >= 2001) form.MessageBox("popup item " + e.Id, "Menu", 0); // Cut or Paste, by its id }; form.MouseDown = (s, e) => { // the popup opens where the user points if (e.Button == MouseButtons.Right) pop.Popup(form, e.X, e.Y); // the NAME: MouseButtons is a script type here }; Application.Run(); // the loop that DELIVERS Command, returning when the last form closes form.SetMenu(null); // take a bar off before destroying the menu it pointed at m.Dispose(); pop.Dispose();

The event carries four values, and each has a job. e.Id is the id the item was added with. e.Time is the raw tick since boot, which is the key for acting ONCE: two events from one delivery carry the same value and a genuine second click a different one, and comparing two ticks needs no clock. e.UtcDateTime is that same moment as a UTC DateTime (its Kind is Utc), which is what a log line wants. e.Hwnd says WHICH window sent the event: a control carries its own handle there, while a menu item carries 0, because a menu is not a window and its id travels in the message instead. So e.Hwnd == 0 tells a menu pick from a control with no extra state.

A control answers the calls that want an hwnd. The handle-taking spelling stays for a window nothing wraps, and the receiver form is that same call with the plumbing done: form.MessageBox(text [, caption] [, type]), where the handle a script would have fetched and handed back is the one the control already holds. MessageBox is the first of these, and the flags are the same values the namespace takes (1024 is MB_SYSTEMMODAL). It is a member the engine adds ONE at a time, where the receiver can supply what the call needs and no engine name already claims it.

The Win32 namespace described in this chapter is the ESCAPE HATCH, and it is meant to stay that way. It is the way to reach a Windows call the engine does not wrap, and above all an EXTERNAL LIBRARY of your own through LoadLibrary and GetFunction, which is nobody else's business to wrap: var k = LoadLibrary("kernel32"); k.Sleep(50); k.FreeLibrary(); The library ANSWERS ITS EXPORTS by name, so no separate lookup call is needed to reach one: k.Sleep(50) is the call, and k.FreeLibrary() is a member of the library object rather than an export. LoadLibrary is a GLOBAL rather than a namespace member: it is the spelling, and the object it answers carries the exports. A call that is part of the engine's OWN model gets a receiver form instead, because the control already holds the handle and the call reads better without it. The two are not competitors: the namespace stays complete for what a script must reach on its own, and the doors grow where the model wants them.

A menu is IDisposable, so using scopes it. The teardown in the sample above is written out because the window outlives it; when a menu's whole life fits in one block, the shorter spelling is the language's own, and the scope disposes it on the way out:

using (var m = Menu.Create()) { m.Add("&About", 1099); form.SetMenu(m); form.SetMenu(null); // take the bar off first: a destroyed menu must not stay on a window } // and the scope disposes it here
Control props UI Design-time control metadata (typed property table)

Designer support used by the RAD form designer: each control's editable properties and its style flags as NAMED rows rather than positional arrays. PropList() answers ControlProp objects (Name, Type, Value) and StyleFlags() answers StyleFlag objects (Name, Bits, Extended, Field, Offered). Both are script types, so typeof(row) names one a script can write back. The table is compiled per kind, so a row costs no runtime reflection of its own.

ctrl.PropList()The control's editable properties, one ControlProp row each (a script type with Name, Type and Value). It IS the design table itself, so a designer and a script read the same one.
ctrl.GetProp(name)Current value of that property, from the same table; a name this kind does not carry throws.
ctrl.SetProp(name, value)Applies the value and returns 1, through the same validation the designer uses; an unsupported name throws. Writing the value the control ALREADY holds is a no-op rather than a write, because several of these setters do more than store (a FontSize re-applies a font) and a document that merely restates a property must not perturb the control it describes.
Style, ExStyleThe two WINDOW-STYLE WORDS, and they are rows like any other, so a saved document carries a control's style. A style is a bit field, so one row per flag would be the alternative: the WORD is what a document needs, and turning a flag into a bit is StyleFlags() and SetStyle.
ClientWidth, ClientHeightA FORM's client area in DESIGN units, the room its children were placed in. The rows exist so a document says the space its layout was designed against and a reader can check it; they are the one pair a row applier never writes, because a client area is what the frame left rather than a request.
ctrl.NameThe name its creator gave it: the designer entry name, or what a script assigned. A handler reads it to tell WHICH control it was handed. Empty until something sets it, and it is a row of the table above too, so GetProp("Name") answers the same thing.
These are the only spellings: the UiDesign and UiStyle namespaces that carried them are gone.
// the control is the door, and the table it reads is the designer's var rows = btn.PropList(); foreach (var row in rows) { print(row.Name + " (" + row.Type + ") = " + row.Value); } print(btn.GetProp("Text")); btn.SetProp("Left", 40); btn.SetProp("BackColor", 0x202020); // the same table whether the control is held as a typed Control or as a plain object

A handler is given the control that raised the event, and can inspect what it was given: s.Name is the name above, s.GetType() answers the control's own type (Button, TextBox, a Form for a form's own events) and that type's own properties read on it, so s.GetType().Name is the type name, s.GetType().FullName the full one and s.GetType().BaseType its parent. A type name written directly still means that type's STATIC members (DockStyle.Bottom), which is why the two never collide: statics are tried first.

A whole control serializes as this very table: Json.Serialize(s, true) in a handler answers the rows, one object per property with Name, Type and Value, for every kind including a Form.

An event's arguments serialize as what they carry: a mouse one answers its position AND what the mouse did (X, Y, Button, Clicks, Delta), a key one its key and modifiers (KeyCode, Alt, Control, Shift), and a click's are an empty object, because that event carries no data at all and the sender is the whole story. A key event answers both halves of a key: KeyCode is its numeric code (65, 123, 17) and KeyValue its name ("A", "F12", "Control"), one shape each whatever key it is. A resize answers its name and its size the same way (Event, Width, Height). A key pressed WHILE ALT IS HELD is reported like any other, and Alt reads as down for the whole combination, the Alt key's own release included.

EVERY value answers four reflection verbs, so code can act on members it cannot name at compile time: o.Get("member"), o.Set("member", value), o.Keys() for the names, and o.Call("member", args...). A handler can also tell WHICH event it is in: the sender records it (s.LastEvent) and the arguments carry the same name (e.Event), so one function can serve several events and still know which one it is answering. Keys() lists the names a script would write: a type that keeps backing fields beside its properties reports the properties, and a struct whose members are fields reports those. A Control answers its design table (the rows above, so Get("Text") and GetProp("Text") agree), a script class answers its fields and methods, and anything else answers its public members. A real member of the same name always wins over a verb, and a name the value does not carry refuses with that name.

Property table: every control exposes Name, Text, Left, Top, Width, Height, Visible, Enabled, FontName, FontSize, ForeColor, BackColor; plus Checked (CheckBox, RadioButton), Items (ListBox, ComboBox), and Minimum / Maximum / Value (TrackBar).

A CONTAINER also exposes its CONTENTS, because they are what a saved form cannot do without: Columns (List<ColumnProp>, each with Text and Width) and Items (a List<List<string>>, one entry per row and its cells in column order) on a ListView, Items (List<TreeItemProp>, each with Text and its own Children, so a tree stays a tree) on a TreeView, and Tabs (List<string>) on a TabControl. Each is READ off the control, so the table says what the control holds now, and writing one back goes through the same control members a script uses (InsertColumn, InsertItem, AddTab).

See assets/language/ui/demos/rad_designer.slc for the consumer.

Style flags UI Style-flag names, bits and the raw word (the design table's sibling)

The NAMES behind a style word. ModStyle, StyleAdd, StyleRemove and the control-side SetStyle / HasStyle / ReadStyle write and read the bits; this table says what the bits are called, so a panel can show what a control has and what it could have instead of a hex word.

ctrl.StyleFlags()Every flag THIS control's kind accepts, as StyleFlag row objects (a script type with Name, Bits, Extended, Field and Offered): the general WS_* / WS_EX_* entries plus that class's own (BS_*, SS_*, ES_*, CBS_*, LBS_*, LVS_*, TVS_*, DTS_*, TBS_*). offered is false for a flag a panel should not show: one that only means something on a top-level window, or one Windows owns.
// the names a panel shows, for the kind of control in hand: var flags = btn.StyleFlags(); foreach (var f in flags) { print(f.Name + " = 0x" + f.Bits); } // the control answers for itself, which is the spelling to prefer: if (btn.HasStyle("WS_BORDER")) { print("bordered"); } btn.SetStyle("WS_VSCROLL", true); print(btn.ReadStyle(false)); // the raw word those flags describe
A flag whose name is a value of a FIELD (a BS_TYPEMASK member, say) is set through SetStyle rather than OR-ed in: setting one value clears its siblings, so BS_CHECKBOX then BS_RADIOBUTTON cannot make 0x7. Offered is false for a flag a panel should not show (one that only means something on a top-level window, or one Windows owns), and Extended says which of the two words the flag lives in. The extended ListView and TreeView families (LVS_EX_*, TVS_EX_*) are deliberately absent: they travel through LVM_SETEXTENDEDLISTVIEWSTYLE / TVM_SETEXTENDEDSTYLE, not through the window's extended style word, so writing them as window styles would set nothing.
ListView UI A report or detail list: columns, rows, and the two cell rectangles an in-place editor needs

Created via form.CreateListView(x, y, w, h), which gives it full-row select, grid lines and double buffering. It is a SysListView32, so its colours do NOT follow the window theme the way a button's do: they come from SetThemeColors, which is also how a Custom form's palette reaches it.

Methods and properties

InsertColumn(index, text, width)Adds a column at that index and returns its index, or -1. The first column is the one a row's own text goes in.
SetColumnText(index, text)Renames a column's header, which GetColumnText reads back. The header's text is also one of the two things FitColumnsToContent sizes a column to, so a rename widens the column as well.
GetColumnText(index)A column's header text, the read that pairs with SetColumnText. Empty for a column that does not exist, and at most 1023 characters of a longer one, exactly as GetItemText reads a cell.
DeleteColumn(index)Removes a column. The columns to its right keep their order and move one index left, so a row's text then reads from the next column.
InsertItem(index, text)Adds a row at that index whose text lands in the first column, returning the row's index. Appending is InsertItem(lv.ItemCount, text).
SetItemText(row, col, text)Sets one cell's text, col 0 being the row's own text.
GetItemText(row, col)The text of one cell, the read that pairs with SetItemText. An empty string for a cell that does not exist, at most 1023 characters of a longer one, and asking never creates the window.
ItemCountThe rows it currently holds.
Clear()Removes every row; the columns stay.
DeleteItem(index)Removes one row.
SelectedIndexThe selected row, or -1 when none is selected. Assigning selects that row and clears the previous selection.
GetCellClientRect(row, col), GetCellRect(row, col)One cell's rectangle, as a Rect. The first is in the list's OWN client coordinates, for a control parented to the list; the second is in the PARENT form's, for a sibling of the list. Both answer Left and Top of -1 when there is no such cell.
CreateOverlayTextBox(text)An TextBox parented to the list, which is the in-place cell editor: position it with GetCellClientRect and show or hide it as the selection moves.
GetColumnWidth(col), SetColumnWidth(col, width)A column's width in pixels; SetColumnWidth refuses a width below 1.
FitColumnsToContent()Sizes every column to its widest cell plus its header (a floor of 24 px each) and then trims from the right until the total fits the client, so the list does not grow a horizontal scrollbar. Call it after filling the rows, and again after a DPI change.
BeginUpdate(), EndUpdate()Wrap a bulk fill so it costs ONE repaint instead of one per row. The pair lives on every control (see the Control rows), a form included; the note below says why a refill that OVERWRITES beats a clear-then-fill.
SetThemeColors(background, text)The two colours the control draws itself with, written 0xRRGGBB. This is the member a Custom form's palette colours a list view through, because the base colour properties only repaint and never tell a SysListView32 what to draw.
RaiseDoubleClick()Fires the control's DoubleClick handler without a mouse, which is how a test drives a row activation rather than posting a click at a guessed position.
SelectedIndexChangedAssign a handler and it runs when the selected ROW changes, by a click in the list or by an assignment to SelectedIndex. It is raised from the LVN_ITEMCHANGED notification, which is the item-state change rather than a tidied "the selection is now N", so it can arrive more than once for a single move; SelectedIndex is where the answer is read. The notification also reaches form.Command with its code packed into the id, which is the escape hatch for what the engine does not name.
RaiseSelectedIndexChanged()Fires that handler without touching the selection, for a test or a script that has to drive it.

A refill that overwrites is not the same as a clear followed by a fill. The cleared state is one a window can be PAINTED in: a form the engine composes repaints a child in the middle of a fill, and BeginUpdate does not suppress that, so a clear-then-fill list is seen empty for a frame. Read ItemCount, overwrite the rows that already exist, add only the missing ones and DeleteItem the tail:

// created with its two columns already in place, through the configure callback
var lv = form.CreateListView(12, 12, 360, 200, (list) => {
    list.InsertColumn(0, "Name", 140);
    list.InsertColumn(1, "Value", 90);
});

lv.BeginUpdate();
var row = 0;
foreach (var p in pairs) {
    if (row < lv.ItemCount) { lv.SetItemText(row, 0, p.Name); }   // overwrite what is there
    else { lv.InsertItem(lv.ItemCount, p.Name); }
    lv.SetItemText(row, 1, "" + p.Value);
    row = row + 1;
}
while (lv.ItemCount > row) { lv.DeleteItem(lv.ItemCount - 1); }
lv.EndUpdate();
lv.FitColumnsToContent();
InputBox UI A modal prompt: a title, a line of text and an input, answered or cancelled

Two spellings. Application.InputBox(title, prompt [, defaultValue [, defaultButton [, timeouts]]]) is the one-shot form: it returns what was typed, or null when it was cancelled or closed, so "cancelled" stays distinguishable from "entered nothing". Application.CreateInputBox() gives the OBJECT instead, for a prompt whose size, font, icon, screen or default button a script decides, and ShowDialog() then answers 1 when it was answered and 2 when it was cancelled or closed, with what was typed left in Value.

It is a window the engine assembles from its own Form and controls rather than a Win32 dialog template, which is what lets it take the theme of the window it opened over, and it runs the engine's own message pump while it is up, so a TIMER still fires inside it. The window it was opened from is disabled until it ends, which is what modality means here. Enter answers it, Escape and the close box cancel it, and its window is a message box: a title bar, no minimise or maximise box, a fixed frame.

A message box is the other prompt, and it has TWO doors because the owner is a real choice: ctrl.MessageBox(text [, caption] [, type]) is that control's window as the owner, and the BARE MessageBox(text [, caption] [, type]) is the same call with NO owner, which is what a tool that has no window prompts with. The bare one is a global rather than a namespace member because nobody owns it.

Methods and properties

Title, Prompt, ValueWhat the window is called, the line above the input, and what is typed. Preset Value before ShowDialog() and read it after.
ShowDialog()Runs the prompt: 1 answered, 2 cancelled or closed.
WindowThe prompt's own window while it is up, and 0 the rest of the time.
PostMessage(msg, wParam, lParam), SendMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)The doors Control has, applied to that window, so a script answers the prompt it is inside without a handle in sight.
Width, HeightIts size in design pixels, as a Form's are. A size too small to hold its parts is raised to a minimum rather than opened as a sliver.
Left, Top, StartPositionWhere it opens, numbered as a Form's is: 0 where Left and Top say, 1 centred on the screen, 2 (the default) centred on the window it was opened over.
ScreenWhich monitor it opens on, numbered the Form's way: left alone it mirrors the window the prompt was opened over, and assigning it (before the prompt is up, or while it is) takes it there through the Form's own Screen, which is also what refuses a number with no monitor behind it.
ModalWhether it OWNS the input while it is up, which it does by default: the window that was active is disabled until the prompt is answered, and false leaves it enabled so the application behind the prompt still takes clicks while the prompt waits.
CloseBoxWhether it carries the X at all. Escape cancels it either way.
TimeoutsWhich button answers on its own, and after how long, as a map of the code to milliseconds: { 1: 2000 } is "the OK button after two seconds" and { 2: 2000 } is Cancel. The codes are the ones ShowDialog() already answers with, the EARLIEST deadline wins when both are named, and an empty map means the prompt waits for a hand. This is also the LAST argument of the one-shot spelling, after the default button: Application.InputBox(title, prompt [, defaultValue [, defaultButton [, timeouts]]]).
DefaultButtonWhich button is the default: 0 for OK, which is what it is, and 1 for Cancel, meaning the one Enter activates and the one Windows draws as the default. The input keeps the caret either way, so a script can still type into it.
ThemeThe theme of the window it was opened over unless the script assigns one, so a prompt in a dark or paletted application matches it.
FontName, FontSize, FontBoldWhat the prompt line, the input and the buttons are written in. Left alone they are the engine's own font ONE STEP UP (10 against roughly an 8pt equivalent), so a prompt reads like a message box rather than a dense panel.
TextHeight, TextPadding, TextLeft, TextRightThe INPUT's metrics: its height (56 by default), the space between the prompt line and it (16), and its side insets. The layout is built from them rather than from constants, so a bigger font or a longer line has room instead of clipping, and the buttons keep a height of their own (28), because a tall input is a place to type rather than a reason for fat buttons.
InputThe input control itself while the prompt is up, the same door every control has, so a script can style or fill its own prompt rather than only answer one.
SetIcon(icon [, size [, color]])The prompt's icon, in the Form's own shapes (a character to render, an ICON handle from Application.ExeIcon, or 0 for none). A WINDOW handle is not one: the engine refuses it by name rather than handing it to WM_SETICON, which accepts any handle and would leave the window without an icon in silence. Asked BEFORE the prompt is up it stores the request and returns 0, since there is no window yet to hold an icon, and asked while it is up it applies at once and returns the handle the window holds. A prompt nobody gives an icon to keeps the running executable's own.
Accept()Answer the prompt the way its OK button does, so the caller's ShowDialog() gets the text that is in the box. It posts the same message that button sends, which is what the prompt's own loop reads, so it is handled exactly as a click would be.
Cancel()Dismiss the prompt the way its Cancel button and the Escape key do: ShowDialog() answers 2.
ReadStyle(), WindowRectThe prompt window's own state, read the way a control reads its own: its STYLE word, and the rectangle it BECAME rather than the size requested. Width and Height above are the REQUEST, and a prompt asked for 10x10 opens at the engine's minimum. The InputBox is not a Control, so it carries these as mirrors beside PostMessage and SendMessage, which is also why GetId and the focus members are not on it.

Example

// Rename a button with a prompt: a form, the control it acts on, and the two shapes of InputBox
var form = Application.CreateForm("InputBox demo");
form.Width = 420; form.Height = 160;
var target = form.CreateButton("Button1", 12, 12, 160, 30);
form.Show();

// The one-shot form: the text comes back, and null means it was cancelled
var name = Application.InputBox("Rename", "New name for the control:", target.Text, 0, { 2: 8000 });   // cancels itself if nobody answers
if (name != null) { target.Text = name; }
print("the one-shot answered: " + (name == null ? "null, so it timed out" : name));

// The object form, for a prompt the script decides the shape of
var box = Application.CreateInputBox();
box.Title = "Rename";
box.Prompt = "New name for the control:";
box.Value = target.Text;
box.FontSize = 12;
box.DefaultButton = 1;      // Enter cancels rather than answers
box.Screen = 1;             // the second monitor, so drop this line where there is only one (Application.MonitorCount())
box.Timeouts = { 1: 4000 };   // answers OK itself after four seconds, so this example needs no hand
if (box.ShowDialog() == 1) { target.Text = box.Value; }
print("the object form answered " + target.Text);


// A prompt runs the engine's pump, so a TIMER fires inside it, and the doors answer it
// with no hand on the keyboard: Accept() is the OK button, Cancel() the Escape path
var auto = Application.CreateInputBox();
auto.Title = "Rename"; auto.Prompt = "New name for the control:";
CreateTimer(400, (sender, e) => { auto.Input.Text = "Renamed"; auto.Accept(); }, false);
if (auto.ShowDialog() == 1) { target.Text = auto.Value; }
print("the timer-driven form answered " + target.Text);
Application.Run();   // keep the window up; close it to end the script
DockStyle enum How a control attaches itself to its parent's edges

What Control.Dock takes, on any control (the form included). The six members are the four edges, Fill for everything the docked neighbours leave, and None for a control placed by hand:

DockStyle.None // 0 positioned by Left/Top/Width/Height DockStyle.Left // 1 DockStyle.Top // 2 DockStyle.Right // 3 DockStyle.Bottom // 4 DockStyle.Fill // 5 takes what the docked neighbours left
var bar = form.CreateStatusBar(0, 0, 200, 24); bar.Dock = DockStyle.Bottom; // pinned to the bottom edge var log = form.CreateTextBox("", 12, 88, 400, 300); log.Dock = DockStyle.Fill; // everything above the bar print(bar.Dock is DockStyle); // True

A whole number is accepted as well (4 is DockStyle.Bottom), which is the general rule for a CLR enum, but the name is the spelling to write: it is also the name typeof(ctrl.Dock) reports, and typename("DockStyle") resolves it. Docking is re-applied by the engine on every resize and after a DPI change, so a docked control stays docked when the window moves to another monitor.

Diagnostics namespace One registry for the engine's run-configuration gates (the diagnostic traces, the two path switches and the frame cap), so a script can read and set any of them while it runs.

The engine's run-configuration gates are readable through Diagnostics rather than only through their environment variables, and there is ONE list of them: the diagnostic traces, the two switches that choose which engine a body runs on (TOPLEVEL_VM and CARRIED_STATEMENTS), and the frame cap (VM_MAXFRAMES, a value rather than a flag). LogTraces(true) turns every trace on and LogTraces(false) takes them all off (the two path switches and the cap are deliberately untouched by it: that switch means the traces), Trace(name, on) sets one gate, and Traces() reports every one with its state, a flag as on/off and the cap as its number. A gate takes effect from the next statement onward, so it is useful in the middle of a run, not only at its start.

Each name is the environment variable's own name without the SLC_ prefix, so Diagnostics.Trace("VM_TRACE", true) and SLC_VM_TRACE=1 are the same gate. The variable is only ever the STARTING value, and ONE rule reads all of them: 1 is on, 0 and false are off, and anything else is the gate's own default. That keeps SLC_TOPLEVEL_VM=false working as the opt-out of a gate whose default is on, and stops a stray value from switching a trace on. An unknown name is refused with the list of real ones rather than ignored.

VM_TRACEThe opcode trace, the same flag as Vm.Trace.A [tr] line per executed unit, with its source position. Use it to see whether a body runs on the VM or is walked.
STACK_TRACEThe live script depth per interpreted call.A [stack:call] and a [stack:unwind] line per call, with the remaining stack, so a recursion's real headroom is visible.
STACK_MAPThe thread's stack regions: commit, guard and reserve.Tens of lines per call, so turn it on alone and briefly. That volume is why Trace(name, on) exists beside the all-switch.
DISABLE_GUARDSBoth recursion guards.Recursion past a cap is no longer refused, so the depth can be measured. Expect a crash rather than an error if it goes too far.
CORO_TRACEThe coroutine walk.Lines for each resume, foreach and yield, which is what a generator that stops early needs.
NAMED_TRACEThe named-argument markers the VM hands to a call.One line per named call, naming the callee and the names it carried. Nothing appears for a positional call.
TOPLEVEL_VMWhether each top-level statement runs on the VM or the tree-walker.The same state VmSetTopLevelEnabled reads and sets, on by default. See that entry for what changing it means.
CARRIED_STATEMENTSWhether the compiler may hand a top-level statement it cannot model to the tree.The same state VmSetStatementCarrier reads and sets, on by default: SLC_CARRIED_STATEMENTS=0 is the opt-out. It governs a COMPILE, not the engine a statement runs on.
VM_MAXFRAMESThe VM's frame cap, a value rather than a flag.Reported as its number, and settable as one: Trace("VM_MAXFRAMES", 50) moves BOTH caps the variable moves, and 0 restores the platform default. The variable fixes it before the first statement.

Every diagnostic the engine prints carries a position. A warning from a builtin, or the end-of-run COM report, prints the same [Lx:Cy] prefix a refusal does, so a warning can be located without a search: when the caller has no position of its own the engine supplies the statement being executed, which is the case for a builtin (a native is handed values, never a node) and for the report raised after the last statement. A diagnostic from a script run through RunScript is attributed to the CALL instead, because the nested text is not in the file you are reading: see RunScript.

Script: Diagnostics.LogTraces(true); turns everything on for a run that is already going, and Diagnostics.Trace("STACK_TRACE", false); quietens the one that is too loud.

ThemeMode enum How a window gets its look, including a palette you set yourself

What Form.Theme and MdiForm.Theme take. Light and Dark are the two native looks, System follows Windows' own app-mode setting, and Custom paints the palette you set on the window:

ThemeMode.Light // 0 the light native look ThemeMode.Dark // 1 the dark native look ThemeMode.System // 2 follows Windows' app-mode setting ThemeMode.Custom // 3 paints the palette below
var form = Application.CreateForm("Palette"); form.Theme = ThemeMode.Custom; // the window and the controls inside it form.ThemeBackground = 0x1E1E32; // what the engine paints form.ThemeText = 0xF0F0F0; form.ThemeDisabled = 0x808080; // text of a disabled control var ok = form.CreateButton("OK", 12, 12, 90, 26); ok.BackgroundColor = 0x2E7D32; // a control's OWN colour wins ok.TextColor = 0xFFFFFF; var cancel = form.CreateButton("Cancel", 112, 12, 90, 26); cancel.BackgroundColor = 0xB00020; // each control takes its own pair cancel.TextColor = 0xFFE0E0; print(form.Theme is ThemeMode); // True

A colour the palette leaves unset comes from the effective leg, so setting only the background is enough. That leg is derived from the palette background's BRIGHTNESS, which is what the parts the engine does not paint (a scrollbar, a themed button face) follow, so a dark palette does not sit beside a light scrollbar. Reading Theme answers the mode that was asked for, which is how a script asks "did I choose Custom" (form.Theme == ThemeMode.Custom), while an internal DarkMode answers the leg in force.

The window's TITLE BAR follows the palette too, where Windows allows it: on Windows 11 and later the caption is painted from ThemeBackground with its text in ThemeText, and it returns to the system's own caption as soon as Theme leaves Custom. On an older Windows the caption keeps the system's dark or light one, so a Custom window shows the palette everywhere but its title bar.

Every colour here is written 0xRRGGBB, red in the high byte, as everywhere else in the engine, and a palette member reads back exactly what it was set to. A GetPixel reading of a painted pixel reports the bytes the other way round (0x00BBGGRR, the order a COLORREF carries), so compare colours through the property rather than through a pixel: a red background reads back as 0xFF0000 from the property and as 255 from the pixel.

Colors namespace The colours by name, plus the byte order a colour is written in and the swap a pixel reading needs

The named colours (Colors.Red, Colors.BlueViolet, and the nineteen beside them) are 0xRRGGBB like everything else, so Colors.Red is 0xFF0000 and assigning one paints the colour it names.

Every colour a script writes is 0xRRGGBB, red in the high byte, and every colour member takes and reports it that way. A GetPixel reading is the one exception: it answers a pixel as 0x00BBGGRR, the order a COLORREF carries, so a pixel is not comparable to a colour without a swap. Measured on a red background: the property reads back 0xFF0000 while the pixel reads 255.

FromArgb([a,] r, g, b)Composes a colour the same way, with an optional alpha first: Colors.FromArgb(255, 128, 0) is the orange 0xFF8000, and Colors.FromArgb(128, 255, 128, 0) carries the alpha in the high byte.
RGB(r, g, b)Composes a colour from its three components, each 0 to 255, so Colors.RGB(0xAA, 0xBB, 0xCC) is 0xAABBCC. A component outside that range, or a value that is not a whole number, is refused by name.
BGR(colour)The value a GetPixel reading reports for that colour, so a pixel can be compared with pixel == Colors.BGR(0xFF0000).
FromPixel(pixel)The colour a pixel reading stands for, so a colour can be READ BACK out of a window: Colors.FromPixel(form.GetPixel(x, y)).
var form = Application.CreateForm("Color"); form.Theme = ThemeMode.Custom; form.ThemeBackground = Colors.RGB(0x1E, 0x1E, 0x32); // the same as 0x1E1E32 // the client is painted 0x1E1E32, and the pixel reports it the other way round: print(form.GetPixel(200, 120) == Color.BGR(0x1E1E32)); // True print(Colors.FromPixel(form.GetPixel(200, 120)) == 0x1E1E32); // True print(Colors.RGB(0xC0, 0x20, 0x20)); // 12591136, a colour to set

BGR and FromPixel are the same swap in opposite directions, which is why swapping twice returns the original: one names the colour you are looking for, the other the pixel you read. Greys need neither, since a swap leaves them unchanged.

MdiForm UI MDI frame container with MDIClient area for document windows

Created via Application.CreateMdiForm(title). Provides an MDI frame with an MDIClient area where MdiChild document windows live. Frame-level controls are positioned above the client area.

Properties

HandleNative window handle (IntPtr).
TextWindow title.
Width / HeightFrame dimensions.
Left / TopScreen position.
ThemeA ThemeMode, so it is written form.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark: Light or Dark, System to follow Windows' own app-mode setting, or Custom to paint a palette. Reading DarkMode answers the effective leg, exactly as on a Form, whose caption follows the palette the same way.
VisibleWhether the window is visible.

Frame control factory methods (all 17 types)

CreateLabel(text, x, y, w, h)Label on the frame.
CreateButton(text, x, y, w, h)Button on the frame.
CreateTextBox(text, x, y, w, h), CreateRichTextBox(text, x, y, w, h)TextBox, or the per-run formatting RichTextBox, on the frame.
CreateCheckBox(text, x, y, w, h, checked?)CheckBox on the frame.
CreateRadioButton(text, x, y, w, h, checked?)RadioButton on the frame.
CreateListBox(x, y, w, h)ListBox on the frame.
CreateComboBox(x, y, w, h)ComboBox on the frame.
CreateListView(x, y, w, h)ListView on the frame.
CreateTreeView(x, y, w, h)TreeView on the frame.
CreateDateTimePicker(x, y, w, h)DateTimePicker on the frame.
CreateTrackBar(x, y, w, h)TrackBar on the frame.

MDI management

>
CreateMdiChild(title [, x, y, w, h, position])Create an MDI child. position: 0=cascade (default), 1=tile, 2=maximized.
TileChildren(horizontal)Tile children horizontally (true) or vertically (false).
CascadeChildren()Cascade all MDI children.
ArrangeIcons()Arrange minimized child icons.
SendMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Send a window message to the FRAME's own window and answer its result. The same member a Control answers, over the same core, so a frame is driven the way a form is.
PostMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Queue the message instead of sending it, answering whether it was queued.
MoveWindow(x, y, w, h [, repaint])Place the frame in PIXELS, exactly as Control.MoveWindow does.
GetActiveChild()Returns handle of the active MDI child (IntPtr).
InitHandle()Create window handle without showing.
Show()Show the MDI frame.
Close()Close the frame (triggers Closing/Closed events).

Events

LoadFires when the form loads.
ClosingFires before close (can cancel via ce.Cancel = true).
ClosedFires after close.
ResizeEventFires on resize, receives Size(w, h).
var form = Application.CreateMdiForm("My App"); form.Width = 900; form.Height = 600; form.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; var btn = form.CreateButton("New Doc", 10, 10, 100, 30); btn.Click = fun(s, e) { var doc = form.CreateMdiChild("Document"); doc.CreateLabel("Name:", 20, 20, 60, 25); }; form.Show(); Application.Run(form);
ChildMdiForm UI Embedded MDI frame an MdiForm parented to another Form

Created via Application.CreateChildMdiForm(title, parentForm). Same as MdiForm but embedded as a child window of another Form. Useful when you want a regular Form to host the MDI workspace (toolbar at the top, MDI children below), rather than using a standalone top-level MDI frame.

Example

var main = Application.CreateForm("Main Window"); main.Width = 1000; main.Height = 700; main.CreateLabel("File Manager with embedded MDI workspace", 20, 20, 300, 30); var mdi = Application.CreateChildMdiForm("Workspace", main); mdi.Left = 10; mdi.Top = 60; mdi.Width = 980; mdi.Height = 600; mdi.Theme = ThemeMode.Dark; var doc = mdi.CreateMdiChild("Doc 1"); doc.CreateLabel("Content:", 20, 20, 60, 25); main.Show(); Application.Run(main);

Notes:

  • The embedded MdiForm inherits its dimensions and position from the parent Form you must set Left, Top, Width, Height explicitly.
  • All control factories, events, and dark mode work identically to a standalone MdiForm.
  • The parent Form's Closing/Closed events should clean up the embedded MdiForm's documents before the parent window is destroyed.
MdiChild UI MDI document window created inside an MdiForm

Created via mdiForm.CreateMdiChild(title, x, y, w, h, positionMode). Each child has its own control collection for document-specific controls. Supports dark mode, DPI scaling, and close via Dispose().

Properties

HandleNative window handle (IntPtr).
TextDocument title (appears in title bar).

Control factory methods (same as Form)

>
CreateLabel(text, x, y, w, h)Label on this document.
CreateButton(text, x, y, w, h)Button supports .Click event.
CreateTextBox(text, x, y, w, h), CreateRichTextBox(text, x, y, w, h)TextBox, or the per-run formatting RichTextBox, as a single or multi-line text input.
CreateCheckBox(text, x, y, w, h, checked?)CheckBox togglable boolean.
CreateRadioButton(text, x, y, w, h, checked?)RadioButton mutually exclusive.
CreateListBox(x, y, w, h)ListBox item selection.
CreateComboBox(x, y, w, h)ComboBox dropdown selection.
CreateListView(x, y, w, h)ListView columns, icons, details.
CreateTreeView(x, y, w, h)TreeView hierarchical.
Show()Show the frame this window belongs to, since a document window is shown by its frame. For a document whose root is a single MdiChild that is the frame the reader made to own it.
SendMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Send a window message to this document window. WM_CLOSE closes it, which is what fires Closing and then Closed.
PostMessage(msg, wParam, lParam)Queue the message instead of sending it, answering whether it was queued.
MoveWindow(x, y, w, h [, repaint])Place the window in PIXELS, exactly as Control.MoveWindow does.
CreateDateTimePicker(x, y, w, h)DateTimePicker date/time selection.
CreateTrackBar(x, y, w, h)TrackBar slider control.

Methods

Dispose()Close and destroy the document window.

Events

LoadFires when the MDI child is created.
ClosingFires before close (can cancel via ce.Cancel = true).
ClosedFires after the document is closed.
ResizeEventFires when the child window is resized. Receives Size(width, height).
var doc = form.CreateMdiChild("Invoice"); doc.CreateLabel("Customer:", 20, 20, 70, 25); doc.CreateTextBox("Acme Corp", 100, 20, 200, 25); var saveBtn = doc.CreateButton("Save", 100, 60, 80, 25); saveBtn.Click = fun(s, e) { print("Saved!"); }; doc.Closing = fun(s, ce) { print("Closing " + doc.Text); }; doc.Closed = fun(s) { print("Closed"); };
ShowConsole UI Show or hide the console window
ShowConsole(true); // show console ShowConsole(false); // hide console (GUI mode)

▼ LINQ Methods

Where LINQ Filter a sequence based on a predicate
Any Iterable works: every LINQ method accepts any Iterable arrays, lists, tuples, dicts (enumerated as KeyValuePairs), HashSets, LINQ results, generators, and strings. Tuples, generators, and dicts materialize on demand when a method enumerates them; a non-iterable receiver (42.Select(...)) is a runtime error.
Where(collection, predicate)
print(Count(Where([1,2,3,4,5], fun(x)=>x > 3))); // 2
Select LINQ Project each element using a selector function
Select(collection, selector)
print(Select([1,2,3], fun(x)=>x*10)); // [10,20,30]
SelectMany LINQ Project each element to a sequence and flatten

Projects each element into a sub-sequence, then flattens all results.

SelectMany(collection, selector)
print(Count(SelectMany(["hi","ok"], fun(w)=>w.ToCharArray()))); // 4
First LINQ Return the first element in a sequence
First(collection [, predicate])
print(First([10,20,30])); // 10 print(First([10,20,30], fun(x)=>x > 15)); // 20
FirstOrDefault LINQ Return first element or default value

Returns the first matching element, or default if none found.

FirstOrDefault(collection [, predicate])
print(FirstOrDefault([5,10,15], fun(x) => x > 8)); // 10
Count LINQ Count elements in a collection
Count(collection)
print(Count([1,2,3,4,5])); // 5
OrderBy LINQ Sort elements in ascending order
OrderBy(collection, keyFn)
OrderBy(collection, keyFn, compareKeys)
print(ElementAt(OrderBy([3,1,2], fun(x)=>x), 0)); // 1
An ordered SEQUENCE, lazily sorted like C#'s: foreach, Count and First() read it, ThenBy adds a second key, and .ToList() / .ToArray() materialize it. The two-argument form takes a comparer that receives two KEYS, so a projection can be ordered by its own rule: people.OrderBy(fun(p) => p.Name, fun(a, b) { return b.CompareTo(a); }).
OrderByDescending LINQ Sort elements in descending order

Sorts in descending order based on a key selector.

OrderByDescending(collection, keyFn)
OrderByDescending(collection, keyFn, compareKeys)
print(ElementAt(OrderByDescending([3,1,4], fun(x)=>x), 0)); // 4
ThenBy LINQ Secondary sort (ascending) after OrderBy

Applies a secondary ascending sort within an ordered sequence.

ThenBy(orderedSeq, keyFn)
var sorted = OrderBy([3,1,2], fun(x)=>x); sorted = ThenBy(sorted, fun(x)=>x);
GroupBy LINQ Group elements by a key
GroupBy(collection, keyFn)
var groups = GroupBy([1,2,3,4], fun(x)=>x % 2); foreach (var g in groups) { print(g.Key); }
Aggregate LINQ Accumulate values using a function

Applies an accumulator function over a sequence.

Aggregate(collection, func)
var sum = Aggregate([1,2,3,4], fun(a,b) => a+b); print(sum); // 10
All LINQ Check if every element satisfies a predicate

Returns true if every element passes the predicate.

All(collection, predicate)
print(All([1,2,3], fun(x) => x > 0)); // true
Any LINQ Check if any element satisfies a predicate

Returns true if at least one element passes the predicate.

Any(collection [, predicate])
print(Any([1,2,3], fun(x) => x > 2)); // true
Average LINQ Compute the average of numeric elements

Returns the arithmetic mean as double.

Average(collection)
print(Average([10,20,30])); // 20.0
Contains LINQ Check if a sequence contains a value

Returns true if the value exists in the collection.

Contains(collection, value)
print(Contains(["apple","banana"], "banana")); // true
Distinct LINQ Return distinct elements from a sequence

Filters out duplicates, keeping only unique elements.

Distinct(collection)
print(Count(Distinct([1,2,2,3]))); // 3
ElementAt LINQ Return element at index
ElementAt(collection, index)
print(ElementAt(["a","b","c"], 1)); // b
ElementAtOrDefault LINQ Return element at index or default value

Returns the element at index, or default if out of range.

ElementAtOrDefault(collection, index)
print(ElementAtOrDefault(["A","B"], 1)); // B
GroupJoin LINQ Group joined collections
GroupJoin(outer, inner, outerKeyFn, innerKeyFn, resultFn)
print(Count(GroupJoin([{id:1}], [{oid:1}], fun(o)=>o.id, fun(i)=>i.oid, fun(o,g)=>o.id))); // 1
Join LINQ Inner join two collections on key

Correlates elements of two sequences based on matching keys.

Join(outer, inner, outerKeyFn, innerKeyFn, resultFn)
print(Count(Join([{id:1}], [{oid:1}], fun(o)=>o.id, fun(i)=>i.oid, fun(o,i)=>""))); // 1
Last LINQ Return the last element in a sequence

Returns the last element, optionally matching a predicate.

Last(collection [, predicate])
print(Last([1,2,3,4,5], fun(x) => x < 4)); // 3
LastOrDefault LINQ Return last element or default

Returns the last matching element, or default if none found.

LastOrDefault(collection [, predicate])
print(LastOrDefault([1,2,3], fun(x) => x > 1)); // 3
LeftJoin LINQ Left outer join two collections
LeftJoin(outer, inner, outerKeyFn, innerKeyFn, resultFn)
print(Count(LeftJoin([{id:1}], [{oid:1}], fun(o)=>o.id, fun(i)=>i.oid, fun(o,i)=>o.id))); // 1
Max LINQ Return the maximum value

Returns the largest numeric value in the collection.

Max(collection)
print(Max([85,92,78,95])); // 95
Min LINQ Return the minimum value

Returns the smallest numeric value in the collection.

Min(collection)
print(Min([72,68,85,70])); // 68
Reverse LINQ Reverse the order of elements

Returns elements in reverse order.

Reverse(collection)
print(ElementAt(Reverse([1,2,3]), 0)); // 3
RightJoin LINQ Right outer join two collections

Joins outer and inner collections, including inner elements even when no outer match.

RightJoin(outer, inner, outerKeyFn, innerKeyFn, resultFn)
print(Count(RightJoin([{id:1}], [{oid:1}], fun(o)=>o.id, fun(i)=>i.oid, fun(o,i)=>""))); // 1
Skip LINQ Skip N elements from the start

Bypasses N elements, returning the rest.

Skip(collection, count)
print(ElementAt(Skip([1,2,3,4,5], 2), 0)); // 3
Sum LINQ Compute the sum of numeric elements

Adds up all numeric values in the collection.

Sum(collection)
print(Sum([100,200,150])); // 450
Take LINQ Take the first N elements

Returns the first N elements from the sequence.

Take(collection, count)
print(Count(Take([1,2,3,4,5], 3))); // 3
Zip LINQ Combine two sequences element-wise

Pairs elements at the same position; stops at the shorter sequence.

Zip(first, second)
foreach (var p in Zip(["a","b"], [1,2])) { print(p); }

▼ Namespaces & Utilities

WeakRef namespace Script-accessible weak reference holds a reference without preventing garbage collection

WeakRef wraps System.WeakReference<object> and allows scripts to hold a reference to an object without preventing that object from being garbage-collected. This is useful for caches, observer lists, or any scenario where you want to reference objects but allow them to be freed when no other strong references exist.

WeakRef.Create(object)

Creates a new WeakRef wrapping the given object. The object is not strongly rooted it may be collected by GC if no other strong references exist.

var wr = WeakRef.Create(myObj);

WeakRef.TryGetTarget()

Returns the wrapped object if it is still alive (not yet collected), or null if it has been garbage-collected.

var target = wr.TryGetTarget(); if (target != null) { /* use it */ }

WeakRef.IsAlive

Returns true if the wrapped object is still alive (not yet collected) without retrieving it.

if (wr.IsAlive) { /* still alive */ }
// Class with WeakRef tracking non-durable Dispose guard public class DisposableRegistry { public bool[] done; public int disposed; private Dictionary<string, WeakRef> store; public DisposableRegistry(bool[] doneFlag) { store = new Dictionary<string, WeakRef>(); done = doneFlag; } public string Track(string id) { store[id] = WeakRef.Create(this); return id; } ~DisposableRegistry() { if (this.disposed > 0) { return; } this.disposed = this.disposed + 1; store.Clear(); done[0] = true; } } var disposedFlag = [false]; using (var dr = new DisposableRegistry(disposedFlag)) { dr.Track("a"); dr.Dispose(); // explicit Dispose destructor guard prevents re-entry } print(disposedFlag[0]); // true destructor ran exactly once
Lifecycle behavior: The WeakRef itself must remain alive for you to query the target. Once the WeakRef goes out of scope and is collected, the reference is lost permanently. For GC testing in AOT, note that native compilation may keep objects alive longer due to stack roots IsAlive may return true even after null assignment and a full GC.Collect().
Native calls namespace Win32 API interop memory, windows, controls, DLLs

Load a native library and call into it by name. The controls, the memory and the window messages have their own homes now (the form factories, the Mem namespace and the events), so what is left here is the native-call surface itself: LoadLibrary and FreeLibrary, CallFunc, and the errors they raise. All methods are in this namespace.

DLL / module

GetModuleHandle(name)Get a module handle (HINSTANCE) by name, or 0 for the calling process.
GetStockObject(index)Return a handle to a stock GDI object (e.g., DEFAULT_GUI_FONT=17).

Dynamic function calls

CallFunc(lib, name, args...)Resolve a function by name from a loaded library and call it with the given arguments. Supports IntPtr (HWND) handles, int, long, short, byte, uint, strings (UTF-8 call the …A entry points), and any convertible type. At most 16 arguments; pass exactly what the native function expects.
// Get text length from any HWND var user32 = LoadLibrary("user32"); var len = CallFunc(user32, "GetWindowTextLengthW", chatLog.Handle); print("Text length: " + len); // Beep kernel32 var kernel32 = LoadLibrary("kernel32"); CallFunc(kernel32, "Beep", 800, 200); // IsWindowVisible check if a window is visible var visible = CallFunc(user32, "IsWindowVisible", textBox.Handle); print(visible == 1 ? "visible" : "hidden");
CallFunc goes through the same native-call step as everything else (NativeCall, with AotInvoker.InvokeCdeclPtr underneath for AOT-compatible dispatch), so it cannot disagree with lib.Invoke(…) or CallNative about the bytes it sends: strings are marshaled as UTF-8 and freed after the call, IntPtr/UIntPtr handles and numerics pass straight through. The result is the machine value as a long an int-returning export is not sign-extended, so -1 arrives as 4294967295.

Array arguments

Instead of passing individual arguments, pass a single array literal as the third argument. Its elements will be spread as individual native arguments:

// Individual args CallFunc(k32, "Beep", 800, 200); // Same call using array spread var args = [800, 200]; CallFunc(k32, "Beep", args);

SizeOfStruct

Mem.SizeOfStruct("StructName") returns the unmanaged size (in bytes) of a named Win32 structure type. This is useful when allocating memory or calling Win32 functions that require the size of a struct (e.g., RegisterClassExW, GetWindowRect, SendMessage with cbSize fields).

var size = Mem.SizeOfStruct("RECT"); print(size); // 16 (4 fields × 4 bytes each)
// Retrieve the window rectangle using ReadStruct + CallFunc (cleaner) var user32 = LoadLibrary("user32"); var rectSize = Mem.SizeOfStruct("RECT"); var buf = Mem.Alloc(rectSize); var ok = CallFunc(user32, "GetWindowRect", form.Handle, buf); var rect = Mem.ReadStruct(buf, "RECT"); print($"Rect: {rect.left},{rect.top} - {rect.right},{rect.bottom}"); Mem.Free(buf); FreeLibrary(user32);
// Or write fields to a struct buffer: var buf2 = Mem.Alloc(Mem.SizeOfStruct("POINT")); var pt = Mem.ReadStruct(buf2, "POINT"); print($"Point: {pt.x},{pt.y}"); Mem.Free(buf2);

ReadStruct / WriteStruct

Mem.ReadStruct(ptr, structName, fieldName) reads a named field from a struct at the given memory address. Mem.WriteStruct(ptr, structName, fieldName, value) writes a value to a named field. Both use the struct layout from SizeOfStruct to compute field offsets.

Script-defined structs are also fully supported. Mem.ReadStruct(ptr, "MyStruct") returns a struct instance with all public/internal fields populated from raw memory. Mem.ReadStruct(ptr, "MyStruct", "fieldName") reads a single field, and Mem.WriteStruct(ptr, "MyStruct", "fieldName", value) writes a single field. Mem.SizeOfStruct("MyStruct") computes the layout from field types with 4-byte alignment packing.

// Script-defined struct only public fields are included public struct MyPoint { public int x; public int y; } // SizeOfStruct computes 8 bytes (4+4, 4-byte aligned) var s = Mem.SizeOfStruct("MyPoint"); // 8 // Allocate and call GetWindowRect into a script-defined buffer var buf = Mem.Alloc(s); var ok = CallFunc(user32, "GetWindowRect", form.Handle, buf); // ReadStruct returns a struct instance with named fields var pt = Mem.ReadStruct(buf, "MyPoint"); print($"Point: {pt.x},{pt.y}"); // Read/write individual fields var val = Mem.ReadStruct(buf, "MyPoint", "x"); Mem.WriteStruct(buf, "MyPoint", "x", 42); Mem.Free(buf);

The following field names are supported for each struct type:

StructFieldsNotes
WNDCLASSEX / WNDCLASSEXWcbSize, style, lpfnWndProc, cbClsExtra, cbWndExtra, hInstance, hIcon, hCursor, hbrBackground, lpszMenuName, lpszClassName, hIconSm80 bytes (x64)
MSGhwnd, message, wParam, lParam, time, pt48 bytes (x64)
RECTleft, top, right, bottomEach field is int (4 bytes)
POINTx, yEach field is int (4 bytes)
MONITORINFOSee Win32 docsMonitor information (rcMonitor, rcWork, dwFlags)
MINMAXINFOSee Win32 docsWindow min/max tracking info
TCITEMWSee Win32 docsTab control item
LVCOLUMNWSee Win32 docsList-view column
LVITEMWSee Win32 docsList-view item
TVINSERTSTRUCTWSee Win32 docsTree-view insert structure
TVITEMWSee Win32 docsTree-view item
TVITEMEXWSee Win32 docsExtended tree-view item
PAINTSTRUCTSee Win32 docsWM_PAINT paint structure
var buf = Mem.Alloc(Mem.SizeOfStruct("RECT")); Mem.WriteStruct(buf, "RECT", "left", 10); Mem.WriteStruct(buf, "RECT", "top", 20); var l = Mem.ReadStruct(buf, "RECT", "left"); print(l); // 10 Mem.Free(buf);

Exception cases

CallFunc throws clear ScriptException with descriptive messages for these error conditions:

ConditionError message (example)
Invalid library handle (null)CallFunc: invalid library handle (zero). Pass a DynamicLibrary from LoadLibrary or a numeric module handle. Got: null
Invalid library type (script class instance)CallFunc: invalid library handle (InvalidCastException). Pass a DynamicLibrary from LoadLibrary or a numeric module handle. Got: ClassInstance
Function not found in DLLCallFunc: function 'NonExistentFunction' not found in the specified library.
Missing function nameCallFunc: function name required (arg[1])
Missing library argCallFunc requires library and function name.
Too many args (>16)CallFunc supports at most 16 arguments.

Note: The first argument must be a DynamicLibrary obtained from LoadLibrary() or a numeric module handle (nint/long). Passing a NativeLib script class instance directly to CallFunc is not supported use NativeLib.Invoke() instead.

NativeLib wrapper class

The NativeLib class wraps LoadLibrary + CallFunc into a clean, disposable object with auto-cleanup. Constructor loads the DLL, destructor frees it, Invoke() calls native functions with params:

// Usage var user32 = new NativeLib("user32"); var len = user32.Invoke("GetWindowTextLengthW", chatLog.Handle); user32.Invoke("Beep", 800, 200); // Auto-freed when variable goes out of scope // Or with array args user32.Invoke("Beep", [800, 200]);
The NativeLib class is available as a script include from assets/language/runtime/nativelib.slc.
LoadLibrary(name) returns a DynamicLibrary that resolves function pointers automatically: kernel.Sleep(1000). It is a global, and so is FreeLibrary(lib).
Cipher namespace AES-256-GCM encryption, plus post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange and ML-DSA signatures

The Cipher namespace provides AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption for string data, and the two post-quantum algorithms .NET 11 ships as stable: ML-KEM (FIPS 203, key encapsulation) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204, signatures). Symmetric keys and ciphertext are base64-encoded for storage and transport, with random 12-byte nonces and 16-byte authentication tags per encryption; the post-quantum members speak byte[], because a key pair is binary.

Cipher.GenerateKey()

Generates a random 256-bit key encoded in base64. Suitable for use with Encrypt and Decrypt.

var key = Cipher.GenerateKey();

Cipher.GenerateRandomToken(int sizeInBytes = 32)

Generates a random token of the specified byte size, encoded in base64. Default size is 32 bytes.

var token = Cipher.GenerateRandomToken(16);

Cipher.Encrypt(string data, string base64Key)

Encrypts the given string using AES-256-GCM with the provided base64-encoded key. Returns the combined nonce + tag + ciphertext as base64.

var enc = Cipher.Encrypt("secret data", key);

Cipher.Decrypt(string base64Cipher, string base64Key)

Decrypts the given base64 ciphertext (produced by Encrypt) using the same key. Throws on wrong key or tampered data.

var original = Cipher.Decrypt(enc, key);
// Full roundtrip var key = Cipher.GenerateKey(); var message = "Hello, secret world!"; var enc = Cipher.Encrypt(message, key); print(enc); // base64 ciphertext var dec = Cipher.Decrypt(enc, key); print(dec); // "Hello, secret world!"
Uses System.Security.Cryptography.AesGcm with 256-bit keys, 12-byte nonces, and 16-byte tags. Each Encrypt call generates a fresh random nonce, so the same plaintext encrypted twice produces different ciphertext.

Cipher.KemGenerate(string algorithm)

Generates an ML-KEM key pair, answering a dictionary with Algorithm, EncapsulationKey (the public half, 800, 1184 or 1568 bytes for ML-KEM-512, -768 or -1024) and DecapsulationKey (the secret half).

var pair = Cipher.KemGenerate("ML-KEM-768");

Cipher.KemEncapsulate(byte[] encapsulationKey, string algorithm)

Encapsulates a fresh shared secret against a peer's encapsulation key, answering Ciphertext (1088 bytes at 768) and SharedSecret (32 bytes). The ciphertext travels to the peer; the secret never does.

var box = Cipher.KemEncapsulate(pair["EncapsulationKey"], "ML-KEM-768");

Cipher.KemDecapsulate(byte[] decapsulationKey, byte[] ciphertext, string algorithm)

Recovers the same 32-byte shared secret from a ciphertext using the secret half of the pair. A ciphertext built for another key answers a different secret rather than an error, which is how ML-KEM is defined: compare the two secrets before trusting one.

var secret = Cipher.KemDecapsulate(pair["DecapsulationKey"], box["Ciphertext"], "ML-KEM-768");

Cipher.SignGenerate(string algorithm)

Generates an ML-DSA key pair, answering Algorithm, PublicKey and PrivateKey. The algorithm names are ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87.

var keys = Cipher.SignGenerate("ML-DSA-65");

Cipher.Sign(byte[] privateKey, byte[] message, string algorithm)

Signs a message, answering the signature bytes (2420, 3309 or 4627 for the three sizes). The message is bytes: Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text) for text, and the same bytes must be passed to Verify.

var sig = Cipher.Sign(keys["PrivateKey"], Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("release 1.2.3"), "ML-DSA-65");

Cipher.Verify(byte[] publicKey, byte[] message, byte[] signature, string algorithm)

Answers true when the signature matches the message and the public key, false otherwise, including when a single byte of the message changed.

var ok = Cipher.Verify(keys["PublicKey"], Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("release 1.2.3"), sig, "ML-DSA-65");
// Key exchange between two parties: only the encapsulation key is published var alice = Cipher.KemGenerate("ML-KEM-768"); var bob = Cipher.KemEncapsulate(alice["EncapsulationKey"], "ML-KEM-768"); print(bob["Ciphertext"].Length); // 1088, the bytes Bob sends back var mine = Cipher.KemDecapsulate(alice["DecapsulationKey"], bob["Ciphertext"], "ML-KEM-768"); print(mine.Length); // 32, and equal to bob["SharedSecret"] // The 32 bytes are a symmetric key: hand them to Cipher.Encrypt or to AesGcm
// A signature over a release note, and a check that the note was not altered var keys = Cipher.SignGenerate("ML-DSA-65"); var note = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("release 1.2.3"); var sig = Cipher.Sign(keys["PrivateKey"], note, "ML-DSA-65"); print(Cipher.Verify(keys["PublicKey"], note, sig, "ML-DSA-65")); // True note[0] = 82; // the same text with one byte changed print(Cipher.Verify(keys["PublicKey"], note, sig, "ML-DSA-65")); // False
The post-quantum members wrap System.Security.Cryptography.MLKem and MLDsa, so a key is standard FIPS 203/204 material. Two differences from the symmetric half are worth knowing: they speak byte[] rather than base64 strings, and an algorithm name is a NAME, so a wrong spelling is refused with the accepted ones printed. To store a key as text, Convert.ToBase64String(key["PrivateKey"]) and Convert.FromBase64String are the bridge. FIPS 205 (SlhDsa) is deliberately not offered: the platform marks it experimental, and a script surface does not rest on an API that may be removed.
GlobalHotKey namespace Register global keyboard shortcuts via raw Win32 RegisterHotKey API

Register system-wide hotkeys that work even when the application is not in focus. Uses raw Win32 RegisterHotKey/UnregisterHotKey from user32.dll no WPF or Windows.Forms dependency. Requires a visible window handle (Form) to receive WM_HOTKEY messages.

Modifier constants

Combine with bitwise OR (|):

ConstantValueDescription
MOD_ALT0x0001Alt key
MOD_CTRL0x0002Ctrl key
MOD_SHIFT0x0004Shift key
MOD_WIN0x0008Windows key
MOD_NOREPEAT0x4000Fire callback only once per keypress (recommended)

Methods

Register(key, modifiers, callback)Register a hotkey. key is a string name ("A", "F1", "Space") or VK code (0x41). Returns non-zero id on success, 0 on failure.
Unregister(id)Unregister by id (returned from Register). Safe to call with invalid ids.
UnregisterAll()Unregister all hotkeys at once.
SetHandle(hwnd)Set the window handle to receive WM_HOTKEY messages. Call once with form.Handle before registering hotkeys.

Valid key names

Letters A-Z, digits 0-9, function keys F1-F24, arrows (Up/Down/Left/Right), Space, Enter, Escape, Tab, Back, Delete, Insert, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, PrintScreen, Pause, numpad (NumPad0-NumPad9, Multiply, Add, Subtract, Divide, Decimal).

// Key name overload var mods = GlobalHotKey.MOD_ALT | GlobalHotKey.MOD_NOREPEAT; var id = GlobalHotKey.Register("S", mods, fun() { print("Alt+S pressed!"); }); // VK code overload var id2 = GlobalHotKey.Register(0x53, mods, fun() { print("Alt+S via VK code"); });
// Create a Form, register hotkeys, run message pump var form = Application.CreateForm("Hotkey Demo"); form.Show(); GlobalHotKey.SetHandle(form.Handle); // CTRL+A → show MessageBox GlobalHotKey.Register("A", GlobalHotKey.MOD_CTRL | GlobalHotKey.MOD_NOREPEAT, fun() { form.MessageBox("CTRL+A pressed!", "Hotkey", 0); }); // CTRL+Z → close the form GlobalHotKey.Register("Z", GlobalHotKey.MOD_CTRL | GlobalHotKey.MOD_NOREPEAT, fun() { form.SendMessage(0x0010, 0, 0); // WM_CLOSE }); Application.Run(form.Handle); GlobalHotKey.UnregisterAll();
Requirements: A visible Form window must exist and have a running message pump (Application.Run). Call SetHandle(form.Handle) before registering hotkeys. Without a window handle, Register returns 0. The callback fires synchronously on the message-pump thread.
Rect function Create a Win32 RECT structure

Creates a Rect with the given Left, Top, Right and Bottom. Used with the Win32 window functions, and the same type every rect-returning call answers.

var r = Rect(10, 20, 100, 200);
// Get window dimensions into a Rect var rect = Rect(0, 0, 800, 600); print("Width: " + (rect.right - rect.left)); // Result: 800
Clipboard namespace The desktop's clipboard text in one call, and the doors for a format the script assembles itself

The clipboard of the MACHINE rather than of a window, so a console tool copies as readily as a form. The text travels as CF_UNICODETEXT, and the whole recipe a correct write needs is the engine's: the MOVABLE global block the clipboard takes ownership of and frees itself, the payload as NUL-terminated UTF-16, the lock a read requires, and the release only when the handover failed.

MemberDescription
SetText(text)Replace the clipboard's text with this one, answering whether it landed.
GetText()The clipboard's text, or an empty string when it holds none.
Clear()Leave the clipboard empty, answering whether it could be opened.
Open([owner])Hold the clipboard, so the calls that follow can read or write ANY format. An owner window is optional (nothing owns it by default) and Close() must release it in a finally, because a script that leaves it held blocks every other process.
Close()Release the clipboard, handing it to the next process.
Empty()Discard what the clipboard holds, whatever its format.
SetData(format, hMem)Hand a block to the clipboard in the format the script names. The clipboard takes OWNERSHIP, so the block must come from Mem.Alloc and must NOT be freed by the caller; it answers the handle, or 0 when the handover failed (and then the block is still the caller's).
GetData(format)The block the clipboard holds in that format, as a handle to lock and read. The block belongs to the clipboard: lock it with Mem, and never free it.
Watch(control, handler), Unwatch(control)Be TOLD when the clipboard changes, instead of comparing GetText() on a timer: the handler is called with the watched control from the pump, on your thread. Watch answers whether the window was registered, Unwatch whether something was being watched, and a closed window drops its own registration.
// copy the log, then read it back: the second half must answer the first if (Clipboard.SetText(logText)) { print("copied " + logText.Length + " character(s)"); } else { print("the clipboard is held by another process"); } var back = Clipboard.GetText();

A failure is a VALUE and not an error, because another process holding the clipboard open is normal on a busy desktop: SetText answers false and GetText an empty string. An empty clipboard and one held elsewhere are the same answer to a reader, so a script that must tell them apart clears it first and checks what it reads.

TEXT is what the pair above covers, and the five doors cover the rest: another format (a dropped-file list, an image) is the script's own blob, handed over with SetData or read back with GetData while the clipboard is held open. The ownership rules a script must obey are on those rows, and they are the reason the pair above exists: a block the clipboard owns is easy to leak or to free twice.

Watching for changes: Clipboard.Watch, not a poll

Windows TELLS a window when the clipboard changes, so a watcher does not have to compare GetText() on a timer. Clipboard.Watch(control, handler) registers the window the control owns and answers whether it did; every change then calls the handler with that control, from the pump, on your thread. Clipboard.Unwatch(control) stops it and answers whether something was being watched, and the registration goes with the window when the window dies, so a closed form does not keep a handler alive.

// print the first text copied after the watch starts, then stop watching var watch = Application.CreateForm("clipboard watch"); // the window exists already (created, hidden): nothing to call here, and it is never shown var seen = [].ToList(); Clipboard.Watch(watch, fun(Control target) { seen.Add(Clipboard.GetText()); }); Clipboard.SetText("first"); for (var i = 0; i < 100 && seen.Count == 0; i = i + 1) { Application.DoEvents(); sleep(20); } print(seen.Count > 0 ? "arrived: " + seen[0] : "no notification arrived"); Clipboard.Unwatch(watch);

Three rules the shape needs. The listener belongs to a WINDOW, so the control must have one: Application.CreateForm creates it (hidden) before returning, so nothing has to be called to make one and a form that is never shown is enough. The handler runs INSIDE the pump, so it is on your thread and can call anything, the clipboard included. And clearing the clipboard is itself a change, so a watcher that runs a snippet and then empties the clipboard must ignore the event its own clear provokes, which is what comparing against the text it just handled answers.

assets/language/probes/clipboard_runner.slc is this watch as a working tool: leave it running in the REPL, copy any script text, and the snippet is executed with RunScript and shown in a dark, centred window whose log box fills it, with a Clear button, a Run in this session (global) check box and a status bar carrying the last run, with the same entry appended to clipboard_runs.log beside it and the clipboard emptied so one paste runs once. Its panel is a SECOND window and deliberately not the watched one: a displaced window procedure also displaces WM_COMMAND and WM_PAINT, so the panel keeps the engine's own procedure and only the hidden notification target is watched, which is what Clipboard.Watch now arranges itself.

Events namespace A feed a script can hold: subscribe to it, publish from any thread, consume it with await foreach

A FEED is a value that carries events instead of owning them. A class event is the shortest way to say "this object tells you something", and it is the right door when the publisher is the object you hold. A feed covers the other shapes: handing the source of events to another function, publishing from a socket thread or a Process output callback while a subscriber writes a window, ending with a reason, and letting a consumer PULL rather than be called.

Values are object, so one feed carries lines, records, numbers or instances without a type per payload. Every subscriber has its own queue of a fixed capacity, so a slow subscriber cannot hold up a fast one and the memory a feed can hold does not grow with the traffic.

Creating one

CallWhat it makes
Create()A feed delivered inline, holding 1024 values per subscriber, dropping the oldest when one is full.
Create(mode)The shorthand for the common case: "inline" or "runThread".
Create({ mode: 'runThread', capacity: 256, overflow: 'block' })All three settings. A name this call does not know is REFUSED, naming the three it takes, so a typo cannot silently leave the default in place.

What a feed answers

MemberDescription
Subscribe(onNext [, onEnd])Call onNext for every value, and onEnd once when the feed ends: with an empty string for a normal end, with the reason after Fail. Answers a handle; a value that is not a function is refused by name.
Start(work [, state [, options]])Run work as the feed's PRODUCER on its own background thread, handing it the feed first and state second when one is given: a normal return ends the feed with Complete, and a script error is reported once and ends it with Fail, so a consumer learns why instead of waiting for an end that never comes. A function of no parameters, of the feed, or of the feed and a state value is accepted, and the state may be null when only options are wanted. The one option is sta: Start(work, null, { sta: true }) runs the body in a single-threaded apartment, which a body that drives COM needs (it refuses on an MTA thread), and it is the non-blocking counterpart of Task.RunSta, which waits for its body. This is what replaces ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem for a feed.
Next(value)Publish one value to every subscriber. Ignored once the feed has ended, which is what a producer that is a moment behind its consumer needs.
Complete(), Fail(reason)End the feed. A subscriber still gets the values already queued for it, then its onEnd.
Dispose()End the feed NOW: what is queued is dropped and no end handler runs. Usable as using var feed = Events.Create();
ReadOnlyA view of the same feed that can subscribe and cannot publish: Next, Complete and Fail are refused there, and its own Dispose does nothing, so a script can hand a feed to somebody else without handing over the right to publish on it.
Count, Subscribers, Closed, DroppedWhat is queued for the subscribers that have not been given it, how many are listening, whether the feed has ended, and how many values the capacity has cost. A pull loop (await foreach) COUNTS in Subscribers and not in Count, because it owns its own queue, which is what lets a producer wait for its consumer with while (feed.Subscribers == 0).
Mode, Capacity, OverflowThe three settings the feed was created with, as the names above.

A subscription is an ordinary IDisposable, so the engine's own using is the idiomatic unsubscribe and no Dispose() call is needed: using (var sub = feed.Subscribe(onLine)) { ... } disposes at the block's closing brace, and using var sub = feed.Subscribe(onLine); disposes at the end of the enclosing block, which is why the declaration form works inside a function. A read-only view's Dispose is a no-op on purpose, so using on a view is harmless.

Json.Serialize(feed) answers the feed's STATE: Mode, Capacity, Overflow, ReadOnly, Closed, Subscribers, Queued and Dropped. The subscribers are deliberately absent, because each is a closure over the run it was made in and nothing could rebuild one from JSON. A read-only view carries the same rows with ReadOnly: true, and Json.Serialize(subscription) answers Closed. Serializing a feed is how a tool reports what its pipelines are doing; it is not a way to move one, so a TYPED read into the type is refused by name (unknown type name 'Subject'): what comes back from JSON is the snapshot, as a dictionary. Serialize, read back, serialize again gives the same text, which is what makes a snapshot comparable across runs.

Where a delivery runs: inline or runThread

inline calls the subscriber on the thread that published, before Next returns. That is what a script publishing from its own statements expects, and it is the default.

runThread queues the value and delivers it on the thread the RUN began on, inside the engine's own pump: between statements, in Task.Wait and inside Application.Run, where a wake-up message makes the delivery prompt rather than waiting for the next mouse move. This is the mode for a producer on another thread: a subscriber that writes a control, or reads interpreter state, must run on the run thread, and a control write from a Process output callback does not land.

The setting is per FEED, not per subscriber, because it is about the source: a socket or a worker thread is runThread, and a value published from your own statement is inline.

Delivery follows the statement boundary, so a script that blocks inside one statement sees its feed when that statement ends. await foreach does not have that limitation: a pull consumer waits on the value itself.

Where a subscriber runs, and the one rule it owes

A subscriber runs on the RUN thread, never on the publisher's: that is what makes runThread safe for a UI, because the box a subscriber writes is the one the message loop owns. The rule that follows is that a subscriber must not pump. If it calls Application.DoEvents (or anything that waits and pumps, such as await) the next value is delivered INSIDE the current delivery, so an app that runs its work in a subscriber and waits there will start a second piece of work inside the first. Keep a subscriber short, and let the loop do the waiting.

Who publishes: feed.Start(work)

Most feeds have one producer, and Start owns the three things that spelling gets wrong when it is written by hand. It runs the body on its own background thread with the stack a run gets, so the run thread (and its window) stays responsive. It ends the feed for you: a normal return is Complete, and a script error is reported once in the engine log and becomes Fail(reason), where an escaping error in a ThreadPool body is fatal and no script can catch it. And it hands the feed to the body as its first parameter, so the producer can be a named function with nothing captured, with the caller's state arriving second exactly where the pool callback's own argument used to be.

What it does not do is abort the body: .NET has no thread abort, so a long-lived producer guards itself with while (!feed.Closed) { ... }, and a consumer that ends the feed stops it at its next check. Publishing from the producer thread is always safe; a subscriber that writes a control still needs runThread, which is the mode that moves the delivery to the run thread.
