When a subscriber is too slow: overflow

PolicyWhat happens to a value that does not fit
'dropOldest'The oldest queued value goes, so a subscriber that catches up reads the NEWEST traffic. The default, and what a log or a price feed wants.
'dropNewest'The arriving value is dropped, so the oldest queued ones survive.
'block'The PUBLISHER waits for room, and after five seconds it gives up and drops the oldest instead, which keeps a dead consumer from stalling a producer for ever. A publisher that is itself on the run thread never waits, since the consumer it would be waiting for is that thread.

Every value a policy costs is counted in Dropped, so a script can tell "the consumer is behind" from "the source is quiet".

Pulling instead: await foreach

A feed is also an async sequence, so a consumer that would rather ask for the next value than be called can loop over it. Each consumer is a subscriber with its own queue, and the loop ends when the feed does; a break unsubscribes. A plain foreach is refused and names await foreach, because a feed has no end until it ends.

The rules worth knowing before using one

A feed is a BROADCAST, not a queue: a value published while nobody is listening is dropped. Start listening first, or keep the values yourself until the consumer arrives.

A subscriber that throws does not break the publisher: the failure is reported once, in the engine's log, and that subscriber is removed so one mistake cannot poison every later value.

A feed belongs to the INTERPRETER that created it, not to the run that happened to create it: in a session it stays open across .runs, and a producer started by one run is still ticking in the next one, and it is closed when that interpreter is disposed, which is also when a detached capture's own interpreter goes away. That is what makes Dispose the script's own way to end a producer early, and it is why a producer that must not outlive its work guards with while (!feed.Closed).

// a worker thread publishes, the window shows the lines: runThread is what makes the control write legal var form = Application.CreateForm("feed"); var box = form.CreateTextBox("", 8, 8, 620, 320); var feed = Events.Create("runThread"); var sub = feed.Subscribe(fun(object line) { box.AppendText("" + line + "\r\n"); }); // the producer receives the feed and runs off the run thread; a normal return ends the feed feed.Start(fun(EventSubject feed) { foreach (var name in Directory.GetFiles(".")) { feed.Next(name); } }); form.Show(); Application.RunFor(1500, form); print("closed by the producer: " + feed.Closed + ", subscribers: " + feed.Subscribers); sub.Dispose();
// pulling: a consumer that asks for the next value instead of being called var lines = Events.Create("runThread"); lines.Start(fun(EventSubject feed) { // the loop attaches when it starts, and a value with no subscriber is dropped: wait for it while (feed.Subscribers == 0) { sleep(5); } for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i = i + 1) { feed.Next(i * 10); sleep(20); } }); await foreach (var value in lines) { print(value); }

The two shapes share one feed, one set of refusals and one bounded queue, so a script can start with Subscribe and move to await foreach without changing how values reach it.

Mem namespace Raw unmanaged buffer access named byte/word accessors, bulk fill, hex dump, disposable buffers

Safe, modern descendants of the classic BASIC PEEK/POKE. Operates only on buffers the script allocated itself (Mem.Alloc / Marshal.AllocHGlobal); there is intentionally no absolute-address byte access (antiquated and dangerous on modern virtual-memory OSes). All buffers are raw pointer values (long) or disposable wrappers.

Buffer lifecycle

var buf = Mem.Alloc(16); // unmanaged 16 bytes, returns a pointer (long) Mem.Free(buf); // release (required when done) print(Mem.LiveBuffers()); // number of live Mem.Buffer wrappers (leak proof)
// Auto-free with using no explicit Mem.Free needed using (var b = Mem.Buffer(64)) { Mem.WriteByte(b.Ptr, 0, 0xAB); print(Mem.ReadByte(b.Ptr, 0)); // 171 } // b.Dispose() frees the buffer automatically

Named byte/word accessors (the PEEK/POKE width)

MethodDescription
ReadByte(ptr[, offset])Read one byte the true PEEK
WriteByte(ptr, value[, offset])Write one byte the true POKE
ReadInt16(ptr[, offset]) / WriteInt16(ptr, value[, offset])16-bit little-endian read/write
ReadInt32(ptr[, offset]) / WriteInt32(ptr, value[, offset])32-bit read/write
ReadInt64(ptr[, offset]) / WriteInt64(ptr, value[, offset])64-bit read/write
ReadString(ptr)UTF-16 string read (Marshal.PtrToStringUni)
ToPointer(text) / FreePointer(ptr)Allocate/free the UTF-16 copy of a string, which is what a native call wanting a wchar_t* takes. The pointer is the caller's to free.

Offset form: the two-argument write forms treat the 2nd arg as the value at offset 0; the three-argument form is (ptr, offset, value). When no offset is given, offset 0 is used.

Bulk operations

Mem.Fill(ptr, length, value); // memset the POKE-loop replacement var dump = Mem.Dump(ptr, length[, bytesPerRow]); // hex + ASCII inspection
// Fill a 200 MB buffer with 0xFF, then hex-dump the first 16 bytes var buf = Mem.Alloc(200 * 1024 * 1024); Mem.Fill(buf, 200 * 1024 * 1024, 0xFF); print(Mem.Dump(buf, 16, 8)); Mem.Free(buf);
Leak detection: unmanaged buffers are invisible to GC.GetTotalMemory. Use GC.PrivateMemory() / GC.WorkingSet() to detect unmanaged leaks (see the GC entry). Mem.LiveBuffers() returns the count of Mem.Buffer wrappers still allocated the direct proof that every using / using var scope released its pointer. using (var b = Mem.Buffer(n)) auto-frees on block exit, even on exception; using var b = Mem.Buffer(n) frees at enclosing scope exit (see the using entry). To release a wrapped buffer manually, call b.Free() (alias of b.Dispose()): it frees the pointer, zeroes b.Ptr, and decrements LiveBuffers() double-call safe. Do not call the raw Mem.Free(b.Ptr) on a wrapped buffer: it frees the bytes but leaves the wrapper counting it (counter stays elevated).
GC namespace Garbage collection control

Provides .NET GC metrics and control collect memory, query usage, and inspect generation counts.

GC.Collect(); GC.CollectAsync([gen]); // non-blocking collect GC.GetTotalMemory(); GC.GetTotalMemoryFormatted(); GC.GetAllocatedBytes(); // thread allocated GC.GetAllocatedBytesFormatted(); GC.GetGeneration(obj); GC.GetCollectionCount(gen); GC.GetMemoryInfo(); // GC memory status GC.GetMemoryInfoFormatted(); GC.GetTotalPauseDuration(); GC.WaitForFinalizers(); GC.SuppressFinalize(obj); GC.ReRegisterForFinalize(obj); GC.Cleanup(); GC.MaxGeneration; GC.WorkingSet(); // OS resident bytes (long) GC.PrivateMemory(); // OS committed private bytes (long) the reliable signal for unmanaged buffers GC.TrimMemory(); // trim the process working set (EmptyWorkingSet) the OS pages out the GC's reserved-but-idle segments
print("Memory: " + GC.GetTotalMemory()); GC.Collect(); print("After GC: " + GC.GetTotalMemory()); print("Gen 0 collections: " + GC.GetCollectionCount(0)); // After a bursty run (big collections, benches): GC.Collect compacts the managed heap but the // GC keeps its reserved segments committed, so the process RAM stays high. TrimMemory() asks // the OS to page those idle pages out the managed heap is untouched. The REPL's .gc collect // does this automatically. GC.TrimMemory();
Json namespace JSON serialization, deserialization with typed reconstruction

Built on System.Text.Json with AOT-safe Utf8JsonWriter/Utf8JsonReader (no reflection). Serializes any interpreter-compatible value and parses JSON back into script objects. Supports typed reconstruction of class and struct instances via Deserialize.

An engine object serializes as what it is, one arm per kind rather than by reflection: an AOT image trims what a reflection walk would have found, so every namespace used to serialize as the type name "Namespace". A namespace answers its own surface, a Form its document, a script class its fields, and a value with no shape of its own the name a script writes for it, never a CLR type name:

var Z = Bytecode.LoadNamespace(one.Bytes, "What"); print(Json.Serialize(Z)); // {"Name":"What","Namespaces":{"A":{"Name":"A","Functions":["add"]}}, // "Properties":["What","__meta"]} the label a load gave it is listed, never walked into

Serialization primitives & collections

Json.Serialize(42); // "42" Json.Serialize(true); // "true" Json.Serialize("hello"); // '"hello"' Json.Serialize(null); // "null" Json.Stringify(value, true); // pretty-print Json.Deserialize<Dictionary<string, object>>(Json.Serialize(value)); // the raw JSON view, as one call

What Serialize returns, and why a nested result looks escaped

Json.Serialize returns a string (its typeof is string), not a JSON value. So handing its result to something that serializes again encodes it twice: the inner call turns the object into text, and the outer one then encodes that text as a JSON string, which by the JSON rules cannot hold a bare " and must write \". The backslashes exist only in the outer text; parse the envelope once and the value is the JSON text you wrote, with real quotes.

// a host that wraps a script's return value in its own JSON envelope Json.Serialize({ "ReturnValue": Json.Serialize(Build()) }); // {"ReturnValue":"{\"X\":3,\"Y\":4}"} text inside text Json.Serialize({ "ReturnValue": Build() }); // {"ReturnValue":{"X":3,"Y":4}} one object, one encoding

So return the value, not its serialization, wherever something else will serialize the answer: the value of a return that a host reads (a SQLite slc_file call, an MCP tool result, an HTTP JSON body, a form document row). The nested call is worth writing only when the consumer wants text: storing into a TEXT column, appending to a log, or printing it. Then the escapes are the correct JSON for a string, and a reader gets the object back by parsing a second time. Json.Stringify behaves the same way (it is a string too), and Json.SerializeToUtf8Bytes is the same encoding as bytes.

Serialization classes & structs

Class and struct instances serialize as flat JSON by default (public fields only, no type metadata). CLR types (like ErrorInfo, CancelEventArgs) also serialize without __type by default pass {"showType": true} to include type metadata for round-trip deserialization:

Json.Serialize(person); // {"name":"John","age":30}

Options are passed via a dictionary: the literal spelling ({"pretty": true}) and an options bag read from JSON both work. Keys are names, so they follow the interpreter's case rule like every other name the spelling the option is declared with in the default C#-strict mode, any case under the REPL's .lax. A key that does not match is reported as a warning and dropped, so neither a typo nor a differently-cased key can quietly become default output. includeNonPublic and nonPublic are two different modes, not two spellings of one: the first adds the non-public members to the public view, the second replaces it so a payload meant to show the non-public side does not have to filter its own output.

Because Json.Deserialize takes no options of its own and returns a dictionary, an options bag can be written as JSON too: Json.Serialize(x, Json.Deserialize('{"showType":true}')). That is the pattern crash_json_serialize.slc uses options read as data, and a typo is visible in the literal.

// A misspelled key is reported, not swallowed, and the keys that were understood still apply Json.Serialize(person, Json.Deserialize('{"showType":true,"typ":true}')); // [hh:mm:ss.mmm] [WARNING] Script: Json.Serialize: ignoring unknown option 'typ'. Valid options: // includeNonPublic, nonPublic, includeType, showType, pretty, omitDefaults. // → {"__type":"Person","name":"John","age":30} (showType still applied) Json.Serialize(person, Json.Deserialize('{"showTyp":true}')); // → {"name":"John","age":30} the same warning names showTyp, which is why the tag is missing
var opts = new Dictionary<string, object>(); opts["includeType"] = true; // {"__type":"Person","name":"John","age":30} the same marker as showType opts["includeNonPublic"] = true; // public AND private/protected fields opts["nonPublic"] = true; // ONLY the non-public ones the complement of the line above opts["showType"] = true; // {"__type":"Person","name":"John","age":30} script classes & structs too opts["omitDefaults"] = true; // only the fields whose value is not their TYPE's default // Native: Json.RoundTrip("hello") → "hello" (serialize + deserialize with __type) // Script-level helper alias (optional): var RoundTrip = (val) => { return Json.RoundTrip(val); }; opts["pretty"] = true; // multi-line indented output Json.Serialize(person, opts);

omitDefaults applies to a script class or struct field whose value is its TYPE's default (0, false, "", or null), so an object that sets a few of its fields emits only those. A field whose declared initializer DIFFERS from the type default is not omitted, because the test is against the type. What is left out reads back as the default it was, exactly, since Deserialize fills an absent key with that same value. A DICTIONARY entry and an ARRAY element are never omitted: there a zero is data or a position, not a default. The comparison is exact, so a 1e-7 is not a zero, and a non-default object is emitted whole. A dictionary ENTRY is a key/value pair rather than a property, so it is never omitted; a dictionary VALUED FIELD that is null goes like any other property, while an EMPTY one does not; and an object held in an object field has its own fields treated by the same rule. That is .NET's WhenWritingDefault condition, spelled as one option.

Serialization a form and its controls

A form, or any control, serializes as its property table: an array of rows, each {"Name":..., "Type":..., "Value":...}, which is the same table ctrl.PropList() answers, followed by the members the control's OWN kind adds (Theme and the palette, Padding, GridSize, and so on, which the base table cannot carry). A control made with CreateWinControl also reports ClassName, Style and ExStyle, which is what it takes to make that window again.

The form's children follow under a Controls row of type list, and each entry is ITSELF a row, so the same triple exists at every depth: {"Name":"Button1","Type":"Button","Value":[ ...the child's rows... ]}. The entry carries the child's IDENTITY, which is why the child's own rows do not repeat it: every control in the document therefore has a name, the one the script set or <Kind><n> counted per kind among its siblings, and the name and the kind each appear once. The ROOT is the exception and has to be, because nothing above it names it: its own rows carry Name and Kind.

The root also states the LAYOUT's version, as its first row: {"Name":"Version","Type":"int","Value":1}. Kind says which host a document is and Version says which layout of it, so a document written by a NEWER engine is refused by name instead of being mis-read, while a version older than this one, and a document with no such row at all (the layout that predates it), is read normally. Only a document ROOT carries it: a child's rows and a document window's rows are part of the same document, and Json.Serialize of a bare control is a fragment of one rather than a document, so it claims no version.

A form also publishes the CLIENT area its layout was designed in, as ClientWidth and ClientHeight. They are in DESIGN units, which are the units of Left, Top, Width and Height and so of every child's geometry, and they are the one pair of rows a document states that a reader cannot set: the document says the room its layout was laid out against, so a script can CHECK that the window it rebuilt has the same room instead of assuming it, which is what a different frame changes (another monitor's DPI, another theme). A control that is not a form has the two members but not the rows, because a form is what lays children out.

An MDI frame and an MDI document window are HOSTS too, and they write the same document: the frame's root says Kind: "MdiForm" and it carries its own controls under Controls and its DOCUMENT WINDOWS under MdiChildren, each of which nests its own Controls, so a frame's whole tree travels. Neither is a Control, so before this they answered a flat object of their public members, with a handle in it and no kind at all. READING one back is what Application.FormFromJson does, and it builds WHICHEVER host the root names: a frame comes back with its document windows, each window with its own controls, and a document whose root is a single MdiChild gets an implicit frame to be parented to (a window belongs to an MDI client, and a client to a frame).

The TYPE column carries a name a SCRIPT can write, and it is as precise as the control makes possible: a scalar's name (int, bool, string, color), a registered type's (ThemeMode), a nullable's (uint?), and a list's ELEMENT type where it is known (List<string> for the item texts of a ListBox or a ComboBox, List<ControlProp> for the children of a form, whose entries are the same rows one depth down). The spelling is the engine's own, so typeof of those value answers List and List<int> is written the same way; a list whose elements were not fixed stays a bare List.

Application.FormToJson(form) writes that document and Application.FormFromJson(doc) builds a NEW form from it, its title and its controls included, and answers how many controls were created. Building is the only direction: the document becomes a fresh host (a form, an MDI frame or a document window, whichever the root names) rather than being re-applied to one a script already holds, so a form a script wants to change is changed through its own members. The pair is what makes a stored form a reusable TEMPLATE: write the document to a database, read it back, and get a live form with the same controls and the same properties. FormToJson is Json.Serialize on the same value, so a control writes one format either way. A row whose property cannot be written is a fact the document merely REPORTS (ClassName, ItemCount, ColumnCount, TabCount, ClientWidth, ClientHeight) and is skipped; any other row the control does not carry is refused by name rather than dropped. An EVENT HANDLER is not in the document and cannot be: a handler is a closure over the interpreter that made it, so serializing one answers megabytes rather than a value (one handler is about 3.8 million characters, against two thousand for a whole form) and it would mean nothing in the process that read the document back. The document carries the names instead, which is what the index is for: a template is the LOOK, and the behaviour is re-attached to it by name (copy["Button1"].Click = ...).

var src = Application.CreateForm("template"); src.Theme = ThemeMode.Custom; src.ThemeBackground = 0x203040; var ok = src.CreateButton("OK", 10, 10, 80, 24); // the row a template table would hold, and a form built back out of it var doc = Application.FormToJson(src); var copy = Application.FormFromJson(doc); print(Application.FormToJson(copy) == doc); // True, at every depth

Typed deserialization

Json.Deserialize("Name", json) maps the payload onto Name, and Json.Deserialize<T>(json) is the same thing with the type as a type argument. The name is not advisory: it has to resolve, and it has to agree with the payload's shape "List<int>" and "IList" want a JSON array (they promise indexing), "Dictionary<string, int>" wants a JSON object, "HashSet" builds a set from an array, "Tuple" takes a positional array, and "Iterable" and "IEnumerable" accept either shape, because that is what those collection predicates mean everywhere else in the language. A declared member type is imposed inside the container as well: Dictionary<string, Person> gives Person values and HashSet<Person> holds them, while a base-type member (int) has nothing to impose. Every spelling the string name, the type argument, and the untyped form that infers from __type reaches one implementation, so they agree. A declared scalar is imposed, not merely tolerated: JSON numbers arrive as long, so List<int> hands back ints, and the conversion is the engine's own (the one behind Result.As<T>(), so 1.5 rounds to 2 and an overflowing value wraps, as unchecked arithmetic does). object means leave the payload as parsed, and a scalar payload that cannot become the named type says which payload it was rather than reporting the name as unknown. A name that resolves to nothing, or one whose shape the payload contradicts, is an error rather than a silent surprise.

// The name and the payload must agree Json.Deserialize("List<int>", '[1,2]'); // a typed list Json.Deserialize("Iterable", '{"a":1}'); // the dictionary Iterable takes either shape Json.Deserialize("Nonsense", '{"a":1}'); // error: unknown type name Json.Deserialize("Dictionary<string, int>", '[1,2]'); // error: array vs a dictionary name // The generic spelling, where the target is a plain class Json.Deserialize<Order>('{"Id":1042}'); // an Order // A type argument that is itself generic works too, and returns what the name form returns: Json.Deserialize<List<int>>('[1,2]'); // as "List<int>" above // Tuples are positional Json.Serialize((1,"a")) is [1,"a"] and the LABELS come from the type // argument, so a tuple's fields are reachable by name, not only as Item1/Item2: var pairs = Json.Deserialize<List<(string s, int i)>>('[["a",1]]'); print(pairs[0].s + "/" + pairs[0].i); // a/1 Json.Deserialize<(string s, int i)>('["a",1]'); // a Tuple as well the bare form works too // An element may name any supported type, containers included: var pair = Json.Deserialize<(int i, Iterable it)>('[1,[2,3]]'); print(pair.i + "/" + pair.it.Count); // 1/2

showType round-trip reference

showType: false (current default) clean output, no __type metadata. For round-trip with CLR types, use the typed Json.Deserialize("TypeName", json) overload.

showType: true includes __type in the output, enabling universal Json.Deserialize(json) auto-dispatch to reconstruct CLR types.

Containers carry a tag too. An object has a member slot for __type, so a dictionary simply gains one: {"__type":"Dictionary","k":1}. A JSON array has no member slot, so a list, tuple or array is wrapped {"__type":"List<string>","Values":["a","b"]}, {"__type":"int[]","Values":[1,2]}. A tuple also carries its labels beside Values {"__type":"Tuple","Names":["s","i"],"Values":["x",3]} because an array has nowhere to put them. The name is the one typeof gives (string[], List<string>, Dictionary, Tuple), and a HashSet is a container too: {"__type":"HashSet<int>","Values":[1,2]}.

A value the engine serves through an INTERNAL class is written by the ROOT of the collection it stands for. The list a typed Json.Deserialize hands back carries the declaration the read was asked for in typeof (List<int>, string[], IList), and its marker is the plain List, the way any other list is written, because the marker names the SHAPE a reader rebuilds and the element type is the wrapper's own business. The same rule covers whatever wrapper comes next, and is LazyDeserializedList still answers.

A dictionary's marker is metadata, not one of its entries. {"__type":"Dictionary<string, int>","k":1} reads back as the single entry k, untyped and typed alike, and a __type key holding anything that is not a container name is ordinary data and is kept. The parser rebuilds what was tagged, so Json.Parse(Json.Serialize(x, opts)) keeps the shape it had before tagging: a list comes back a list, and a tuple comes back a Tuple with its labels. A class instance with a field literally called Values is not affected the unwrap happens only when the type name is a container name.

// A real payload: an order with a list of lines and a totals dictionary class Line { public string Sku; public int Qty; } class Order { public int Id; public List<Line> Lines; public Dictionary<string, int> Totals; } // o = Order 1042, lines A-1×2 and B-7×5, totals {"qty": 7} Json.Serialize(o); // default: clean, no metadata // {"Id":1042,"Lines":[{"Sku":"A-1","Qty":2},{"Sku":"B-7","Qty":5}],"Totals":{"qty":7}} var opts = new Dictionary<string, object>(); opts["showType"] = true; Json.Serialize(o, opts); // the same payload, self-describing // {"__type":"Order","Id":1042, // "Lines":{"__type":"List","Values":[{"__type":"Line","Sku":"A-1","Qty":2}, // {"__type":"Line","Sku":"B-7","Qty":5}]}, // "Totals":{"__type":"Dictionary<string, int>","qty":7}} // ↑ three shapes in one payload: the object tags itself as a member, the list needs the // Values wrapper (an array has no member slot), and the dictionary's tag is just another // key. A container's tag is the name typeof gives it, and a callable is tagged "Function" // with its signature beside the marker (a JSON string has no member slot of its own). var typed = Json.Serialize(o, opts); Json.Deserialize(typed); // Order auto-dispatch through __type var strict = Json.Deserialize("Order", typed); // strict.Id == 1042, strict.Lines is a List with 2 items, strict.Totals is a Dictionary // the wrappers are unwrapped, so the containers come back as containers and not as the // {"__type":…,"Values":…} objects that carried them.
Can auto-roundtrip without showTypeNeeds showType: true
Primitives int, string, bool, nullCLR types in JsonTypeMap (CancelEventArgs, ScriptErrorInfo)
Collections (arrays, List, Dictionary)CLR types nested inside arrays / dicts
DateTime / TimeSpan (via typed Deserialize)ScriptFunction (fun lambdas)
Script classes (via typed Deserialize)

Deserialization overloads

// 1. Universal returns Dictionary (like Parse) var dict = Json.Deserialize('{"name":"John","age":30}'); print(dict["name"]); // "John" // 2. Typed by class/struct reference var p = Json.Deserialize(Person, '{"name":"Alice","age":30}'); print(p.GetInfo()); // methods and field access // 3. Typed by class/struct name string var p2 = Json.Deserialize("Person", '{"name":"Bob"}'); // 4. Typed by instance (infers type from prototype) var p3 = Json.Deserialize(new Point(0,0), '{"X":10}'); // infers Point // 5. Case-sensitive option the DEFAULT is the interpreter's case flag: C#-strict (like System.Text.Json), // so `x` ≠ `X`; a REPL `.lax` session makes the default tolerant. An explicit argument overrides either way. var p4 = Json.Deserialize(Point, '{"x":10}'); // case-SENSITIVE: 'x' ≠ 'X' → X=0 var p5 = Json.Deserialize(Point, '{"x":10}', false); // case-insensitive: matches 'X'

Parse (universal)

var obj = Json.Parse('{"name":"John","age":30}'); // Dictionary var arr = Json.Parse('[10,20,30]'); // List

Validation & Format

Json.Validate('{"a":1}'); // true Json.Format(json); // pretty-print existing JSON string Json.Minify(json); // strip whitespace

UTF-8 bytes (no string allocation)

var bytes = Json.SerializeToUtf8Bytes(data); // byte[] var obj = Json.Deserialize(bytes); // Dictionary from bytes // Deserialize also accepts byte[] no separate method needed var d = Json.Deserialize(bytes); // universal var p = Json.Deserialize(Person, bytes); // typed from bytes var p2 = Json.Deserialize("Person", bytes); // by name from bytes
Which form is cheaper depends on the work, and assets/language/repl/bench_json_string_vs_bytes.slc measures it on your own machine: one 1.5 MB document written and read both ways, interleaved, every round printed, with the minimum reported, plus what each call ALLOCATES, which is the reading that does not drift. Allocation states the difference plainly: writing to a string allocates two extra copies of the document (the bytes it built, then the string it decoded) and reading from a string allocates one (the encode), while the byte forms build neither. WRITING is otherwise dominated by building the JSON, so the two forms land close to each other in TIME. READING is where the byte form earns its keep. The larger lever is Deserialize against Parse: the typed form also walks the result to rebuild __type objects, which on that document allocates many times the document's own size. Reach for the byte form when reading a big payload, and for Deserialize when the payload has to come back as objects. Deserialize is ONE door, reading a string and a byte[] alike, and both serializers take the same options, read by one reader.

File I/O

Json.ToFile("out.json", data); Json.ToFile("out.json", data, true); // pretty-print var loaded = Json.FromFile("out.json");
// Serialize class with options var p = new Person(); print(Json.Serialize(p)); // {"name":"John","age":30} var opts = new Dictionary<string, object>(); opts["includeType"] = true; print(Json.Serialize(p, opts)); // {"__type":"Person","name":"John","age":30} var opts2 = new Dictionary<string, object>(); opts2["includeNonPublic"] = true; print(Json.Serialize(p, opts2)); // includes private fields // Deserialize 3 ways var d = Json.Deserialize('{"name":"Alice","age":30}'); // Dictionary var c = Json.Deserialize(Person, '{"name":"Alice","age":30}'); // ClassInstance var c2 = Json.Deserialize("Person", '{"name":"Bob"}'); // by type name // Case-sensitive matching (default: true) var p = Json.Deserialize(Point, '{"x":10}'); // 'x' ≠ 'X' X=0 (not set) var p2 = Json.Deserialize(Point, '{"x":10}', false); // case-insensitive: X=10 // Enum serialization enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } print(Json.Serialize(Color)); // {"Red":0,"Green":1,"Blue":2} var col = Json.Deserialize(Color, Json.Serialize(Color)); print(col.Red); // 0 (dictionary key access) // Round-trip: class → flat JSON → typed class var orig = Json.Serialize(c); var restored = Json.Deserialize(Person, orig); print(restored.name); // "Alice" // Nested classes deserialize recursively var co = Json.Deserialize(Company, '{"name":"ACME","addr":{"city":"Paris","zip":75001}}'); print(co.addr.city); // "Paris"

Merge & Select

Json.Merge(dictA, dictB); // deep-merge B into A (A is mutated) Json.Select(dict, "path.to.field"); // dot-path access into nested dicts
Supported types: null, primitives, dictionaries, lists, class instances, struct instances, arrays. A Task is none of them and answers null by design, since it is a handle to running work rather than data: serialize its result, or the inputs and the outcome (see async / await). Cyclic references detected. AOT-safe via Utf8JsonWriter/Utf8JsonReader zero reflection. JSON keys are matched to field names case-insensitively. Missing fields keep type defaults ("", 0, false). If the type name specified in Deserialize is not found, that is an error rather than a fallback a typo must not be mistaken for a deliberate cast. Bytes support: SerializeToUtf8Bytes avoids the string allocation, and Deserialize accepts a string and a byte[] alike, so no separate parse method exists for bytes.

Extending namespaces

Any namespace (including Json, File, Http, etc.) can be extended with user-defined functions or properties by simple assignment. This works because namespaces are reference types modifications are visible to all importing scripts.

// Add a function to the Json namespace Json.Reverse = (x) => { var chars = [c for c in x]; var result = ""; var i = Count(chars) - 1; while (i >= 0) { result = result + chars[i]; i = i - 1; } return result; }; // Call it like a native method print(Json.Reverse("hello")); // "olleh" // Also works for properties Json.Version = "1.0"; // Re-defining an existing method shows a warning: Json.Serialize = (x) => "overridden!"; // ⚠ Warning: Json.Serialize already exists.
// In an include file (json_utils.inc), import once and use everywhere: // json_utils.inc contents: Json.Pretty = (value) => Json.Serialize(value, true); Json.Get = (obj, path, def) => { /* nested access */ }; Json.Pick = (obj, keys) => { /* filter keys */ }; // Usage: import "../json_utils.inc"; print(Json.Pretty([1, 2, 3]));
Bytecode namespace Compile your functions once, save them to a .slcbc file, and run them later same process or a completely different one

Bytecode lets you save a compiled function to disk and run it later without the original source. Think of it as a tiny "DLL" for ScriptLangCore: your function is compiled to the internal bytecode format, written to a binary .slcbc file, and re-loaded in any later interpreter even a separate process. No parser and no AST are involved: the blob carries only value data (literals + type info) and nested-lambda shells.

Only functions the VM can compile are exportable, which includes a plain value-yield coroutine: its body compiles like any other and the loaded call wraps it so the yield sequence survives. Anything else (a body that falls back to the tree-walker, or a coroutine the VM cannot back, such as one that requests a yield) is skipped and reported (see Limitations).

Quick start 30 seconds

// writer.slc build once, save to disk int sumTo(int n) { var s = 0; for (var i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) { s = s + i; } return s; } print(Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/mylib.slcbc")); // "exported 1, skipped 0" // loader.slc run later, source file not needed Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/mylib.slcbc"); print(sumTo(10)); // 55 the function exists again, from bytecode

A .slcbc as a program

A bundle is not only a library. --compile writes one without running the script, and the executable runs a bundle the way it runs a .slc file:

ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc // builds app.slcbc, runs nothing ScriptLangCore.exe app.slcbc // runs the program ScriptLangCore.exe app.slcbc --quiet // the CLI switches a .slc accepts work here too

What the bundle carries explains how it runs. Its functions travel as bytecode, and its top level travels as source, so the program starts exactly as the file does. That second half covers the shapes a compiled entry cannot: a top-level const, whose const-ness the interpreter registers at declaration, or a body the compiler declines. The source travels deflated, so a bundle's bytes do not contain the program's text.

--source=strict, which --no-source is shorthand for, leaves the source out entirely. The top level then runs from bytecode, and its declarations, the bundle's classes and structs, travel as descriptors. A program whose top level the compiler cannot compile is refused by name instead of being written. An instance field's initializer travels as a compiled body of its own, so public int V = 5; and public int Doubled = 5 * 2; build the same instances from a bundle as from the file; one that reads the instance (public int W = this.V + 1;) is refused by name, because the body that carries it has no this. A ref/out argument whose target is a top-level variable travels as a cell over that variable, so a swap, an out and a ref at the top level run from a bundle as they do from the file. An interface's default bodies and property accessors travel the same way, and a class carries the interfaces it implements, so x is IBox<int> answers from a bundle as it does from the file. An import travels as its own data (the path, an alias when it has one, and the statement's position), and the loader re-imports the module before the entry runs, so a one-line import no longer costs the whole file its source. An optional parameter's default value travels with its declaration as a compiled body of its own, so a stripped bundle answers F(1) for int F(int a, int b = 3) exactly as the file does. A default that a loaded body cannot answer is refused by name: one that reads the instance (this) or a name the bundle cannot resolve. A top-level const is compiled into the entry and keeps both its value and its const-ness, so a write to it is refused from a stripped bundle exactly as from the file. Without a flag the bundle CARRIES the program text, which is the default and what a plain --compile has always done; --source=strip leaves the text out whenever that is honest and carries it, saying which in the report, when it is not; and --source=strict (what --no-source is shorthand for) leaves it out or refuses the compile by name. So a bundle written with strip or strict always tells you what it is:

ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc --source=strict // no source in the bundle, or a refusal naming why [bc] app.slc -> app.slcbc: exported 1, skipped 0, entry __program__, source stripped, 1 class(es), 0 struct(s) Error: could not write app.slcbc: Bytecode: cannot strip the source: the stripped form cannot carry the initializer of 'K.W' (an instance field's initializer, and its expression reads 'this', which a loaded body has no instance for), so an instance it builds would not hold the value the script gives it. Compile without --no-source, which carries the source and behaves as the script does. ScriptLangCore.exe --compile big.slc --source=strip // strip when honest, carry when not, and say which [bc] big.slc -> big.slcbc: exported 4, skipped 0, entry __program__, source carried instead (the stripped form carries no default value for 'K.M.a' (its expression reads 'this', which a loaded body has no instance for), so a call that omits it would be refused at run time instead of using the default) ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc // the default: the source travels, and the report says nothing about it

What the stripped form carries

Every declaration below, and the verdict each one gets from the strip gate. A refused shape is refused by name, before the bundle is written, because a bundle that silently differed from its script is the one outcome worth an error; --source=strip never refuses, it carries the source instead and says so in the report. So --source=strict, or its --no-source shorthand, is the opt-in that promises the bundle IS the program, and a file it cannot promise that for is still compilable, one flag short.

Declaration--source=strictNotes
the file's top level✅ carriedit becomes the bundle's ENTRY, the synthetic __program__, so the bundle runs the program rather than being a function library
functions, and local functions✅ carriedbytecode bodies. A local function declared INSIDE a block travels too, and a call to it resolves. One declared inside a lambda is the same: that body has no scope dictionary of its own, so the declaration travels in the bundle's function table and the call finds it. One declared inside a plain function travels as its source TEXT instead, which runs that body on the tree exactly as the file does
methods (instance and static), constructors, operators, destructors✅ carriedbytecode bodies, including a bare sibling call inside one
classes and structs✅ carriedas descriptors: fields, properties and the bodies above. A static field's value travels with it
enums, delegates, interfaces, extension blocks✅ carriedthe declaration sections, so the four kinds that have no class or struct descriptor of their own still travel
an interface's DEFAULT body, or a property accessor✅ carriedas member shells, like every other body, so a class that does not implement the member runs the same body from a bundle as from the file. A class also carries the interfaces it IMPLEMENTS, which a generic contract is matched by
import "./mod.inc", bare or with an alias✅ carriedas the statement's own data: the module is re-imported, through the same visitor a source run uses, BEFORE the entry runs, with the bundle's own directory resolving a ./ path. A CONDITIONAL import is not carried (replaying it would make it unconditional), so it declines the top level and the strip refuses by name
a top-level const✅ carriedcompiled into the entry with its const-ness, so a write to it is refused from the bundle exactly as from the file
an optional parameter's default value✅ carrieda compiled zero-parameter body of its own, so F(1) answers for int F(int a, int b = 3) as the file does
an instance field's initializer✅ carriedthe same shape as a default, so public int V = 5; and a computed one build the same instance. One that reads the instance is refused below
a params tail✅ carriedassembled before the call, and the tail does not count towards the required arguments
a generator (yield)✅ when the VM can back ita plain value yield travels and its drive steps it. A body that also makes a REQUEST (sleep, http, an event, ReadLineAsync) is refused below
an async body✅ carriedits await is an opcode, and the async-ness travels with the declaration, so a call from a compiled body hands its caller a Task as the file does
a ref/out argument on a METHOD call (c3.Bad(out v3), Interlocked.Increment(ref counter))✅ carriedthe argument travels as a cell over its target (a local slot, or a global), the callee writes through it, an out is checked on return, and the call site's keyword travels with the call so a swap is still refused by name
a ref/out argument on a FUNCTION call, an OVERLOADED name included✅ carriedthe same cell, and the keyword travels with the call, so the picker chooses the member the keyword fits (Bump(ref n) beside Bump(int, int)) and a call no member can honour is still refused by name, as a flag whose position falls in a params tail is
a top-level statement the compiler cannot model (o is int n, an await, a var lambda that calls itself)✅ carried, as its own SOURCE TEXTthat one statement runs on the tree exactly as in a source run, while the rest of the top level compiles as usual. This is the statement carrier (VmSetStatementCarrier, on by default); SLC_CARRIED_STATEMENTS=0 turns it off, and then a declined statement refuses the file instead. What a carried statement DECLARES (var g = fun(...) { ... g ... }) lands in the global scope when it runs, so a later compiled statement calls it normally
every statement of the top level declined, or one with no source text to carry❌ refusedthere would be no entry to run; the message names the statement kind
a class whose instance field has an initializer that reads the instance (public int W = this.V + 1)❌ refusedan initializer travels as a body of its own, which has no this, so the compiled form would read a null instance; the message names the field (Owner.field)
a generic class (class Box<T>)❌ refuseda descriptor does not reproduce it, so an instantiation would be missing at run time
a QUALIFIED interface receiver (IShape.area(x))❌ refuseda script interface is a name with no VALUE, and the VM stops at that instruction; a bundle's body is compiled only, so the run would end part-way. The message names the interface
an out var declaration✅ carried, as its own SOURCE TEXTit names a variable the TREE creates, so a compiled body has no declaration for it: the statement is carried and the variable exists in the bundle exactly as in the file (Give(out var made) then a read of made answers the same from both)
a ref or out argument naming a FIELD, a PROPERTY or an ELEMENT (Fn(ref h.F), Fn(ref a[i]))✅ carriedthe target travels as a cell built by the engine's own resolver (__ref_field__ / __ref_elem__), the same storage a compound assignment writes through, and the call site's keyword travels with it. Only a CHAINED index (a[i][j]) and a range stay on the tree, because the resolver would hand back a copy of a struct element
a REF RETURN (ref int F() { return ref x; })✅ carriedthe body travels as BYTECODE and the header's flags byte says it is a ref return, because the RETURN has to know: it dereferences for a value consumer and hands the cell back to an lvalue use. An lvalue call carries a marker of its own, so a bundle keeps F(..) = 7; and ref int r = ref F(..); working, or box.F() = 7; on a method
a ref LOCAL (ref int r = ref x;, var r = ref h.F, var r = ref a[i])✅ carriedthe target is a global, a FIELD or an ELEMENT, so the local holds the TARGET cell (the VM REPLACES the slot cell rather than nesting two, so the binding is the reference itself). Over a LOCAL variable it is an ALIAS: the two names are ONE storage, so the compiler maps the name to the target slot and emits nothing at all
a want-reference call as an LVALUE in the two shapes the compiler does not compile: a BARE call to the class's own method (Cell() = 12; inside a method), or one that NAMES its argument (box.Cell(add: 0) = 9;)✅ carriedthe BARE form works and the method's body travels as its own text, so the bundle answers what the file answers (that body is walked rather than compiled). The NAMED form is a LANGUAGE limit rather than a bundle one: assigning through a call that names its arguments is refused, with the same message from a file and from a bundle, while READING the same call is fine
an in parameter (int Scale(in int v))✅ carriedits declared TYPE travels with the parameter, which is what a call checks; read-only-ness is a PARSE-time rule, so a body that writes the name never existed and there is nothing to carry
an await foreach (an async stream)✅ carried, as its own SOURCE TEXTthe bytecode VM has no state for an async enumerator, so the STATEMENT stays the tree's: the compiler declines it and the statement carrier (VmSetStatementCarrier) hands it over by its own text, at the top level and inside an async body alike (a body holding one travels as its own text). The bundle of a file with a top-level await foreach prints what the file prints
an await using (an awaited disposal)✅ carried, as its own SOURCE TEXTthe disposal is a CLR ValueTask awaited from inside a statement, which the bytecode VM has no state for, so the statement (or the body holding it) travels as text and runs on the tree as in a source run
an extension property, an extension operator, a generic extension block❌ refusedno descriptor slot for the first two, and a generic block's members are compiled per instantiation, so there is no bytecode to carry
a member whose body the compiler did not take, a CONSTRUCTOR included✅ carried, the class or struct as its own SOURCE TEXTa body the compiler left to the tree (or a coroutine it cannot call from a compiled body) has no bytecode for a descriptor, so the DECLARATION travels as text and the loader re-registers it, members and constructors together. It used to be refused by name; measured, constructor_test is 28 passed from the file AND from its bundle now
the same NAME declared as both a class and a struct✘ refuseda source run resolves names in DECLARATION ORDER, while a bundle registers every declaration before its entry runs, so the later one wins from the first statement and the earlier one's members are unreachable; the message names the name
an optional parameter's default that reads this, or a name a loaded body cannot resolve❌ refuseda default travels as a body of its own, which has no instance; the message names the parameter (Owner.Method.param)
a call to a name the bundle cannot resolve❌ refusedthe call would fail at run time instead of resolving as it does in the file, and the message names what is missing

From a script, Bytecode.ExportProgram(outPath, source [, entryName] [, options]) does the same for a source text you hold, compiling it in a fresh interpreter so your own session is untouched. It strips the source by default, unlike ExportScript, and takes the same { "source": ... } options, so { "source": "carry" } keeps the program text instead.

In the REPL, .loadslcbc loads the functions and registers what the file declares (its classes, structs and extensions) without running the top level, so a loaded function that builds its own class works:

// app.slc: class Box { public int V = 3; public int Twice() { return V * 2; } } // int MakeBox() { var b = new Box(); return b.Twice(); } // in the REPL: .loadslcbc app.slcbc .functions // MakeBox MakeBox(); // 6, with Box registered from the carried source

Keeping a bundle honest

The verifier that runs at LOAD proves a bundle's format: every body's operands, jump targets, table indices and operand-stack balance, the format version, and the opcode fingerprint. It cannot say whether somebody edited the file after it was built, so --compile also SEALS the bundle: a SHA-256 of the whole file lives in the bundle's own header, and every load refuses a file whose bytes no longer match it. One file, nothing to keep in step.

// Error: Bytecode.LoadScript: this bundle does not match the digest it carries: // the file changed after it was built (the digest differs from byte 5 on: it says 6EAFA7D872BD5225..., // the bytes say C9E9969C30CF5F20...). Rebuild it with --compile, or rebuild it from its source; // a bundle with a sidecar (`<name>.slcbc.sha256`) is checked against that too.

What the digest covers, and what it cannot. The 32 bytes sit at offset 12 of the header and are computed over everything else: every body, every table, the carried source, the version and the fingerprint (a field cannot hash itself, so its own bytes count as zeros). A truncated download, a bad copy and a hand-patched body are all caught, which is what an integrity check is for. It is not a signature: the digest lives in the file it describes, so somebody who edits a body and recomputes that field produces a file that passes. For that question keep the expected hash somewhere the artifact cannot reach: Bytecode.WriteBundleManifest(path) writes a sha256sum-compatible sidecar, a sidecar you place beside a bundle is still honoured by every path load, and a mismatch is refused by name.

No sidecar means no second check, which keeps a bundle a script exported into a temp folder working exactly as before, and a blob from an older engine answers its clean version refusal before the digest is even looked at.

A bundle whose sections do not line up says so. A reader and a writer of this format disagreeing about one field is what a broken format change looks like, and a length read from the wrong place used to ask the runtime for that many bytes, so it surfaced as Out of memory on a file of a few hundred bytes. A string whose declared length is past the end of the blob, and bytes left over after the last section, are refused as what they are: the bundle's descriptor stream is out of phase: a string at byte 122 declares 127 byte(s) while 46 remain. The sentence names the position and the counts and says to rebuild with --compile, because a bundle this engine wrote cannot be in that state.

Command line

ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc // writes app.slcbc beside it, runs nothing ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc out.slcbc // writes the bundle where you say ScriptLangCore.exe --compile app.slc --source=strict // ...without the source: bytecode and descriptors only ScriptLangCore.exe app.slcbc // runs the bundle as a program ScriptLangCore.exe --dump-bytecode app.slc // prints what compiled, without running it ScriptLangCore.exe --dump-bytecode app.slc --program // ...and whether the top level itself compiled

--compile always builds, so a second run overwrites the bundle. In the REPL the -bc option is load-or-build instead: it loads the .slcbc sibling when one is there and only builds it when it is not, so a stale sibling is what runs unless you delete it or name another output.

--dump-bytecode prints the constant table, the locals, the global slots and every compiled function of a file, then one summary line per script:

[dump-bytecode] app.slc: 3 compiled function(s), program body: compiled (code=412 globalSlots=9) [dump-bytecode] lib.slc: 2 compiled function(s), program body: declined (while compiling an ExprStmt)

A body the verifier cannot balance is reported as a refusal, and the command fails instead of running it. That is what keeps a corrupted or hand-written bundle away from the executor:

[dump-bytecode] REFUSED __program__: ip 928: POP needs 1 value(s) on the operand stack, but 0 is/are there

A bundle written before the current format version is refused by version, so rebuild it with --compile; a bundle written from a session with no file on disk carries no source, and then the entry recorded at export is what runs. A bundle the engine cannot read at all (another version, a truncated or foreign file) is refused with ONE line that names the version it found and the fix, and a REPL session keeps running: the file counts as a file, the next statement still runs, and the CLR stack trace is printed only when SLC_STACK_TRACE=1 asks for it.

The REPL commands

.run app.slc // run one file .run app.slc -bc // load app.slcbc if it is there, else run the source and build it .run app.slc -bc app.v2.slcbc // the same, writing the bundle where you say .run app.slcbc // run the bundle: its carried source is the program .run stress_*.slc // a glob, or .run a.slc|b.slc for a list of files .run app.slc -q // quiet: the program's own output is suppressed .looprun 50 app.slc // 50 runs of one file; it takes -bc like .run does .loadslcbc lib.slcbc Lib // a library bundle: its functions arrive as namespace Lib .loadslcbc app.slcbc // a program bundle: its functions arrive flat, by name .functions // what is loaded now, with each function's signature

.run accepts several files at once, separated by | or matched by a glob, and each file's Check verdict is its own, so running one twice in a session reports each run separately.

Bytecode.ExportScript(path [, entryName] [, options])

string Bytecode.ExportScript(string path [, string entryName] [, options])

Writes every VM-compiled top-level function of the current script into path as a single-script bundle. Returns an "exported N, skipped M (names)" report so you can see what was saved and what was not. The optional entryName pins which function the bundle declares as its entry (the one LoadScript returns).

Where the program text goes: by default the bundle carries the script's own text, so a bundle whose top level the compiler declined still runs the file it came from. { "source": "strip" } leaves the text out when the strip is honest, and carries it (the report saying source carried instead (...)) when it is not. { "source": "strict" } refuses rather than carrying, naming what could not be stripped, which is what the CLI's --no-source does. An unknown key or spelling is an error, never a silently ignored option.

// the same export, three source modes Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/s1.slcbc"); // carries the program text Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/s2.slcbc", { "source": "strip" }); // strips when honest, carries otherwise Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/s3.slcbc", { "source": "strict" }); // strips, or refuses // the options dictionary also fits the entryName slot, so no placeholder null is needed: Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/s4.slcbc", { "source": "strict" });

Basic use export, then load in the same process:

// same-process round trip: export the current script's functions, load them back int myMath(int n) { var sum = 0; var i = 0; while (i < n) { sum = sum + i * 3; i = i + 1; } return sum; } print(Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/myMath.slcbc")); // "exported 1, skipped 0" Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/myMath.slcbc"); print(myMath(10)); // 135 same result as before the round trip print(myMath(100)); // 14850 loops are part of the bytecode

Advanced use cross-process: write in one run, load in another:

// writer.slc process #1 exports the bundle int myMath(int n) { /* ... as above ... */ } Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/myMath.slcbc", "myMath");
// loader.slc process #2 (days later, myMath source deleted) var entry = Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/myMath.slcbc"); // returns the entry function print(entry(10)); // 135 executed from bytecode, no parser involved print(myMath(10)); // 135 every bundle function is also defined by name

Edge cases:

// 1) entryName must be an exported function, else ExportScript throws try { Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/x.slcbc", "noSuchFn"); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // Bytecode.ExportScript: entry function 'noSuchFn' is not VM-compiled or not found in this script. // 2) a value-yield coroutine exports like any other function int countTo(int max) { var i = 0; while (i < max) { yield i; i = i + 1; } return -1; } print(Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/y.slcbc")); // "exported 2, skipped 0, entry __program__" (countTo and the top level) // 3) a single-script bundle has NO metadata import "x.slcbc" as Z will not work for it. // Use LoadScript for single-script bundles; import needs a library (ExportLibrary).
A value-yield coroutine IS exported, and the loaded call wraps it so the yield sequence survives. What stays out is a coroutine the VM cannot back from a compiled call, one that REQUESTS a yield (sleep/HTTP/event): it is skipped and named in the report.

In-memory bundles: the ...Bytes forms

Every member that reads or writes a .slcbc file also has a form that takes or returns byte[]. Use them when a bundle should not touch the disk: a blob in a database column, bytes from a socket, or a test that builds a library in memory. The file form is the memory form plus one read or one write, so the two cannot disagree about what a bundle is. A library's inputs need no files either, and the two forms differ in what a spec's string means: ExportLibrary reads it as a path, while ExportLibraryBytes reads it as the script text, so no Encoding call is needed for a script you hold. A byte[] spec is the script's text in both, and the member decides, so nothing is guessed from the value.

BytecodeResult Bytecode.ExportScriptBytes([string entryName] [, options])
BytecodeResult Bytecode.ExportProgramBytes(string source [, string entryName] [, options])
BytecodeResult Bytecode.ExportLibraryBytes(meta, scriptOrTuple... [, string[] ignoreVars])
BytecodeResult Bytecode.MergeLibraryBytes(meta, libOrBytes...)
Namespace Bytecode.LoadNamespace(byte[] bytes [, string alias])
Function Bytecode.LoadScript(string|byte[] pathOrBytes)  ·  string Bytecode.GetSource(string|byte[] pathOrBytes)  ·  string Bytecode.MergeLibrary(string outPath, meta, libOrBytes...)

The exporters return a result value with two members: .Bytes (the blob) and .Report, the same report string the file form returns, which is where skipped names and a carried source are named. A { "source": ... } dictionary means the same here as it does for the file form.

LoadNamespace(bytes [, alias]) is the memory form of import "x.slcbc" as Z. It returns the library as a namespace value, because import takes its path in the syntax. The alias is the label the library is reached by: it names the namespace being returned, and that label is a path segment through the value, so Z.What.A.add(2, 3) works beside Z.A.add(2, 3). It is deliberately NOT a name in scope: What.A.add(...) is undefined, because the path starts at the value you already hold. With no alias there is no label to spell, and the value is simply the namespace. Assign it and call through it like any namespace, and a merge may mix the two spellings, so a library on disk can join ones in memory.

Composition nests: a merged blob can be merged again, and a library's own function may call MergeLibraryBytes and hand the result back, so one library can know how to combine others. The only rule is that a function name stays unique across everything being merged, in its namespace, or the merge is refused and names the collision. There is no limit on how many libraries one call takes.

// two scripts to one namespaced library, nothing written to disk var meta = Bytecode.Meta("pair", "1.0"); var a = Bytecode.ExportLibraryBytes(meta, ("int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }\n", "A")); // the script TEXT, no file var b = Bytecode.ExportLibraryBytes(meta, ("int mul(int x, int y) { return x * y; }\n", "B")); print(a.Report); // "exported 2, skipped 0" var one = Bytecode.MergeLibraryBytes(meta, a.Bytes, b.Bytes); // "merged 4" var Z = Bytecode.LoadNamespace(one.Bytes, "Z"); print(Z); // "Z" the alias names it print(Z.A.add(2, 3)); // 5 the namespaces survive the merge print(Z.Z.A.add(2, 3)); // 5 the label is also a segment through the value var prog = Bytecode.ExportProgramBytes("print(\"hi\");", { "source": "carry" }); print(Bytecode.GetSource(prog.Bytes)); // the text those bytes carry

Bytecode.LoadScript(pathOrBytes)

Function Bytecode.LoadScript(string|byte[] pathOrBytes)

Reads a single-script bundle, defines every function into the current interpreter's global scope, and returns the entry function (or null when the bundle declared none). Every function body is decoded and verified at load, so a body that does not verify refuses the load here, naming the function, instead of failing when something first calls it.

Basic use load and call by name:

var entry = Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/lib.slcbc"); print(entry(10)); // 55 the returned entry function print(sumTo(10)); // 55 same function, also bound by name in global scope print(myMath(10)); // 135 non-entry bundle functions are defined too

Advanced use the entry as a "main": combine entryName at export time with the returned value at load time to give a bundle a clear entry point:

Bytecode.ExportScript("C:/Temp/lib.slcbc", "sumTo"); // pin the entry var main = Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/lib.slcbc"); print(main(10)); // 55 main is sumTo print(typeof(main)); // "Function" it is a normal callable

Edge cases:

// a bundle with no functions returns null var nothing = Bytecode.LoadScript("C:/Temp/empty.slcbc"); print(nothing == null); // True // loaded shells are VM-only: no tree-walker fallback exists for them (they carry no AST). // If the environment is incompatible the error surfaces AT CALL TIME see Limitations.

Bytecode.ExportLibrary(outPath, meta, scripts... [, ignoreVars])

string Bytecode.ExportLibrary(string outPath, meta, scriptOrTuple... [, string[] ignoreVars])

In memory: Bytecode.ExportLibraryBytes(meta, scripts... [, ignoreVars]) is this member without the output path, returning a result value to read .Bytes and .Report from (see In-memory bundles under Bytecode.ExportScript). Each script is written as a (script, ns) tuple or a bare script. Here a spec's string is a path (use ExportLibraryBytes to give the script TEXT instead), and a byte[] spec is the script's text, which is what makes a library buildable with nothing on disk.

Builds a library from several scripts into one .slcbc file. Each argument is either a script path (its functions land flat) or a (script, namespace) tuple (its functions land under namespace.*). A library also snapshots the modules' classes, structs, and top-level variables. Libraries carry metadata, so they can be loaded with import "lib.slcbc" as Z and expose Z.__meta.

An exported function keeps its optional parameter defaults, so Z.add(2) answers for int add(int x, int y = 3) just as the script does. A default that the library cannot carry is refused at export, naming the parameter: one that reads the instance (this), reads a name the library cannot resolve, or reads a top-level variable (a library's variables are snapshots, not bare names, so a function body cannot read one either).

meta is a Bytecode.Meta(name, version, description) value or a dict { "name": ..., "version": ..., "description": ... } both accepted.

Basic use one script, import as a namespace:

// build.slc merge one script into a library var meta = Bytecode.Meta("TestLib", "1.0", "my library"); print(Bytecode.ExportLibrary("lib.slcbc", meta, "math.slc")); // "exported 3, skipped 0"
// user.slc any later process import "lib.slcbc" as Z; print(Z.add(2, 3)); // 5 flat functions live directly on Z print(Z.__meta.Name); // TestLib the metadata round-trips

Advanced use namespaces, variables, and classes:

// a.slc has add/mul; b.slc has greet and a top-level var var meta = Bytecode.Meta("TestLib", "1.0", "two-module lib"); print(Bytecode.ExportLibrary("lib.slcbc", meta, ("a.slc", "Math"), // a.slc's functions land under Math.* "b.slc")); // b.slc's land flat
import "lib.slcbc" as Z; print(Z.Math.add(2, 3)); // 5 a.slc's add at Z.Math.add print(Z.Math.mul(6, 7)); // 42 print(Z.greet("bob")); // Hello bob flat print(Z.LIB_CONST); // 42 top-level variable snapshots travel too var g = Z.sumTo; print(g(5)); // 15 namespace members are usable as values

Edge cases the strict variable contract and the ignoreVars escape hatch:

// STRICT default: an unserializable top-level variable ABORTS the export and // NO file is written a partial library would silently lose state. try { Bytecode.ExportLibrary("bad.slcbc", meta, "module_with_proc.slc"); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // Bytecode.ExportLibrary: variable 'proc' is not serializable (value of type ProcessHandle // cannot be serialized). Remove or make it serializable before exporting the export is // aborted and no file is written. // ESCAPE HATCH: list the name in a trailing array those variables are skipped with a warning print(Bytecode.ExportLibrary("ok.slcbc", meta, "module_with_proc.slc", ["proc"])); // [WARNING] Bytecode.ExportLibrary: variable 'proc' is in ignoreVars skipped (not exported). // "exported 1, skipped 0" // duplicate function names across modules abort the export try { Bytecode.ExportLibrary("dup.slcbc", meta, "a.slc", "a.slc"); } catch (var ex2) { print(ex2.Message); } // duplicate function 'add'.
import requires an alias: import "lib.slcbc" as Z a bare import "lib.slcbc" is an error for bytecode libraries. And a library is required: single-script bundles (ExportScript) have no metadata and cannot be imported this way use Bytecode.LoadScript for those.

Bytecode.MergeLibrary(outPath, meta, libPaths...)

string Bytecode.MergeLibrary(string outPath, meta, string libPath1 [, string libPath2...])

Merges already-compiled .slcbc libraries into one file. The per-module namespaces are preserved, and the caller-supplied meta becomes the merged library's __meta. Returns "merged N". Each input may also be the library's byte[] rather than a path, so a merge can combine a library on disk with ones in memory, and Bytecode.MergeLibraryBytes(meta, libs...) takes and returns bytes with no file involved at all.

Basic use combine two libraries:

print(Bytecode.MergeLibrary("merged.slcbc", { "name": "Merged", "version": "1.0" }, "libA.slcbc", "libB.slcbc")); // "merged 7"
// import the merged library namespaces survive the merge import "merged.slcbc" as M; print(M.Math.add(2, 3)); // 5 libA's Math namespace print(M.greet("x")); // Hello x libB's flat function print(M.__meta.Name); // Merged the caller-supplied meta

Edge cases:

// inputs must be libraries, not scripts MergeLibrary reads .slcbc files // duplicate function names (same namespace + name in two libs) abort the merge try { Bytecode.MergeLibrary("m.slcbc", meta, "libA.slcbc", "libA.slcbc"); } catch (var ex) { print(ex.Message); } // duplicate function 'add'.

Bytecode.GetSource(pathOrBytes)

string Bytecode.GetSource(string|byte[] pathOrBytes)

Returns the program text a bundle carries, as a string, with the engine doing the unpacking. A whole-script bundle carries its top level, so this is the source the bundle was built from; a library bundle carries no program of its own and answers "". Use it to read what a bundle holds, or to keep a bundle's source without keeping the original file beside it.

Inside the file, that text is stored compressed, which is why a bundle's bytes no longer contain it in the clear. That is an implementation detail of the format rather than something a caller has to undo. A file that is not a bundle is refused by name: Bytecode.GetSource: not a ScriptLangCore bytecode bundle.

var text = Bytecode.GetSource("app.slcbc"); print(text.Length); // the program's size in characters print(Bytecode.GetSource("lib.slcbc")); // a library: empty

Bytecode.Meta(name [, version, description])

Meta Bytecode.Meta(string name [, string version, string description])

Creates the metadata value used by ExportLibrary / MergeLibrary and returned by imports as Z.__meta. A plain dict { "name": ..., "version": ..., "description": ... } is accepted anywhere a Meta is expected.

Basic use:

var meta = Bytecode.Meta("TestLib", "1.0", "two-module lib"); print(typeof(meta)); // Meta print(meta is Meta); // True Bytecode.ExportLibrary("lib.slcbc", meta, "math.slc");

Advanced use the dict form, and reading it back on import:

// dict form is equivalent var meta2 = { "name": "TestLib", "version": "1.0", "description": "hi" }; Bytecode.ExportLibrary("lib.slcbc", meta2, "math.slc"); // on import, Z.__meta exposes the fields import "lib.slcbc" as Z; print(Z.__meta.Name); // TestLib print(Z.__meta.Version); // 1.0 print(Z.__meta.Description); // hi

Edge cases: a "entry" key in a dict is intentionally ignored (metadata is informational). After an export/merge, __meta.Sources lists each function's namespace ("" = flat) useful for diagnostics.

REPL commands

.export -bc <file.slc> [out.slcbc] [ns] runs a script and exports its VM-compiled top-level functions to a bytecode LIBRARY (it carries no source, so a source flag is refused there); .export -bundle <file.slc> [out.slcbc] [--source=carry|strip|strict] writes a PROGRAM bundle instead and runs nothing, with the same flags as the CLI; .loadslcbc <file.slcbc> [alias] loads a bundle a library becomes a namespace under the alias (default: file stem), a single-script bundle loads flat; .run, .looprun and .bench accept -bc [out.slcbc] and .run loads a .slcbc path directly.

Limitations what is NOT supported yet

  • Only VM-compiled functions can be exported. Functions whose body falls back to the tree-walker have no bytecode and are skipped at export (reported in the "exported N, skipped M" report): coroutines (yield) their bytecode is only valid when driven through the in-process generator/coroutine VM machinery (VmSuspendState); an exported bundle calls bodies plain and would run them eagerly, losing the yield sequence, so they are still skipped at export and any body containing a construct the VM does not yet compile (unknown shapes). The VM does compile ref/out params, self-recursive functions (with VM tail calls), bare-name method calls inside class/struct methods (self-recursion, sibling methods resolve through the class context), try/catch/finally, foreach, switch statements and expressions (constant, type, var, discard patterns, when guards, multiple labels), new, ternary/??, prefix and postfix ++/-- on locals, globals, and property/index targets, compound assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=, &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=) on locals, globals, and property/index targets, named arguments (f(x: 1) the VM reorders them against the callee's parameter list), using bodies that return/break/continue, const declarations (reassignment throws), and lambdas with capture-free, read-only local, or global captures (write-capturing lambdas fall back to the tree); local functions are compiled to bytecode with VM captures too.
  • Whole-script bundles. ExportScript exports all VM-compiled top-level functions into one bundle; classes, structs, enums, delegates, and globals are not serialized a bundle only loads where those are already defined. (Libraries built with ExportLibrary do carry classes, structs and top-level variable snapshots.)
  • Environment-coupled. A bundle that references a script class/struct/delegate/global only runs in an environment that defines them. The mismatch is caught at call time with a clear error referenced types and globals must exist when the loaded function runs.
  • No tree fallback for loaded shells. A loaded function is VM-only: if the VM cannot execute it at call time (e.g. an unsupported construct slipped through), it raises an error instead of silently tree-walking loaded shells have no AST body.
  • Compiler-coupled. The blob format is pinned to a deterministic opcode fingerprint; the bundle version number is deliberately kept stable at 1 (on-disk layout changes are documented in code, not by bumping the number). Bytecode written by a different ScriptLangCore build is rejected on fingerprint mismatch, not migrated there is no cross-version compatibility layer.
  • Binary format. Blobs are opaque binary files (.slcbc); there is no textual/disassembly export and no safe way to hand-edit them.
  • Nested lambdas are shell-only. Lambdas inside an exported function are serialized as parameter/return-type shells plus bytecode their captured state is rebuilt at runtime, so they must be capturable by the VM (capture-free, read-only local, and global captures work; lambdas that write a captured local fall back to the tree).
VmXXX bytecode VM control built-in Inspect & control the bytecode VM VmStats, VmSetEnabled, VmSetTopLevelEnabled, VmSetStatementCarrier, VmReset, VmSetTrace

ScriptLangCore executes functions through an internal bytecode VM (compiled at parse time from the AST) with a silent fallback to the tree-walker for constructs the VM does not yet compile. These built-ins let a script inspect and control that behavior useful for diagnostics, A/B benchmarks, and tracing.

VmStats()

Returns a string reporting how many function invocations ran in the VM vs. the tree-walker since the last reset, e.g. "VM: 26 (92.9%) | Tree: 2 (7.1%) | Total: 28 | cacheHits: 0 misses: 0 | gfast: 100011/100007". The trailing gfast: N/M counts global fast-path accesses LOAD_GLOBAL_FAST / STORE_GLOBAL_FAST operations executed. When a function reads/writes globals in a hot loop, N and M grow large, proving the global slot cache is in use (it skips a per-access dictionary lookup). A trailing toplevel: N counts the top-level statements this run executed on the VM (see VmSetTopLevelEnabled below); it is part of the short form too, because a script whose work is all at file scope reports VM: 0 (no function invocations yet) while statements are running on the VM.

var stats = VmStats(); print(stats);

VmSetEnabled(bool)

Globally enables or disables the bytecode VM. With VmSetEnabled(false) every function runs through the tree-walker (the VM is bypassed entirely) use it for A/B comparisons of the same workload under VM vs. tree. The switch reaches the calls a running compiled body makes after it too, not only the ones the top level makes, so a function that turns the VM off hands its own callees to the tree. One boundary worth knowing: a body loaded from a bundle has no syntax tree to walk, so it keeps running on the VM whatever the flag says.

VmSetEnabled(false); // force tree-walker VmSetEnabled(true); // re-enable VM
Recursion depth limits (runaway guard): a runaway recursion throws a catchable ScriptException Maximum call depth exceeded (N) possible runaway recursion. it never crashes the process, and the guard is silent (no console warning). The limit N depends on the execution path and the build:
  • VM enabled (default): N = 1000000 under NativeAOT, 30000 in Debug/JIT. The VM runs calls on a flat heap frame list the C# stack never grows (measured 100% VM-flat at 1,000,000 levels), so the cap is bounded by memory, not the thread stack: ~370 MB of working set per million levels (the process OOMs catchably at ~20.3M levels).
  • VM disabled (tree-walker): N = 3000 under NativeAOT, 24 in Debug/JIT. The tree-walker recurses on the native C# stack and .NET exception dispatch costs ~3× the recursion's own stack per level, so the guard fires well below the physical limit (~15800 AOT levels) to leave headroom for the guard's own throw to unwind.
Tail-recursive calls are optimized into a loop and run in constant stack, bounded only by the 1000000-iteration tail-loop guard (tailRec(100000, 0) passes). The guard counts every tail call the same invocation makes, so its boundary is a property of the emitted stream rather than of the recursion's depth: pin it with SLC_VM_MAXFRAMES when a specific boundary is wanted. Diagnostic override: the environment variable SLC_VM_MAXFRAMES=N replaces the VM frame cap in both builds.

VmSetTopLevelEnabled([bool])

Runs top-level statements (the code outside every function) on the bytecode VM instead of the tree-walker. Called with no argument it reports the current state; called with one it sets it and answers what it set, so a script can turn it on, compare the two engines, and turn it off again in the same run. Function bodies are unaffected: VmSetEnabled governs those. Statements already executed keep the engine they ran on, so a switch made here applies to the statements after it.

On by default, and the reason to know before changing it: a top-level statement the VM cannot finish is refused rather than re-run, because by then it may already have stored a global and running it again on the tree would repeat that work. Turning it off is for comparing the two engines, or for a session that wants the tree-walker: SLC_TOPLEVEL_VM=0 in the environment does it for a whole run, and VmSetTopLevelEnabled(false) for the statements after the call.

VmSetTopLevelEnabled(true); // the top level runs on the VM (the default) VmSetTopLevelEnabled(false); // ...and on the tree-walker (this run only; SLC_TOPLEVEL_VM=0 does it for every run) print(VmSetTopLevelEnabled()); // read the state: false or true
// The `toplevel:` field of VmStats() is what shows the switch working VmSetTopLevelEnabled(true); VmReset(); var total = 0; for (var i = 0; i < 3; i = i + 1) { total = total + i; } print(VmStats()); // ends with `toplevel: N`, the statements that ran on the VM VmSetTopLevelEnabled(false);

VmSetStatementCarrier([bool])

Controls the statement carrier, a compile-time mechanism: when a program body cannot be compiled as one unit, each top-level statement the compiler cannot model is handed to the tree-walker by its own source text instead, so a file stops having to carry its whole source in a bundle. Called with no argument it reports the current state; called with one it sets it and answers what it set.

On by default since 2026-10-21: it takes --source=strict from 471 stripped of 514 suites to 501 (43 refusals down to 13), and every suite it newly strips has been measured against its own source by tools/bundle-parity.sh, which is why the eleven bundle defects that gated the flip are closed rather than reasoned (a generic call naming its type parameters, a generic body resolving its own T, an out _ discard, a tuple name in a generic position, an async Task<int> that falls off, a carried statement writing the global where the body reads a local slot, two capture-free lambdas at the same position in two snippets). It governs the compile (the bundle a script exports after the call), not the engine a statement runs on, and the carrying itself is decided per statement, so a file whose top level compiles as one unit is unaffected.

Pass false to compare the two states in one process, and SLC_CARRIED_STATEMENTS=0 to do it for a whole run; the compiler then REFUSES a file whose top level it cannot model, as it did before the flip. The env-var-only era is why the switch exists: Process.Start takes no environment, so before it no suite could reach the carrier. assets/language/repl/statement_carrier_test.slc pins it, through a strict Bytecode.ExportProgramBytes compile.
VmSetStatementCarrier(false); // the opt-out: refuse such a file instead of carrying print(VmSetStatementCarrier()); // read the state: true or false VmSetStatementCarrier(true); // back to the default

VmReset()

Zeroes the VM/tree invocation counters so a subsequent VmStats() reflects only the work since the reset. The top-level statement count is zeroed with them.

VmReset();

VmSetTrace(bool)

Enables per-opcode execution tracing. Every VM instruction prints a line to the console: [vm] fn=<name>[depth] [Lx:Cx] ip=N OP sp=N ; decode (e.g. [vm] fn=Inner[1] [L1:C20] ip=7 LOAD_CONST sp=1 ; push const 2). A one-time --- source: file.slc --- banner is printed when the executed source file changes (import boundaries). The tree-walker prints matching [tree] lines. Use VmSetTrace(false) to stop.

VmSetTrace(true); // start tracing // ... run your code ... VmSetTrace(false); // stop
See also the REPL .vm command, which exposes the same controls interactively. The Bytecode entry documents export/load of VM-compiled functions.
Http namespace HTTP client and form decoding GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, timeout, forms

Blocking HTTP requests. In coroutines, yields an HttpRequest for non-blocking dispatch. Returns the response body as a string.

All methods accept an optional timeoutMs parameter (default 30 000 ms).

Forms.
