Http.DecodeForm(text) decodes one application/x-www-form-urlencoded component: a + is a space and %XX is one byte, so a multi-byte character survives ("caf%C3%A9" is café), and an escape that does not introduce two hex digits is left as it stands rather than refused. Http.EncodeForm(text) is the inverse, a space written +. Http.ParseForm(body) decodes a whole body into a dictionary, one entry per field: a repeated field keeps its last value and a pair with an empty key is ignored. Test a field with ContainsKey before reading it, because reading an absent key is refused.

// the two lines a form handler needs, instead of splitting on "&" and "%" by hand var f = Http.ParseForm(ctx.Body); var text = f.ContainsKey("text") ? "" + f["text"] : "";

Cancellation. Every verb also accepts an optional CancellationToken, recognised by its runtime type (anywhere after the URL) or with the named form token:. With no token the call binds to the ambient token, readable as Http.Token (read-only): the current host request's token inside the MCP HTTP server, otherwise a process token fired by Ctrl+C, abort() or shutdown. Link your own deadline with the short form CancellationToken.Create(a, b, ...) (returns the token; the engine owns the linked source).

// explicit token cancel a group of calls from one source var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(); var body1 = Http.Get("https://api.example.com/a", 5000, cts.Token); var body2 = Http.Get("https://api.example.com/b", token: cts.Token); cts.Cancel(); // in-flight calls abort // link the ambient token with your own: whichever fires first wins var mine = new CancellationTokenSource(800); // 800 ms deadline var t = CancellationToken.Create(Http.Token, mine.Token); Http.Post("https://api.example.com/data", '{"k":1}', t); // tell cancellation from a timeout without string matching if (Http.LastErrorKind == "cancelled") { print("aborted by caller"); }

Failure values. Failures are returned (not thrown) as __HTTP_ERROR__:<message>. Two causes are named explicitly: __HTTP_ERROR__:cancelled (the ambient or an explicit token fired) and __HTTP_ERROR__:timeout (the per-call timeout fired). Http.LastErrorKind holds "cancelled", "timeout" or "network" for the most recent call, and "" after a success. The two Async members below THROW instead, because a byte count and a byte array have no sentinel slot: their refusal arrives as a catch-able error carrying the engine's own wording, and Http.LastErrorKind is set the same way.

Server-side note. Inside the MCP HTTP server each request gets its own token, exposed to http.Use middleware as ctx.RequestAborted, and cancelled when the server stops or a socket failure is detected. Because HttpListener provides no Kestrel-style abort event, that detection is best-effort: a client that disconnects mid-handler is noticed when the engine next touches the socket. Pass an explicit token or a short timeoutMs when a hard deadline matters.

Http.Get("https://api.example.com/data"); Http.Get("https://api.example.com/data", 5000); // 5s timeout Http.Post("https://api.example.com/data", '{"key":"val"}'); Http.Post("https://api.example.com/data", '{"key":"val"}', 3000); // 3s timeout Http.Put("https://api.example.com/data/1", '{"key":"val2"}'); Http.Delete("https://api.example.com/data/1"); // the BYTES doors: a binary body, and a download that never passes through a string var png = await Http.GetBytesAsync("https://example.com/logo.png"); var written = await Http.DownloadAsync("https://example.com/big.zip", "./big.zip"); print(png.Length + " bytes read, " + written + " written");
MemberDescription
GetBytesAsync(url [, timeoutMs] [, token])The response body as a byte[], read INCREMENTALLY (ResponseHeadersRead, so the body is never buffered whole before it is handed over). Use it for anything binary: Http.Get decodes a body as text, which is wrong twice over for a PNG. It answers the engine's Task, so await it, and the Async postfix is the repository's naming rule for a member that really is asynchronous.
DownloadAsync(url, path [, timeoutMs] [, token])The same transfer written straight to a FILE, answering the byte count, so a large download never becomes a script string. The path follows the one path rule (./x is beside the run), the copy runs chunk by chunk and asks the token per chunk, so a cancellation stops the transfer rather than only its start, and a ./ path needs a run directory (a bare or absolute path needs none).
var resp = Http.Get("https://httpbin.org/get"); print(resp); // raw JSON response // With timeout (100ms will time out on slow/unreachable hosts) try { var data = Http.Get("https://192.0.2.1/test", 100); // unroutable IP } catch (var ex) { print("Timeout: " + ex.Message); // "__HTTP_ERROR__:..." } // In a coroutine non-blocking with timeout var coResp = yield Http.Get("https://api.example.com", 5000);
Timeout behavior: The timeout parameter applies a CancellationTokenSource to the underlying HttpClient call. In synchronous mode, the current thread blocks for at most timeoutMs. In coroutine mode, the background Task.Run is cancelled after timeoutMs, and the scheduler resumes the coroutine with an error result. Default: 30 000 ms (30 seconds).
MCI namespace Media Control Interface audio playback

Play, pause, seek, and control audio files via the Windows Media Control Interface.

MCI.Open("song.mp3"); MCI.Play("song.mp3"); MCI.Pause("song.mp3"); MCI.Close("song.mp3"); MCI.Status("song.mp3"); MCI.Seek("song.mp3", 5000); // seek to 5s
MCI.Open("background.mp3"); MCI.Play("background.mp3"); sleep(10000); // play for 10 seconds MCI.Pause("background.mp3"); MCI.Close("background.mp3");
Com namespace COM interop create objects, access properties, call methods via IDispatch, and embed ActiveX controls in windows (Com.HostActiveX)

COM (Component Object Model) automation via native IDispatch vtable calls. All operations are AOT-compatible (no reflection, no dynamic). Every COM object the bridge hands back is tracked in a ComScope, and the scope releases the bridge's references to them when it exits see the lifecycle below for what that does, and what it does NOT do.

The whole surface seven methods

MethodWhat it doesWhose the application is
Com.Run(callback [, extraArgs…])Turns the thread into an OLE/STA apartment, creates a ComScope and calls the callback with it, and returns the callback's value. At its LAST scope out it releases its interfaces and reports every server this process started that nothing quit.Nothing is ended here the script quits, inside the callback.
Com.CreateObject(progId)Starts a fresh instance (a ComNode), and records it as this process's own work.Yours: call Quit() on it, or the run reports it.
Com.GetObject(progId)
also (path, progId)		Finds a running instance through the Running Object Table the ATTACH path. Nothing is recorded.Its owner's: never reported, never touched.
Com.GetOrCreate(progId)Attach-or-create in one call: it reuses a running instance, and starts (and records) one when nothing of that class is up.Decided by which half it took see the two rows above.
Com.IsAlive([progId | node])Is it still there, or still usable? Prefer the scoped forms. A node: is THIS handle still usable? the tightest scope, answered without dispatching when its run released it, so it is safe on a handle held past its run. No argument: has THIS PROCESS started anything still up? A ProgID: is anything of that class running? the loosest scope, and the only one that cannot tell YOUR instance from a stranger's. The tool for waiting out a real shutdown instead of guessing a sleep.Answers the lifetime question without taking a side.
Com.Stats()The bridge's counted facts: name lookups and hits, parameter lookups and hits, safe arrays created/destroyed, enumerations, the process handle count, type-cache entries, and StillRunning / .StillRunningNames. Every property is dynamic.Reads only it ends nothing.
Com.HostActiveX(node, parentHwnd [, x, y, w, h, verb])Hosts an ActiveX control in-place inside an existing Win32 window and returns the control's child HWND.The control and its OLE site live on the STA thread see its own section below.
Seven methods is the WHOLE surface, and none of them ends an application. Quitting is the script's line to write (Quit(), inside the callback), and the engine's part is to REPORT what was left running which is what the lifecycle below describes.

Lifecycle Com.Run(callback)

All COM operations MUST happen inside Com.Run(callback). It initializes the thread as OLE/STA (OleInitialize, which Com.HostActiveX needs for embedding ActiveX controls), creates a ComScope, and disposes it when the callback returns. The callback receives that scope as its parameter Com.Run(fun(scope) { … }) and a callback that ignores it (fun() { … }) is equally fine. Anything after the callback is handed to it after the scope Com.Run(fun(scope, progId) { scope.CreateObject(progId); }, "Excel.Application") so a helper can pass values explicitly instead of relying on capture. Use the parameter to create objects in a scope you name yourself, which is what makes helpers and nested runs composable; Com.CreateObject is the shorthand for the scope that is current on the thread.

// the callback receives the scope its objects will be released by Com.Run(fun(scope) { var app = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); // a ComNode: the CURRENT scope tracks it var fso = scope.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject"); // the same call, spelled with the scope print(fso.Drives.Count); // scope.GetObject(pathName, progId) also exists // nothing typed to end `app`: this run started it, so its last scope out ends it (below) });

scope is the tracker, not an object. It owns every COM object created inside its run and releases them when it exits, while app and fso are the objects themselves (ComNode handles) so app.Quit() and fso.Drives are the SERVER's members, and the scope has nothing to do with them. Inside one callback Com.CreateObject and scope.CreateObject are the same call: the first is the shorthand for the scope that is current on the thread, and that is this one. They differ only when the scope you mean is NOT the current one, which is the nested case inside an inner Com.Run, Com.CreateObject registers in the INNER scope (released when that block ends) while scope.CreateObject, with an outer scope value, registers in the OUTER one (still alive). So: use Com.CreateObject for the run you are in, and pass scope to a helper when its ownership should be explicit. Whose an APPLICATION is, the RUN decides rather than the scope: it ends the ones this process STARTED, and leaves an instance it merely attached to alone see the lifecycle below.

What "the scope disposes it" means 
WhenAt that scope's Dispose the end of its Com.Run, or the end of the nested block it belonged to. Deterministic: not the garbage collector's timing, and GC.Collect() has nothing to do with it.
What happensThe bridge releases its COM reference. For an IN-PROCESS server (Scripting.FileSystemObject, ADODB.Stream) the last reference going destroys the object, so it is gone once the scope exits usable until then. Repeated wrappers of one interface are deduped, so a scope releases each object exactly once.
What ELSE happens the reportWhen the LAST scope on the thread closes, the bridge REPORTS every application this process STARTED through Com.CreateObject or Com.GetOrCreate that is still running: a line on stderr naming it, plus Com.Stats().StillRunning / .StillRunningNames. It does not end it: quitting is the script's own Quit(), inside the callback. An instance this process merely ATTACHED to is never recorded, so it is never reported; an IN-PROCESS server has no server to quit and is never reported either.
The variable is not cleaned up that is the half people miss. When the scope exits it releases the interface, but the value in your variable is left untouched and nothing nulls it for you, so what you are holding is a dangling handle. What that costs depends entirely on the server:
  • an OUT-OF-PROCESS server (Excel, WMI) answers through its dead proxy with a clear error: the COM object is disconnected: its server is gone;
  • an IN-PROCESS server (Scripting.FileSystemObject, scrrun.dll) is freed memory, and calling into it kills the process SILENTLY: a run printed the object's value inside the scope, then stopped with no error at all when the same handle was used after that scope had exited. (Com.IsAlive(node) is the test for it, and it is safe to ask: a released handle is answered WITHOUT dispatching, so it does not become the crash it is asking about.)
So treat an object as valid only until the run that created it ends: do not stash it in a global, and do not use it after a nested block that owned it. If it must outlive the current block, create it in an OUTER scope that is what the scope parameter is for.
One out-of-process activation leaves one connection handle until that server exits. Measured with cdb's !handle: each Com.CreateObject of a LocalServer (Excel, WMI) leaves an ALPC Port the connection to that instance and 45 seconds after the instances had QUIT, with their processes gone, about 70% of those handles were still held. It is the COM/RPC runtime's handle, not a reference the bridge forgot to release: an IN-PROCESS server leaks nothing over 200 activations. So a program that keeps ONE instance per run costs one handle and then none, while a script that activates a server in a loop accumulates one per activation (bounded by the activations, never by time). If you must activate repeatedly, Com.GetObject attaches to the running instance instead of starting another; if the result is just a file, writing it directly avoids the activation altogether.
The engine does not end applications it REPORTS the ones you forgot to quit. When the run's LAST scope closes (the end of the outermost Com.Run, or an early scope.Dispose() taken while no other run is live), the bridge releases its COM interfaces so the handles from that scope stop working ("the COM object is disconnected: its server is gone") and then it looks, in the Running Object Table, at every server this process STARTED. Whatever is still there is named on stderr and counted in Com.Stats().StillRunning / .StillRunningNames. Quitting it was, and stays, the script's job: Quit() inside the callback, the only place its handles are alive. That division is deliberate an engine that quits a server is guessing at a lifetime that is not its own.
Two consequences, stated plainly. Quit() DISCARDS unsaved edits in a server this process started: marking a document Saved and closing it without saving is exactly what lets the server end, so a workbook the script never wrote to disk is gone when the script quits it. And there is NO engine-side opt-out in EITHER direction: the bridge never ends a server, so "keep it alive" is not a flag you set — it is simply not calling Quit(), which is the case the run reports — while a server the script DOES quit cannot be asked to survive the run. Com.CreateObject means "this process started it", and whether it outlives the run is the script's own Quit(). An instance somebody ELSE started is the opposite case and is never touched. If work has to outlive the script, write it to disk inside the run. And not every server can be ended this way: PowerPoint's Application.Quit is not reachable through IDispatch at all, so a PowerPoint this process started stays running even when the script does everything right, and the run's leftover report is the only signal there is. Excel and Word (with a document open) both end correctly when the SCRIPT quits them.
// the script quits it the engine only REPORTS what was left running Com.Run(fun() { var app = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); app.Visible = false; app.Workbooks.Add().Sheets(1).Cells(1, 1).Value = 42; app.Quit(); // YOUR line: a forgotten one is reported, never fixed for you });
A forgotten Quit() is the case it exists for, and a script that DID quit is not reported any more. An application that keeps a document does not die with the scope: a workbook left DIRTY keeps EXCEL.EXE alive 25 seconds after the scope had disposed, and without the script's Quit() that process is an invisible window nobody notices which is exactly what this report names. The line reads [WARNING] [L244:C5] Com: 'X' may still be running; Quit() it inside the callback (Com.Stats().StillRunning), where the position is the LAST statement the run executed (the report is made after the run, so it belongs to no statement of its own) and names NO OWNER, because the Running Object Table matches by CLASS: it cannot tell your instance from a stranger's (a foreign instance of the same class gets reported too). Read it as "check this", not as a verdict, and when you want a precise answer ask per SCOPE instead: Com.IsAlive(node) for one handle, Com.IsAlive() for this process's own work. Give a real shutdown 10-15 seconds before counting processes as well.
THE RELEASE COMES FIRST: the scope releases its interfaces and only then asks the table, because an interface still held in this process is what stops an out-of-process server from exiting, so asking before the release could only ever answer "still running" and reported scripts that had already quit. Measured after that order: the table stops resolving 115 ms after the release, inside the 500 ms grace. A script whose last statement is Quit() therefore says nothing; one that never quits still gets the line.
AND A PRISTINE INSTANCE IS NOT REPORTED EITHER, which is the same rule one step further: an instance with no document and no window exits by itself about a second after the scope's references go, so once the release comes first there is nothing left to report. What the report names is the case that really leaks, an instance holding a document: give it a document (even an unsaved cell in a new workbook) and it survives the release, which is exactly what the line warns about. A later run can still end one of those by attaching and quitting it.
Wrap the run in your own helper when a script repeats the same bridge work. Com.Run hands its callback the scope FIRST and then every extra argument it was given, so a helper can take the body as a parameter and inject the subject itself: a typed delegate (Func<…>) or a generic method parameter both accept a script lambda.
The generic form is a helper in the language, not a namespace: a caller that injects a subject takes a FACTORY and a BODY, and using releases the subject when the body returns (a subject that is not IDisposable is simply not disposed that is what using means here).
// the generic caller, in the language: the factory makes the subject, `using` releases it object Scoped(Func<object> factory, Func<object, object> body) { using (var subject = factory()) { return body(subject); } } Com.Run(fun(scope) { print(Scoped(fun() { return scope.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject"); }, (fso) => fso.Drives.Count)); // 3 });
There is deliberately no Scope.Run / Method.Run in the surface. Two namespaces already own a Run, and each injects what it owns: Com.Run a Com scope (whose last scope out also reports unquit servers), Task.Run a task while Invoke is the NAKED dynamic call, injecting nothing and holding no lifetime. A generic X.Run would therefore be a second spelling of one of those jobs rather than a third behaviour, which is the reason Com.Dispose was removed instead of aliased.
// a reusable caller, in the language: the subject is injected, the body decides object WithFso(Func<object, object> body) { return Com.Run(fun(scope) { return body(scope.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject")); }); } print(WithFso((fso) => fso.Drives.Count)); // 3

Nested Com.Run scoped lifetimes inside one apartment

Com.Run nests: each call creates its own scope, and an inner scope releases the objects created in it while the outer scope keeps its own. The thread's apartment and the bridge's internal array bookkeeping belong to the last scope out, whichever that is, so an inner run can never tear down the state an outer one is still using.

Com.Run(fun() { var app = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); // a book opened, read and released on its own, while the app stays alive Com.Run(fun() { var wb = app.Workbooks.Open(@"report.xlsx"); print(wb.Sheets.Count); }); // wb released here; app still alive app.Quit(); });
Excel wants \ in a COM path, and has its own idea of array shapes. Measured: SaveAs("C:/temp/x.xlsx") a folder that exists, a unique name, no leaked instances was refused, Excel rendering the path as C:\//temp/x.xlsx; normalize / to \ and pass a FULL path a bare name is not refused: Excel resolves it against its OWN documents folder and writes nothing where you looked, which is what Path.GetFullPath prevents. And Range.Value over more than ONE cell is an array-backed VARIANT (VT_ARRAY|VT_VARIANT): the engine reads it as a 2-D value, and for writing, a 1-D array maps to a row while a jagged array gives the 2-D shape a column needs (a 1-D list aimed at a column range was accepted and then broadcast its first value into every cell).
The shape that misleads. Com.Run(fun() { Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); }); does not end that application: it REPORTS it, and the instance keeps running. Attached instances are the other side of the coin Com.GetObject, and the attach half of Com.GetOrCreate, is never recorded at all, so nothing about an instance somebody else started is ever reported or touched. A trap worth knowing while you are here: Quit() on an instance you ATTACHED to answers HRESULT 0x80004005, so attaching is not a way to end a server either its starter owns it.

CreateObject / GetObject / GetOrCreate

var obj = Com.CreateObject("ProgID"); // CoCreateInstance var running = Com.GetObject("ProgID"); // ROT lookup

CreateObject starts a new COM instance. GetObject finds a running instance via the Running Object Table.

Com.GetOrCreate(progId) is the attach-or-create idiom in one call: it reuses a running instance when there is one, and starts a new instance otherwise. That is the difference between ONE COM connection handle and one per activation a loop calling CreateObject each iteration leaks an ALPC Port per iteration while attaching leaks none, and the runtime reclaims an idle connection only after minutes. Which of the two happened decides who has to END it: an instance it had to CREATE is this process's own work, so the script quits it (and a run in which the script forgets is reported); an instance it merely found ALREADY RUNNING belongs to whoever started it, and the script must leave it alone querying it is fine, quitting it is not, and it is never reported.

An application is ended by the SCRIPT that started it, with Quit() inside the callback. The engine's part is the report above: Com.Stats().StillRunning (a count) and .StillRunningNames (the ProgIDs, comma-separated), raised at the end of every run for each server this process started and nothing quit. An instance this process merely ATTACHED to is not the script's to end and is never reported; an in-process object has no server to quit, so it is not reported either (it dies with the last reference). The record is cleared once reported, so one forgotten server is named once never twice, and never mistaken for an instance the USER starts later.

Com.IsAlive([progId | node]) is the same question from the SCRIPT's side, and it exists so a script can WAIT instead of guessing: Quit() returns long before the server actually leaves, so while (Com.IsAlive("Excel.Application")) { sleep(250); } is the honest way to know. The argument picks the question: a node asks "is this HANDLE still usable?" (true inside the run that owns it, false once that run released it and the false is answered WITHOUT dispatching, which is what makes it safe on an in-process handle whose memory is gone); no argument asks "has this process started anything still up?"; a ProgID asks "is anything of that class running?", where a true for an instance somebody else started is simply not yours to undo. Scope is why all three exist: ask about the HANDLE you hold when you have it, about THIS PROCESS's own work when you do not, and by class only when the question really IS about the class it is the one form that cannot tell your instance from a stranger's, which is why the report it mirrors is worded the way it is.

That wait is CROSS-RUN. An application cannot be gone while the run that holds its interface is still alive: polling Com.IsAlive() inside the run that created it stayed true for every poll the scope is keeping the server up. A LATER Com.Run holds nothing of its own, and there the answer turned false immediately (measured, 0 polls) once the earlier run had quit it. So: quit inside the callback, then wait in a following run if you need certainty. That wait asks BY CLASS on purpose, even though the scoped forms are preferred in general: the no-argument form answers about the names the engine still has on its books, and a name it has already reported is forgotten so it can answer false while the application is still up.
// one call, three questions the ARGUMENT picks which Com.Run(fun() { var app = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); app.Visible = false; print(Com.IsAlive(app)); // true: is THIS handle still usable? print(Com.IsAlive("Excel.Application")); // true: is anything of that class running? (may be somebody else's) print(Com.IsAlive()); // true: did THIS PROCESS start something? app.Quit(); }); // the wait for a real shutdown belongs in a LATER run a run holding the interface keeps the server up Com.Run(fun() { while (Com.IsAlive("Excel.Application")) { sleep(250); } }); // ...and the safe way to ask about a handle you KEPT: a released one answers false without making the call var held = null; Com.Run(fun() { held = Com.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject"); }); Com.Run(fun() { print(Com.IsAlive(held)); }); // false its run released it, and asking cannot crash
A namespace answers the names it registered plus Dispose(), which is a rule rather than a hole. Dispose() is the by-name counterpart of what using does to an instance, and it resolves through IDisposable: for a namespace tree this run OWNS (an imported bundle) it really releases that tree, and for one with nothing to release it is simply a NO-OP which is what being IDisposable means. Every OTHER name a namespace never registered is REFUSED (Method 'X' not found in namespace) exactly like a typo anywhere else: resolution stops at what the namespace REGISTERED, so a name it never declared is refused rather than quietly doing nothing.

The record lives on the PROCESS, and an entry is cleared as soon as it has been reported, INCLUDING when the name no longer resolves the ROT is the only handle on "the current instance", so a spent name could otherwise be mistaken for an instance the USER starts later. A DIFFERENT process is never reached: nothing on the machine records who STARTED an instance, so nothing of another process's is ever ended or reported, which is exactly what keeps this surface away from a stranger's application. Two related facts worth knowing: Com.Run returns its callback's VALUE (var n = Com.Run(fun() { … return 42; }) ), and the callback's scope parameter IS the lifetime handle, whose Dispose() is idempotent, so you may call it early which, when no other run is live on the thread, is when the report is made.

HostActiveX embed an ActiveX control in a window

Com.HostActiveX(ctrl, parentHwnd [, x, y, w, h, verb]) embeds any Com.CreateObject-able ActiveX/OCX control in-place inside an existing Win32 window (e.g. form.Handle) and returns the control's child window handle. It is a generic OLE host: IOleObject → SetClientSite → OleRun → DoVerb → GetWindow. IE (Shell.Explorer) and Windows Media Player (WMPlayer.OCX) are two validated instances the control only needs to implement IOleObject and tolerate a minimal site; automation servers (Excel/Word/...) are rejected with a clear error.

var child = Com.HostActiveX(ctrl, form.Handle); // 640x480 at 0,0 var child = Com.HostActiveX(ctrl, form.Handle, 0, 40, 900, 600);

The optional verb selects the activation verb: 0 (default) = AUTO try OLEIVERB_INPLACEACTIVATE and fall back to OLEIVERB_SHOW if the control refuses it; 5 = in-place only; -1 = show only. After hosting, drive the control through its normal IDispatch members (ctrl.Navigate(...), ctrl.URL = ..., …). The control and its OLE site must live on the same STA thread as the window's message pump keep everything inside one Com.Run on the main thread. To keep the child fitted to the form, adopt it with form.AdoptChild(child, insets…) (auto-sizes on resize); otherwise size it manually on the form's Resize event with ctrl.SetBounds(...). See assets/language/ui/demos/music_player.slc for a full working player.

// Example a web browser in a Form (see assets/language/ui/demos/web_browser.slc) Com.Run(fun(scope) { var form = Application.CreateForm("Script Browser"); // the window exists from here, hidden var ie = Com.CreateObject("Shell.Explorer"); var child = Com.HostActiveX(ie, form.Handle, 0, 40, 900, 600); form.Show(); // a control that PAINTS (Explorer) only loads once its window is on screen ie.Navigate("https://example.com/"); var title = ""; while (title == "") { Application.DoEvents(); sleep(100); if (ie.Busy == false && ie.ReadyState == 4) title = ie.Document.title; } print("page title: " + title); // "Example Domain" read through the hosted control Application.Run(); ie.Quit(); });
// Example a second, independent control: Windows Media Player (msdxm.ocx) // (regsvr32 C:\Windows\System32\msdxm.ocx first) see assets/language/ui/demos/wmp_ocx_test.slc Com.Run(fun(scope) { var form = Application.CreateForm("Media Player"); var wmp = Com.CreateObject("WMPlayer.OCX"); Com.HostActiveX(wmp, form.Handle, 10, 40, 480, 320); // hosted while the form is still hidden wmp.uiMode = "none"; // bare video area wmp.URL = "file.mp4"; // play a file wmp.settings.volume = 50; // nested dispatch object form.Show(); // LAST: everything is set up, the window appears once Application.Run(); });
ActiveX hosting prerequisites: the control's OCX must be registered (regsvr32) and match the process bitness (ScriptLangCore is 64-bit); the demo window needs a desktop session; Office Click-to-Run vfs OCX copies refuse standalone registration. Com.CreateObject returns ComNode values whose returned COM objects chain (ie.Document.title, wmp.settings.volume).

Native property syntax

Properties are accessed with natural object.Property syntax no explicit getters/setters.

excel.Visible = true; // set property var vis = excel.Visible; // get property → bool var pid = process.ProcessId; // get numeric property var mem = process.WorkingSetSize; // get numeric (long)

Native method calls

Methods are called with natural object.Method(args) syntax. Arguments are converted to VARIANT automatically.

excel.Quit(); // void method var wb = excel.Workbooks.Open(@"C:\file.xlsx"); // chained property + method var sheet = wb.Sheets("Sheet1"); // indexed property (COM method) var svc = locator.ConnectServer("localhost", "root\\cimv2");

Named arguments and optional parameters

COM methods take the same name: value spelling as script functions, so a parameter can be addressed by the name the server publishes:

wb.SaveAs("out.xlsx", AccessMode: 3, ConflictResolution: 2); // the names the SERVER knows, not positions: AccessMode = xlExclusive, ConflictResolution = xlLocalSessionChanges // (overwrite without asking) naming the pair settles the question instead of leaving it to the server

The bridge resolves the name through the object's type library (IDispatch::GetTypeInfo → ITypeInfo::GetNames), which returns a member's parameters in order, and then sends the parameter's position as its DISPID the mechanism VBA compiles AccessMode:= into. It is cached per object, member and name, so only the first named call on a given object pays for the type library. A name the server will not publish is refused with an error naming the parameter, never silently re-pointed at the next one: a value one position early turns AccessMode: 3 into FileFormat = 3, and Excel then writes a 7-byte text file named .xlsx. Naming a pair such as AccessMode + ConflictResolution is also how you settle a question the server would otherwise ask what to do about an existing file inside the call itself: with DisplayAlerts = false suppressing that prompt, Excel reports the opaque "Impossible de lire la propriété SaveAs de la classe Workbook", which reads like a broken bridge rather than a suppressed dialog.

// Workbook.SaveAs(Filename, FileFormat, Password, WriteResPassword, ReadOnlyRecommended, CreateBackup, AccessMode, ConflictResolution, …) // 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 wb.SaveAs(path, null, null, null, null, null, 3, 2); // positionally: xlExclusive, xlLocalSessionChanges
Positional recipe null for every gap. For a server whose names cannot be resolved, or when a positional call simply reads better, pass the arguments in order and use null for each parameter to skip. null becomes a VARIANT of type VT_ERROR carrying DISP_E_PARAMNOTFOUND that IS VBA's Missing, and the only thing that makes an optional parameter skippable at all. Stop at the last parameter you set; every gap before it needs one null.
Two limits worth knowing. A member's parameter list is read up to 24 names, and a name past that is refused rather than guessed at Excel has one member that exceeds the buffer (Application.Run, 32 names), so its last parameters cannot be addressed by name through the bridge. And the type library is only reached when the object has one: a server that publishes none yields the same loud refusal.
Judge a save by the FILE, not by wb.FileFormat. A never-saved workbook already reports 51 (xlOpenXMLWorkbook), so an assertion written against that number passes for a call that wrote nothing at all which is how a broken named-argument path once passed review while Excel answered "the method failed" and no file appeared. Check that the file exists, its size, and its PK header. A sheet/workbook layer built over this bridge struct handle, class, extension members lives in assets/language/com/com_excel_sheets_test.slc, and the gate's Excel coverage is assets/language/repl/com_excel_smoke_test.slc.

Com.Stats() what the bridge actually issues

Counters read at the call sites rather than inferred from timing. Each one is a live property, and they are process-wide. They answer the questions that keep coming up: what a shape really costs in round trips, whether a generator re-enters a collection, and how often a named argument pays for the type library.

PropertyMeaning
NameLookupsGetIDsOfNames calls issued for member names
NameHitsmember lookups satisfied by the per-object or per-type cache
ParameterLookupsGetTypeInfo + GetNames pairs issued for a named argument
ParameterHitsnamed-argument lookups satisfied by the per-object parameter cache
EnumerationsCOM collections for which an enumerator was created
Handlesthe process's kernel-handle count, read on demand the figure a COM or native leak consumes, and one no managed counter can see
SafeArraysCreatedSAFEARRAYs the bridge built for an array-valued argument or a block write
SafeArraysDestroyed...and destroyed. A FAILED destroy is not counted, so created == destroyed after a block write is the leak check. An array-valued property PUT is destroyed when its scope exits rather than at the call, because the server may still be reading it
TypeCacheEntriestype-level (vtable-keyed) dispid cache entries
var s = Com.Stats(); print(s.ParameterLookups + " lookups, " + s.ParameterHits + " hits");
Measured shape of the named-argument cache (JIT and the AOT publish agree): a named call on a NEW object costs one lookup; the same member+name on the SAME object is a hit; a second OBJECT pays again. It is per object, like the member cache and Excel hands out a new Range/Cells object on every access, so hold on to the object you mean to reuse.

Collection enumeration

COM collections are enumerated via .ForEach(fun(item) { ... }). Each item is a ComNode tracked in the current scope. Alternatively, use .AsEnumerable() to get a foreach-compatible iterator. Prefer the iterator form when the loop is hot: measured over 2,000 items, ForEach(fun) costs about 2,650 ticks/item against 1,870 for foreach + AsEnumerable(), because the callback form carries the lambda as a CLR delegate while the iterator feeds the script's own foreach. A script coroutine works too and costs almost nothing for script-side data (43 ticks/item against a 34-tick control), but driving a COM collection through one measured slower than both (2,379 ticks/item), so prefer AsEnumerable() over COM and yield over script data. Better still, avoid enumerating a collection for BULK data: one Range.Value read of 10,000 cells measured 6 ticks/cell against ~1,700 per ENUMERATED item, because each item is its own COM round trip. Read the block, then walk the script-side value.

For bulk writes, the lever is CALCULATION, not the screen. Measured on 500 ten-cell row writes over a sheet with a formula column, each configuration run twice with a baseline repeat as a drift check (assets/language/com/excel_speed_bench.slc): Application.Calculation = xlCalculationManual (-4135) cut the time by 35-40%, well beyond the run-to-run spread; Application.ScreenUpdating = false moved it less than that spread, both with the window hidden and with Visible = true the COM round trips and the recalculation dominate, and suppressing repaints has little to suppress. Restore the automatic setting afterwards. On the AOT publish the same bench measured Calculation = manual at -46% (-2,087,834 ticks) with a ~5% drift, and ScreenUpdating = false on a VISIBLE window at -0.35% nothing. The shipping build was also the QUIETER benchmark target (5% drift against 12-40% on the JIT build), so measure there.
VBA inside Excel, or the bridge from a script measured, per cell.
Same 1,000-cell write+read, minimum of seven samples with the work repeated inside each timed span (assets/language/com/excel_vba_bench.slc, AOT):
  • per cell, cell-by-cell loops: VBA 30 µs vs bridge 1.31 ms (VBA 43x faster)
  • per cell, BLOCK shaped: VBA 7 µs vs bridge 14.5 µs (VBA 2x a near tie)
  • one COM call: ~110 µs round trip, so the bridge's cost is per CALL, not per cell
  • the SHAPE is worth 4x inside VBA and 90x through the bridge more than the choice of side
Reading it: VBA wins per call because it never marshals; the bridge ties on a block, and wins on reach JSON, sqlite, files, regex, coroutines, structs, and a test harness which VBA does not have. So the question is not which side is faster but how many calls you make: for work that must stay inside Excel, VBA (or VBA's own block idioms); for anything needing the language, the bridge, shaped in blocks.
processes.ForEach(fun(p) { print(p.Name + " " + p.ProcessId); }); // or via foreach + AsEnumerable (used in WMI tests) foreach (var item in processes.AsEnumerable()) { print(item.Name); }

Bulk range operations (Excel)

Read/write 2D arrays to Excel ranges via SAFEARRAY:

range.SetRangeValues([["Name", "Score"], ["Jan", 42.314]]); var data = range.GetRangeValues(); // lazy row-by-row IEnumerable

Fluent API (alternate syntax)

Explicit get/set/invoke calls as alternatives to native syntax:

node.Get("Workbooks") // same as .Workbooks node.Set("Visible", true) // same as .Visible = true node.Invoke("Quit") // same as .Quit() node.Get("Range", "A1:B2") // indexed property get node.Set("Value", 42, "A1") // indexed property set

Example Excel automation

Com.Run(fun() { var excel = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); excel.Visible = true; excel.DisplayAlerts = false; var wb = excel.Workbooks.Open(@"report.xlsx"); var sheet = wb.Sheets("Sheet1"); sheet.Range("A1:C3").SetRangeValues([ ["Name", "Score", "Grade"], ["Alice", 95, "A"], ["Bob", 82, "B"] ]); var score = sheet.Range("B2").Value; print("Score: " + score); });

That example opens a workbook and quits, but it does not release the book or mark it clean first see Lifecycle above for the recipe that reliably ends the process.

Example a block export: sqlite to Excel to CSV (advanced)

The shape that matters at scale: ONE Range.Value write for the whole table instead of one call per cell, a boundary query instead of a row scan, and the release recipe. The tracked sample is assets/language/com/sqlite_excel_csv_test.slc 50,000 rows, 9 checks.

// sqlite (in memory) -> a 2-D script list -> ONE Range write -> SaveAs CSV var rows = Sqlite.Query(lib, db, "SELECT id, Age, Name FROM people"); var grid = [].ToList(); foreach (var r in rows) { grid.Add([r.id, r.Age, r.Name]); } Com.Run(fun() { var app = Com.CreateObject("Excel.Application"); var wb = null; try { app.Visible = false; app.DisplayAlerts = false; app.Calculation = -4135; // xlCalculationManual: the bulk-write lever wb = app.Workbooks.Add(); var ws = wb.Sheets(1); ws.Range("A1:C" + grid.Count).Value = grid; // ONE call for the table wb.SaveAs(Path.GetFullPath("export.csv"), FileFormat: 6, AccessMode: 3, ConflictResolution: 2); } finally { try { wb.Saved = true; } catch (var e1) { } try { wb.Close(false); } catch (var e2) { } app.Quit(); } });
Judge the save by the FILE. wb.FileFormat == 51 is not evidence that anything was written a never-saved workbook already reports 51. Check the file's existence, its size and its PK header. And note the named pair in SaveAs: with DisplayAlerts = false, leaving Excel to decide what to do about an existing file makes it fail with an opaque message instead of asking.

Example WMI query

Com.Run(fun() { var svc = Com.CreateObject("WbemScripting.SWbemLocator") .ConnectServer("localhost", "root\\cimv2"); var processes = svc.ExecQuery( "SELECT Name, ProcessId, WorkingSetSize FROM Win32_Process"); processes.ForEach(fun(p) { print(p.Name + " PID: " + p.ProcessId); }); });

Example Scripting.FileSystemObject

Com.Run(fun() { var fso = Com.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject"); var folder = fso.GetFolder(@"C:\Windows"); print("Subfolders: " + folder.SubFolders.Count); print("Files: " + folder.Files.Count); });

Threading

COM Automation requires an STA thread. Com.Run initializes COM as STA automatically. The interpreter uses [STAThread] on the entry point.

mcp.Use namespace Register MCP tool call middleware logging, blocking, caching

The mcp namespace is available in MCP mode. mcp.Use(fn) registers middleware that intercepts every tool call before the handler runs. Middleware can log, block, cache, or modify tool calls.

The middleware receives the call as an McpContext and the pipeline's own continuation as an Action, so both can be declared: fun(McpContext ctx, Action next).

mcp.Use((McpContext ctx, Action next) => { print("tool=" + ctx.ToolName); next(); // continue to next middleware or tool handler });

Context properties

PropertyTypeDescription
ctx.ToolNamestringName of the tool being called
ctx.ArgslistArguments passed to the tool
ctx.Resultobject?Set to bypass handler and return directly
ctx.ErrorMessagestringSet it (or call ctx.Error("...")) to stop the pipeline with an error: the tool call is not run and the message is what the caller receives

Blocking a tool

mcp.Use((McpContext ctx, Action next) => { if (ctx.ToolName == "delete_file") { ctx.ErrorMessage = "blocked by policy"; return; // don't call next() } next(); });
tcp.Use namespace Register TCP connection middleware RemoteAddress, Close

tcp.Use(fn) registers middleware for the connections the engine's own TCP server accepts: Server.Create(port, ...) then Server.Start(). The middleware runs on the accept thread, BEFORE the server reads anything from the socket, so it sees every connection alike, the ones the file handler would answer and the ones meant for a WebSocket. A tcp.Use registered after the server started runs too: the server holds the same pipeline.

The middleware receives the connection as a TcpContext and the pipeline's own continuation as an Action, so both can be declared: fun(TcpContext ctx, Action next). Calling next() lets the connection through to the rest of the chain and then to the server's own handling; returning without calling it stops the chain there.

Context properties

MemberTypeDescription
ctx.RemoteAddressstringThe peer endpoint as the server sees it (127.0.0.1:54321), which is what lets a middleware allow or refuse by address
ctx.Close()voidCloses the connection immediately: the rest of the chain does not run, even if this middleware calls next() afterwards, and the server does not handle the connection at all
tcp.Use((TcpContext ctx, Action next) => { print("connection from " + ctx.RemoteAddress); next(); // let it through to the rest of the chain });
// Refuse by address: Close() ends the connection AND the chain, so nothing else sees it tcp.Use((TcpContext ctx, Action next) => { if (ctx.RemoteAddress.StartsWith("192.168.")) { ctx.Close(); return; } next(); });
http.Use namespace Register HTTP routes and request middleware

The http namespace is available in MCP+HTTP mode. http.MapGet and its siblings register an endpoint, and http.Use(fn) registers middleware for the requests no route matched.

http.Use((HttpContext ctx, Action next) => { if (ctx.Url == "/hello" && ctx.HttpMethod == "GET") { ctx.ResponseBody = "Hello!"; ctx.ResponseStatus = 200; return; } next(); });

Routes

http.MapGet(pattern, handler), http.MapPost, http.MapPut and http.MapDelete register an ENDPOINT rather than a middleware. A route table belongs to the application, so it is registered once on the http namespace and not on a request's ctx.

http.MapGet("todos/{id}", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => "<b>" + args["id"] + "</b>"); http.MapPost("todos", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => { var text = Http.ParseForm(ctx.Body)["text"]; // ... store it ... return "<ul>...</ul>"; });
RuleDescription
The patternMatched on the PATH, so the query string is ignored and a trailing slash is the same route. A segment is literal ("todos", "stats/fragment") or {name}, which captures one segment; the root is "/".
The handlerfun(HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args), where args holds the pattern's {name} segments by name, as in args["id"]. Its RETURN is the answer, and there are four cases: a string is the body written as text/plain; an http result (http.Text, Html, Json, Status, NotFound, Created) decides its own content type and its own status; any other object (a { } literal, a class, a list) is serialized as application/json; and a byte[] is sent as bytes. A handler that writes ctx itself (or a void one) returns nothing, which is a 200 with an empty body. A handler may declare a THIRD parameter, CancellationToken ct, and then it receives the request's own ctx.RequestAborted, so its work can stop when the client goes away; the DECLARATION is what decides, so a two-parameter handler is untouched.
Resultshttp.Text(s) / Html(s) / Json(v) / NotFound([body]) / Status(code [, body]) / Created(location, value) / File(path [, contentType [, fileName]]) / Bytes(data [, contentType [, fileName]]) / StreamLines(source [, contentType]) / StreamEvents(source), where Created also sets the Location header. NotFound() with no argument is a 404 with no body, the way Results.NotFound() is, and NotFound(body) writes the text the script chose; Status(code) with no body is the same shape for any code. There is deliberately no Ok beside Status(200, ...), and no TypedResults either: what makes a result "typed" is a compile-time return type, which a script does not have.
Files and downloadshttp.File(path) answers a file on disk: the bytes go out with an exact Content-Length and the content type is GUESSED from the extension with the very table the engine's own file server uses, so a route and that server cannot disagree about what a .pdf is. http.File(path, "", "report.pdf") and http.Bytes(data, type, "report.pdf") turn the answer into a DOWNLOAD with Content-Disposition: attachment, and a name that is not ASCII uses the RFC 5987 form (filename*=UTF-8''...), because a header is ISO-8859-1 by spec. http.Bytes takes a byte[] (what File.ReadAllBytes and Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes answer) or a list of numbers, and REFUSES one that is not a byte rather than truncating it. A route's ./x means beside the FILE THAT REGISTERED the route, captured when the route was registered, because a served request outlives the run that registered it.
Streaminghttp.StreamLines(source) and http.StreamEvents(source) answer a body written ONE ELEMENT AT A TIME, with chunked framing: no Content-Length, because the length is not known when the answer starts, and one flush per element, so a client sees each line as it is produced. That is what makes a big export possible without holding it in memory. StreamLines writes one JSON value per line (application/x-ndjson, so a string arrives quoted), and StreamEvents writes data: <text> then a blank line (text/event-stream, so a browser's EventSource reads it natively; a multi-line value becomes one data: line per line, which the grammar requires). The source is a list, a generator, an Events feed, or an async sequence such as File.ReadLinesAsync(path): the producer is pulled on the request thread, so a script generator is resumed and an async step is awaited exactly as await foreach would. A feed is the one source with a condition: it must be created in inline mode, because a runThread feed delivers its values on the thread the run began on, which the writer is holding (one created that way is REFUSED, rather than losing values and leaving the server unable to answer). A stream is answered by a ROUTE HANDLER's return value: a http.Use middleware writes a whole body through ctx.ResponseBody and cannot stream, because a middleware returns nothing for the pipeline to interpret. Three things follow from the status going out with the FIRST element: an error part-way cannot change the status (the stream ENDS there, the client is told the body is incomplete, and the cause goes to the server's log), nothing that buffers may sit in front of the client (curl -N, or HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead, or the batching is the CLIENT's), and a stream blocks the other requests this server takes while it is open, because it serves one request at a time.
The orderThe FIRST route that matches wins, in registration order, so a table is an ordered list rather than a specificity puzzle: "order/{x}" registered before "order/fixed" answers the wildcard. A pattern the table ALREADY holds is therefore a route that never runs, and registering it is REPORTED at warning level, naming the member, the pattern and the file that registered it: the table lives for the session, so a second .run of the same file re-adds its routes (harmless, it is reported), and a tool the --mcp startup loaded from <exe>/tools keeps what it registered first. That is the one collision worth knowing: the engine's sample mcp_httpserver.slc serves GET /, so a page route registered by a script you then .run never answers, and the remedy is --tools-dir pointing at a folder holding only your own tools.
Asking firsthttp.IsServed(method, pattern) answers whether THIS session already serves that method and pattern, so a program can claim a pattern only when it is free instead of registering a route that can never run: if (!http.IsServed("GET", "/")) { http.MapGet("/", page); }, which is what the htmx board does and why it stays silent in a session that kept the engine's sample tools (its page is always at /board as well). The comparison is the table's own, so "/x/" and "x" are one pattern and the method follows the interpreter's case rule; both arguments are strings, and a call without them is refused by name.
No matchnext(), exactly as a middleware that does not answer, so an http.Use middleware registered after the routes can still handle the request, log it or 404 it. The engine's 404 line then names what the session does serve (nothing is registered for '/todos'. This session serves GET /, GET time, POST echo, from mcp_httpserver.slc.), because a route that is missing because its file never ran looks exactly like a typo otherwise: a session with the engine's sample tools loaded has six routes registered from mcp_httpserver.slc, which is what --tools-dir pointed at an empty folder keeps out of the way.
Who writes the bodyA status the engine sets carries NO body, and a status the script chose carries what the script wrote. That is ASP.NET Core's rule: a request nothing answered is a 404 with Content-Length: 0 (the "page not found" text a browser shows for it is the browser's own), an unhandled exception is a 500 with no body in production, and 204/304 never carry one by spec. So a 404 an app wants to explain is http.NotFound("...") or ctx.ResponseBody; a 500 an app wants to explain is ctx.ErrorMessage = "...", whose text IS the body. When the engine answers instead, the reason goes to the server's LOG rather than into the response, so nothing is lost for the author and nothing is invented for the caller. The engine's own file server follows the same rule (404, 405 with Allow: GET, 403, all with no body).
A method as a handlerBoth http.Use and the Map* members take a function or a bound method: a method named where a field would be is its own value, so http.Use(app.Handle) carries app's receiver with the method. A value that cannot be called at all is refused by name, never dropped.
An async handlerA handler may be async, and its value IS the answer: the pipeline waits for the Task a script async body answers, then uses its result exactly as it would a synchronous one. A failure after an await becomes the 500 whose cause goes to the server's log, like any other handler failure. Two limits are properties of THIS server rather than of the language, and both are worth knowing before reaching for await: it serves one request at a time on one thread (a script's interpreter is thread-affine, so serving concurrently would run two bodies at once on one interpreter), and a handler must therefore never await a request to its own server, because that request can only be served after this one returns. Calling another service is the shape that works. A THIRD parameter is the request's own CancellationToken (fun (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args, CancellationToken ct)), which fires when the client goes away, so an await can be cancelled with it; that token is cancelled when a WRITE to the client fails, which is the only evidence this server gets of a disconnected client.
// A tiny JSON API: a result decides the status and the type, a plain object is serialized for you http.MapGet("/", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => "<h1>Tasks</h1>"); // text/plain http.MapGet("todo/{id}", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => { "id": args["id"] }); // application/json http.MapGet("missing", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => http.NotFound("no such todo")); // 404 http.MapPost("todo", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => http.Created("/todo/7", { "id": 7 })); // 201 + Location http.MapDelete("todo/{id}", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => http.Status(204)); // no body http.Use((HttpContext ctx, Action next) => { print(ctx.HttpMethod + " " + ctx.Url); next(); // no route answered, so this one runs }); // An ASYNC handler: its value is the answer, and a failure after the await is the same 500 as any other async Task<string> Report() { await Task.Delay(20); return "ready"; } http.MapGet("report", Report); // A file, and a DOWNLOAD named report.pdf (the type is guessed from the extension) http.MapGet("file", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => http.File("./report.pdf", "", "report.pdf")); // An EXPORT that streams: one JSON value per line, written as the generator produces it int Rows() { for (var i = 0; i < 5000; i = i + 1) { yield { "id": i }; } return 0; } http.MapGet("export", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => http.StreamLines(Rows())); // An IMPORT of the same shape, read line by line, counting the lines it cannot use http.MapPost("import", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args) => { var ok = 0; var bad = 0; foreach (var line in ctx.BodyLines()) { try { var row = Json.Parse(line); ok = ok + 1; } catch (var e) { bad = bad + 1; } } return { "imported": ok, "skipped": bad }; }); // Server-sent events, and the request's token as the optional third parameter http.MapGet("ticks", (HttpContext ctx, Dictionary args, CancellationToken ct) => { var feed = Events.Create("inline"); feed.Start(fun(EventSubject self) { while (!self.Closed && !ct.IsCancellationRequested) { sleep(1000); self.Next("tick"); } }); return http.StreamEvents(feed.ReadOnly); });

Context properties

The request arrives as an HttpContext, so a middleware or a handler may pass it to a helper typed with its real name: string Panel(HttpContext ctx) { ... }.

A RESPONSE header is set with ctx.ResponseHeaders["X-My-Header"] = "value", the flat shape the other fields on the context already have (ctx.ResponseStatus, ctx.ResponseContentType, ctx.ResponseBody, ctx.ResponseBytes). ASP.NET spells it ctx.Response.Headers[...]: ctx.ResponseHeaders IS that dictionary here, because this context carries its own answer fields rather than a nested response object, and a second spelling of one thing is what this language retires rather than aliases.

PropertyTypeDescription
ctx.HttpMethodstringHTTP method (GET, POST, etc.)
ctx.UrlstringRequest path (/hello)
ctx.Bodystring?Request body for POST/PUT, as TEXT. It is read from the request the first time it is asked for, so a handler that never reads it costs nothing, and the answer is kept: reading it twice pays once. Null when the request carried no body, which is how a GET reads. A request body is read ONCE, so this and ctx.BodyLines() cannot both be used (the second one is refused by name). There is no size limit: this member is what reads all of it into memory.
ctx.BodyLines()IEnumerable<string>The request body LINE BY LINE, for a body too big to hold: foreach (var line in ctx.BodyLines()) { ... } reads one line at a time from the request's stream. A line is the raw TEXT, not parsed, so the handler owns the format and can skip and COUNT what it cannot use, which is what a bulk import needs. A body may DECLARE its length or arrive as a chunked stream with no length at all, and both are read the same way, so an upload never has to fit in memory. A line ends at CRLF, LF or CR alone, so a file written on Windows, on Unix or on an old Mac reads the same, and the terminator is never part of the line. Three rules: the body is consumed once (a second call, or a ctx.Body read, is refused by name); the lines are only readable while the request is being handled; and an aborted request THROWS at the next line rather than ending quietly, so a truncated import cannot read as a complete one. If a handler ASSIGNS ctx.Body first (to normalise or decompress what arrived), the lines read come from that text rather than from the request, which is what ctx.Body itself reports.
ctx.ResponseStatusintHTTP response status (default 200)
ctx.RequestHeadersDictionaryRequest headers. Read one by name, ctx.RequestHeaders["HX-Request"]; an absent header answers null, so no guard is needed
ctx.RequestAbortedCancellationTokenFires when the client goes away or the request times out
ctx.ResponseBodystring?Response body text
ctx.ResponseBytesbyte[]?Response body as bytes, for an icon or any binary answer
ctx.ResponseContentTypestring?Content type of the answer, for anything that is not HTML text
ctx.ResponseHeadersDictionaryHeaders to send with the answer: a result's own Location, or one a handler sets itself (ctx.ResponseHeaders["Cache-Control"] = "no-store"). Written before the body, and a name the platform refuses is reported rather than dropped in silence
ctx.ErrorMessagestring?Set it to refuse the request: the answer is a 500 whose BODY is this text, because the application is the one refusing. An UNHANDLED exception is a 500 with no body instead, with the cause in the log.
What a middleware can reach. It runs inside the request pipeline, on the interpreter that started the server, and it is a normal script body: it may call the file's own functions, read its top-level variables and use its classes, and it may name a CLR type as a static (Uri, Stopwatch, Version, IPAddress, CultureInfo, Regex). It can index the request's header dictionary directly, and a { } literal or a script list indexes as it does anywhere else. Http.ParseForm is still the way to read a whole form body: it splits the pairs and decodes each component once, so a multi-byte character survives, where Uri.UnescapeDataString would need the splitting and the + handling written out by hand.
StringBuilder type Efficient string concatenation Append, AppendLine, ToString

For building strings efficiently without creating intermediate copies. Use new StringBuilder() to create one, then call Append() / AppendLine() to add content, and ToString() to retrieve the final string.

var sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.Append("hello"); sb.Append(" world"); print(sb.ToString());
// Build 100 lines O(n), single buffer var sb = new StringBuilder(); var i = 0; while (i < 100) { sb.Append("line " + i + "\n"); i = i + 1; } print(sb.ToString()); // 100 lines, single allocation // 1 MB stress test ~82 ms with StringBuilder vs ~4000 ms with + var big = new StringBuilder(); var block = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\n"; i = 0; while (i < 16000) { big.Append(block); i = i + 1; } print("1 MB: " + big.Length + " chars");
Performance: Using + to concatenate N strings creates N intermediate copies O(n²). Using StringBuilder grows a single internal buffer O(n). For large payloads (100 KB+), the difference is dramatic: 1 MB takes ~82ms with StringBuilder vs ~4000ms with +.
StrBuilder namespace Script-friendly StringBuilder wrapper StrBuilder.Create()

The StrBuilder namespace provides a convenient wrapper around System.Text.StringBuilder that's ergonomic from script. StrBuilder.Create(initialCapacity?) returns a StringBuilder instance with chainable .Append(), .Clear(), .Length, and .Capacity.

var sb = StrBuilder.Create(); sb.Append("hello").Append(" ").Append("world"); print(sb.ToString()); // "hello world"
// With initial capacity var sb = StrBuilder.Create(256); // Chaining sb.Append("a").Append("b").Append("c"); print(sb.ToString()); // "abc" // Clear and reuse sb.Clear(); sb.Append("new"); print(sb.ToString()); // "new"
StringComparison enum String comparison mode

Enum values for controlling string comparison behavior in .NET method calls.

StringComparison.Ordinal StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase
print(StringComparison.Ordinal); // Result: 4 print(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase); // Result: 5
DialogResult enum Message box result values

Numeric values returned by a message box use these for readable comparisons.

DialogResult.OK // 1 IDOK DialogResult.Cancel // 2 IDCANCEL DialogResult.Yes // 6 IDYES DialogResult.No // 7 IDNO
var form = Application.CreateForm("Confirm"); var result = form.MessageBox("Save changes?", "Confirm", 4); if (result == DialogResult.Yes) { print("User clicked Yes"); }
TypeInfo namespace Type metadata at runtime

Provides type information at runtime. Access type metadata via the TypeInfo namespace.

// Access type info via TypeInfo namespace // Provides base type, nullable info, array rank, etc.
Process namespace Launch and manage external processes

Launches external executables with optional stdout/stderr callbacks. Use proc.ExitCode (after WaitForExit()) to get the process exit code available immediately, no sleep() needed. Note: ExitCode returns -1 if the process has not exited yet (including after Kill() Windows does not set an exit code for killed processes). Stdout/stderr callbacks run asynchronously add sleep(300) after WaitForExit() when collecting output lines.

var proc = Process.Start("ffmpeg", "-i in.mp4 out.avi", fun(line) => print("[OUT] " + line), fun(line) => print("[ERR] " + line));
// Fire-and-forget var p = Process.Start("cmd.exe", "/c echo hello"); p.WaitForExit(); print("exit: " + p.ExitCode); // Capture output lines var lines = new List<object>(); var p2 = Process.Start("cmd.exe", "/c dir", fun(line) => lines.Add(line), null, null); p2.WaitForExit(); sleep(300); // drain async streams print("Got " + Count(lines) + " lines"); // Kill mid-execution var p3 = Process.Start("cmd.exe", "/c timeout 30"); sleep(500); p3.Kill();
// Exit code via WaitForExit preferred pattern var p4 = Process.Start("cmd.exe", '/c "timeout /t 5 /nobreak >nul & exit 42"', null, null); p4.WaitForExit(); print("Exit code: " + p4.ExitCode); // 42 works on any thread
Returns a ProcessHandle with .Kill() (safe on exited processes), .WaitForExit() (no-arg returns exit code, with timeout returns bool), .IsRunning, .ExitCode. The handle is IDisposable: using (var h = Process.Start(...)) { ... } releases it at the end of the block, h.Dispose() does the same by name, and h is IDisposable answers the question. Disposing releases THIS side's process handle and cached state, it does not end the process, so Kill() is what stops it. A QUERY on a released handle is refused with the engine's own sentence (this process handle was released: Dispose() ran, so the process cannot be queried) rather than the runtime's wording for it, which on an invariant-globalization build is its resource key; Kill() stays a safe no-op, as its contract says. Errors (Win32Exception) are caught and re-thrown as ScriptException with the native error code. Callbacks serialized per handle. WaitForExit() double-calls Process.WaitForExit() to drain async output streams. Add a sleep(300) after WaitForExit() when using callbacks.
File namespace Read/write text and binary files

Provides text and binary file I/O: read, write, append, copy, move, delete, and size queries.

File.ReadAllText("data.txt"); File.WriteAllText("data.txt", "content"); File.AppendAllText("log.txt", "entry\n"); File.ReadAllLines("data.txt"); File.ReadAllBytes("data.bin"); File.WriteAllBytes("data.bin", bytes); File.Exists("data.txt"); File.Delete("data.txt"); File.Copy("src", "dst", true); File.Move("src", "dst"); File.GetSize("data.txt");
File.WriteAllText("out.txt", "hello"); var content = File.ReadAllText("out.txt"); File.Delete("out.txt");

A relative path is resolved against the process directory, unless it starts with ./ or ../. "./data.txt" (and "../data.txt") means "in the directory of the script being run", which is also the process directory in the REPL. Any other relative spelling means "in the working directory the executable was started in", so "data.txt", "sub/data.txt" and the backslash form ".\data.txt" all name the SAME file, and none of them names one beside the script. An absolute path is used as given. This is the rule for Directory and for the bundle paths of Bytecode too.

// beside the script, wherever the process was started File.WriteAllText("./report.txt", "beside the script"); // beside the executable: a bare name is NOT "beside the script" File.WriteAllText("report.txt", "beside the exe"); // ask for either side explicitly print(Script.Directory()); // the run's directory print(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory()); // the process directory

A member this list does not hold is resolved on System.IO.File itself, so the whole .NET surface is reachable without being restated here: File.ReadAllTextAsync, File.GetLastWriteTime, File.OpenHandle. The members above always win, and two rules keep a fallback member behaving like them: a parameter that IS a path follows the ./ rule above, while an argument that is content stays exactly as written (WriteAllTextAsync(path, contents) resolves path and passes contents through), and a failure reads the engine's own way, naming the member and the position. A name neither the engine nor the type has is still refused, with the list of what this namespace holds.

// the task awaits like the engine's own var text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync("./report.txt"); print(File.GetLastWriteTime("./report.txt")); // a DateTime

Reading a file line by line. File.OpenRead(path) answers a reader you dispose: ReadLine() gives the next line without its terminator, and null at the end; ReadToEnd() gives every REMAINING line as a string array; Close() releases the handle, and a using block does that for you. A line ends at CRLF, LF or a lone CR, and no empty line follows a final terminator, so the reader and File.ReadAllLines answer the same rows for the same file.

using (var reader = File.OpenRead("./data.txt")) { var header = reader.ReadLine(); foreach (var line in reader.ReadToEnd()) { print(line); } }

Which one to use on a big file. ReadToEnd() and File.ReadAllLines keep every line at once: one string per line plus one pointer array, and an array over 85,000 bytes (about 10,600 lines) is allocated on the large object heap, which only a full collection reclaims. A ReadLine() loop keeps one line alive at a time, so it is the shape for a file too big to hold.

Directory namespace Create, delete, list directories

Directory operations: create, delete (recursive), list files by pattern, list subdirectories, and query current directory.

Every path follows the File rule: "./x" is beside the script, and any other relative spelling is beside the executable. A member this list does not hold is resolved on System.IO.Directory itself, with the same rules as File (Directory.GetFileSystemEntries, Directory.GetLastWriteTime).

Directory.Exists("path"); Directory.CreateDirectory("path"); Directory.Delete("path", true); var files = Directory.GetFiles("path", "*.txt"); var dirs = Directory.GetDirectories("path"); Directory.GetCurrentDirectory();
Directory.CreateDirectory("output"); File.WriteAllText("output/test.txt", "data"); Directory.Delete("output", true);
Path namespace Path manipulation utilities

Path segment combination, filename/directory/extension extraction, and path resolution.

Path.Combine("folder", "sub", "file.txt"); Path.GetFileName("C:\\dir\\file.txt"); Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension("archive.tar.gz"); Path.GetDirectoryName("C:\\dir\\sub"); Path.GetExtension("data.json"); Path.ChangeExtension("photo.jpg", ".png"); Path.HasExtension("readme.md"); Path.GetFullPath("relative\\path.txt");
var full = Path.Combine("folder", "file.txt"); var ext = Path.GetExtension(full); // ".txt"
All methods delegate directly to System.IO.Path. Path separator is platform-specific (\\ on Windows, / on Unix). A member this list does not hold is resolved on System.IO.Path itself, with the same rules as File (Path.GetRandomFileName, Path.GetRelativePath).
pause ref cell Wait for key press

Blocks execution until the user presses any key. Useful in scripts before exiting, or between test phases.

pause;
print("Press any key to continue..."); pause; print("Continuing...");
exitcode ref cell Get/set process exit code

A reference cell (RefCell) that reads and writes the process exit code (Environment.ExitCode). Validates integer range.

exitcode = 0; print(exitcode);
exitcode = 42; abort(exitcode); // exits with code 42

▼ REPL Commands

.help REPL Show the list of available commands

Displays a reference of all available dot commands, REPL features, and script expression/statement syntax. Grouped into Commands (all dot commands) and Expressions & Statements (script constructs available directly at the prompt).

In a FILE, a dot command is stripped before the file is read, so a session pasted into a script still runs: a line whose first character is . and whose name is one of these commands is removed (and .time / .echo are honoured, the way they are at the prompt). Both halves matter: a line that only looks like a command is left alone as code, so an indented .Replace(...) continues a chained call and .row .text { ... } inside a template stays part of its stylesheet.

.help
.help Commands .help Show this help .infos Show version, build info, AOT status .echo on/off Toggle echo mode .reset [all] Clear state ...
.exit / .quit REPL Exit the interpreter

Exits the REPL and terminates the process. All interpreter state is discarded. .quit is a synonym.

.exit or .quit
.clear / .cls REPL Clear the console screen and show the banner

Resets the terminal, clears all visible text, and re-displays the script banner with version info, admin warning color, and the .help / .exit hint line.

.clear or .cls
.reset REPL Clear all global variables and reset interpreter state. .reset hard creates a new Interpreter instance.
.reset
.reset all wipes user-defined types, classes, delegates, modules, and frees native library handles
.reset hard disposes the entire Interpreter and creates a new instance frees ALL state, caches, static dictionaries, and GC segments
Ctrl+C REPL KeyboardInterrupt cancel current input or running script

Pressing Ctrl+C interrupts the current operation without exiting the REPL, like Python's behavior. A yellow Interrupted by user message is printed and a fresh prompt appears. Works both at the prompt (clears partial input) and during script execution (interrupts at the next statement boundary). When this session is serving HTTP (--mcp), pressing it also stops that server and says so: the prompt stays, and serving again is one .run away: a session launched to serve re-arms the listener when it runs a script. A session whose input is piped keeps the older rule instead and ends on the key, because there a closed input is the only other way out.

// At the prompt clears current line >>> KeyboardInterrupt >>> // During infinite loop interrupts execution while (true) {} // press Ctrl+C KeyboardInterrupt >>>
.vars REPL List user-defined global variables (name, type, line, column)

Lists user-defined global variables in a formatted table with columns: Name, Type (script type name), Line, and Col (declaration location). Entries are sorted by declaration position. Only variables the user explicitly created are shown built-in namespaces, types, and functions are excluded.

.vars
.vars Name Type Line Col ────────────────────────────── x int 5 2 name string 10 3
.varsall [cat] REPL List ALL global scope keys, grouped by category. Optionally filter by category name.

Categories: types, native, delegates, namespaces, functions, user, lists, dictionaries, ref cells, other. Multiple categories can be combined: .varsall types native.

.functions REPL List user-defined functions, classes, and structs

Lists all user-defined declarations (functions, classes, structs) with their Name, Type, Line, and Column. Sorted by declaration order. Useful for checking the current scope after a series of REPL inputs.

.functions
.functions Name Type Line Col ────────────────────────────── square int 5 2 Point class 12 1
.tree <var> REPL Display a variable's structure as a tree (lists, dicts, nested)

Displays a variable's structure as a visual tree. Supports lists, dictionaries, arrays, and raw .NET IDictionary types up to 10 elements (remaining are summarized as ... (N more)). Scalars show their ToString() value.

.tree variableName
.tree mydict mydict: Dictionary (3 entries) ├── name: Alice ├── scores: List [3] │ ├── [0]: 10 │ ├── [1]: 20 │ └── [2]: 30 └── tags: null
.strict REPL Enable case-sensitive mode (default). 'A' and 'a' are distinct.

Enables case-sensitive identifier matching. After switching, MyVar and myvar refer to different variables. This is the default mode. Clears the method and property caches when toggled.

Keywords are case-sensitive in every mode: if is the keyword and IF is an ordinary name, so IF (x) { } is not an if statement and a whole number is written int, never Int. The same holds for a keyword used as a name, where the engine only warns for the keyword's own spelling: var class = 5; warns, var Class = 5; does not.

A type name follows the same rule. The engine registers string, int, long and their siblings, and refuses the CLR spelling in a declaration while naming the one to write: String name; reports write 'string'. A value's printed form is the engine's, too, so a string parameter and a concatenation render the same value the same way.

.strict
.lax REPL Enable case-insensitive mode. 'A' and 'a' refer to the same variable.

Enables case-insensitive matching. MyVar and myvar refer to the same variable. Useful when working with imported code that uses inconsistent casing. When toggled, the method and property caches are cleared and a Reset(keepGlobals: true) is performed.

.lax
.time REPL Toggle execution timing shows elapsed ms after each result

Toggles execution timing on/off. When on, each expression or statement shows elapsed milliseconds in parentheses after the result. Works like a stopwatch the time includes parsing, interpretation, and any I/O.

.time
.time Timing mode: ON >>> var x = 0; >>> while (x < 1000) { x = x + 1; } (1.23 ms)
.echo on/off REPL Toggle echo mode each input line shown before execution (useful when piping)

Toggles echo mode. When ON, each input line is reprinted with the >>> prompt prefix before execution. Useful when piping scripts via stdin so you can see what was executed.

.echo on or .echo off
.echo on Echo mode: ON >>> echo on >>> print(42) = 42
.run <file> [-q|--quiet] [-bc [out.slcbc]] [-- <script args>] REPL Execute a script file. Supports glob patterns, pipe-separated paths, and .state. -bc loads/builds the .slcbc sibling. -- passes the script its own arguments.

Executes a script file in the current interpreter context. Supports glob patterns (*.slc) and pipe-separated file lists. The file is resolved first as an absolute path, then relative to the configured base directory, then in assets/language/.

Whether state persists after execution depends on the .state setting (default: .state keep). Use .state reset to automatically clear all variables, classes, and modules after each .run.

A class, struct or enum a file declares therefore SURVIVES its run, which is what lets a later request reach it (an http.Use middleware calling a helper the file itself declared). Re-running the same file replaces its own declarations silently, so an edit takes effect; a different file declaring a name the session already has still warns (Class 'X' already declared. Skipping redefinition.) and keeps the first one.

.run "test.slc"
.run "stress_*.slc" // glob
.run "a.slc|b.slc" // batch
.run "tool.slc" -- a "b c" // the SCRIPT's own arguments

Everything after -- is the script's command line rather than another file, so a tool whose input IS its arguments can be driven from a session: .run slc-pack.slc -- launcher.exe app.slc app.exe --version 1.2.3.4. Inside the run, Application.Args is [the script's path, ...those arguments], which is exactly what the CLI gives a script, so a file written for the command line needs no second form. A QUOTED argument survives as one argument (-- "C:\Program Files\app.exe"), because a path with a space is the common case; only the tail is split this way, so .run a.slc|b.slc -bc is unchanged. Two rules to know: the arguments belong to that RUN and are put back afterwards, so the next statement reads the session's own Application.Args; and a script's arguments arrive with no shell, so a wildcard is not expanded (*.slc is the literal text) and there is no redirection or piping.

.run "test.slc reset" // run then clear state
.run "test.slc -q" // quiet: the script's own output is discarded
.run -bc "test.slc" // load the .slcbc sibling if present, else run the source and build it

A .run file runs exactly as the command line runs it, its top level included: the statements outside every function are compiled and run on the VM. A line TYPED at the prompt is the one thing that stays on the tree walker, because its value has to echo (= 42).
