The difference is not academic for a script that builds a window: the designer demo's setup measures about 0.5 s on the VM path and about 4.3 s walked, so routing FILE runs through the tree made the same file look ten times slower for no benefit.

-q and -bc belong to the command, not to the script. -q discards everything the run prints, and it does so at the ENGINE's writer as well as at Console.Out, so it silences the same way when the REPL is driven by a host (ScriptLangCore.Launcher.exe is one): a flag that only swapped Console.Out left a hosted run printing at full volume.

.looprun <N> <file> [-bc [out.slcbc]] [-- <script args>] REPL Run a script file N times. Resets state between iterations unless .state keep is set. -bc also exports the .slcbc sibling.

Runs the specified script file N times in sequence. By default the interpreter is reset between each iteration, so each run starts with a clean state. Set .state keep to preserve variables across iterations (useful for incremental accumulation benchmarks).

Supports the same glob patterns and pipe-separated paths as .run. Catches per-iteration errors without aborting the benchmark. After all iterations complete, a summary line shows total time and runs/second.

Warning suppression: Non-critical warnings (e.g., "Variable already declared", "Class already declared") are automatically suppressed during .looprun and .bench to keep benchmark output clean.

What reaches the console while it runs: the FIRST iteration shows the script's own output, every later one is silenced, and one progress line (a percentage) is rewritten in place on stderr, so a 5000-iteration run reads as a single screen instead of a flood. The same rule holds when the REPL is driven by a HOST (the launcher is one): the silencing covers the engine's own output writer as well as Console.Out, which is the difference that used to let every iteration through into the host's pane. .run -q and .bench -q silence the same way.

.looprun 100 "test.slc" // 100 iterations
.looprun 1000 "stress_*.slc" // glob pattern × 1000
.looprun 5000 "lib.slcbc" // load a bytecode bundle 5000 times (no source parse)
.looprun 20 "bench.slc" -- 1000 // the SCRIPT's own arguments, each iteration

Everything after -- is the script's command line, the same rule .run follows, so a benchmark or a generator that takes its size from Application.Args can be looped from a session. Every iteration gets the SAME arguments ([the script's path, ...those arguments]), a quoted one survives whole, and the session's own list is back when the loop ends. Only the first iteration's output is printed by design, which is what a benchmark wants.

.looprun 50 "crash_memory_leak_fix.slc" // Output: // Running crash_memory_leak_fix.slc × 50 = 50 total executions... // Done: 50 runs in 12144 ms (4 runs/s)
.loadslcbc <file.slcbc> [alias] REPL Load a bytecode bundle: library → namespace under alias (default file stem); single-script bundle → flat

Reads a .slcbc bundle (see Bytecode) and magic-detects its type. A library bundle becomes a Namespace defined under the given alias (default: the file stem) call its functions as alias.fn(...) (or alias.ns.fn(...) when the library declares namespaces). A single-script bundle loads flat: every function is defined into the current interpreter's global scope. Every body is decoded and verified at load, so a body that does not verify is refused here, naming the function, rather than when something first calls it. Prints the load report (e.g. Imported library as namespace 'lib'. or Loaded N function(s)).

.loadslcbc "C:/Temp/lib.slcbc" // library → namespace 'lib' (file stem) .loadslcbc "lib.slcbc" Z // library → namespace 'Z' (explicit alias) .loadslcbc "single.slcbc" // single-script bundle → flat
.loadslcbc "lib.slcbc" print(lib.sumTo(10)); // 55 library under namespace 'lib' (file stem) .loadslcbc "lib.slcbc" Z print(Z.sumTo(10)); // 55 same library, explicit alias 'Z' .loadslcbc "single.slcbc" print(sumTo(10)); // 55 single-script bundle loads flat
.state keep/reset REPL Toggle whether .run and .looprun preserve or clear global variables between executions

Controls whether the interpreter state (variables, classes, modules) is preserved across .run and .looprun executions.

  • .state keep (default) state is preserved. Variables set by .run are accessible after it finishes.
  • .state reset state is cleared after each .run and between each .looprun iteration.
.state reset // clear state after each .run .state keep // preserve state (default)
.state reset .run "stress.slc" // clears globals after running .looprun 10 "test.slc" // each iteration is clean
.reset and .reset all are manual commands unaffected by .state they always clear state immediately regardless of the current setting.
Variable redeclaration warnings: With .state keep, running a script that declares variables (var x = ...) will print a warning when the same variable is re-declared in subsequent runs. The warning is informational the new value replaces the old. These warnings are automatically suppressed during .bench and .looprun.
.import <file> REPL Import a script into the current session (keeps state no reset)

Imports a script into the current session without resetting state. Unlike .run, this keeps all existing variables, functions, and classes. Multiple imports accumulate. Equivalent to typing the file contents at the prompt.

.import "utility.inc"
This is the REPL equivalent of the import statement. It runs in the current interpreter's scope rather than creating a module interpreter.
.cd [dir] REPL Show or change the script base directory for .run and .import

Shows or changes the script base directory used by .run, .import, and glob resolution. When called without arguments, prints the current base directory. The path supports environment variable expansion (%USERPROFILE%).

.cd // show current
.cd "C:/Projects/Scripts"
.cd "%USERPROFILE%/scripts"
.debug on/off REPL Enable or disable the interactive script debugger

Enables or disables the interactive script debugger. When enabled, you can set breakpoints with .break <line>. The debugger pauses execution at breakpoints and allows you to inspect variables. Toggle off to return to normal execution mode.

.debug on or .debug off
.break <line> REPL Set a breakpoint at the specified line (requires .debug on)

Sets a breakpoint at the specified line number. The debugger must be enabled first (.debug on). Execution pauses when reaching that line, allowing variable inspection. Line numbers are relative to the current script or REPL input.

.break 42
.debug on .break 10 .run test.slc
.gc collect / .gc stats / .gc info / .gc diff / .gc top / .gc leak / .gc handles / .gc handletypes REPL Show memory info, force garbage collection, show GC statistics, or run a one-shot leak check
.gc show memory usage
.gc collect force GC
.gc stats collection counts
.gc info per-gen sizes, fragmentation, pause
.gc diff memory delta since last .gc call
.gc top [N] top N object types by instance count (default 5)
.gc leak <file> [count] [thresholdKB] one-shot leak detector
.gc handles handle count and private bytes now, with the delta since the previous .gc handles/.gc collect

The OS-side counterpart of .gc collect: handles and private bytes are invisible to GC.GetTotalMemory, so a COM or native leak appears here and nowhere else. A count that climbs across repeated calls is a leak with one exception worth knowing: the connection handle a COM out-of-process activation costs (one ALPC Port) is reclaimed by the runtime within minutes of that server exiting (9 → 5 over a 4-minute idle), so read DELTAS rather than absolutes. The handle TYPE tally needs cdb (tools\cdb-gc-leak.cmd -handles); this is the count, in-process, without a debugger.

Parameters:

  • <file> script to run repeatedly (fresh parse each iteration, like .looprun)
  • [count] number of measured runs (default 100; a warmup pass always runs first to absorb one-time startup state)
  • [thresholdKB] per-run retained-memory threshold in KB (default 64). If the measured per-run delta exceeds it, the verdict is LEAK; otherwise PASS. Raise it for scripts that legitimately retain per-run state; lower it to catch small leaks.

While it runs: the first measured run prints the script's own output and the rest stay quiet, with one percentage line rewritten on stderr, the same rule .looprun follows and for the same reason: a leak check of a few thousand runs must not bury its own verdict in script output.

Threshold noise floor: a thresholdKB below 16 KB is below the engine's GC allocator noise floor any workload trips LEAK on ordinary variance, not real retention. The command prints a warning in that case but still honors your chosen value. Use ≥ 16 KB (the 64 KB default is the calibrated value) for a meaningful verdict.

.gc info shows detailed memory diagnostics:

  • Heap total managed heap size
  • Fragmented memory lost to fragmentation
  • Gen0/1/2 size per-generation heap size
  • Paused duration of the last GC pause (important for real-time scenarios)
  • Frag ratio fragmentation percentage (high → compacting needed)
  • Memory load OS-reported memory pressure
// Typical output after a heavy bench: Heap: 96459.4 KB Fragmented: 12345.6 KB Gen0 size: 2100.3 KB Gen1 size: 8400.2 KB Gen2 size: 89100.0 KB Paused: 5.2 ms (last GC pause) Frag ratio: 12.4 % Memory load: 42.3 MB (OS) Gen0: 241 Gen1: 62 Gen2: 23
.gc diff Managed: +12.3 KB (delta since last .gc call) Gen0: +2 Gen1: +0 Gen2: +0 .gc top 1. ScriptBoxedDictionary 12,847 2. ClassInstance 8,492 3. Dictionary<String,Object> 6,103 4. List<Object> 4,221 5. ScriptFunction 2,018
// Memory-leak diagnostic workflow .gc top 10 → snapshot before .bench my_script.slc 100 -gc 50 -q → run 100 iterations .gc top 10 → snapshot after .gc diff → delta memory .gc history → collection counts + memory snapshot Gen0: 24 collections Gen1: 6 collections Gen2: 2 collections Memory: 12450.3 KB
Workflow tip: Chain .gc top 10 → .bench ... -gc 50 -q → .gc top 10 → .gc diff to identify memory leaks. If the same types grow linearly with iterations (visible in top before/after), clear the relevant caches or check for undisposed objects.
// One-shot leak check: baseline → run N times → forced collect → verdict .gc leak stress.slc 500 64 File: stress.slc × 500 Base: 363.8 KB After: 444.9 KB Retained delta: +81.1 KB Per run: 0.16 KB (threshold 64 KB) gen0=63 VERDICT: PASS no significant per-run retention // With a real leak (e.g. per-iteration rooted state): .gc leak leaky.slc 100 64 Per run: 31.25 KB (threshold 64 KB) VERDICT: LEAK retained memory grows per run and survives full collection
.gc leak automates the manual leak workflow in one command: it runs a warmup pass (absorbing one-time state like script globals, type registration, and cache warmup), measures a baseline after a forced full collection, runs the script count times (fresh parse each iteration, like .looprun), forces another full collection, and reports the per-run retained delta between runs. Growth that survives a full collection is rooted (a genuine leak e.g. a static or interpreter-held collection growing per iteration); reachable live state and one-time startup costs are absorbed by the warmup. Raise thresholdKB if a script legitimately retains per-run state; lower it to catch small leaks.
.history [N] REPL Show last N REPL commands (default: all, max 500)
.history or .history 10

Multi-line entries show with indented continuation lines. Use .edit <line> to inspect an entry.

.edit <line> REPL Display a history entry for editing

Shows the exact code from a history entry. Use .history first to find the line number, then .edit <N> to display it. Copy-paste and correct any typo.

.edit 1
.history 1 var x = 10; 2 var y = 20; .edit 2 2 var y = 20;
!<N> REPL Re-execute a history entry (bash-style)

Type !<N> to re-execute history entry N. The entry is printed then executed. Useful for replaying commands or re-running a function definition after fixing it.

!3
.history 1 var x = 10; 2 var y = 20; 3 print(x + y); !2 >>> var y = 20; Warning: Variable 'y' is being redeclared at line 4.
.type REPL Show type of an expression

Evaluates an expression and shows its type and value.

>>> .type 42 int => 42 >>> .type "hello" string => hello >>> .type 1 + 2 * 3 int => 7
Note: The expression is evaluated in the current interpreter scope, not a sandbox. Side effects (e.g. calling functions) persist.
.stats REPL Show execution metrics

Shows uptime, statements executed, function calls, and managed memory.

.stats
.stats Uptime: 00:12:34 Statements: 1 523 Function calls: 342 Managed memory: 4.2 MB
.search <pattern> REPL Search command history

Searches the interpreter's command history for lines containing the given pattern. The search is case-insensitive.

.search "pattern"
.search var History matches for 'var': 1: var x = 10 3: var name = "hello" 12: foreach (var i in range)
.alias REPL Create or remove command aliases

Manages in-memory command aliases. Aliases are not persisted between sessions.

  • .alias list all current aliases.
  • .alias name=value create an alias (e.g., .alias ll=.looprun).
  • .alias name remove the specified alias.
.alias // list aliases .alias ll=.looprun // create alias .alias ll // remove alias
.alias ll=.looprun Alias 'll' => '.looprun' .alias ll => .looprun .alias ll Alias 'll' removed.
.eval <expression> REPL Evaluate expression silently

Evaluates an expression without printing prompts. If the expression fails, the interpreter tries to parse it as a statement.

.eval x + 1
.eval 2 + 2 4 .eval var msg = "hello" // (no output statement executed silently)
.export [filename] | -bc <file.slc> [out.slcbc] [ns] | -bundle <file.slc> [out.slcbc] [--source=carry|strip|strict] REPL Export variables to a script file, or -bc: run a script and export its VM-compiled top-level functions to a bytecode LIBRARY (.slcbc), or -bundle: write a PROGRAM bundle without running anything, with the source mode of --compile

Writes current user variables to a script file. If no filename is given, defaults to session_state.slc.

With -bc, instead of exporting variables it runs <file.slc> and exports its VM-compiled top-level functions to a bytecode LIBRARY (.slcbc). The optional trailing ns becomes the namespace for this script's functions in the library; functions the compiler did not take are skipped and reported. Load it back with .loadslcbc. A library names functions and namespaces and carries no source at all, so a source flag has nothing to act on here and is refused by name.

With -bundle, it writes a PROGRAM bundle instead: the artifact --compile writes and .run <file> -bc runs, with an entry. Nothing is executed, so a script that opens a window or never ends can still be compiled, and the compile happens in a fresh interpreter, so this session's own variables and classes cannot reach the artifact. The output path and the flags are the same as on the command line: the path is the first argument after the file that is not a flag, and --source=carry|strip|strict decides what the bundle carries (carry keeps the program text, strip strips it when the strip is honest and carries it otherwise, saying so in the report, strict refuses rather than carry, which is what --no-source means on the command line). Without a flag it carries.

Exported types: string, int, long, double, float, bool, null. Complex types (functions, classes) are skipped.

.export // writes to session_state.slc .export "backup.slc" // writes to backup.slc .export -bc "app.slc" // runs app.slc, writes app.slcbc as a bytecode LIBRARY .export -bc "app.slc" "app.slcbc" My // explicit output file + namespace 'My' for this script's functions .export -bundle "app.slc" // nothing runs; writes app.slcbc as a PROGRAM bundle, source carried .export -bundle "app.slc" --source=strip // the source is stripped when that is honest, and carried with a reason when it is not
.export myvars.slc Exported 3 variables to 'myvars.slc'. // Contents of myvars.slc: // var x = 42; // var name = "hello"; // var flag = true;
_ / _last REPL Previous expression result variables

After every REPL expression evaluation, the result is stored in _ (most recent) and _last (previous). These are regular global-scope variables inspectable with .vars, usable in subsequent expressions. Note: REPL input requires a trailing ; for all statements, including variable references.

42; // = 42, _ = 42 _ * 2; // = 84, _ = 84, _last = 42 _last; // = 42 (previous value)
// REPL session: >>> 2 + 2; = 4 >>> _ * 10; = 40 >>> _last; = 4 >>> .vars _ = 40 _last = 4
Cleared on .state reset. Explicitly defining _ or _last in a script replaces the automatic values on the next expression evaluation.
.save [--all] [file] REPL Export session state to a script file

Writes current user variables (and optionally declarations) to a script file for reuse. Defaults to session_state.slc.

Without --all: exports scalar variables (string, int, long, double, float, bool, null). With --all: also exports function, class, and struct declarations.

.save // writes to session_state.slc .save my_session.slc // writes to my_session.slc .save --all full.slc // includes functions and types
.save backup.slc Saved 3 item(s) to backup.slc // backup.slc contents: // var x = 42; // var msg = "hello"; // var flag = true;
.trace on|off REPL Enable/disable execution call tracing

When enabled, prints [trace] lines showing every function call and REPL expression evaluation useful for debugging complex scripts or understanding control flow.

.trace on // enable tracing .trace off // disable tracing
// REPL session with trace on: >>> .trace on Trace: ON >>> var x = 2 >>> print(x); [trace] print(2) → null = null >>> 2 + 2; [trace] <repl> → 4 = 4
Function call tracing only fires for user-defined functions and script visible calls, not for internal built-in operations. Variable declarations and control-flow statements are not traced.
.vm [trace on|off] REPL Inspect & control the bytecode VM trace toggle and enabled state

Interactive control of the bytecode VM, mirroring the script-side VmXXX built-ins.

.vm // show VM trace + enabled state .vm trace on // enable per-opcode VM tracing ([vm] ip=… OP sp=…) .vm trace off // disable
// REPL session: >>> .vm VM trace: OFF VM enabled: ON (.vm off re-enables the tree-walker...) >>> .vm trace on VM trace: ON
The trace sub-command toggles VmSetTrace(bool); the enabled/disabled state reflects VmSetEnabled(bool). Trace lines use the format [vm] fn=<name>[depth] [Lx:Cx] ip=N OP sp=N ; decode with a one-time --- source: <file> --- banner at file/import boundaries.
.bench <file> [N] [-q|--quiet] [-gc N] [-bc [out.slcbc]] REPL Benchmark a script file (or a .slcbc bundle: loads it per run)

Runs a script file N times (default 10) and reports timing statistics. Reports total time, average time per run, and throughput (runs/s). Use -q or --quiet to suppress script output during benchmarking. Use -gc N to force a full garbage collection every N runs. The actual number of runs may be less than N if interrupted by Ctrl+C or if the script encounters an error.

.bench "test.slc" // 10 runs .bench "test.slc" 100 // 100 runs .bench "lib.slcbc" 100 // loads a bytecode bundle 100 times
.bench test.slc 50
.bench "test.slc" 1000 -gc 50 // GC every 50 runs`n.bench "test.slc" 100 -q // 100 runs, quiet
Runs: 50 Total: 2 340 ms Average: 46.8 ms Throughput: 21.4 runs/s
Note: State is reset between runs by default. Use .state keep before benchmarking to preserve state across iterations. When .state keep is active, SQLite database handles from setup scripts remain valid across all benchmark iterations they are not closed on reset.
Memory diagnostics: Combine .gc top 10 → .bench ... -gc 50 -q → .gc top 10 → .gc diff to detect memory leaks. If the same object types keep growing linearly across iterations, investigate the relevant caches (_pureMemoCache, _pureYieldCache) or undisposed object references.

Warning suppression: Non-critical warnings are automatically suppressed during .bench and .looprun execution to avoid noise in benchmark output.

.infos REPL Show version, build date, AOT status, OS info

Displays system and build information: version number, file version, build date, Debug/Release configuration, AOT compilation status, .NET runtime version, OS description, process architecture (32/64-bit), and admin privilege status. Useful for diagnostics and confirming AOT compatibility.

.infos
.infos Version: 1.0.0.0 Configuration: Debug AOT compiled: No Runtime: .NET 11.0.0 OS: Windows 10.0.22631 Process: 64-bit Admin: Yes
.mcp REPL List registered MCP tools (MCP server mode)

Shows all tools registered via RegisterMcpTool() and resources via RegisterMcpResource() with parameter signatures. Also lists built-in protocol methods (ping, initialize, logging/setLevel, resources/list). Only in --mcp --repl mode.

.mcp
.mcp Registered MCP tools (6): read_file(path: string) Read the full contents of a text file from disk. write_file(path: string, content: string) Write text content to a file. test_echo(message: string) Echo back the input. [Protocol methods: ping, initialize, logging/setLevel, resources/list]
.call <name> <json> REPL Invoke an MCP tool directly

Calls a registered MCP tool with JSON arguments. Tests the same code path as the AI. Only in --mcp --repl mode.

.call test_echo {"message":"hi"}
.call test_echo {"message":"hi"} ECHO: hi .call test_add {"a":3,"b":4} Result: 7
.log <level> REPL Set MCP server log level

Sets the MCP log level for diagnostic messages. Messages go to stderr. Only in --mcp --repl mode.

LevelShowsExample
debugEverything[MCP debug] → tools/call id=1
infoTool calls + errors[MCP infos] tool:system_info args:0
noticeSame as info (reserved)
warningErrors only
errorErrors only[MCP error] tool:read_file failed: ...
offNothing

.log off disables all logging.

.log debug
.log debug Log level set to: debug .log warning Log level set to: warning .log off Logging disabled.
> file REPL Persistent stdout redirect all output goes to file

Redirects all REPL output (results, print, errors) to a file. Stays active until > console restores console output. Survives .state reset and works with .run, .import, .bench.

> file.txt 42 // goes to file.txt print("hi") // goes to file.txt > console // back to console
< file REPL Execute a script file (alias for .run)

Shorthand for .run <file>. Same file resolution (direct path, glob, relative to script base directory).

< test.slc
REPL limitations:
  • Class declarations (class Foo {}) work in the REPL but instantiation (new Foo()) may not resolve the type immediately. Use .reset and retry, or define classes in a file and run with .run.
  • Multi-line input (e.g., function bodies, loops) is supported via ... continuation prompts.
  • Variables declared with var persist between commands. Use .reset or .reset hard to clear state.
  • Arrow keys (up/down) recall command history. Tab inserts a literal tab (no auto-completion).
  • Press Ctrl+C to interrupt a running script and return to the prompt.

▼ Sqlite Namespace

Sqlite namespace SQLite cursor + UDF functions (requires sqlite3.dll loaded via LoadLibrary)

The Sqlite namespace provides high-level wrappers around the SQLite C API. It uses the same dynamic library handle obtained from LoadLibrary("sqlite3"). All cursor operations return IEnumerable objects that stream rows lazily the database is kept open until the enumerator is disposed. All handles use SafeHandle wrappers with critical finalizers to prevent native memory leaks. Methods that accept SQL parameters use params Array values can be passed as individual arguments or as an array literal.

Row access: by name or by ordinal

Cursor rows are returned as dictionary-like objects. You can access columns by name (r["id"]) or by ordinal position (r[0]). Both forms are equivalent ordinal lookup is O(1) and uses the query's column order. Mixed access within the same row is fine.

foreach (var r in db.Query("SELECT id, name, price FROM products")) { print(r["id"]); // by column name print(r[0]); // same by ordinal (0 = first column) print(r[1] + " $" + r[2]); // name + price by ordinal }

Methods

MethodReturnsDescription
Query(path, sql[, params]) or Query(db, sql[, params]) or Query(lib, path, sql[, params]) or Query(lib, db, sql[, params])SqliteIteratorUnified cursor: pass path (string) for new connection, db (Int64 from OpenDb) for existing handle, or lib (DynamicLibrary) for explicit library handle. Auto-detects form by argument types. Enumerable + IDisposable.
QueryLazy(db, sql[, params]) or QueryLazy(lib, db, sql[, params])SqliteIterator of SqliteRowSame cursor over an existing handle, but each row reads a column only when the script asks for it the win on a wide row a script reads partly. Enumerable + IDisposable.
OpenDb(path) or OpenDb(lib, path)longOpen a database and return the raw dbHandle (Int64). OpenDb(path) auto-loads sqlite3.dll; OpenDb(lib, path) uses a pre-loaded handle.
CloseDb(db)boolClose a database previously opened with OpenDb. Returns true on success. Handles are also automatically closed when the interpreter is reset or disposed.
CreateFunction(db, name, argCount, deterministic, callback) or CreateFunction(lib, db, name, argCount, deterministic, callback)boolRegister a script function as a SQLite UDF. Pass 0 for lib to auto-resolve. Use UnregisterFunctions(db) to free the callback handle.
Query<T>(path|db|lib, path|db, sql[, params])SqliteMappingIteratorTyped cursor (each row mapped to a T class instance). Auto-detects form by argument types (same as Query). Enumerable + IDisposable.
Query<T, V>(path|db|lib, path|db, sql[, params])VFlexible return (List, Dict, instance, scalar). Same source detection.
UnregisterFunctions(db)boolUnregister all UDFs on a connection
BulkInsert(lib, db, table, colNames, rows[, batchSize[, useTransaction]])longBulk INSERT: script-list path (prepared statement bind); binary path when colNames is byte[]
SerializeRows(colNames, rows)byte[]Serializes script rows to binary format accepted by BulkInsert
CsvImport(lib, db, table, csvPath, batchSize, hasHeader, colNames)longStream CSV file into table, auto-detect delimiter
LoadExtensions(lib, db, firstExt, ...)boolLoad SQLite extension DLLs (FTS5, math, etc.)
AttachDatabase(lib, db, path, alias)boolAttach another database file for cross-DB queries
DetachDatabase(lib, db, alias)boolDetach a previously attached database

The script functions SQL can call

The six slc_* functions are a second way into this engine. The methods above let a SCRIPT talk to a database; these let a DATABASE talk to a script, because ScriptLangCore.dll is itself a SQLite loadable extension. From then on SQL has real logic in it: an expression, an aggregate, a whole set, or a file's own functions, all written in this language and all running on one interpreter per connection.

The purpose is worth stating plainly, because a REPL session is where it pays off first. The sqlite3 shell is a REPL for data, and with the DLL loaded its expressions are no longer limited to what SQLite can spell: a WHERE clause can call a function you wrote, an aggregate can be any fold, and a set can be mapped with one script expression instead of a chain of CASE. Nothing needs to be installed, because the DLL is the engine itself, and each connection gets its own interpreter, so what a script declared stays callable for as long as the connection lives.

Loading the DLL from the command-line shell. From a sqlite3 session the load is one line, and the entry point is init: 
sqlite> .load ./ScriptLangCore init
sqlite> select slc_eval_scalar('a0 * 2', 21);
42
The path is the DLL without its .dll suffix, and SQLite finds the file itself. The entry point is exported under three names: init (the short one), sqlite3_scriptlangcore_init (the name SQLite DERIVES from the file, i.e. the basename without its extension, without a leading lib, lowercased, so a bare .load ./ScriptLangCore works too) and init_sta (the same, and it makes the calling thread the main STA so a script can drive COM; see the note under the table). If the shell answers no such function the entry point was not found: spell it, as .load ./ScriptLangCore init. It can also be done without the REPL, one shot per invocation: sqlite3 my.db ".load ./ScriptLangCore init" "select slc_eval_scalar('a0 * 2', 21);", and as a SQL statement with select load_extension('./ScriptLangCore', 'init');. The statement form needs extension loading enabled in the host (the shell has it on; an application asks for it with SQLITE_DBCONFIG_ENABLE_LOAD_EXTENSION before opening the connection it will use), while .load is the shell's own door and needs nothing. The floor is SQLite 3.31, an older host is refused by name, and the functions are registered DIRECTONLY, which is why a schema cannot carry a reference to them (see the note under the examples). The sqlite> in these examples is the shell's prompt and not SQL: from SQLite 3.54 the shell shows its application and version there instead, and its continuation prompt spells the characters still needed to close a statement, which the embedding howto covers with the two lines that pin the classic pair.

A script can load the same DLL for a connection it already holds, which is the same registration done from this side: Sqlite.LoadExtensions(lib, db, "<path>/ScriptLangCore.dll"). Then a scalar question can be answered from inside the connection: Sqlite.Query(lib, db, "select slc_eval_scalar('a0 * 2', 21)").

A script that drives COM needs an STA thread, and the shell's own thread is not one (Windows reports it as an implicit MTA, because the shell never initialized COM), so the plain entry point answers COM Automation requires an STA thread for it. That thread never chose MTA, so it can still become the main STA, and the third entry point does exactly that before the session exists: .load ./ScriptLangCore init_sta, also select load_extension('./ScriptLangCore', 'init_sta'). It is the host's thread, so the cost is stated: after an init_sta load that thread is the main STA for the rest of its life, and a host that later asks for MTA on it gets RPC_E_CHANGED_MODE. A thread whose host did choose MTA cannot be converted, and init_sta refuses it by name.

print goes nowhere through this door, so a payload reports through Console.Error. The extension gives its session a sink that discards text (TextWriter.Null), because a host's console is not the script's to write on: a SELECT that evaluates print(...) once per row would flood the shell. The door for a diagnostic is therefore stderr, which is where the engine's own log already goes: Console.Error.WriteLine("phase 2: " + rows + " rows"); shows up in the shell, while print(...) is dropped. A payload that has to answer with data returns it (slc_file, slc_eval) rather than printing it, which is why assets/language/sqlite/excel_matrix_roundtrip.slc builds one object holding its verdict and its matrix.

FunctionAnswerWhat it is for
slc_eval(code, a0, ...)TEXT, the run's result as JSONThe one that carries a failure: the JSON holds HasError, ErrorMessage, ReturnValue, ExitCode and the position, so a failing row is a value rather than a broken query.
slc_eval_scalar(code, a0)The value, as a native SQL valueA number, text, blob or NULL that a WHERE, an ORDER BY or a sum() can use directly. A failing run is a SQL error here, since a bare value has nowhere to carry the failure.
slc_agg(code, value)The fold's final stateAny aggregate in one function: a0 is the running state (NULL on the first row) and a1 the row's value, and the expression's answer becomes the new state.
slc_map(code, rows)TEXT, a JSON array of valuesA whole set in one call, for a document you already hold: rows is a JSON array, and an element that is itself an array supplies the arguments in order.
slc_map_agg(code, a0, ...)TEXT, a JSON array of valuesThe same answers with the rows coming from a query, arguments spelled as slc_eval spells them.
slc_file(path)TEXT, the run's result as JSONRuns a script FILE in the connection's interpreter, once per call: the file is re-read, re-parsed and re-compiled every time, so it is a LOADER rather than a per-row door (about 165 KB of allocation for a 120-byte file and 12 MB for a 7 KB file of 200 functions, against about 18 KB for calling a function the file already declared). Afterwards its functions are callable from the other five, which is how a schema carries its logic instead of one expression. What the file returns is its top-level return <value>, or else the value of its last top-level expression statement, so a file that ends in Build(); answers {"HasError":false,"ExitCode":0,"ReturnValue":{...}} and one that only declares things answers no ReturnValue member at all. A path holding a compiled bundle is run too, decided by the file's content rather than by its extension: a program bundle (--compile, with or without --source=strip) answers exactly what its source answers, and a library blob, which names no entry, is refused naming import and .loadslcbc.
-- slc_eval: the whole run as JSON, which is the form that carries the failure fields select slc_eval('a0 + a1', 2, 3); -- {"HasError":false,"ExitCode":0,"ReturnValue":5} select json_extract(slc_eval('{n: a0 * 2}', 7), '$.ReturnValue.n'); -- 14 (the run answered a document) -- slc_eval_scalar: one value per row, so a script can decide what a WHERE or an ORDER BY keeps select slc_eval_scalar('a0 * 2', 21); -- 42 select n from t where slc_eval_scalar('a0 > 2 && a0 < 5', n); -- the rows the script accepts -- slc_agg: any aggregate in one expression, a0 being the running state and a1 the row with t(n) as (values (1),(2),(3),(4),(5)) select slc_agg('(a0 ?? 0) + a1', n) from t; -- 15 (a sum) select slc_agg('(a0 ?? 0) + a1 * a1', n) from t; -- 55 (a sum of squares) -- slc_map: a whole set in one call, for a document you already hold select slc_map('a0 * a0', '[1,2,3]'); -- [1,4,9] select slc_map('a0 + a1', '[[1,10],[2,20]]'); -- [11,22] (an array row supplies a0 and a1) -- slc_map_agg: the same answers with the rows coming from a query, and no JSON in the middle with t(a,b) as (values (1,10),(2,20)) select slc_map_agg('a0 + a1', a, b) from t; -- [11,22] select key, value from json_each((select slc_map_agg('a0 + a1', a, b) from t)); -- 0|11 and 1|22: rows back out -- slc_file: a whole script, so its functions stay callable for the connection select json_extract(slc_file('D:/rules/grades.slc'), '$.HasError'); -- 0 select slc_eval_scalar('Grade(a0)', score) from results; -- the file's own Grade(), per row

A file's ReturnValue is what the file answers: its top-level return <value> when it has one, because a top-level return ends the run and hands its value over, and otherwise its last top-level expression statement. So return Build(); and a trailing Build(); answer the same thing, and json_extract(slc_file('…'), '$.ReturnValue.X') reads a field of the object either way, while a file that only declares classes and functions answers {"HasError":false,"ExitCode":0} with no ReturnValue member. A value of null is the same: the member is absent rather than null. Any value travels, a class instance included, whose fields become the document, which is how a script hands back a whole report (return log;) and a query reads it with json_each. The returned value is not the exit code: read ExitCode for that, and exitcode = N (or exit(N)) is what sets it.

From a SCRIPT the same run is RunScript(path, true), whose .ReturnValue is that identical value and whose Json.Serialize(result) is byte for byte the text slc_file answers; the one difference is scope, since RunScript runs in an isolated interpreter by default (pass preserveContext: true when the caller wants the file's functions to stay callable, which is what slc_file does for the connection).

Each function declares the arity it really has, which is what pragma_function_list reports and what makes SQLite refuse a wrong argument count itself, at prepare time, naming the function (wrong number of arguments to function slc_map()), where an extra argument used to be accepted and silently ignored. Four are fixed (slc_file 1, slc_map 2, slc_agg 2, slc_eval_scalar 2) and two are variadic, reported as -1 because the count is the caller's: slc_eval reads a0..aN and slc_map_agg sees every row's a0..aN, and both then refuse a call that supplies no code at all. A NULL code (or a NULL path) answers NULL rather than an error.

The six are registered SQLITE_DIRECTONLY, so a schema cannot use them: an expression index, a CHECK constraint and a generated column are refused when you create them, while a VIEW, a TRIGGER and a DEFAULT clause are created and then refused with unsafe use of slc_eval_scalar() when something reaches them. That is the property the flag exists for: a database that arrives from elsewhere must not be able to carry a schema that runs script code with the host's permissions, so such a reference simply fails when used, and without the DLL loaded a statement naming one is unknown function. The functions also run on the connection's own interpreter, so what a script declares stays callable for the connection's lifetime. docs/embed/howto.html has the rest: the entry point, threads, what a script's print does, and what a row costs.

SQL parameter binding

All cursor methods accept SQL with ? placeholders. Parameters can be passed as individual arguments (via params Array) or as an array literal [val1, val2]. The underlying sqlite3_bind_* functions handle type dispatch: integers → sqlite3_bind_int64, floats → sqlite3_bind_double, strings → sqlite3_bind_text, null → sqlite3_bind_null, byte arrays → sqlite3_bind_blob.

Bulk insert PRAGMAs

BulkInsert applies optimization PRAGMAs before inserting and restores them to defaults afterwards regardless of the useTransaction flag (script-list path). The optimization PRAGMAs are synchronous=OFF, temp_store=MEMORY, foreign_keys=OFF, cache_size=-80000. They are restored to synchronous=NORMAL, temp_store=DEFAULT, foreign_keys=ON, cache_size=-2000 after completion. Disabling foreign keys during bulk inserts eliminates per-row FK constraint checks, which can dramatically speed up inserts on tables with foreign key relationships. The script-list path also uses savepoints (SAVEPOINT/ROLLBACK TO/RELEASE) for partial rollback safety when useTransaction=true. The binary path always uses a single transaction with savepoints.

Blob columns

A BLOB column arrives as a byte[]: Sqlite.Query, the typed mapping and the cursors all take the copy route, so the bytes stay valid for as long as the script holds them. The binding also has a zero-copy route, internal only: SqliteBlobManager is a MemoryManager<byte> over the pointer sqlite3_column_blob returns, handed out as ReadOnlyMemory<byte> by SqliteIterator.ReadBlobMemory(stmt, iCol) and SqliteNative.ReadBlobValueMemory(valPtr). Neither is exposed to scripts, and that is deliberate SQLite invalidates that pointer on the next sqlite3_step(), on a reset or finalize, and on a type conversion of the same column (reading it as text, for instance), a lifetime only the caller knows when it will end. If a script ever needs to avoid the copy, the shape that survives stepping is SQLite's incremental blob API (sqlite3_blob_open / blob_read / blob_close), which holds a handle per blob instead of a pointer per row not currently bound here.

Wide rows: read the columns you need

The row objects Sqlite.Query yields materialise every column of every row, so a SELECT * over a wide table is dominated by columns the script never reads. Measured on an 80-column table (500 rows, 100 iterations, AOT, :memory:, best of two): SELECT * takes 685 ms against 68 ms for five named columns and 34 ms for one a 20× spread that is per-column materialisation, not sqlite3_step cost, which is why it is invisible on narrow tables (the 4-column benchmark below reads all of its columns for the same time as it reads none of them in the lazy case). Three ways to stay on the fast side: name the columns (SELECT c1, c2 …), map into a small class with Sqlite.Query<T> whose fields are only the ones the query returns, or when the query is written by someone else and SELECT * is what you have use Sqlite.QueryLazy.

Sqlite.QueryLazy(db, sql[, params]) yields SqliteRow objects that read a column when the script asks for it, copy it, and cache it for that row. On the same 80-column table, reading one column of a SELECT * through the lazy row costs 123 ms against 685 ms for the eager path 5.6×, 18% of the eager reading and the ceiling, naming the column so the query returns nothing else, is 30 ms (4%). It is ahead on narrower selections too, for the same reason it skips the per-row dictionary: SELECT c1…c5 through the lazy row measured 49 ms against 68 ms eager. What it uniquely rescues is the SELECT * nobody wants to rewrite. A row that outlives its cursor position (kept past the next MoveNext, or past Dispose) throws a clear error instead of reading native memory the statement has already released; copy what you need inside the loop.

The wide-row figures come from one interleaved run on the AOT build (best of two), so the eager and lazy numbers in this section are directly comparable; the eager path has not changed, so an earlier revision's higher spread (534/48/18 ms, a 30× reading of the same effect) is the same effect measured on another day, not a different code path. The step-0 probe recorded in docs/reasonix/plans/2026-09-12-sqlite-wide-row-plan.md also settled a design question: positional storage is only ~3% cheaper than the eager dictionary row (652 ms vs 672 ms for a whole-row read), because the cost is per-column read-and-copy, not per-row dictionary overhead so QueryLazy needs no separate "eager positional" mode, and row.Values() covers "give me the whole row". assets/language/repl/sqlite_lazy.slc is the tracked suite for the behaviour values, accessors, lifetime guard and asserts structure rather than timing, so it stays portable across builds.

Performance measured on the AOT build, bytecode VM ON vs OFF (500-row table in :memory:, 100 iterations per read = 50 000 rows per read phase; 10 000 rows per write):

OperationVM onVM offThroughput (VM on)Throughput (VM off)Notes

Write 10k rows, Sqlite.BulkInsert12–13 ms12–13 ms~770k–830k rows/s~770k–830k rows/sOne prepared INSERT … (?1..?N) reused per row reset, clear_bindings, binds, step in one transaction. ~7× the row above, and VM-insensitive: the binds and the step dominate
Read, lazy (foreach over cursor)100–101 ms99–109 ms~495k–500k rows/s~460k–505k rows/sNo materialization. The few-% mode difference is inside the run-to-run spread
Read, lazy row (QueryLazy, 1 column read)93–99 ms95–105 ms~505k–538k rows/s~476k–526k rows/sOne column read per row through a SqliteRow. On this 4-column table it lands in the same band as the rows around it the lazy row pays off on wide rows (123 ms vs 685 ms over 80 columns, in the section above), and a cheaper reading here would mean it was not doing the work asked of it
Read, materialized List<T>95–98 ms89–102 ms~510k–526k rows/s~490k–560k rows/sPer-row ClassMapping through a cached map
Read, materialized Dictionary102–103 ms99–106 ms~485k–490k rows/s~470k–505k rows/sAs List, plus the Dictionary insert

Measured with assets/language/repl/crash_memory_bench_sqlite.slc phase 1a is the library handle's resolved-export lists and their JSON, phase 0 the per-row write loop, phase 8 the read benchmarks, 8b the write-path comparison and 9 the heap readout, all in that one file, so every row and figure below can be reproduced by running it (its timing, throughput and heap readings come from the shared assets/language/repl/_bench.inc module, so they are one implementation rather than three); VmSetEnabled(false) disables the bytecode VM to produce the "VM off" column. Ranges are over the passes measured, at least three per row and per mode, because a range's lower end against a single reading can look like a regression that is not there. Run-to-run spread reaches ~6%, so anything below that is not a result. Where the write time goes: the per-row row's ~4.6× VM gap is the script-side helper call, not the SQL the same inserts written without the helper call phase 8b's inline per-row loop measured 90–94 ms in both modes (VM on 91–92, tree 90–94), so the VM-sensitive work is the call, just as the few-% spread between modes on the reads says the SQL work is not. The real per-row cost is the parse: removing it, as Sqlite.BulkInsert does by preparing the INSERT once, takes 10k rows from ~90 ms to 12–13 ms. The caller transaction is worth ~2.2× (28–29 ms without it). The binary path (SerializeRows + BulkInsert, one multi-row INSERT per batch) measured 19–21 ms real, but not faster than the script-list BulkInsert, so it is not the one to reach for on this shape. Every write path is VM-insensitive; a write that looks VM-bound is a script-side loop, not SQLite.

On the read side the rows vary only a few % between modes, which is why they are reported as VM-insensitive no read row was faster on the tree than on the VM by more than one drift step. The reads land within a few ms of each other in both modes because the native sqlite3_step plus the per-row work dominates, and on a narrow table QueryLazy is simply one of those reads: its win is on wide rows 123 ms against 685 ms for an 80-column SELECT * whose script reads one column which is why it exists at all. Memory, produced by the suite's own phase 9 rather than read by hand: 0.56 MB managed heap after a forced collection before the workload starts, 14.4–14.5 MB at the end in VM-on mode against 7.4–7.5 MB in tree mode, and 1.52 MB after a forced collection in both modes the same live set either way, so that end-of-run gap is memory not yet collected rather than memory retained, and a full collection releases ~89% of the VM-on end reading and ~80% of the tree one. (The end reading is higher than an earlier revision of this table carried: phase 8b allocates ~10k rows per repetition, which is exactly why the after-collection figure is the one that means something.) What remains is engine state that survives a full collection, and it is not the caches a script can clear: ClearPureCache() and VmReset() leave the reading unchanged (both measured after the run), so the pure-memo and compiled-function caches are not it. The working set ends at 31,629,312–31,662,080 bytes on the VM and 30,683,136–31,051,776 on the tree 30.2–30.3 MB and 29.3–29.6 MB in the same unit as the heap lines above, the suite printing the working set in raw bytes not the 97 MB an earlier revision of this row reported; the smaller peak and the ~100× faster reads point at one cause a mapping path that no longer reflects per row. The AOT build uses OptimizationPreference=Speed + IlcInstructionSet=native.

Sqlite.OpenDb method Open a database and return the raw dbHandle

Opens a SQLite database and returns the raw handle as an Int64. Two calling forms are supported:

  • OpenDb(path) auto-loads sqlite3.dll from standard library paths.
  • OpenDb(lib, path) uses a pre-loaded library handle obtained via LoadLibrary("sqlite3.dll") (for custom DLL paths).

The handle can be used with Query and CreateFunction to share the same connection. It is automatically tracked for cleanup when the interpreter is disposed no explicit sqlite3_close needed from script code.

var db = Sqlite.OpenDb(":memory:"); // auto-loads sqlite3.dll var lib = LoadLibrary("tools/sqlite3.dll"); // custom path var db2 = Sqlite.OpenDb(lib, "/path/to/file.db");
// Open in-memory DB, register a UDF, iterate with kv.Key / kv.Value var db = Sqlite.OpenDb(":memory:"); // auto-loads sqlite3.dll Sqlite.CreateFunction(db, "doubleVal", 1, true, fun (int x) { return x * 2; }); foreach (var kv in Sqlite.Query(db, "SELECT doubleVal(21)")) print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value); // "doubleVal(21) = 42" Sqlite.CloseDb(db); // optional auto-closed on reset/dispose
Note: sqlite3_open is a lazy operation an invalid path won't fail until the first SQL operation. Use :memory: for temporary databases. The returned value is a native Int64 handle, treated as a number in script.
Calling convention: When calling Query(lib, db, sql) or CreateFunction(lib, db, ...), Query(db, sql, ...) and CreateFunction(db, name, ...) auto-resolve the lib. Query(lib, db, sql, ...) and CreateFunction(lib, db, name, ...) use an explicit DynamicLibrary handle.
Sqlite.CloseDb method Close a database previously opened with OpenDb

Closes a SQLite database handle that was obtained from Sqlite.OpenDb. Returns true on success, false if the handle is already closed or invalid. Uses sqlite3_close_v2 internally (with fallback to sqlite3_close for older SQLite versions).

Calling CloseDb is optional for :memory: databases and short-lived scripts handles are automatically closed when the interpreter is reset (.reset all) or disposed. For long-running scripts that open many databases, explicit close prevents resource exhaustion.

Sqlite.CloseDb(db);
var db = Sqlite.OpenDb("mydb.sqlite"); Sqlite.CloseDb(db); // explicit close
Sqlite.Query method Open a lazy cursor over a SQL query

Executes a SQL query and returns an IEnumerable that yields each row as a dictionary with string keys and object? values. Four calling forms are supported auto-detected by argument types:

  • Query(path, sql[, params]) opens a new connection. Auto-loads sqlite3.dll.
  • Query(db, sql[, params]) reuses an existing handle from OpenDb(). Auto-resolves lib.
  • Query(lib, path, sql[, params]) new connection with explicit library handle.
  • Query(lib, db, sql[, params]) reuses existing handle with explicit library handle.

Important: Forms that open a new connection (Query(path, sql), Query(lib, path, sql)) do not have access to UDFs registered via CreateFunction. Use Query(db, sql) to share the same connection.

Row iteration: Each row supports foreach(var kv in row) access the column name via kv.Key and the cell value via kv.Value. Alternatives: row["colName"] or row[0].

// Auto-load + new connection, iterate with kv.Key / kv.Value foreach (var kv in Sqlite.Query(":memory:", "SELECT 1 AS x")) print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value); // "x = 1" // Reuse existing db handle (UDFs available) var db = Sqlite.OpenDb(":memory:"); Sqlite.CreateFunction(db, "doubleVal", 1, true, fun (int x) { return x * 2; }); foreach (var kv in Sqlite.Query(db, "SELECT doubleVal(21)")) print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value); // "doubleVal(21) = 42" Sqlite.CloseDb(db); // close when done // Explicit library handle + path var lib = LoadLibrary("sqlite3.dll"); foreach (var kv in Sqlite.Query(lib, ":memory:", "SELECT 1 AS x")) print(kv.Key + " = " + kv.Value);
Sqlite.QueryLazy method Cursor whose rows read a column only when asked

Same SQL execution as Sqlite.Query, over an existing handle, but the rows it yields are SqliteRow objects that materialise a column on access: the value is read from the native statement, copied, and cached for that row. A script that reads three of eighty columns pays for three.

Two calling forms both need a handle from OpenDb():

  • QueryLazy(db, sql[, params]) existing handle, library auto-resolved.
  • QueryLazy(lib, db, sql[, params]) existing handle with an explicit library handle.

Lifetime: a row is valid only while it is the cursor's current row. Once the cursor steps again or is Disposed every read on the old row throws ("This SQLite row is no longer live…") instead of returning data from a statement position that has already moved. Copy what you need inside the loop; collecting rows for later use is what the eager Query path is for.

Row access: by name or by ordinal

A SqliteRow is a read-only dictionary with the same two access forms the eager rows have: by name (r["c1"], case-insensitive) or by ordinal (r[0], the position in the SELECT list, 0-based). Both resolve to the same slot, so they share the per-row cache and the same lifetime rule mixing the two in one loop is fine. Assigning to a column throws.

MemberReturnsNotes
r["c1"]objectBy column name, case-insensitive. An unknown name throws Column 'x' not found in the query result.
r[0]objectBy ordinal, in Keys() order. Negative, or past the last column, throws Column index N is out of range: the row has M column(s).
r.GetValue(i)objectThe ordinal form as a method.
r.GetKey(i)stringThe column name at that ordinal.
r.CountintHow many columns the query returned.
r.Keys()string[]Column names in query order so r[i] == r[r.Keys()[i]].
r.Values()object[]The whole row, positionally. Reads (and caches) every column on the first call.
r.ContainsKey(k)boolTakes a column name or an ordinal.
foreach (var kv in r)KeyValuePairName/value pairs, in query order.

Any of these reads is what triggers the native read and only for the column asked for. A name and its ordinal are the same slot, so r[2] after r["c2"] copies nothing twice.

var db = Sqlite.OpenDb(":memory:"); // ... fill a wide table ... // By name reads only c1 and c7, whatever else SELECT * returns foreach (var r in Sqlite.QueryLazy(db, "SELECT * FROM wide")) print(r["c1"] + " / " + r["c7"]); // The same columns by ordinal 0-based position in the SELECT list foreach (var r in Sqlite.QueryLazy(db, "SELECT id, c1, c2, n FROM wide")) { print(r[0] + " | " + r[1] + " | " + r[3]); // id | c1 | n print(r[2] == r["c2"]); // True same slot } // The name at a position, or the whole row positionally foreach (var r in Sqlite.QueryLazy(db, "SELECT * FROM wide")) { print(r.GetKey(2) + " = " + r.GetValue(2)); var vals = r.Values(); print(vals[0]); }

An ordinal only means something for that query: it follows the columns the SELECT actually returned, in order. r.Keys() reports that order, and GetKey(i) turns a position back into a name the pair to reach for when the query is SELECT * and the column order is not yours to fix.

When not to use it: for a narrow row, or when you keep every row, plain Query is the simpler call same values, no lifetime rule to respect. On an 80-column table, reading one column of SELECT * through QueryLazy measured 123 ms against 685 ms for the eager path (5.6×); naming the column in the SQL (SELECT c1) stays the fastest at 30 ms.
Sqlite.Query<T> / Sqlite.Query<T, V> generic method Typed cursor maps rows to class instances

Two typed overloads same source detection as untuned Query:

  • Query<T>(...) typed cursor (1 type arg). Each row is mapped to a T class instance. Call it from sqlite.inc wrappers as db.Query<Person>(sql).
  • Query<T, V>(...) flexible return (2 type args). V can be List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, a class name, or a scalar type. Also available as db.Query<Person, List<Person>>(sql).
class Person { public int Id { get; set; } public string Name { get; set; } } // Typed cursor foreach (var p in Sqlite.Query<Person>(lib, db, "SELECT * FROM people")) print(p.Id + " " + p.Name); // Flexible return var list = Sqlite.Query<Person, List<Person>>(lib, db, "SELECT * FROM people"); var cnt = Sqlite.Query<Person, int>(lib, db, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM people");

The second type argument V controls the return shape:

VReturns
T (a class)Single ClassInstance (first row only)
List<T>List<T> with all rows
Dictionary<K, T>Dictionary keyed by first column
scalar (int, string, ...)First column of first row, coerced to V
Iterator types: Query returns a SqliteIterator (row cursor) and Query<T> returns a SqliteMappingIterator (maps each row to a class instance). Both are enumerable (foreach), implement IDisposable (.Dispose() releases the statement), and are usable with is / typeof / as under these exact names.
Sqlite.BulkInsert method Multi-row INSERT with parameterized prepared statements

Multi-row INSERT using parameterized prepared statements with ?1..?N placeholders. Prepares the INSERT once, then reuses it per row via sqlite3_reset + sqlite3_clear_bindings + sqlite3_bind_*. By default wraps the operation in BEGIN TRANSACTION/COMMIT with savepoints. Pass false as the 7th argument to skip the transaction. Returns the number of rows inserted.

Signature (script-list path)

Sqlite.BulkInsert(lib, db, "table", colNames, rows[, batchSize[, useTransaction]])
  • colNames string[], List<string>, or any IList
  • rows object[] (each element: object[] or IList of values), List<T>, or script struct/class instances (fields extracted by name)
  • batchSize rows per batch (default: 1000)
  • useTransaction bool, default true

Signature (binary path)

Sqlite.BulkInsert(lib, db, "table", byteData[, batchSize])

Auto-detected when args[3] is byte[]. Uses multi-row VALUES SQL internally.

// Full form with explicit lib and db handles var lib = LoadLibrary("sqlite3.dll"); var db = Sqlite.OpenDb(lib, "test.db"); var colList = ["Name", "Value", "Active"]; struct Row { public string Name; public string Value; public int Active; } var rowList = new List<Row>(); rowList.Add(new Row("a", "hello", 1)); rowList.Add(new Row("b", "world", 1)); var inserted = Sqlite.BulkInsert(lib, db, "my_table", colList, rowList, 1000); print("Inserted " + inserted + " rows"); Sqlite.CloseDb(db); FreeLibrary(lib);

SQL injection safety: Values are never concatenated into SQL strings. All data is passed via sqlite3_bind_* special characters, quotes, and null bytes in column values are handled safely by SQLite's binding API.

Sqlite.BulkInsert (binary path) method Multi-row INSERT from a pre-serialized byte[] auto-detected by BulkInsert

Takes a pre-serialized byte[] in compact binary format and builds multi-row INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (v1),(v2),... SQL strings. BulkInsert auto-detects byte[] at args[3] and routes to this path (instead of the prepared-statement path used for script lists). Useful when data originates from host C# code that can produce the binary format directly, avoiding script-object allocation entirely. Wraps the operation in BEGIN IMMEDIATE TRANSACTION / COMMIT with savepoints, applies optimization PRAGMAs before and restores defaults after. Returns the number of rows inserted.

Binary format

[4B colCount][4B rowCount]
for each col: [4B nameLen][nameBytes] (UTF-8, not null-terminated)
for each row, each col: [1B tag][value]
  tag=0: no value bytes (NULL)
  tag=1: [8B int64]
  tag=2: [8B float64]
  tag=3: [4B strLen][strBytes] (UTF-8)

Tags 1 and 2 correspond to SQLite INTEGER and REAL. Tag 3 is TEXT (string values are single-quote-escaped). The column names in the header are used in order one per column per row is required. A column count mismatch between the header and actual row data will produce broken SQL.

SerializeRows helper

To generate the binary byte[] from script row data, use Sqlite.SerializeRows(colNames, rows) (This native C# function reads the same List<object> input as BulkInsert and serializes it to the binary format in native code no script-side allocations per row, and no hardcoded test data.

// Build rows, serialize to byte[], then bulk insert
var cols = new string[] {"id", "value", "label"};
var rows = new List<object>();
rows.Add([1, 1, "odd"]);
var byteData = Sqlite.SerializeRows(cols, rows);
Sqlite.BulkInsert(lib, db, "bulk_bytes", byteData, 1000);
(binary path) uses multi-row VALUES SQL internally it concatenates values into SQL strings rather than using prepared statements. This means string values are single-quote-escaped rather than bound via the SQLite binding API. The binary format must match the table's column types and order exactly. Use SerializeRows to generate the binary payload from script row data without hardcoding the binary format. Call BulkInsert(lib, db, table, byteData, batchSize) the method detects byte[] at args[3] and routes here automatically.
Sqlite.CsvImport method Stream CSV file into a SQLite table (auto-detects delimiter)

Reads a CSV file line-by-line (streaming, no full file load), auto-detects the delimiter, and inserts rows into a SQLite table using a prepared statement with periodic batch commits. Handles quoted fields with embedded commas and escaped quotes.

The delimiter auto-detection scores candidate characters (, ; | : ^ ~ \t # @ ! % & * / \ ) by counting occurrences outside quoted regions and picks the one with the most hits. Falls back to comma if none scores ≥2.

Parameter handling

colNames controls column naming:

  • If a string[] is provided, those names are used and the first CSV row is treated as data
  • If hasHeader = true (default), the first CSV row provides column names
  • If hasHeader = false and no explicit names, auto-generated col1, col2, ... are used

If the table does not exist, it is created with all columns as TEXT (SQLite flexible typing). Wraps the operation in a transaction with savepoints, applies optimization PRAGMAs before and restores defaults after. Returns the number of rows inserted, or -1 on error (fully rolled back).

Sqlite.CsvImport(lib, db, "my_table", "./data.csv", 10000, true, null);
// Auto-detect pipe delimiter, header row, create table Sqlite.CsvImport(lib, db, "csv_products", "./data.csv", 10000, true, null); // Custom column names, first row is data Sqlite.CsvImport(lib, db, "users", "./users.psv", 10000, false, ["uid", "uname"]);
Sqlite.CreateFunction method Register a script function as a SQL UDF

Registers a script lambda as a callable SQL function via sqlite3_create_function. Deterministic functions can be optimized by SQLite.

// Short form auto-resolves lib from db handle var upper = fun (arg) => arg != null ? arg.ToString().ToUpper() : null; Sqlite.CreateFunction(db, "MY_UPPER", 1, true, upper); foreach (var row in Sqlite.Query(db, "SELECT MY_UPPER('hello')")) print(row["MY_UPPER('hello')"]); // HELLO
// Long form explicit library handle Sqlite.CreateFunction(lib, db, "MY_UPPER", 1, true, upper);

Return type mapping: int/short/byte/bool/char → INTEGER, long/uint/ulong → INTEGER (64-bit), float/double/decimal → REAL (decimal is converted to double), string/DateTime/TimeSpan → TEXT, byte[] → BLOB. Arguments read as long (INTEGER), double (REAL), string (TEXT), or byte[] (BLOB).

Sqlite.LoadExtensions method Load SQLite extension DLLs (FTS5, math, ICU, etc.)

Loads one or more SQLite extension DLLs via sqlite3_load_extension. Automatically enables extension loading on the handle if not already enabled. Extensions like FTS5 (fts5), math functions (math), ICU, JSON1, and others can be loaded if the sqlite3.dll was compiled with extension support. Returns true on success, false if the extension file does not exist or loading fails.

Sqlite.LoadExtensions(lib, db, "./path/to/ext.dll"); Sqlite.LoadExtensions(lib, db, "./fts5.dll", "./math.dll");
Loading a non-existent extension file throws ScriptException. On Windows, the DLL must be in the same directory as sqlite3.dll or on the system PATH.
Sqlite.AttachDatabase method Attach another SQLite database for cross-DB queries

Attaches another SQLite database file to the current connection under a logical alias. Once attached, tables from that database can be queried using the alias.table_name syntax. Returns true on success, false if the file does not exist or the SQL operation fails. Use AttachDatabase to join tables across databases, or to perform bulk operations across multiple files.

Sqlite.AttachDatabase(lib, db, "path/to/other.db", "other"); // Then query: SELECT * FROM other.table_name
// Cross-database join Sqlite.AttachDatabase(lib, db, "./sales.db", "sales"); foreach (var r in Sqlite.Query(db, "SELECT p.name, s.total FROM products p " + "JOIN sales.orders s ON p.id = s.product_id")) print(r["name"] + " " + r["total"]);
Sqlite.DetachDatabase method Detach a previously attached database

Detaches a database previously attached via AttachDatabase. After detach, the alias.table_name syntax no longer resolves for that alias. Does not delete the database file only removes the logical attachment. Returns true on success, false if the alias does not exist.

Sqlite.DetachDatabase(lib, db, "alias");
DetachDatabase returns false if the alias does not exist no exception is thrown. Check the return value if you need to know whether the detachment succeeded.
